**M1 · the one that decides whether this project is easy or hard.** Read-only.

## Why

625 commits of upstream include schema migrations, and they run against Postgres on relay startup. The relay's database is shared by everything: Peek, Ship, the agent CLI, the MCP server.

**At least one upstream migration is known to refuse rather than migrate.** `crates/buzz-db/src/migration.rs` blocks the NIP-RS pre-0007 path when existing `kind:30078` rows have ambiguous `d`/`t` tag cardinality:

> `NIP-RS migration blocked: pre-0007 database contains kind-30078 rows with ambiguous d/t tag cardinality; repair or remove those nonconforming rows before retrying`

That is a *good* migration — it fails loudly rather than corrupting. Assume there are others, and assume some of them fail less loudly.

## What to produce

**1. The list.** Every migration between our current schema version and upstream's head. Where it lives, what it does, and whether it is additive, destructive, or conditional.

**2. The refusers.** Which ones can *block*, and what data shape triggers each. For the NIP-RS one specifically: **do we currently have any `kind:30078` rows at all?** Cross-app read state (CRO-2) grants that kind, so if that project lands first the answer changes from "no" to "yes, ours" — and this ticket's answer has a shelf life.

**3. The irreversibles.** Anything that drops or rewrites a column. Those set the requirement for M4's throwaway and for whether a backup is taken first.

**4. Row counts that matter.** For any conditional migration, how much production data hits its condition. A migration that is instant on 100 rows and locks a table on 10 million is the same code.

## Traps

- **Read the production schema version, do not assume it.** The fork has been deployed by hand for months.
- Do not run anything against production. This is a reading exercise; M4 is where migrations actually execute.
- `docker compose exec -T postgres psql …` on the box reads the live schema. See `operations/PRODUCTION.md`.
- Migrations may be ordered by a mechanism that does not match commit order. Read the migration runner, not just the files.

## Done when

The four lists are on this issue, and there is a plain answer to: **would deploying upstream today break, block, or silently change production data?** If yes, say which migration and what it needs first. That answer is the gate for M2.

**M1 · un-gated.** Small, and it makes the two refetch tickets actually look fixed rather than half-fixed.

## Why

`peek-app/src/nostr/foreign.ts:78` holds `knownPeople`, a **module-level** `Map` with **no TTL** that also **caches misses**:

> "Misses are cached too — someone with no published profile would otherwise be asked about on every single resolve... The cost is that a profile published mid-session appears on the next reload rather than immediately"

That cost was reasonable when nothing else refreshed either. Once the topic sync and the project panel re-read on a timer, this cache becomes the remaining reason a newly named person still renders as `nostr:<8 chars>` until a full reload — and it will read as "the refresh does not work".

The negative caching is the sharp end: the common case is someone who has not finished setting up their Estiva ID, which is exactly the person whose name is about to arrive.

## What to change

Give entries an expiry and re-ask when stale. Suggested shape:

- hits: a long TTL (names change rarely) — 10 minutes is generous
- **misses: a much shorter TTL** — a minute or so, because a miss is a profile that may be about to exist

Keep the cache module-level and shared. The reason it is not per-call is real: a topic with ten reference widgets otherwise asks who the same handful of people are ten times, and the sidebar and every widget should share one answer.

## Traps

- Do not drop the batching. `cachedPeople` collects the unknown pubkeys and makes **one** relay lookup for the set. A rewrite that resolves per-pubkey turns one query into N.
- `syncStaleProfilesFromRelay` in `src/nostr/sync.ts` is a different path (it asks Convex who is *missing* a profile and writes rows). This cache is the render-time one in `foreign.ts`. Do not merge them.

## Done when

Publish a `kind:0` profile for an identity currently rendering as a placeholder in an open Peek tab. The name and avatar appear within the miss-TTL without a reload.

**M2.** Depends on the grant and the probe. This is the "start a conversation" half.

## Why

Peek's `dmConversations` table exists but has no relay counterpart — DMs are Convex-only today. This gives each one a real channel on the relay, using the same pattern `topics.channelUuid` already establishes.

## What to build

**Publish `kind:41010`** when a DM is first needed, with one `#p` tag per other participant. The relay builds the full participant set as self + others, deduplicated, so **do not include your own pubkey** in `#p` — it is added server-side and duplicates are collapsed by the participant hash either way.

**Record the returned channel uuid** on the `dmConversations` row, mirroring `topics.channelUuid`. Follow the existing shape in `convex/nostr/data.ts`: `storeChannelUuid` is an `internalMutation` with **first-write-wins** semantics (`if (t.channelUuid) return { minted: false }`). Use the same rule — two tabs opening the same DM simultaneously must converge on one channel, not race.

**Lean on idempotence rather than bookkeeping.** Because the channel id is derived from `compute_participant_hash`, re-opening a DM with the same people returns the same channel. So "message this person" never needs to ask whether a DM already exists — publish `41010` and use what comes back. `find_dm_by_participants` is the relay's own lookup and it is keyed the same way.

## Where it belongs

The unsigned event should be built in Convex, signed and published in the browser, and the resulting id recorded back — the three-step division in `src/nostr/bridge.ts`. Convex has the data and needs no credential to shape the event; the browser has the token and is the only place it belongs; the channel uuid is a fact, not a secret.

Add an `unsignedDmOpen` query alongside `unsignedMessage` in `convex/nostr/outbox.ts` rather than inventing a second pattern.

## Traps

- **`HTTP 200` does not mean accepted.** A duplicate returns `200 {"accepted":false,...}`. For this command a duplicate is success — the DM already exists. Read the field; do not treat the status code as the answer, and do not treat a duplicate as an error.
- **Do not publish a `kind:9007`.** `41010` creates the channel itself.
- The relay caps participants at **8 others, 9 total** (`command_executor.rs:330`). Enforcement in the UI is a separate task, but this code should fail legibly rather than passing 12 pubkeys and reporting the relay's rejection verbatim.
- `41010` is a *command*, persisted for idempotency. Republishing an identical one is safe.

## Done when

Opening a DM in Peek produces a channel on the relay, the uuid is on the `dmConversations` row, and opening the same DM again from a second tab yields the same uuid with no duplicate row.

**SHA-3 put the socket in the right package on the wrong footing, and this is the ticket that pays for it.**

`createLiveRelay` and `createChannelSubscriptions` are in `@estiva-app/protocol` as of 0.1.0. Everything else in that package arrived as a **byte-identical duplicate** pinned by 21 wire vectors, so the extraction could not change behaviour and needed no second consumer to find the seam — SHA-3 says so in its own first paragraph. The socket was never duplicated. It is a single implementation with a single caller, and no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API. That is exactly the failure SHA-4 and SHA-5 avoid by extracting *during* REW-2 and REW-3, and the socket skipped it.

## What is Peek-shaped and unproven

Not `live.ts` itself — the plumbing that stayed behind in `peek-app/src/nostr/liveTopics.ts`, which the second app will otherwise write again from scratch:

- **One instance per tab, as a module singleton.** `max_subscriptions` is per connection and the relay authenticates a connection once, so a connection per component mount is wrong rather than merely wasteful. React StrictMode makes it concrete: anything owned by an effect is built twice.
- **A credential provider read on every connect, never captured.** A token captured at module load survives a silent renewal as a dead credential, and a reconnect then signs `22242` with it.
- **`navigator.onLine` → `relay.reconnect()`.** A socket whose peer became unreachable stays OPEN until TCP gives up, reporting `live` and delivering nothing. Reconnection is driven by `onclose`, which never fires.

None of that interprets events, so "share the wire format, never the fold" does not send it back to an app. It is browser lifecycle, which makes it **`@estiva-app/platform`'s (SHA-2), not `protocol`'s**. `freshness.ts` is the opposite case: its four states and their copy are product voice and stay in the app.

## Sequence it after the cutover, not inside it

REW-6 keeps Ship's 5s poll deliberately (`apps/ship/app.ts:85`), and the roadmap already calls "adopting Peek's conventions naively" a release blocker. Do not swap Ship's transport during the rewrite. Land this after REW-8.

## A cheaper second consumer, if the API wants stressing before then

`estiva-agent` already imports `@estiva-app/protocol`, and `live.ts` declares its own `WebSocket` types and reads the global *inside function bodies* precisely so a non-browser runtime can use it — Node 22 has a global `WebSocket`. A live tail in the agent would exercise the API from a second runtime for very little code.

**It is not free, and the cost is in Estiva ID, not here.** `claude-agent` has no `22242` in `allowed_kinds` and an empty `relay_auth_urls`. PEE-4 is the shape to copy — a grant has two halves, and `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` is the deployment half.

## Done when

A second consumer holds a live authenticated socket against `wss://estiva.estiva.app` and receives an event **it did not publish** (a two-window test of one identity proves nothing — PEE-8 learned that), the per-tab / credential / online plumbing lives in a package rather than in two apps, and whatever the second consumer forced to change in `live.ts` or `subscriptions.ts` is written on this issue — including "nothing", which is the answer that retires the worry.

**Depends on SHA-1** (registry decision) and is most useful once SHA-2/SHA-3 exist to wire in. This is the half of ADR 0001 that actually enforces it — the document is the other half.

## Why a template, when this project is otherwise about packages

Packages give inheritance for behaviour. They cannot set a **default**. Nothing about `@estiva/protocol` existing stops a new app from also adding Convex on day one — and a developer starting a React app in 2026 reaches for a backend-as-a-service by reflex, because that is the normal instinct and because Peek is sitting there as precedent.

That is exactly how Peek got Convex, and the asymmetry is unforgiving: **adding a backend later is easy, removing one is a rewrite.**

So the point of this ticket is not convenience. It is that **relay-canonical becomes the physical default** — you have to add a database on purpose, in a commit, where somebody can ask why. See `estiva-docs/decisions/0001-relay-canonical-by-default.md`.

## What to build

A scaffold that produces a working, deployable Estiva app with:

- **No backend.** No Convex, no Supabase, no database client, no server directory. Reads the relay, folds in the browser.
- The foundation packages wired: `@estiva/protocol`, `@estiva/identity`, `@estiva/platform` (PWA), `@estiva/ui`.
- A working sign-in through Estiva ID, and a relay read that renders something. **The scaffold must run and authenticate out of the box** — a template that needs three undocumented steps before it starts is a template people abandon.
- Build config, folder layout, lint and CI — the things ADR 0001 and the project description agree should *not* be shared as a package, because each app will diverge on them immediately and that is fine.
- A `CLAUDE.md` seeded with the working rules that have actually held: the data-access seam, tokens-not-raw-hex, and the layer rule from ADR 0001.

Delivery mechanism is open — `npx create-estiva-app`, a GitHub template repo, or a documented `degit` target. Pick the cheapest thing that works; the enforcement comes from what the output contains, not from the tooling.

## Encode the layer rule where the decision gets made

The scaffold should make the right thing easy and the wrong thing visible:

- A commented example of **layer 2** storage (`kind:30078`, app-namespaced `d_tag`, NIP-44 encrypted) for per-user app state, so the obvious home for "starred items" is right there and is not a database table.
- A short section in the generated `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` stating the two-question test — *does another app need to see it? would the person expect to own it?* — and that **"only this app reads it" is not grounds for a database.**
- No placeholder for a backend. Do not scaffold an empty `server/` or a commented-out database client; an empty slot is an invitation.

## Traps

- **Do not make the scaffold depend on Peek.** It should be generated from the packages, not extracted from Peek's tree. A scaffold shaped like Peek carries Peek's Convex assumptions — the whole reason this project extracts during Ship's rewrite rather than from Peek alone.
- **Do not let it become a fifth package to maintain.** A template is copied once and diverges by design; that is its purpose, not a flaw. Resist adding a mechanism to push updates into generated apps — that is what the packages are for, and conflating the two gives you the costs of both.
- Prove it before believing it: generate an app, deploy it somewhere real, sign in with Estiva ID, read a Folder. A scaffold verified only by `npm run build` is a scaffold that does not work.
- The generated app must not assume Vite forever. Peek is Vite and Ship's rewrite will be, but the packages are meant to be toolchain-agnostic, and the scaffold is where an accidental hard dependency would hide.

## Done when

A generated app runs, authenticates against Estiva ID, reads a Folder from the relay, is installable as a PWA, and contains **no database of any kind**. Someone who has not read this ticket can generate an app and ship something without ever deciding to have a backend — and if they later need one, they add it deliberately and can say which feature demanded it.

**CAT-2 said all five hunks were keep-both. Two were not.**

- **`ingest.rs` is one sorted `use` list both sides edited.** Keep-both would have duplicated ~50 identifiers and not compiled. Correct resolution is a **set union**: 58 ours + 55 theirs = **61** (52 common, our 6 Estiva kinds, upstreams 3 new ones). Re-wrapped by hand — `cargo fmt` is forbidden here.
- **Both `buzz-db` hunks share the closing brace that sits AFTER the `>>>>>>>` marker.** Deleting markers alone would have let `is_owner_channel_member` swallow the next functions signature. Each ours-side needed its own brace. This one would have compiled into something wrong rather than failing loudly.

**The real find: a semantic conflict that produced no marker at all, and broke the build.**

The fork widened `enforce_relay_membership` from `(state, community: CommunityId, …)` to `(state, tenant: &TenantContext, …)` — that is #10, *"Record a proven owner on every gated path"*. Upstream kept the narrow signature and added **two new endpoints**, `api/gifs.rs` and `api/workflows.rs`, calling it the old way. **Neither file exists on the fork**, so both auto-merged with no conflict and the tree did not compile: two `E0308`s.

**Narrowed to Topic on 2026-08-31.** This ticket asked for Topic *and* Message. A Message cannot be declared in a manifest at all today — see **PRO-11** — so the Message half moved there, where the mechanism that makes it possible lives. Topic is unaffected and unblocked.

## Why this ticket exists

**Peek has only ever been a consumer.** It reads Ship's manifest and renders Ship's objects. It has never published one, so no other app can render a Peek object — and the projection layer has never been exercised in that direction at all.

This is the producer half of the second consumer. PRO-7 is the reader half. Together they close a loop that has run one-way since the mechanism was built.

## What to publish

A `kind:31990` declaring a projection for **Topic** — a channel, addressable as `kind:39000` per RFC 0.4 §5.2, whose `d` is exactly the channel uuid (measured across all 50 production channels).

A Topic wants a **`list` slot** for its recent conversations, which per SPEC §7.2 is now a `children` source — found by the tag on the child that names the parent, not by a list the parent maintains. That inversion matters here: a topic cannot maintain a list of its own messages, because a relay-signed record is not something Peek can rewrite.

## The trap, and it is specific to this object

**A `kind:39000` is signed by the relay, not by a person.** So:

- a consumer resolving "who authored this" gets the relay's pubkey, and must not render it as a person
- **Peek cannot add any tag to it** — the record is not Peek's to write. Anything Peek wants to say *about* a topic has to live somewhere Peek can sign. This is the same constraint that shapes facet declaration in RFC 0.5 §3.1

## Done when

Peek publishes a `kind:31990` declaring Topic, the manifest verifier passes it, and a second app resolves it from the relay by `#k` query and renders a real production topic.

Message follows in PRO-11.

**Renaming a project does not fix its refs, and that is deliberate. Recording it so nobody tries it twice.**

Hit today: a new project *Peek's Intelligence* produced `PEE-1`…`PEE-6`, colliding with *Peek: Feedback & Bugs*, which produces the same prefix. Renaming it to **Intelligence in Peek** changed the project title and **left all six issues on `PEE-`**.

**Why.** The ref is computed once at `create-issue` — `nextRef(refPrefix(project.title), siblings)` — and written onto the issue event as a `['ref', …]` tag. `edit-project --title` cannot reach into six already-published events, and `edit-issue` has no `--ref`.

**That is the right design, not the bug.** `store.ts` says so: refs are *"display-only, per the spec: never used for addressing, never authoritative"* and the collision is *"cosmetic… the address is the identity."* Re-stamping on rename would break every prior citation of a ref in a PR or a comment.

**One consequence worth knowing before the fix is designed:** after a rename, `nextRef` counts only siblings already carrying the new prefix, so the next issue in that project is `INT-1`, not `INT-7`. A renamed project therefore ends up holding `PEE-1…6` followed by `INT-1…`, which is worse than either consistent option. Whatever this ticket does, it should decide what happens to a project that has already been renamed.

Left as-is deliberately: re-filing six issues would mean six permanently cancelled ones, since `kind:5` is refused to this identity (AGE-2).

**The migration is the steady state, not a window that closes.** Depends on RIC-1.

## What cannot move

Measured on production 2026-08-28:

| corpus | events | carrying structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| messages (`kind:9`, `kind:1111`) | 398 | 165 |
| descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 89 with a body | 76 |

A `kind:9` is **not replaceable at all**. A `30850`/`30851` is replaceable only by its author, and REW-11 established that rewriting stamps a `created_at` the relay will not backdate. So whichever format RIC-1 picks, **every one of these events keeps its current shape permanently.**

## What this ticket owns

- the declaration: how a reader knows which form it is holding, in the shape `emits.alsoRead` already uses one level down — the owner is the only party that knows what it used to write
- **one safe renderer**, imported by both apps. Ship's plain-text stance is a security position and the renderer has to honour it rather than route around it
- the read path in both apps handling both forms, permanently, with no flag day

## The failure to avoid

A reader that handles only the new form shows a thread that begins in the middle — newest content present, everything older silently gone. Nothing reports it. That is exactly why `alsoRead` exists, and it is written up in SPEC §7.3.

## Done when

Both apps render both forms, a message written before the cutover and one written after appear identically to a reader, and the compatibility declaration is in SPEC rather than only in code.

Almost no new logic, as the ticket predicted — batch, partition by kind, call three actions in order. 468 tests, 19 new.

## The ticket's kind list is incomplete, and it would have shipped broken

`kind:9 → importChannel` alone makes **every Ship comment vanish from live delivery.** Comments moved to NIP-22 `kind:1111` with REW-10, and a Ship comment is posted into the project's Folder — which *is* a Peek topic's channel. No error, no empty state, just a conversation that stops updating.

Not hypothetical: **the first live events seen on this socket during PEE-6's two-channel check were `kind:1111`, not `kind:9`.** The HTTP path in `src/nostr/sync.ts` already asks for both and explains why at length; the live path now matches it, and `KIND.COMMENT` exists so the two cite one constant rather than a literal.

## Two keys, and this ticket names only one

The import actions are keyed by **`topicKey`** — the client-facing topic id — while a subscription is keyed by **channel uuid**. Neither is derivable from the other without a query, so `watch()` takes both. PEE-8's caller holds both already, and looking one up here would put a Convex query inside an event handler.

Worth flagging because the RFC 0.3 note on PEE-6 asks that a topic id never become a subscription key, and this is the seam where the two meet. They stay separate: subscribe by channel, import by topic.

## Two things the ticket left implicit

**`importChannel` runs on every flush, even one with no messages.** It is the only source of `known` and `deletable`, and a reaction-only batch still needs them — skipping it would hand empty lists to `importReactions` and silently fail to attach. Safe because `syncTopic` guards on `incoming.length > 0` while the three lookups run regardless.

**A fixed window, not a trailing debounce.** "Debounce ~250ms" read literally keeps resetting while events keep arriving, which starves on a busy channel. The window opens on the first event of a burst and fires once — latency bounded at one window, burst still collapsed to one call per kind group.

## Found by its own test

`flushNow()` returned early on an empty buffer **even with a call in flight**, reporting "flushed" while work was outstanding. Fixed to return the in-flight promise. That is the shape that makes a test green and loses the last batch on unmount.

## One deliberate gap for M4 to know about

**No profiles reach `importChannel` on the live path.** `kind:0` is not channel-scoped, so a `#h` subscription never delivers one and there is nothing to pass. A first-time author renders under a placeholder until `pubkeysMissingProfile`/`recordProfiles` fills it in — the gap PEEK-72 built that pair to close, running on its own schedule. Live delivery makes it more visible than the HTTP path did, since that fetched `kind:0` per author in the same run.

## What PEE-8 has to observe

All three modules are merged and **none has ever run inside the app**. PEE-8 is where the chain becomes real, and this ticket's done-when is part of what it should check: a message published from Ship appearing in an open topic **with no `POST /query` in the network panel**. The StrictMode double-mount caution from PEE-5 still applies.

tags:
**A message cannot be declared in a manifest, and that is measured rather than inferred.**

Confirmed on production while building PRO-6: *"A Message carries no `d` and is not addressable."* Every resolver in the consumer runtime starts from an `AddressPointer`.

## The gap

| object | identified by |
| --- | --- |
| project, issue, document, folder | address — `naddr` |
| Peek topic | address — `naddr` (the relay's `39000`) |
| **a conversation** | **the root event's id — `nevent`** |
| **a message** | **its own event id — `nevent`** |

`projections` is keyed by kind and resolved from an `naddr`; Ship's manifest declares its `web` template as `naddr` outright. So a manifest cannot say how a message renders, and a consumer holding a `nevent` has nothing to look up.

**Why it stayed hidden:** every Ship object is addressable, so the layer works in the one direction it has ever run. It only appears when you ask what a *message* widget would resolve through.

## This is one of six, and the other five are on PRO-6

PRO-6's comment records six things the manifest could not express, all measured against production. **Read them before starting here** — they are siblings of this one, not background:

- `list` matched the parent's *address* while Peek's `h` holds a bare uuid
- `title` is required and a message has none
- **`records` was required by both resolvers**, so an app that folds nothing rendered as *nothing* — §13.3's worst outcome, never caught because Ship was the only publisher and Ship folds
- a `changeKind: -1` sentinel passed 53 tests and was refused by production, because a kind is a `u16`
- a Topic carries no `h` — it is not *in* a container, it *is* one

The third is the most severe and the least specific to messages: **any app that does not fold got an empty render.** Worth deciding whether it belongs here or against the runtime extraction in PRO-1.

## What to change

- a projection may be declared for an event-identified object, not only an addressable one
- the consumer resolves `nevent` alongside `naddr`
- the `web` template learns a second form, so "open this in the app that owns it" works for a message

**A message is not replaceable and has no folded state**, so most of what `records` describes does not apply to it. A projection for an event-identified object is a thinner thing, and the manifest should say so rather than leaving a consumer to infer which halves are meaningful.

**Not declaring actions was the right call in PRO-6** and stays true until this lands: a reply names an *event id*, and the action vocabulary only names a parent *address*, so declaring one would tell a consumer to publish a malformed reply.

## Done when

The consumer resolves `nevent`, Peek's manifest declares a Message projection, a second app renders a real production message through it, and its `web` link opens that message in Peek. **RFC 0.4 §13.6 records the gap** — update it to record the resolution.

**M1 · first ticket.** Decision plus scaffold. No views ported.

## Decide: in place, or a parallel app directory

`build.mjs` iterates every directory under `apps/`, so both work with no build changes.

- **Parallel (`apps/ship-next`)** — a working app throughout, an incremental cutover, and the old one stays runnable for comparison. Costs some bookkeeping and a period where two apps exist.
- **In place** — less bookkeeping, but Ship is broken for the duration.

Recommend parallel, because M5 asks you to verify the new app against production before deleting the old one, and that is much easier when both can be served. Record the choice on this issue.

## Stand up the stack

React 19 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind, matching Peek, with `@estiva/ui` tokens (SHA-5) for the palette. Nothing ported yet — the goal is an empty shell that builds, serves and deploys.

**Do not touch `src/` or `lib/nostr/`.** `estiva-agent` vendors both by copy at identical paths so `diff -r` is a check anyone can run (commit b990b57). This rewrite is the UI layer above them.

## Build-time config — keep it build-time

`build.mjs` bakes three values through esbuild `define`, and this is deliberate: the relay URL *is* the workspace, not a runtime choice. Peek reads its relay origin from a Convex query instead, precisely so bundle and backend cannot drift — **Ship has no backend, so build-time is the right answer here.** Under Vite these become `import.meta.env`.

Two traps, both of which fail in a way that looks like something else:

- **The `RELAY_URL` default must stay exactly `http://localhost:3000`.** `scripts/smoke.ts:323` asserts the profile menu names the relay as the workspace, and `smoke.ts:122` intercepts that origin. Change the default and the smoke test fails for a reason that has nothing to do with what broke.
- **An empty `ID_BASE` must keep meaning "sign-in is not offered at all."** That is a deliberate fail-closed default, matching `RELAY_URL`'s shape. A rewrite that treats empty as "use production" turns a safe default into a live one.

`CLIENT_ID` stays `estiva-ship`, which is what Estiva ID knows this app as.

## Tests

Move the suite to Vitest, matching Peek — **with one exception that must not be missed.**

**`scripts/conformance.test.ts` stays a plain `tsx` script.** It is byte-identical with `estiva-agent`'s copy, over the shared `conformance/fold-fixture.json`, and the agent runs `tsx`. Converting it to Vitest destroys the property that makes it a cross-repo check, and nothing would fail to tell you. Leave it, and leave the way `npm test` invokes it.

## Traps

- Type-check with `npx tsc -b`, never `tsc --noEmit` — matches what Peek's build runs, and the rewrite should match Peek's conventions from the first commit rather than being corrected later.
- Do not scaffold a backend, a `server/` directory, or a commented-out database client. See `estiva-docs/decisions/0001-relay-canonical-by-default.md` — Ship is relay-canonical and an empty slot is an invitation.
- `apps/ship/index.html` is 14KB. Some of it is styling Tailwind replaces and some is structure that must survive. Work out which before deleting any of it — that question is open question 3 on the project.

## Done when

The new app builds, serves, signs nothing, renders an empty shell with `@estiva/ui` tokens applied, and deploys through the existing `deploy/` path. `npm test` passes, including the conformance test, still as a `tsx` script.

**Reported by Miky, 2026-08-25**, while testing M3's live delivery in two browser windows.

## What happens

Delete a message or a reply in one window. In another window on the same topic, signed in as the same person, the message **sometimes stays on screen**. Reloading that window clears it.

Replies and new messages propagate correctly. Only deletion was observed sticking.

## What the reload tells us

**Convex had already deleted the row.** If it had not, a reload would have brought the message back — instead the reload is what removes it. So this is a *rendered state* problem, not a data one: the stale window is holding a view that no longer matches the query it was built from.

That also rules out the obvious suspect. Peek deletes the Convex rows **first** and publishes the `kind:5` afterwards — `src/api/actions.ts` says "the rows are gone by the time this runs" — so the other window should lose the message by Convex reactivity, before the relay is involved at all. The relay path is not in the loop for a same-account delete.

## Where to look

`src/api/messages.ts`, the merge that produces a topic's groups. Two layers there could hold a message past its row:

- `o.deletedIds` — a **per-tab** override set. The deleting tab adds to it; the other tab's copy is empty, so it is not filtering anything, and it is only the Convex row's disappearance that should remove the message there.
- `sentLocal` / `o.sentMessages[topicId]` — the optimistic copy, filtered by `remoteIds`. A locally-sent message whose row later vanishes is a shape worth checking: `sent = sentLocal.filter((c) => !remoteIds.has(c.id))` keeps the local copy precisely *when the remote row is absent*, which is also exactly what a deletion produces.

That last one is a plausible mechanism for "the author's own tab keeps it" and is cheap to test, though it does not obviously explain a *second* tab keeping someone else's.

## What is not established

**Whether this predates M3.** It was found on the day PEE-8 shipped live delivery, and PEE-8 touches `useTopicView` — but only by adding an effect and a returned value, and it does not touch the merge path above. It is very likely older and simply unnoticed until somebody watched two windows at once, which is not a normal way to use Peek. Worth confirming rather than assuming: the same repro with the socket disabled would settle it in a minute.

## Done when

A message or reply deleted in one tab disappears from every other open tab without a reload, and the mechanism is understood rather than papered over with a refetch.

PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-id/pull/55 — batched with CRO-1 as one Gate 1 deploy. Not done until the row is verified on the box.

**The unverified note was right to check, and the answer was reassuring.** Production's `allowed_kinds` matched `seed.ts` exactly before anything was edited — `estiva-peek` had the 14 kinds from PR #54 and no 22242, so no drift to reconcile.

## Where the allowed relays come from — the open question, decided

A **new deployment bound (`SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS`) and a new per-app column (`app_credentials.relay_auth_urls`)**, intersected exactly the way the NIP-98 pair is. Both default to empty, which refuses.

Reusing `nip98_url_prefixes` was rejected for the reason the scoping comment gives, and one more found while implementing: the schemes do not even match. A `u` tag is `https://estiva.estiva.app/...`; a NIP-42 `relay` tag is `wss://estiva.estiva.app`. Sharing the column would have needed scheme-rewriting on one side, which is a second place for the two capabilities to disagree.

**One correction to the scoping comment:** it says there is "no `RELAY_URL` in Estiva ID's config at all". There is one — `RELAY_BRIDGE_URL`, the origin of Buzz's HTTP bridge. It is still the wrong thing to derive from, for a sharper reason than being merely adjacent: *empty means profile publishing is off*. Deriving relay auth from it would give two unrelated capabilities one switch, so turning profile publishing off would also stop Peek authenticating to the relay. Worth knowing it exists before the next person greps for it and concludes the same thing.

## Exact match, not prefix — a deliberate divergence from the pattern

The ticket says to copy the NIP-98 URL-prefix branch. The structure was copied; the **match rule was not**, on purpose.

A NIP-98 `u` tag is a full request URL with a path, so a prefix is the only workable shape. A `relay` tag has no path, so a prefix buys nothing and costs something:

```
allow  wss://estiva.estiva.app
admits wss://estiva.estiva.app.attacker.example/    ← under prefix matching
```

That is precisely the hazard `config.ts` already documents for redirect URIs ("Exact, never prefix"). A trailing slash would have saved it by accident; a value configured without one would not. WHATWG normalization folds `wss://x`, `wss://x/` and host case together first, so exact matching costs no ergonomics — the test environment configures `ws://relay.test` without a slash while every event under test carries one, so the normalization is exercised on every run rather than assumed.

## The pin is gone, and what replaced it

`seed.test.ts`'s `not.toContain(22242)` is deleted as instructed. What replaced it asserts the **invariant** rather than either number, in both directions across every seeded app: an app has relays iff it has the kind. The kind without relays is PEEK-133's shape — passes the kind check, then refused for every relay there is. Relays without the kind sit there looking like a grant until somebody adds 22242 and gets no scope with it.

Ship is given `relay_auth_urls: []` rather than the deployment's list, so adding the kind there later cannot be a one-line unscoped grant.

## What is proven, and what is not

Six DB-backed tests in `sign.test.ts` alongside the unit tests, because the rule being a pure function is not the risk — the *column* surviving `seed.ts` → `findAppPolicy` → `evaluateSignPolicy` is. A `relay_auth_urls` missing from that SELECT would have refused every relay while every `policy.test.ts` test still passed.

**Still unproven, and it stays that way until M3:** a browser-signed 22242 accepted by the live relay, and a REQ returning events on that connection. That needs a live Peek user token, which this session has no way to mint — the service-credential grant available to the agent is `claude-agent`, which is not granted 22242. What *will* be verified on the box is the row plus the container's env var, and the second half matters: the deployment bound is the other side of the AND, so an empty `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` refuses every relay while `allowed_kinds` looks perfectly correct.

events.content:
**M5 · deploy.** Blocked by the throwaway rehearsal. Do not start until every migration is accounted for.

## The relay is the exception in this ecosystem

Every other service has an update timer. **Buzz does not.** Deploy is manual, by design, and `operations/PRODUCTION.md` says so:

```bash
cd /opt/buzz && docker compose pull relay && ./run.sh restart
```

**Pull `relay` only.** `run.sh pull` also pulls postgres, redis and minio — which on a catch-up deploy means changing the database engine and the relay in one step, with two candidate causes if it goes wrong.

## Order, and the verify step is not optional

**merge → confirm the image built → confirm the box pulled it → restart → verify by image id → exercise the apps.**

`relay-image.yml` builds `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb` from `nfb-demo-kinds`. A merged change sits in the registry until someone pulls it, so a "deployed" relay can be running last month's code indefinitely.

**Verify by comparing the running image id to `:nfb`, never by health.** A healthy relay serving a stale image is precisely the state this project can produce, and it is invisible from the health endpoint. This ecosystem has shipped that failure before — a production re-seed that ran before the new image had been pulled, wrote the old values back, and exited 0.

## Before the restart

- **Take a fresh production backup and confirm it restores.** M4 established the procedure; this is the moment it matters.
- Announce the window. The estimated outage comes from M4's measured migration timings against production row counts.
- Have the rollback ready: the previous image id, written down, before the pull.

## Traps

- Migrations run on startup, so the restart *is* the migration. There is no separate step to abort at.
- The relay's CORS list in `/opt/buzz/.env` names each app's origin, and **omitting an origin turns that app off**. A merge should not touch it, but confirm it survived — it is environment, not code, and an upstream change to how origins are read would be silent.
- If the relay does not come up, the fastest correct move is rolling back the image, not debugging in place. Both apps are down while you think.

## Done when

The running image id matches `:nfb`, the relay serves reads and writes, and the actual outage duration is recorded on this issue against M4's estimate — the gap between them is the useful number for next time.

**Normative already, and worth a ticket because getting it wrong is silent.**

SPEC §6.5 says a NIP-09 `kind:5` is **author-scoped**: a relay honours a deletion only from the pubkey that signed the original, and *"an app MUST therefore hide the control from non-authors rather than offer one that silently fails."*

Archive and delete also have genuinely different reach and MUST NOT be offered as two styles of the same control — archive is a change event on a field, reversible and available to anyone in the Folder; delete is a request that relays MAY decline and that leaves children untouched.

## Why now

The *Conversation standard* project is aiming at a package other apps adopt. **Whatever that package does about deletion is what every adopting app will do**, so the semantics need to be right before it exists rather than discovered by an app that shipped a button doing nothing.

## The consequence this workspace keeps paying

**An identity that cannot sign `kind:5` publishes permanently, and no other identity can clean up on its behalf** — NIP-09 is author-scoped, so the author is that identity. That is AGE-2, still open, and it is why several probe records and verification comments are on production for good.

Any app or agent adopting this model needs to know its own signing ceiling *before* it publishes something it may want to remove, not after.

## Done when

Both apps hide delete from non-authors, archive and delete are visibly different affordances rather than two labels on one, and an identity without `kind:5` is told **before** it publishes rather than at the failed deletion.

## A correction to this ticket's own description first

The description says 14 changes target the 13 issues (6 status, 7 assignee, 1 project) and concludes **"six of them would render as `todo` when they are not"**. That conclusion is wrong, and it was mine. Six is a count of change *events*, not of issues — six status changes turned out to be one ticket moved through its lifecycle repeatedly.

Measured properly, by folding both ways and diffing:

    change events targeting the 13: 14
       status    6 events → 2 distinct issue(s)
       assignee  7 events → 2 distinct issue(s)
       project   1 events → 1 distinct issue

    Without the Folder widening, of the 13:
      would show the WRONG status : 2
      would lose their assignee   : 2

So the argument holds and the magnitude was 3× overstated. Two rows, both `done` and assigned, both of which would have come back `todo` and unassigned. Still worse than thirteen missing rows — a missing row is noticed, a wrong status is believed — but two, not six. The code comment carries the measured figure.

## What shipped

Both passes, because the first alone is the harmful one:

1. discovery asks for `kind:30851` unscoped alongside `kind:30850` — the same query `coverage()` already used to *count* them
2. the widening set now includes each discovered issue's own `h`, so its changes arrive with it

The 4-pass bound is unchanged; the extra filter rides the same round trip, since `POST /query` takes an array.

## The app needed nothing, which was not obvious

I expected this ticket's third done-when — "a parentless issue has a defined place in the app" — to be the real work. It was already satisfied. The **Issues** surface never filtered on having a project, `ctx.folderOf` uses the issue's own `h` rather than its project's, and the issue view already renders a missing parent. So the thirteen were never displayed wrongly; they were only never fetched. `apps/ship/` is untouched, which also keeps this clear of the React rewrite.

## The coverage block stays, and starts being useful

At 13 it was counting a known defect. At 0 it measures the real thing — an issue in a Folder the reader genuinely cannot read — which will be non-zero the first time anybody makes a Folder private. Production has no private channel today (all 50 are open), so that case has never occurred here.

Closed by PRO-4, not separately. On peek origin/main `submitAction` publishes through `applyAction`, and all three legs hold: a person created a Ship issue from the launcher (this project's untitled-ref row), Ship's fold lists it as ordinary, and a refusal sets submitError from the runtime's own reason. The optimistic-close risk named here is handled a layer down — bridge.ts reads the relay's `accepted` field. 29 tests green.

The file's "Inert v1: close" comments are stale text, not stale code; fixed in the PEE-2 PR.

**A recommendation on the three kinds still refused, since `1111` is done and the rest are a decision rather than work.**

**`kind:5` — grant it.** This is the one with a cost that compounds. Today anything this identity publishes to production is undeletable **by anyone**: NIP-09 is author-scoped, so the author is the agent key and no human can clean up on its behalf. That has already produced permanent artefacts this week — a verification comment on REW-10 and three archived probe project records that exist only because deletion was refused after the fact. Archiving hides them from lists; it does not remove them, and the workspace accretes.

The usual argument against is that a bot should not be able to destroy work. It is weaker than it looks: NIP-09 is author-scoped, so `kind:5` lets the agent delete **only what the agent itself wrote**. It cannot touch a human's issue, comment or project. The capability is "clean up after yourself", not "delete things".

Compare the shape with the two apps: `estiva-peek` and `estiva-ship` both already have `5`, for exactly this reason.

    PATCH /admin/credentials/claude-agent/kinds
    {"allowedKinds":[27235,1851,9,30851,30850,9007,1111,5]}

**`31989`/`31990` — leave refused.** The agent has no business publishing Ship's NIP-89 manifest or a handler recommendation; `publish-manifest.ts` signs those with a separate local key by design, and that separation is worth keeping. Nothing this session wanted them.

**`30078` — leave refused** (CRO-2 asks for a deliberate answer). Read state records that a *person* read something. A bot marking things read is a reading nobody did, and it would corrupt the cross-app read-state model the moment the agent listed issues.

So: one grant, two deliberate refusals, and the ticket can close once `5` is decided either way. I am not going to widen my own ceiling by writing to the database directly — the admin route exists with an audit trail precisely for this, and it is the one case the control is for.

**M4 · the milestone that exists because there is no staging.** Blocked by the merge and the migration audit.

## Why this cannot be skipped

Upstream migrations run against Postgres on relay startup, and the relay's database is the only shared dependency in the ecosystem — Peek and Ship both read and write it, Estiva ID signs for it, the agent CLI and MCP server read through it. A failed or destructive migration takes everything down at once.

There is **no staging workspace**. So this ticket builds the rehearsal that would otherwise not exist.

## What to build

A relay instance running the merged image against a **production-shaped database** — same schema version, and data whose *shape* matches: the same kinds present, the same tag cardinalities, comparable row counts on anything a conditional migration touches.

Shape matters more than volume. The known refuser triggers on `kind:30078` rows with ambiguous `d`/`t` tag cardinality — a copy with no `30078` rows at all would pass and prove nothing.

**Options, in order of fidelity:** a restore from a production backup into an isolated instance; a synthetic database built to match the audit's row-shape findings; or the local suite's database seeded to match. The audit (M1) says which shapes must be present.

## What to record

- every migration that ran, in order, and how long each took
- anything that refused, with its exact message and what data triggered it
- anything destructive, and whether the result is what was intended
- the schema version before and after
- whether the relay serves reads and writes afterwards — start it, publish an event, read it back

## Traps

- **Do not point this at the production database**, and do not run it on the production box where a misremembered `docker compose` could reach it. Use a separate machine or a clearly-named isolated stack.
- **Take a production backup first regardless**, and verify the backup restores. A backup nobody has restored is a hope. `~/estiva-backups` exists; confirm it covers the relay's Postgres and not only other services.
- A migration that is instant on a small copy may lock a table on production. Note timings against row counts so M5 can predict the outage window.
- If a migration refuses, that is a **finding, not a blocker to work around**. Record what data it wants repaired and file it; do not edit production data to make a rehearsal pass.

## Done when

The merged relay starts against a production-shaped database, every migration is accounted for, the relay serves a read and a write afterwards, and the expected production outage window is estimated from measured timings. If anything refused, M5 does not start until it has its own ticket.

**Depends on the publishing decision.** Mechanical: this deletes a verified duplicate rather than inventing an abstraction. Do it before `@estiva/identity` or `@estiva/ui`, because unlike those it needs no second consumer to find the seam.

## Why this one is safe to do first

The duplication is not a judgement call. These functions are **byte-identical** across `peek-app/convex/nostr/` and `estiva-ship/lib/nostr/`, verified by extracting and diffing them:

```
computeEventId   threadTags   toNostrSeconds   canonicalChannelName   normalizeUrl
```

`computeEventId` is the event-id preimage — a hash over an exact serialisation that the signature covers and the relay verifies. Two copies that agree today, with no test binding them together across repos, is the most dangerous shape available. `peek-app/src/nostr/bridge.ts` states the rule about one function crossing a folder boundary *inside a single repo*:

> a second copy would not be duplication, it would be a silent divergence the relay notices and we do not

That rule is already broken across repos. And per the project notes, Ship's `lib/nostr/` originated as a copy from `~/nfb-demos`, which has no git remote — so its provenance exists on one machine.

## First, spend an hour on `nostr-tools`

Before packaging a hand-rolled hash function, check whether an existing library covers it. The wider ecosystem does not hand-write this layer — `nostr-tools`, `rust-nostr`, NDK — and Buzz itself uses the `nostr` crate.

What to check specifically:
- event id / canonical serialisation, and Schnorr verification
- NIP-19 encode/decode for the `naddr` forms actually used (Peek needs `addressToPointer` / `pointerToAddress` / `findNaddrs`)
- NIP-98 auth event construction
- NIP-44 v2

What it will **not** cover: the Estiva/Buzz kind constants, the tag layouts Buzz validates (the `h` channel tag, NIP-10 marked reply form, the `about` reference tag), and the `accepted`-field semantics of the HTTP bridge. Those stay ours regardless.

A hybrid is a fine outcome — `nostr-tools` for crypto and NIP-19, our own thin layer for kinds and tag builders. Record the decision and the reasoning on this issue either way.

## What to extract

Into `@estiva/protocol`:

- event building and `computeEventId`, `threadTags`, `toNostrSeconds`, `canonicalChannelName`
- kind constants and the shared limits (`MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES`, `MAX_MENTIONS`, `MAX_EMOJI_CHARS`)
- NIP-19: address/pointer conversion, `naddr` discovery in text
- NIP-98: `buildUnsignedAuthEvent` and the `Authorization: Nostr` header, plus `normalizeUrl`
- the HTTP bridge client — `POST /events`, `POST /query`, `POST /count` — including the rule that **`HTTP 200` does not mean accepted** and the `accepted` field is authoritative
- NIP-44 helpers once CRO-1 lands, if there is anything client-side to share

Deliberately **not** in this package: the fold, and anything that interprets events. See the project description.

## Reconcile one real divergence

Peek split `buildAuthEvent` into `buildUnsignedAuthEvent` plus a signing wrapper, because Peek holds no keys and must sign via Estiva ID. Ship never received that refactor and still has the combined form.

**Peek's shape is correct** and should be what the package exports: an unsigned builder plus a caller-supplied signer. Ship then signs through `estivaIdSigner` instead of a secret key, which is what it already does everywhere else anyway.

## Traps

- **Must stay browser-safe and runtime-agnostic.** Peek imports these modules from *both* its Convex tree and its browser bundle, and `convex/nostr/sync.ts` documents a real deploy-time failure caused by runtime assumptions — a Node-runtime Convex file may export only actions, and that failure appears at deploy, not at type-check or test. No Node built-ins. `@noble/hashes`, `@noble/curves` and `btoa` only.
- **Prove byte-compatibility, do not assume it.** Add a fixture of known events with their expected ids and signatures, and assert the package reproduces them. This is the one place where a shared test vector genuinely belongs — unlike the fold, where the conformance fixture stays per-app.
- **Peek's build must still pass as configured.** Type-check with `npx tsc -b`, never `tsc --noEmit` — that is what Vercel runs.
- The agent (`estiva-agent`) vendors Ship's `lib/nostr/` by copy at identical paths, kept honest by `conformance/fold-fixture.json`. Migrating the agent to the package is probably right but is **open question 4** in the project description — do not resolve it silently here. Leave the agent's copy alone and note what it would take.

## Done when

Both Peek and Ship import these from `@estiva/protocol`, their local copies are deleted, the shared test vectors pass, and an event published from each app is accepted by the live relay. Verify the last part against `estiva.estiva.app` — the relay is the only authority on whether the wire format is still right, and a passing test suite is compatible with a rejected event.

**GA for the conversation standard, and the guide is the deliverable that tests the claim.**

The goal from 2026-08-28: Leaf, *"and in future other apps"*, get full comment functionality — reactions, formatting, edit, delete, read/unread — by reusing rather than rebuilding. Until somebody does that in an hour, the claim is untested.

## The guide

**A decision, not an implementation.** Per roadmap rule 2, the tickets that depend on this are deliberately not filed until it is made — filing them now would be a backlog that looks like progress.

## What is true today, measured on production

| corpus | events | carrying structure | dialect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| messages (`kind:9`, `kind:1111`) | 398 | **165 (41%)** | `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `__underline__`, `#`, `>`, `-`, `1.` |
| descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 89 with a body | **76 (85%)** | the above **plus tables, fenced code, links** |

**Two undocumented dialects, three producers, two renderers that disagree.** Peek's composer serialises TipTap to an ad-hoc marker syntax; Ship's composer is a plain textarea; the agent CLI writes freehand markdown and is the heaviest producer of structure on the relay. Peek parses the markers back; Ship renders them literally. So 41% of messages read formatted in one app and raw in the other, right now.

They do not even agree among themselves: the agent uses backticks constantly, Peek's editor has code spans **disabled** and its parser has no backtick rule.

## Ship's position is correct and must survive

Ship renders bodies as text on purpose — *"untrusted text from other people and other apps: rendered as text, never as markup."* **The fix is not to make Ship render markdown.** It is to specify a format and ship one renderer that is safe by construction.

## The three candidates (RFC 0.4 §14.5)

1. **Specify the existing marker dialect** — cheapest, matches the message corpus, caps expressiveness near what Peek's editor emits.
2. **A CommonMark subset** — standard parsers, matches what descriptions already contain, but it is a *superset* of the message dialect so the two models diverge further.
3. **Structured blocks as JSON** — what block editing and §6 anchoring actually need; costs the most and makes `content` opaque to anything that does not parse it.

RFC 0.4 §14.5 **recommends a split** — (1) for messages, (3) for rich text, sharing an inline layer — but recommending is not deciding.

## Whichever is chosen

**The 487 existing events do not move.** They are non-replaceable or replaceable-only-by-author, and REW-11 established that rewriting stamps a `created_at` the relay will not backdate. Every candidate needs an `alsoRead`-shaped answer: a declaration of the old form, and a reader that handles both permanently. **The migration is the steady state, not a window that closes.**

## Done when

The format is written into SPEC as a numbered section, the compatibility story for the existing corpus is stated, and this issue records which candidate was chosen **and what it costs** — not only which one won.
tags: Decide the content format, knowing 487 published events cannot move

**A decision, and a small one, but it is currently made by an undocumented constant.**

SPEC §6.6 now records the mechanism: a reaction is a `kind:7`, and **it carries no `h` tag**, so reactions cannot be found the way messages are. They must be fetched addressed by target — collect the event ids on screen, query for reactions pointing at them.

That forces a choice of N, and the choice is invisible: reactions on older messages simply do not appear, and **nothing reports that they were not asked for.** The reference client's N is `REACTION_TARGET_LIMIT = 100`.

**An undocumented cap is indistinguishable from "nobody reacted"** — which is the failure shape PEE-10 fixed elsewhere in Peek, where an empty container and an unreadable one had to become different things on screen.

## What to decide

- what the horizon **should** be — a fixed target count, a time window, or "everything currently rendered"
- whether it is a guarantee an app states, or a per-app choice the spec only requires be documented
- what a reader sees at the boundary, if anything

## Done when

SPEC §6.6 carries the answer, the constant is named after it rather than the other way round, and this issue records the reasoning — this is RFC 0.4 open question 10.

`peek reply <topic> <conversation>` resolves a conversation *root* and publishes with `replyTo: { rootId: thread.id, parentId: thread.id }` — the two are hardcoded equal. `Store.postMessage` already takes a distinct `parentId`, and the wire format already carries a root/reply pair for a reply to a reply, so nothing new is needed on the protocol side.

The effect is that the agent can join a conversation but cannot answer a particular person in it. In a thread with several participants its reply attaches to the opening message, which reads as answering whoever started the thread rather than whoever it is actually responding to.

This is almost certainly the second half of AGE-3. The request there was "give claude the ability to reply to its own message", and the answer to whether the agent can do that is: it *can* reply to a conversation it started — `peek reply` has no author check — but it cannot reply to a specific message within one, whoever wrote it. The limitation is threading depth, not authorship.

Shape: let `reply` take a message id as well as a conversation id, resolving to `{ rootId: <conversation>, parentId: <message> }`. `peek topic` already prints the messages, so the ids are available to whoever is calling.

Done when: the agent can reply to a named message inside a conversation and Peek renders it nested under that message rather than under the thread root.

Is it necessary? No.

That said it's addictive (maybe just for me and because i'm biased). What's nice at least in my workflow is that I brainstorm, create the plan (project and issues in Ship with description and comments) and then when Claude is shipping those task, it writes comments to the tickets. So the tickets become nice knowledgebase.

**M3.** Depends on the NIP-44 endpoints and the 30078 grant. This is the write half; the read half is the next task.

## What to build

`peek-app/src/nostr/readState.ts` — publishing a NIP-RS blob.

**Slot identity.** On first run, generate and persist locally (localStorage, not sessionStorage — it must survive a browser restart):

- `slot-id`: 32 random hex chars. The `d` tag is `read-state:<slot-id>`.
- `client_id`: a stable string, 1–64 chars, identifying this installation.

These are per **installation**, not per app-version and not per session. Peek-in-Chrome and Ship-in-Chrome own different slots by design; that is what makes the merge meaningful.

**The event:**

```json
{
  "kind": 30078,
  "tags": [["d", "read-state:<slot-id>"], ["t", "read-state"]],
  "content": "<nip44 ciphertext of the blob below>"
}
```

Exactly one `d` tag and exactly one `["t","read-state"]` tag — the spec says events with zero or more than one of either MUST be ignored, so getting this wrong produces silence, not an error.

**The plaintext blob:**

```json
{ "v": 1, "client_id": "<client-id>", "contexts": { "<context-id>": <unix-seconds> } }
```

Context ids come from the convention task — `h:<folder-uuid>`, `thread:<root>`, `msg:<id>`. Do not invent Peek-private ids.

Encrypt via the Estiva ID `/nip44/encrypt` endpoint; sign via `/sign`. Peek never holds a key.

## Write discipline — the rule that is easy to break

Marking a **thread** read advances only its `thread:<root>` context. Marking a **message** read advances only `msg:<id>`. Neither may advance the parent `h:` context. Advancing the container from a thread read silently marks later top-level messages as read, which users experience as lost messages.

Peek's `readState` table already models two granularities (container id, or a message id for one thread's replies — ruling 2026-07-09), so the distinction already exists locally. Map it faithfully rather than flattening it.

## Traps

- **Debounce publishing.** Opening five topics must not publish five events. 30078 is parameterized-replaceable so a rapid series just overwrites, but it is wasteful and each publish costs a `/sign` and a `/nip44/encrypt` round trip. Batch on a few seconds' idle, and flush on `visibilitychange` to hidden.
- **Publish the whole blob, always.** It is a replaceable snapshot, not a delta. A partial blob silently *loses* contexts — and because the merge is grow-only across *other* slots, the loss is invisible until it is the only slot left.
- Respect the caps: ≤10,000 context entries, context id ≤256 bytes, timestamps 0–4294967295, total event under the relay's size limit.
- Timestamps are **unix seconds**, matching `created_at` semantics — not milliseconds. Peek stores milliseconds internally; convert at the boundary.

## Done when

A blob appears on the relay for the viewer, decrypts to valid JSON with the expected contexts, and marking a thread read leaves the container context untouched — verify by reading the blob back, not by reasoning about the call.
tags: NIP-RS client: slot identity and publishing the read-state blob

**M5 · cutover.** Depends on the whole parity checklist passing.

## Deploy order, and why the verify step is not optional

Ship deploys through `deploy/` — `docker-compose.yml`, `nginx.conf`, `update.sh`, and an `estiva-ship-update.timer`.

**Verify the deployed thing, not the build.** This ecosystem has shipped three failures of exactly this shape, each silent and each invisible from the tool that reported success:

- a production re-seed that ran before the new image had been pulled, wrote the old values back, and exited 0
- a stacked PR reported *merged* whose content never reached `main`
- a canvas re-encode that reported success while the bytes it produced were rejected

So the order is **merge → wait for the pull → restart → verify**, and verification means opening the deployed URL and checking the app, not checking that a build passed.

## What to verify against production

1. Sign in with a real Estiva ID identity.
2. A project list that matches what the old app shows.
3. An issue with its status, assignee as a name, history and conversation.
4. A write — create an issue, comment, change a status — and confirm it by reading it back from the relay, not from the UI.
5. The 5-second refresh working in a second browser.
6. The PWA installing.
7. The relay's CORS list still names Ship's origin. It is configured in `/opt/buzz/.env`, and **omitting an origin turns that app off**. If the cutover changes the origin at all, that is a relay-side change with its own deploy.

## Traps

- **Do not delete the old app in this ticket.** That is the next one, deliberately separate, so that a problem found after cutover has something to fall back to.
- If the deployment path changed at all, the update timer's assumptions may have changed with it. Check `update.sh` actually updates the thing now being served.
- `estiva-ship-update.timer` means deploys can happen without anyone watching. Make sure a broken build cannot be picked up automatically mid-cutover.

## Done when

The new app is what `ship.estiva.app` serves, all seven checks above pass against production, and the results are recorded here. If anything fails, it belongs on this issue as a comment with what was measured — a cutover that is 90% verified is not verified.
tags: Cut over: deploy and verify against production

**A hazard caught at push time, worth recording because the branch looked finished.** The merge commit was cut from `0bd67427b`, *before* CAT-11 merged to `nfb-demo-kinds` as `e6766311e`. Pushing it as-is would have **silently dropped CAT-11's fix** — the exact silent-revert shape this ticket exists to guard against, arriving from our own side rather than upstream's. `git merge-base --is-ancestor e6766311e b09aeba7f` returned false, which is how it was found. Merged `origin/nfb-demo-kinds` into the branch: clean, 97 insertions, no conflicts. Both changes now verified to coexist.

**Upstream moved 8 further commits (`69096c9a8` → `b49675894`) and those are deliberately not included.** This is the tree that was verified end to end; re-merging would invalidate the migration rehearsal (CAT-6) and the live-relay probe (CAT-5). Being 8 behind at merge time is not meaningful when the gap was 702. Re-measure with `git merge-tree` if it sits unmerged for long.

**Re-verified after bringing CAT-11 in**, on the exact tree in the PR:

    cargo clippy -p buzz-relay --all-targets -- -D warnings   clean, 0 warnings
    cargo test -p buzz-relay --lib (migrated Postgres)        927 passed, 0 failed
    all 34 migrations apply                                   yes
    Estiva kinds with a scope arm                             10/10
    kinds that lost a scope arm                               0
    panicking expect() in the reaction path                   0
    KIND_LL_PROJECT as a requires_h_channel_scope arm         0
    a_project_record_may_be_global…()                         ok
    config::tests::a_drift_window_past_the_commit_floor…      ok

The last two are the pair a 702-commit merge is most likely to break quietly, and both hold.

**Still `in_progress`, not done** — the PR is unmerged, and an unmerged PR is not done. Merging it fires `relay image`; it does not deploy.

**Half done. The stale bundle is fixed; the mechanism that let it go stale is not.**

estiva-agent#9 (`b7d43d4`) rebuilt it. Verified the way this ticket asks — by running the check against `origin/main` itself rather than against a branch:

    npm ci && npm test && git status --porcelain -- plugin/
    → clean

The committed bundle now carries SHI-7's issue-Folder widening and REW-10's comment reader, and no absolute paths. So **anyone installing the plugin from `main` today gets a current agent**, which was not true this morning.

**The second done-when is untouched.** Nothing yet prevents this recurring, and it will: the check still validates the branch rather than the merge result, so any pair of open PRs where only one regenerates reproduces it exactly. Branch protection's *"require branches to be up to date before merging"* remains the cheap fix and is a checkbox nobody has ticked.

One thing learned while fixing it, worth having here because it makes the check itself untrustworthy if you get it wrong: **do not build this bundle in a worktree with a symlinked `node_modules`.** esbuild writes each module's path relative to the outbase; through a symlink that resolves outside the tree, so the build silently emits
`../../../../../../home/miky/estiva-agent/node_modules/...` — 180 times, in my first attempt at the fix. Every test passed. It is visible only in the diff, and it would also make anyone *checking* whether main is stale get a false positive. `npm ci` in the worktree and take the minute.

**Half of this is already right.** `buildMessage` takes `mentions: string[]` and emits `p` tags, so **who** was mentioned is on the wire and resolvable by anyone.

**The inline token is the problem.** It is the person's display name — `@Ada Lovelace` — and the parser that turns it into a chip resolves it against a local directory: `textParsing.ts` imports Peek's own `PEOPLE` and `TOPICS`. Two consequences, and the second is permanent:

- another app cannot render the chip without holding the same directory, so a mention degrades to plain text across the ecosystem
- **message content is immutable, so a rename desynchronises the text from the `p` tags forever**

## The fix

NIP-27's inline `nostr:npub…` (and `nostr:naddr…` for objects), which is the specified answer and is not currently used inside message bodies. A mention becomes self-describing: resolvable by any app, stable across renames.

**It is additive.** The `p` tags stay. Existing messages keep working because the old display-name form is still parseable — this is `alsoRead`'s shape applied to inline content: publish the new form, read both.

## Why this is filed while the format decision is not

The mention encoding is separable from the bold/italic question. It is about *reference resolution* rather than *presentation*, its defect is diagnosed, and its fix is a ratified NIP. If the format decision later subsumes it, this ticket folds into that work rather than being wasted.

## Also note

`textParsing.ts` importing app fixtures is what makes it un-extractable today, so this ticket moves the parser toward being packageable as a side effect. See the projection layer's extraction constraints.

## Done when

Peek publishes mentions as inline `nostr:` references, both forms render, a mention resolves in a second app with no shared directory, and a renamed person's old messages still resolve to the right identity.

**`@estiva-app/interop` is published and its exhaustive suite is not in it.** The 67-case `projection.test.ts` lives in `peek-app/interop/`, where the code used to be. The package carries 9 tests of its own — the public surface, README accuracy, and core resolution against the built artifact.

That is backwards. ADR 0002 §10 constraint 3: *its tests run with no app; untested code does not travel.* These tests need no app — they run against an array standing in for the relay — so nothing excuses them staying behind. The consumer that happens to have been first is not their home.

## What makes it more than a move

The suite is **vitest** (`describe/it/expect`); the foundation packages are **node:test** (`assert`). Adding vitest to one package would make it the only one, so the cases have to be converted.

**Do not do this with a regex.** I tried, and it produced assertions that had silently lost their assert:

```
expect(found?.openCount, 2)        // was expect(...).toBe(2)
expect(found?.tickets).length, 10) // syntactically mangled
```

11 of them, and the dangerous ones are the ones that still parse. A suite that looks converted and asserts nothing is worse than no suite, because it reports success. Convert by hand, or with a codemod that is itself tested against the before/after of a few known cases.

## The one wrinkle

`resolveFolderProjectSlotsForTest` is used twice and is deliberately **not** exported from the package's public entry point — a test helper in a public API is a promise nobody meant to make. Import it from `../dist/projection.js` rather than `../dist/index.js`; that keeps the public surface honest while giving the suite what it needs. Protocol's `.ts` tests already run against `dist`, so the pattern exists.

## Done when

The 67 cases run in `packages/interop/test` under `node --test`, Peek's copy is deleted rather than left beside it, and the count is checked: 76 tests in the package, not 9. **Spot-check that a few converted assertions still fail when the behaviour they cover is broken** — that is the only thing that distinguishes a real conversion from the one above.

**Unblocked by RIC-1.** This is the project's premise: the block model is proved in a field that exists today, with a second app already reading it, rather than in Leaf. It is also the escape from RFC 0.3's deadlock — Leaf should not start before §6 is answered, and §6 should not freeze before something can test it.

## What Ship does today

Every body goes through `textContent` in `apps/ship/ui.ts`'s `h()`, deliberately: *"no template strings holding user data — a project title goes through `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, because on a shared relay the titles are written by other people."*

**That position does not change.** [SPEC §13.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) makes it explicit that rendering a body as plain text stays conformant; what is forbidden is *interpreting* one as markup. Ship gains structure by rendering a parsed model through the same node construction, not by relaxing anything.

## What must keep working

Measured 2026-09-02, and none of it moves:

| corpus | bodies | carrying structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| root descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 157 | 135 (86%) |
| description changes (`kind:1851`) | 26 | 21 (81%) |

The change events are the easy ones to miss: **a description edited after creation lives in the `value` tag of a `kind:1851`, not in anyone's `content`.** RFC 0.4 §14.2 missed them and so did the first RIC-1 probe. §13.4's rule is per event, not per object — a description created as text and later edited into blocks is an untagged root plus a tagged change, and the fold must read the tag from the event it took the value from.

## Moved here from RIC-4: the one safe renderer

**Moved 2026-09-02.** SPEC §13.5's *"one renderer that is safe by construction"* was RIC-4's third build item and shipped as neither — Peek got a React renderer of its own, and Ship still has nothing. It belongs here because **Ship is the app that needs it**, and building it in RIC-4 meant designing it against no caller.

One open question comes with it, and it is why this was not obvious: **Ship renders with vanilla `h()` and Peek with React.** "One renderer" therefore cannot mean one component. It has to mean the package emits a node tree — marks and blocks already resolved, nothing to interpolate — and each app maps that to its own DOM. That is what makes §13.5's guarantee structural rather than a convention every app has to remember.

Peek's `MessageBody` is the working reference for the mapping; it should not be the second implementation of the parsing.

## Before starting

The shared `~/estiva-ship` checkout was **123 commits behind `origin/main`** on 2026-09-02, and the layouts differ: `CLAUDE.md` names `web/src/pages/IssuePage.tsx` while that checkout has `apps/ship/views/issue.ts`. Read `origin/main` from a worktree.

## Done when

The package emits a renderer-agnostic node tree and Ship maps it through node construction that cannot interpolate markup; an untagged legacy description still renders exactly as it does now; **Peek reading the same description does not regress**; and the check is run against a production description of each kind — a root, and one whose current value came from a `kind:1851` — rather than against a locally created issue.

*Amended on closing, 2026-09-02.* Two changes, both stated rather than quietly absorbed:

- **"Ship writes a block document with the `content-format` tag" moved to RIC-8.** Nothing in this ticket wrote one, and holding the write back was deliberate: a published event cannot be unpublished, so the read path should be seen working on production first. It now has been.
- **"the same `textContent` node construction it uses today"** was written when Ship rendered with a vanilla `h()`. Ship's UI is React + Vite and has been since before this ticket started; the guarantee is unchanged — every string reaches the DOM as a React child, no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, nothing to interpolate — but the mechanism named was already wrong.

## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.9.0` — `toRenderTree`, one resolved tree for either content model, plus `contentFormatOf` moved down from interop so two folds could read a tag without depending on the projection layer. estiva-foundation#29, #30.
- `@estiva-app/ui@0.3.0` — `EditableText.displayNode`, because the component moved into the shared library mid-ticket. estiva-ui#4.
- Ship renders both descriptions: ship#80 (issue), ship#82 (project).
- The fold carries the format, identically in two repositories: ship#80 and estiva-agent#32, with the conformance fixture's `expected` re-recorded and its `events` and pinned checksum untouched.

## What the verification was worth

The browser check found what four green suites and three green CI runs did not: after ship#80, the **project** description — the longest real body in the workspace at 6,446 characters — still rendered 49 literal `**` and `#` markers. ship#82 fixed it, and `scripts/ric6-live-check.ts` is kept as the check that catches it next time.

**Peek cannot have regressed**, and it is worth saying why rather than asserting it: nothing Ship publishes changed shape. Every description is still the marker text it was. That stops being true the day RIC-8 lands, which is why a Peek check is in *that* ticket's done-when.

Two corrections, both measured.

SIZE. The ticket says max_content_len is 65536 on the live relay. That number is in NIP-11 `push` object — it bounds the NIP-PL push executor, not stored events. push.limitation.max_plaintext_len (32768) is also the push executor. limitation.max_message_length (524288) is the whole websocket message. The ticket says the relay refuses to channel-scope a 30078 so a stray `h` merely signals confusion. ingest.rs classifies the kind global-only on WRITE, but its own comment records the read path treating explicit `h` tags as authoritative — so a stray `h` does not scope the event AND does make it answer #h queries. That asymmetry is why 12.2 is a MUST NOT rather than a style note.

So "stars" was one candidate and is two problems. Not bolting it onto a docs PR because it moves production per-user state and wants its own review. Say the word and I will do the DM half plus a Convex-to-relay read merge, or pick a different first case.
