**M3.** Depends on DM channels existing. Self-contained and can be done in parallel with the projection task.

## Why

A DM list needs a way to say "I do not want this in my sidebar" without leaving the conversation or losing its history. Buzz models this as two halves, and both already exist:

- **`kind:41012` `KIND_DM_HIDE`** — the client's request to hide a DM. Peek publishes this.
- **`kind:30622` `KIND_DM_VISIBILITY`** — the relay's per-viewer snapshot of the hidden set. Parameterized replaceable with `d = viewer_pubkey`, carrying one `h` tag per hidden DM, republished by the relay on every hide/unhide so **the latest event is always the authoritative hidden set**.

## What to build

- **Publish `41012`** to hide a DM.
- **Read `30622`** for the viewer and treat it as authoritative for which DMs are hidden. Do not maintain a separate Convex `hidden` column as the source of truth — the relay owns this state, and a second copy is a divergence waiting to happen. Cache it if useful, the way read state is cached.
- Unhide: per `moderation_notices.rs:121`, `open_dm` *resurfaces* a hidden DM — so re-opening the same participant set clears the hidden flag. Check during the probe whether an explicit unhide command exists or whether re-open is the intended route; the comment suggests the latter.

## Traps

- **Never sign a `30622`.** It is relay-signed and result-gated: `buzz-core/src/kind.rs` lists it in `RESULT_GATED_KINDS`, and `filter.rs:reader_authorized_for_event` requires the reader to equal the event's `#p` tag. Peek reads only its own, and `ingest.rs` would reject a client-authored one anyway.
- **Hiding is not leaving and not deleting.** The DM, its participants and its history all survive; only the sidebar entry goes. Make sure the UI copy says that — "hide" that reads as "delete" is a support ticket.
- The snapshot is a full replacement, not a delta. Apply the newest event wholesale rather than merging successive ones.
- A hidden DM that receives a new message: decide deliberately whether it resurfaces. `open_dm`'s resurfacing behaviour suggests yes, but confirm against the relay rather than assuming, and record the answer here.

## Done when

Hiding a DM removes it from the sidebar, the relay's `30622` for that viewer lists its `h`, a second device reflects the same hidden set, and no other identity can read that snapshot.

**Small, and the reason to do it now is timing rather than value.**

An action declares `{ id, label, appliesTo, emits, input }`. That is enough to draw a control and not enough for anything else to decide to use one — `label: "Change status"` is a button caption.

Add two optional fields (RFC 0.4 §13.4):

| field | for |
| --- | --- |
| `description` | prose describing what the action does and when it applies, distinct from `label` |
| `effect` | `safe` \| `writes` \| `destructive` — whether invoking without confirmation is acceptable |

## These are fields, not a design

The layer that would consume them is **deliberately parked** — no app has a harness yet, and designing against zero implementations is worse than SHA-7's single-consumer problem. See the roadmap's "not filed, and why".

**The argument for adding them anyway is `alsoRead`'s argument one level up:** adding a field now costs a line each; adding one after several apps have published manifests is a migration across every one of them, and a manifest is republished by its owner alone.

`effect` also has an immediate non-agent use: a consumer can require confirmation for a `destructive` action without knowing what the action does.

## Done when

Both fields are in the manifest schema and Ship populates them for its six actions. Consumers may ignore them; nothing yet reads `description`, and that is expected.

**Reader half open: ship#36 + estiva-agent#9. The writer is blocked, and the Peek trap this ticket predicted is the wrong one.**

## Blocked on the Estiva ID ceiling, and it belongs in Gate 1

Measured rather than read off the `allowed_kinds` query (which needs the box):

    Estiva ID refused to sign kind:1111 — App claude-agent may not sign kind 1111

The relay registry already has `1111` (`ffeb41606`), so this is the *other* ceiling and it is per-app. `estiva-ship` needs checking too and almost certainly needs the same grant, since the browser app is the main comment writer and the agent is the other.

**This is a Gate 1 dependency the ROADMAP does not record.** Gate 1 batches exactly this — CRO-2 `30078`, PEE-4 `22242`, DMS-1 `41010–41012` — into one deploy and one manual re-seed. `1111` for `estiva-ship` and `claude-agent` should ride that batch rather than earn its own trip to the box.

## The Peek trap, corrected

This ticket says: *"Peek renders a Ship issue widget above a conversation because the message carries `about`. If Peek reads `about` specifically, 1111 comments will lose the widget."* Checked, and it is the opposite way round on both halves.

**The widget path already works and was designed for this.** `convex/nostr/projection.ts` has `KIND_COMMENT = 1111`, and better, `commentKindOf(manifest)` reads the comment kind off the app's **own NIP-89 manifest** instead of hardcoding it — the comment there says hardcoding "would quietly stop finding comments the moment an app said something different." It queries `{ kinds: [commentKind], "#a": [address] }`, which is exactly what a `1111` presents.

But that only adapts **if Ship republishes its manifest**. `src/manifest.ts` currently declares `emits: { kind: KIND.MESSAGE, scope: "address" }` for the `comment` action. Republishing it is a required step this ticket does not list.

Also worth correcting: Ship does not emit a custom `about` tag. The parameter is called `about`; the wire tag is already `["a", address]`. What is non-standard is the *kind*, not the tag.

**The timeline breaks, and that needs a Peek ticket.** `peek-app/src/nostr/sync.ts` fetches `kinds: [9]`, hardcoded, `#h`-scoped. A Ship comment published as `1111` disappears from the Peek topic conversation **entirely** — not "loses its widget". That is a real break in the ecosystem's flagship interop claim, so **the writer half must not land before Peek reads 1111 in `sync.ts`.**

## What shipped

The fold reads `1111` alongside `kind:9`, both landing in the same thread under the same issue. NIP-22's case is the whole spec — uppercase `A`/`E`/`K`/`P` for the thread root, lowercase for the immediate parent — so `about` reads uppercase `A`, `parentId` reads lowercase `e`, and `rootId` reads uppercase `E` only when a thread roots at an event. Ship's roots at an address, so a top-level comment is its own conversation root exactly as a `kind:9` with no `e` is.

Reader-first is even more load-bearing here than for REW-11: a `kind:9` comment is **not replaceable at all**, so unlike a project record it cannot be rewritten even by its author. There is no migration window to miss — there is only "every comment ever written stays kind:9".

One thing the reader cannot fix, flagged where the writer will look: `1111` is channel-scoped with an `h` and **global without one**, so a comment published without it is world-readable however private its issue.

One correction to the ticket, measured not reasoned. The container context is the BARE channel uuid, not `h:<folder-uuid>`.

NIP-RS declines to prescribe context ids but grandfathers one — "a bare channel identifier remains the channel context" — and Buzz own clients write exactly that: contexts.set(channelId, …) at desktop/src/features/channels/readState/readStateStorage.ts:34, same in mobile, with msg: and thread: for the finer grains and no h: anywhere.

So a prefix does not namespace an empty space, it creates a SECOND convention for an object the ecosystem already agrees about. The failure is not an error message: one app marks a container read, the other still shows it unread, and both are behaving correctly. Blobs are grow-only, so reconciling later means tolerating both keys forever or migrating published blobs — the permanence this ticket comment warned about.

The folder model was the strongest argument for namespacing and does not survive it. RFC 0.3 7.1 is "one channel per folder, not one per file", so the container context still identifies the same object upstream identifies. What the folder model adds is that the finer grain matters more — thread: already covers that, same spelling — and that "everything in this folder" becomes a distinct frontier, which is why 11.5 reserves folder:<address> as the ticket comment asked.

Promoted from tidy to load-bearing: marking a thread read advances only thread:<root>, never the parent. Today a container holds one topic so getting it wrong is invisible. A container holding five topics marks four of them read — so this rule starts mattering exactly when RFC 0.3 lands.

And the horizon has no protocol default — NIP-RS only says blobs are "best-effort recent activity hints bounded by a time horizon", so the 7 days CRO-6 assumes is a client choice, which is what makes CRO-6 a real prerequisite rather than an optimisation.

tags:
**Write documents and descriptions in blocks** — drop in a table, a code snippet, or a live widget from another app, and comment on any single block rather than the whole page.

---

# Context

## Source

> **Miky (2026-08-21)** — "Support code snippets in rich formatting"

> **Miky (2026-08-24)** — "You will be able to comment on specific blocks in Leaf." … "You will be able to reference in Peek or Ship conversation not just whole Leaf document, but just specific block like a table or paragraph."

> **Miky (2026-08-28)** — "Build rich text field based on block where you can embed widgets from other apps. Before building Leaf, I will make it work in Ship."

## Problem

Every app has description fields and none of them agree what text is. Measured on production 2026-08-28: **76 of 89 issue descriptions carry markdown structure** — tables, fenced code, links — and Ship renders all of it as literal characters. Deliberately, because the body is untrusted text from other apps. So the person who wrote a table sees a table nowhere.

The deeper job is addressability: **let me point at one paragraph, not the whole document.** That is also the thing Leaf needs in order to exist.

## Usage scenarios

> **Miky, 2026-08-21, writing feedback in Peek**
> Asked for code snippets in rich formatting. Today a code fence he types is stored, rendered raw in Ship, and rendered raw in Peek too — Peek's editor has code spans disabled while the agent writes backticks constantly.

> **Miky, 2026-08-24, describing Leaf to Katerina**
> Wants to reference "just specific block like a table or paragraph" from a Peek or Ship conversation. Nothing addressable exists below the document today.

## Less about / More about

- **Less about** — a better editor in one app.
- **More about** — one content model that survives being read by an app that did not write it.

---

# Solution

Two content models, kept apart, sharing only their inline layer.

A **message** carries inline marks on immutable content. A **rich text field** is a tree of blocks, and **a block is addressable** — which is what answers RFC 0.4 §6. Attachments sit below a message and inline in a field; messages carry reactions and blocks do not.

Build it in **Ship's description field**, not in Leaf.

## Options considered and rejected

- **Build it in Leaf first.** This is the deadlock RFC 0.3 wrote down and could not escape: Leaf should not start before §6 is answered, and §6 should not be frozen before Leaf can test it. Ship's description field is a block-structured field that exists today with a second app already reading it.
- **Make Ship render markdown.** Ship's plain-text rendering is a security position — *"untrusted text from other people and other apps: rendered as text, never as markup"* — not an oversight. The fix is a specified format and one safe renderer.
- **One content model for both messages and fields.** Rejected on Miky's correction, 2026-08-28, and the production corpora agree: two dialects are already in use.
- **Which format** — three candidates, decided in RIC-1, not pre-empted here.

## Prior art

Notion's block model is the target experience. ProseMirror / TipTap is already in Peek and stays the *editor* — what is shared is the format, never the editor.

---

# Milestones

**MS1 — Framing & Shaping · complete.** RFC 0.4 §14 accepted; §6 unfrozen; Ship's description named as the test bed rather than Leaf.

**MS2 — Internal Beta.** RIC-1 (decide the format) and RIC-2 (NIP-27 mentions).

**Filed 2026-09-02, the day RIC-1 landed**, per roadmap rule 2 — held back until then because implementation tickets against an undecided design are a backlog that looks like progress:

- **RIC-4** — inline mark vocabulary in `@estiva-app/protocol`, with one safe renderer
- **RIC-5** — the block model for a rich text field
- **RIC-6** — Ship's issue description becomes blocks
- **RIC-7** — anchor a comment to a single block — the §6 answer, and the thing Leaf is waiting on. Depends on RIC-5 persisting block ids

**MS3 — GA + GTM.** Roll the format out against the existing published corpus, **re-measured at 731 bodies on 2026-09-02** — the 487 in RIC-3's title is five days stale, and the growth is itself the argument for a permanent reader. They cannot move whichever candidate wins, so the compatibility story is `alsoRead`-shaped and permanent rather than a window that closes.

events.content:
**Blocks PRO-6, and it is invisible from the direction currently in production.**

Found while writing RFC 0.5. Every Ship object is addressable, so the projection layer works today for the direction it was built for — and cannot work reciprocally.

## The gap

| object | identified by |
| --- | --- |
| project, issue, document, folder | address — `naddr` |
| Peek topic | address — `naddr` (the relay's `39000`) |
| **a conversation** | **the root event's id — `nevent`** |
| **a message** | **its own event id — `nevent`** |

`projections` is keyed by kind and resolved from an `naddr`. Ship's manifest declares its `web` template as `naddr` outright. So **a manifest cannot declare how a message should be rendered**, and a consumer holding a `nevent` has nothing to look up.

## Why it is not a wire problem

NIP-22 already spans both — uppercase `E` names an event root where `A` names an address — so the bytes are fine. What is missing is that a projection cannot be *declared* for an event-identified object, and a `web` template cannot be built for one.

## What to change

- a projection may be declared for an event-identified object, not only an addressable one
- the consumer resolves `nevent` alongside `naddr`
- the `web` template learns a second form, so "open this in the app that owns it" works for a message

**Watch the author.** A `kind:39000` topic is signed by the *relay*, so a consumer resolving "who wrote this" gets the relay's pubkey rather than a person. Any attribution slot has to account for that instead of rendering the relay as a person.

## Done when

A manifest declares a projection for a message, a second app renders a real message from production through it, and following its `web` link opens that message in the app that owns it. **RFC 0.4 §13.6 records the gap** — update it to record the resolution.

## Note

This is why PRO-6 could not have worked as written. Not a mistake in PRO-6 — the gap was invisible until somebody asked what a *message* widget would resolve through.

**Amendment — this issue was written assuming two layers, and there are three.** Read it with the following in place of the framing above. The measurements are unchanged; what they decide is narrower.

**What changed.** `kind:30078` (NIP-78, arbitrary app data) is usable for app-private, user-owned state, and Buzz already does exactly this for itself — `is_buzz_mesh_status` (`buzz-db/src/lib.rs:3688`) stores mesh member status as a `BOOKMARK_SET` with a namespaced `d_tag`. Ingest performs no `d_tag` validation on 30078, and NIP-RS handling is a narrow predicate matching only `read-state:<32 hex>`. So there is a middle layer between "on the relay for interop" and "in Convex":

1. interop → relay, standard kinds
2. **app-private but user-owned → relay, `30078` with an app-namespaced `d_tag`, NIP-44 encrypted** — see CRO-11
3. app backend → Convex, for what genuinely needs a database

**Why it matters here.** This issue's premise was that `screenerItems` and `deskOpenWork` are irreducibly Convex-shaped because only Peek reads them. That reasoning was wrong: "only this app reads it" is not the same question as "this needs a database". All three of `stars`, `deskOpenWork` and `screenerItems` are small per-user lists that fit layer 2, and `stars` may belong in a standard NIP-51 bookmark list instead. So the residue this spike is weighing is smaller than described, and the ownership argument — one `authors:[pk]` export, NIP-IA archival on offboarding, NIP-09 deletion — now covers it.

**Revised outcome space.** The three outcomes still stand, but the third is now the likely one and the first two shift meaning:

- *Convex stays in the read path* — as a materialization layer, justified by cold-start numbers rather than by holding state nothing else can.
- *Convex leaves the read path* — and, with layer 2 available, may be left holding little beyond **file blobs** (`_storage`; Buzz has media routes plus `KIND_FILE_METADATA` 1063 and Blossom auth 24242, so even that has a relay home).
- *Hybrid* — fold live, materialise a small denormalised summary (per-container last-message-at and unread frontier). Most likely to be right if the cliff is real.

**Two things to add to the measurement.** First, cost layer 2 as a destination: what a `30078` round trip costs on boot for three or four small blobs, and whether whole-blob replaceable writes are acceptable for a screener that gets snoozed often. Second, note the concurrency constraint — replaceable events are last-write-wins on a *seconds* timestamp, so two tabs can silently lose a write unless the blob is a CvRDT the way NIP-RS is.

**What has not changed.** Layer 3 is permanent and will grow as Peek ships features that genuinely need queries, indexes, server-side compute or scale, and Convex may be exactly the right tool for it. The point of this spike is not to remove Convex. It is to decide whether it belongs in the read path for content the relay already owns — and now, additionally, to confirm nothing sits in it that a person would reasonably expect to own.

**Dependency added:** CRO-11 (the layer-2 convention) should be settled before this runs, or the spike will measure a two-layer world that is no longer the plan.

Measured against production, 3 references on one issue: 10 requests/tick -> 3 warm, i.e. 1 per reference. Same render (title, kind, comments, children, widget all equal).

Manifest memoised per kind+author with a 5min TTL; children merged into the object's own round trip, since the child filter never needed the root. The object, changes, comments and children are still re-read every tick — caching those is how a live widget becomes a screenshot.

**Unblocked by RIC-1.** [SPEC §13.1](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) names six marks — bold, italic, underline, code, link, reference — and two serialisations of them: markers in a message, JSON nodes in a block document. This ticket is the one implementation.

## Why it belongs in the package

Wire-visible content, so SPEC §10's test applies: *would the relay notice if two apps disagreed?* It already does. Today there are **three producers and two renderers and no shared code** — Peek's `src/lib/textParsing.ts` is the only implementation of the marker dialect anywhere, and Ship has none on purpose.

## What to build

- **Marker text** (§13.2) — parser and serialiser, including the two conservatism rules that keep published text unchanged: no whitespace at the inner edges, no alphanumeric adjacent to a marker.
- **Inline JSON nodes** (§13.1, right column) — parser and serialiser, for the block model to consume.
- **One renderer** that constructs nodes and never interpolates markup (§13.5). This is the artefact that lets Ship render structure without abandoning its position.

## `code` is the new part, and it is the point

Measured 2026-09-02: **200 of 548 published messages carry a backtick span** — more common than bold (179) — and **no renderer has ever handled one.** Peek's editor has code spans disabled and its parser has no backtick rule. This is Miky's 2026-08-21 request, and it is one mark, not a project.

## Two things to be careful about

- **`textParsing.ts` is not all mark code.** It also holds mention and bracket-reference regexes bound to Peek's mock fixtures (`PEOPLE`, `TOPICS`, `APP_FILES`). **Only the mark layer moves.** The mention layer is RIC-2's.
- **A `nostr:` reference is the token, not the product behaviour.** This ticket makes the token parse and render; RIC-2 decides what a mention *does*.

## Done when

The package exports a parser, serialiser and renderer for both serialisations; **Peek's marker code is replaced by it rather than duplicated**; a body containing a backtick span renders as code in Peek; and the round-trip is checked against a sample of the **real published corpus**, not hand-written fixtures — 548 message bodies exist to test against and a fixture that agrees with the parser proves nothing.

**Method.** A fresh archive was taken with `KEEP=15` so the 14-day retention pruned nothing (it prunes at `KEEP=14`, and there were exactly 14 — worth knowing before anyone runs it by hand).     kind 1111    76 backup / 77 prod   (+1 written after the dump)
    kind 1851   292 backup / 293 prod  (+1 written after the dump)
    totals     1399 backup / 1401 prod

Separately, the three 37 KB archives in `~/estiva-backups` are from 2026-08-07, old-key, and far too small to be a useful restore point.

One measured warning from SHA-3, because this package will hit it harder than protocol did.

tsconfig.base.json sets types: [] and lib: ["es2022"], and that is not style — it is what makes one published .d.ts compile in Peek (types: ["vite/client"]) and in Ship (types: ["node"]). es2022 contains none of: URL, btoa, fetch, WebSocket, TextDecoder, setTimeout. A service worker and an install prompt cannot avoid far more than that.

What worked in protocol: declare each global INSIDE the module that uses it and read it INSIDE a function body. The first keeps it out of every consumer global scope; the second means importing the package touches no global, which matters because an eager read at module scope throws on import in a runtime that lacks it. Transport-shaped things (fetch, WebSocket) are also parameters with the global as the default.

That will not stretch to a service worker, whose whole body is ServiceWorkerGlobalScope. Expect to need a separate entry point with its own tsconfig and lib: ["webworker"], emitted separately and never imported by the app-side entry — and to say so in the ADR, because it is the first package that genuinely cannot obey section 4a as written.

Also: the ticket says SHA-2 exists to force the release process into existence. That process now exists and has shipped three packages, so this is just a feature. There is no reason to do it before somebody wants a PWA.

**A capture form with only a title is worse than the context switch it replaces.** `add-issue` declared `{title}` alone, so filing an issue from a Peek conversation had nowhere to put what was actually said.

> **Miky, 2026-09-02** — "we should add description to add-issue. Having only title is not good experience"

## Why it is not a one-line manifest edit

The runtime writes each declared property to a **tag of its own name**, so a foreign consumer's issue arrives with `["description", …]` and empty content. Ship's own composer does the opposite — body in `content`, no tag. Both of Ship's readers only knew about content:

- `fold.ts` — `fields.description ?? event.content`, so Ship's own UI would render it blank
- the issue projection's `body` slot — `{fold, field}` with no `tag`, so every *other* consumer would too

Declaring the input without both fixes publishes descriptions that are on the event, correct, and rendered nowhere. Nothing fails.

## Done when

Filing an issue from Peek's launcher with a description shows that description in Ship's own UI and in a foreign consumer's widget, a title-only capture still works, and the manifest has been read back off production rather than trusted.

Peek has only ever been a *consumer* — it reads Ship's manifest and renders Ship's objects, and has never published one. This is the producer half of the second consumer that stops the projection layer coming out Peek-shaped; PRO-7 is the reader half.

events.content:
**One line in the relay, plus a deploy. It is the only thing standing between REW-11's merged reader and its writer.** Measured against production 2026-08-24.

## Why

Ship's project record is meant to go global so it can be discovered without channel access — `["h", uuid]` becomes `["buzz-channel", uuid]`. The relay refuses:

```
200 {"accepted": false, "message": "invalid: channel-scoped events must include an h tag"}
```

Probed in three shapes against `estiva.estiva.app`: with `buzz-channel`, without it, and a control still carrying `h`. The first two get that message; the control gets past this gate. So the refusal is the `h` requirement specifically, not the tag vocabulary and not the kind.

This is a **third gate**, separate from the two that were known. The kind is fully registered and Estiva ID signs it happily; `requires_h_channel_scope` is a different list and nobody had read it.

## What to change

`crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:494`, `requires_h_channel_scope` — remove **one** line:

```rust
    | KIND_LL_PROJECT      // ← delete this
    | KIND_LL_ISSUE        // ← keep
    | KIND_LL_CHANGE       // ← keep
```

**Issues and changes must keep the requirement.** The comment above those lines is right about them: the Folder is both how objects are grouped and how access is enforced, and an issue without one has no owner and no reader. Only the *record* goes global. Removing all three would be a different and much larger change, and is not wanted.

### This shrinks the fork rather than growing it

Worth knowing before anyone prices it as new divergence: those three lines are **ours**, added by `d207a1148` (the commit that registered 30850/30851/1851) — `git blame` confirms it. The function itself is upstream's, untouched. So this removes one line from one of our own commits and leaves the fork *closer* to upstream, not further.

That also means it is not new conflict surface for [CAT-2] or [CAT-4]. Related observation while checking: the fork is now **8 commits** past the upstream merge-base, not the four CAT-2's title names — four `feat(kind):` commits plus #1, #3, #5 and #6. CAT-2 was accurate when written; the fork has grown since.

## Where it goes, and how it deploys

- **Branch `nfb-demo-kinds`, never `main`.** Our `main` carries **zero** `KIND_LL` entries in that function — it does not have the Linear-lite kinds at all — so a PR against `main` would be meaningless or actively wrong. `relay-image.yml` builds `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb` from `nfb-demo-kinds`.
- `nfb-demo-kinds` is not rustfmt-clean. Do not run `cargo fmt` — it reflows unrelated comments.
- **The relay has no update timer.** estiva-id, peek and ship each have one; buzz does not. Deploy by hand on the box: `cd /opt/buzz && docker compose pull relay && ./run.sh restart` — pull `relay` only, since `run.sh pull` also pulls postgres/redis/minio.

## Traps

- **HTTP 200 does not mean accepted.** This gate returns `200` with `accepted: false`. Any verification that checks the status code will report success against a relay that still refuses. Read the `accepted` field.
- **Verify by image id, not by health.** A healthy relay serving the old image is the exact shape that has cost hours here before.
- **Sequencing against the catch-up.** Doing it *before* the 625-commit merge means CAT-4 has to carry it through; doing it *after* means REW-11 waits for the entire catch-up. Before is better — it is a one-line deletion inside a commit CAT-4 is already preserving, and it unblocks work that is otherwise finished.
- **This does not finish REW-11.** After the deploy, `buildProject` in `estiva-ship/src/events.ts` still has to emit the new tag array, mirrored into `estiva-agent`. The comment there carries the exact shape. The reader side is already merged and needs nothing.
- **A global project record is world-readable** — its name becomes public to anyone on the relay. That trade is argued in RFC 0.3 §4.2 and stated on REW-11; this ticket is the mechanism, not the decision.

## Done when

A `kind:30850` carrying `buzz-channel` and no `h` is accepted by production — confirmed by reading `accepted: true` off the response, not the status code — while a `kind:30851` and a `kind:1851` without `h` are both still rejected. The running relay's image id matches `:nfb`.

`assign <ref> <pubkey|me>` takes a 64-character key or `me`, and has no way to express "nobody". Once an issue is assigned, the assignment cannot be cleared from the CLI or from MCP at all.

The asymmetry is with the command written next to it: `edit-project --lead none` clears a project's lead perfectly well, writing an empty value rather than removing anything, because an append-only stream has no undo and "set to nobody" is a fact like any other. The fold reads issue `assignee` from the same kind of change field, so the mechanism is identical and only the surface is missing.

Found while verifying AGE-15 (#23). The end-to-end check there wanted to take a key from `ship people` and assign it to a throwaway issue — and could not, because that assignment would have been permanent. The check was run against an already-assigned issue instead, which is a weaker test chosen only to avoid an irreversible write.

That is the real cost: a write nobody can undo makes the safe way to test it unavailable, so the command is exercised less than the ones that are reversible.

Shape: accept `none` (and an empty value) in `assign`, exactly as `--lead` does, writing an empty assignee. The note should read "Unassign" — which is already what the Ship UI writes for a cleared assignee (`web/src/pages/IssuePage.tsx`), so the activity feed stays one vocabulary.

Worth checking while there: whether any other write in the CLI can set a value it cannot clear.

Done when: a person can clear an issue's assignee from the CLI and from MCP, and the change reads as an unassignment on ship.estiva.app.

**M3.** Do this before the cutover task, or the cutover regresses unread for every quiet container.

## Why — a real regression risk, not a theoretical one

NIP-RS fetches with `since: now - horizon`, default **7 days**, and the spec is explicit about the consequence:

> Absence of a context in all fetched blobs means the read state for that context is **unknown** — clients SHOULD treat unknown contexts as unread (conservative default). [...] *Contexts that were read but have aged out of the time horizon are indistinguishable from never-read contexts.*

For Peek this bites hard. A topic read three weeks ago and untouched since has no blob inside the horizon, so it reads as **unread** and lights up the sidebar. Peek has long-lived topics; this would look exactly like the freshness bugs this whole programme is trying to fix.

The spec names the mitigation: *"Clients MAY extend the horizon or maintain a local cache."*

## What to build

**Keep `convex/readState.ts` — change its job.** It stops being the source of truth and becomes the durable local cache that outlives the horizon. Concretely:

- merged NIP-RS state is written into `readState` as it arrives, taking the max per context (never lowering — same monotonic rule)
- the UI reads from `readState`, as it does today, so nothing downstream changes
- a context absent from the relay fetch but present in `readState` keeps its cached value rather than reverting to unread

This is a happy fit: `watermarks()` in `readState.ts` is already a per-container watermark map, which is the same shape as a NIP-RS `contexts` map. The table is not being retired — it is being repurposed, and it earns its place.

Consider also extending the fetch horizon beyond 7 days for Peek, since the relay stores the events anyway. Cheap, and it narrows the window the cache has to cover. Do both rather than choosing.

## Traps

- **Max, never overwrite,** in both directions. Relay-into-cache and cache-into-relay must both take the later timestamp. An overwrite in either direction can lower a read position, which the protocol forbids and users experience as messages un-reading themselves.
- Do not let the cache become a second source of truth that diverges. It holds exactly what the merge produced, plus history the horizon has forgotten — never a value the merge did not produce.
- Convex is per-deployment, so the cache is per-app. That is fine and expected: the relay is the shared layer, the cache is local.

## Done when

Set a container's read timestamp older than the horizon, clear the relay's recent blobs, and confirm the container still reads as read. Then confirm a genuinely never-read container still reads as unread — the two must stay distinguishable, which is exactly what the horizon alone cannot do.
tags: Repurpose Convex readState as the horizon cache

So --since 7, which anybody would write meaning seven days, would have become a cutoff twenty-five years ago and returned the whole workspace in an answer indistinguishable from a correct one. The date form is now shape-checked before it is parsed.

What the feed showed the moment it ran is the argument for it: every ticket update made from the shared checkout today carries no note, because ~/estiva-agent is 8 commits behind and predates AGE-16. The same commands from a current worktree wrote Assign and Unassign correctly. That is a live AGE-6, and nothing in a status listing could have surfaced it.

**The code already works and lives in one app.** `peek-app/convex/nostr/projection.ts` does `resolveManifest → resolveForeignObject → resolveActions → buildActionEvent` — roughly 1,300 lines, and none of it is Peek-specific in its logic. It is the single highest-value extraction available.

**It is already most of the way there, and its own header says so:** *"takes a query function and knows nothing about Convex."* That is why this is tractable; contrast `textParsing.ts`, which imports Peek's own `PEOPLE` and `TOPICS` fixtures and cannot leave the building.

## The four constraints, checked while writing rather than after

1. No imports from the app's data layer, store or config — the dependency runs one way.
2. Every environment touch is an injected parameter: query function, signer, clock. Never a module-level global.
3. Its tests run with no app. A test needing a deployment or a browser cannot travel with the package, and untested code does not travel.

SHA-7 is the warning: `@estiva-app/protocol` took the live socket as a single implementation with a single caller, and no second consumer ever pushed back on its API. **The second consumer here is Ship rendering a Peek object**, and it should exist before this is a published package. The runtime is a standalone module with no app imports, its tests run with neither Convex nor a browser, Peek consumes it with no behaviour change, and whatever the second consumer forces to change is written on this issue — **including "nothing", which is the answer that retires the worry.**

**Unblocked by RIC-1.** [SPEC §13.3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) specifies a rich text field as a JSON block document. Nothing writes one today — this is the first implementation, and §13.3 was written ahead of it deliberately.

## What a block document is

```jsonc
{ "type": "doc", "content": [
  { "type": "paragraph", "id": "b1", "content": [ … ] }
] }
```

Block types: `paragraph`, `heading` (level 1–3), `bulletList`, `orderedList`, `listItem`, `blockquote`, `codeBlock`, `table`, `horizontalRule`, `attachment`, and `widget` — which names a §7.5 widget and inherits that section's fallback chain.

## The `id` is the whole reason this is JSON

**Every block carries an `id` unique within the document, stable across every edit that does not replace the block.** That is what a comment anchors to, and it is the only thing JSON buys over text. An implementation that generates ids at render time has built a tree and not an addressable one — the anchor ticket then has nothing to bind to.

## What to build

- parse, serialise and **validate** a block document in `@estiva-app/protocol`
- id generation and preservation across edits
- write `["content-format", "estiva-blocks-1"]` on publish; **honour its absence on read** (§13.4)
- an unknown block type renders its inline text and is never dropped silently

Inline content comes from the vocabulary ticket. This ticket owns the block layer only — the two are separate on purpose, because the inline layer is shared with messages and the block layer is not.

## Done when

The package can round-trip a block document; ids survive an edit that does not replace the block; a document containing an unknown block type still renders its text; the `content-format` tag is written on publish and its absence is treated as marker text on read; and **a legacy description that begins with `{` is still read as marker text** — §13.4 forbids deciding by sniffing, and that is the case which proves it.

This ticket's done-when — *a message from Ship landing in Convex and appearing in an open topic with no HTTP relay read* — was never observable while nothing imported this module. It is now, and it works.

## The finding, restated because it is the one worth keeping

The ticket's routing table said `kind:9 → importChannel`. **Messages are kinds 9 and 1111.** Ship's comments moved to NIP-22 with REW-10, and a Ship comment is posted into the project's Folder — which *is* a Peek topic's channel. Routing only `kind:9` would have made every Ship comment vanish from live delivery: no error, no empty state, just a conversation that stops updating.

It was caught only because PEE-6's live two-channel check happened to show the first real events arriving as **kind:1111**, not `kind:9`. Reading the ticket alone would have shipped it broken, and the HTTP path — which already asks for both and explains why at length — would have kept working, so the two paths would have quietly disagreed about what a topic contains.

`KIND.COMMENT` now exists so both paths cite one constant rather than a literal.

## Still true and worth carrying into M4

**No profiles reach `importChannel` on the live path.** `kind:0` is not channel-scoped, so a `#h` subscription never delivers one and there is nothing to pass. A first-time author renders under a placeholder until `pubkeysMissingProfile`/`recordProfiles` fills it in.

The HTTP path fetched `kind:0` per author in the same run, so this is more visible now than it was: someone speaking in a topic for the first time can appear as `nostr:<8 chars>` until that pair runs. That is PEEK-72's gap, not a regression, but live delivery is what makes it noticeable.

**Peek has only ever been a consumer.** It reads Ship's manifest and renders Ship's objects. It has never published one, so no other app can render a Peek object — and the projection layer has never been exercised in that direction at all.

This is the producer half of the second consumer (see the sibling ticket for the reader half). Together they close a loop that has run one-way since the mechanism was built.

## Two kinds

**Topic** — a channel, addressable as `kind:39000` per RFC 0.4 §5.2, whose `d` is exactly the channel uuid (measured across all 50 production channels). A topic wants a `list` slot for its recent messages, which is the slot the pattern was missing.

**Message** — a `kind:9`. **Neither `card` nor `row` nor `table` nor `stat`**, so this is the first genuine use of the fallback chain: `widget: ["message", "card"]`.

## Why these two specifically

They stress the layer exactly where it is weakest — a new widget type, a list slot, and a relay-signed object whose author is the relay rather than a person. A Message rendered elsewhere is also, in itself, the unified cross-app comment experience the *Conversation standard* project is aiming at, so one artifact proves two things.

## Note the author

A `kind:39000` is signed by the **relay**, not by a user, so a consumer resolving "who wrote this" gets the relay's pubkey. Any NIP-22 `P` tag or attribution slot has to account for that rather than rendering the relay as a person.

## Done when

Peek publishes a `kind:31990` declaring both kinds, the manifest verifier passes it, and a second app resolves it from the relay by `#k` query.

events.content:
**M3 · the core.** Blocked by the kind:22242 grant. Buildable before it lands, but not verifiable — plan to test only after.

## Why

Convex cannot hold a socket: its functions are request-scoped. `convex/nostr/sync.ts:18-20` says so and proposes an external consumer; `convex/crons.ts` explains why that consumer cannot exist as a service identity (see the design note at the bottom). The browser is where the socket goes, for the same reason the relay *reads* already live there (PEEK-106): the viewer's token is the only credential that can see their channels.

Peek has **no nostr library dependency** and does not need one. Raw `WebSocket` plus the existing types in `convex/nostr/events.ts` is enough.

## What to build

`peek-app/src/nostr/liveRelay.ts` — one shared connection per tab.

1. **Connect** to the relay origin from `api.nostr.config.relayConfig` (a Convex query; deliberately not a `VITE_` build-time var, so do not add one). Convert `https://` → `wss://`.
2. **Answer AUTH.** On `["AUTH", challenge]`, build an unsigned kind:22242 carrying the `relay` and `challenge` tags and sign it with the existing `signViaEstivaId` from `src/nostr/bridge.ts`. Send `["AUTH", <signed event>]`.
3. **Reconnect** with exponential backoff and jitter. On reconnect: re-authenticate first, then re-issue every live subscription. A reconnect that restores the socket but not the subscriptions is the silent half of this failure.
4. **Re-auth on token rotation.** `useEstivaIdAuth.ts` renews the access token on a timer; the socket must not keep running on a dead identity. Signing a fresh 22242 is cheap — prefer re-auth over reconnect.
5. **Surface state** — `connecting | authenticating | live | reconnecting | failed` — for the connection-state ticket in M4 to consume. Do not render anything here.

## Traps

- **`expectedPubkey` on every `signViaEstivaId` call.** `/sign` ignores any pubkey it is handed and signs as the token's subject, so a mismatch returns HTTP 200 with a valid event authored by somebody else. The existing helper takes the guard as an argument — pass it. The comment in `bridge.ts` says not to drop it; that applies here too.
- **Do not reimplement the auth event's tag layout.** Reuse the builders from the `convex/nostr/` tree the way `bridge.ts` does — a second copy is not duplication, it is a silent divergence the relay notices and we do not.
- **Never log or persist the AUTH event or the access token.** Buzz never stores kind:22242 by design. Convex surfaces function arguments in its dashboard logs, which is the entire reason the relay credential lives in the browser — do not undo that by passing the token to an action or into a log line.
- A relay that is down must leave the app working off its Convex rows, exactly as today. Failures are logged and swallowed at this layer; visibility is M4's job.

## Done when

The socket reaches `live` against production, survives a forced disconnect (kill the network, restore it) with subscriptions restored, and survives a token renewal without dropping. Nothing is projected yet — that is the next two tickets.

## Design note: why not a server-side consumer

Worth settling once so it is not revisited. An identity is obtainable — `estiva-id/src/domain/roles.ts` has role identities with a client-credentials grant, built for server-side bots. But Buzz gates reads **per channel**, not per relay: `buzz-relay/src/handlers/event.rs:181-196` filters live fan-out through `is_member_cached(community, channel, pubkey)` and fails closed on private channels. A service identity would need membership in *every* topic — a product decision (a bot in every conversation), not an implementation detail.

nostr:naddr1qqjr2vr9vvur2cek95urzce4956rvwt995urqv3395urjdesxcenvvf489nrzqgedp68gurn8ghj7etnw35hvcfwv4ehg6tkvyhxzursqgst8r7jdpa30w7796q8j4muhfspjd4vlcdhx8fd9wnummef5p3ak3srqsqqq7yrdac49a

Observed 2026-08-28 while closing out track F. **Not diagnosed** — filed so it is not lost, with what was ruled out.

## What happened

`npx tsx scripts/agent.ts ship projects` returned **11 projects** earlier in the session, including *"Catch up the Buzz fork"*. Roughly an hour later, the same command in the same checkout returned **9**, and *"Catch up the Buzz fork"* was absent from the list.

Between the two runs I published about fifteen events — issue comments (`kind:9`, `kind:1111`) and status changes (`kind:1851`) — plus filed two new issues. Nothing that should touch a `kind:30850` project record.

## What is ruled out

- **The project still exists and still resolves.** `ship issues --project "Catch up the Buzz fork"` returns its 11 issues, so the record is readable and `resolveOne` finds it by name. Only the *list* omits it.
- **It is not archived.** The record `30850:…:5b2701f3-da02-47f1-9ff5-14bdfb1dd822` is on the relay, `created_at 2026-08-24 10:38:56`, with no `archived` tag.
- **It is not the page ceiling.** This was my first hypothesis — the relay's `max_limit` halved to 1000 with the Buzz catch-up, and this checkout predates SHA-8. But running the same command from a worktree at `origin/main`, which has `queryAll` and `@estiva-app/protocol` 0.2.0 installed, **also returns 9**. So paging is not the difference.
- **It is not a shortage of records.** The relay holds **43** `kind:30850` events with **43 distinct `d` tags**. The command lists 9 of them.

## Why it matters

43 records to 9 listed is a large filter, and whatever it is moved between two runs an hour apart. `ship projects` is the first command anyone runs, and `--project` accepts a name — so a project that silently drops out of the list while remaining addressable is the kind of gap that makes a summary confidently wrong. It is adjacent to the `coverage` block's purpose, but coverage counts *issues*; nothing reports a project the listing cannot see.

Two candidate directions I did not pursue: whether the fold filters projects on something recency-dependent (which would explain the change over time), and whether 43 records include duplicates or test records that a dedupe rule is collapsing inconsistently.

## Done when

The listing is either stable, or it reports what it filtered — the same argument the `coverage` block already makes for issues. If the 43-to-9 filter is intentional, one sentence in `ship projects`' output saying so is enough.

```
claude-agent|{27235,1851,9,30851,30850,9007,1111}|{}
estiva-peek|{9,7,5,9007,27235,1851,9101,9002,9008,1111,30078,41010,41011,41012,22242}|{wss://estiva.estiva.app}

pc-0a4935|{27235}|{}
```

And the pairing invariant asserted in SQL rather than read by eye — `(22242 = any(allowed_kinds)) = (relay_auth_urls is not empty)` is **true for all four rows**, including the two bot credentials that have neither.

## update.sh really does not seed — observed, not assumed

Worth recording because it was visible mid-deploy this time. Immediately after the timer pulled the image and ran migrations, before the manual seed:

```
009_relay_auth_urls.sql | applied 13:36:19    ← migration ran automatically
estiva-peek | {…,41011,41012} | {}            ← no 22242, empty relay list
```

The migration applies itself; the seed does not. A deploy that stopped there would have left a new column, a healthy container, a green timer log, and the feature entirely absent.

## The other half of the AND, which the row does not show

`allowed_kinds` containing 22242 is **not sufficient**, and this is the part that would fail silently. `evaluateSignPolicy` ANDs the app's column with the deployment bound, so an empty `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` refuses every relay while the row above looks perfectly correct. It is a new env var, so it had to be added to `/opt/estiva-id/.env` by hand — **before** the new container started, so the timer's `--force-recreate` picked it up with no window in between. Confirmed inside the serving container, not in the file:

```
docker compose exec -T estiva-id printenv SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS
→ wss://estiva.estiva.app
```

**For anyone doing a fresh deployment or a restore: this is a required setting now.** It is in `.env.example` and `deploy/env.production.example`; empty means every 22242 is refused.

## Regression check on the neighbouring path

The 27235 branch shares the file that changed, so it was re-verified live: `https://estiva.estiva.app/query` still signs (200), `https://evil.test/steal` still refused (`nip98_url_not_allowed`). And a 22242 signed as `claude-agent` — which has neither the kind nor a relay — is refused `kind_not_allowed`, confirming the kind check still runs before the relay branch.

## Why this is still in_progress

The done-when is *"a browser-signed kind:22242 carrying the relay's challenge is accepted, and a REQ on that connection returns events instead of auth-required."* **That last leg is unproven and cannot be proven yet** — it needs a WebSocket client and a live Peek user token, which is PEE-5. There is no way to mint a Peek browser session from a terminal, and the service credential available to the agent is not granted 22242 (correctly).

So: everything this ticket controls is shipped and verified, and **M3 is unblocked — PEE-5 onwards are testable now**. The first socket that answers a challenge is what closes this, and it should close it by observation rather than by assumption: if the relay refuses, the two things to read are this row and `printenv SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS`, in that order.

One correction carried over from the scoping comment: Estiva ID *does* have a relay URL in config — `RELAY_BRIDGE_URL` — it is just the wrong one to derive from, because empty means "profile publishing is off" and sharing it would give two capabilities one switch.

**Writer half open: ship#37 + estiva-agent#10.** CI green on both. That is the last code in this ticket.

    a comment about an object   → kind:1111, A/K/P root, a/k/p parent, h, ts
    a message about nothing     → stays kind:9
    a reply                     → stays kind:9, see below
    the manifest                → emits { kind: 1111, scope: address, alsoRead: [9] }

## Three decisions in there worth reviewing rather than skimming

**`K` and `P` are derived from the address, not passed in.** An address is `<kind>:<pubkey>:<d>` and already carries both; a second argument could only ever contradict the `A` sitting beside it.

**Replies stay `kind:9`, and that is the right answer rather than a shortcut.** A `1111` MUST name its root, and a reply's root is the *object*, not the comment it answers — so building one needs the thread's anchor, which `replyTo` does not carry and no caller passes. A `1111` with no `A` would be malformed rather than merely old. Supplying the anchor is a change in `apps/ship/`, which this ticket is scoped out of. Nothing breaks meanwhile: the fold reads both kinds into one thread and Peek has since peek#58. Worth picking up in the rewrite.

**The `h` has a test rather than a comment.** It would never fail a build: a `1111` is channel-scoped with an `h` and global without one, the relay takes both, and a comment published without it is world-readable however private its issue. Nothing errors.

## What still has to happen after merge

**Republish the manifest** — `npm run manifest`. Peek reads `emits.kind` to decide what to publish and the union with `alsoRead` to decide what to fetch, so until the *event* on the relay carries the new declaration, Peek keeps publishing `kind:9` and keeps querying only `kind:9`. The code change alone does nothing for Peek.

It signs with `.manifest-key`, a local key that is **not** subject to the Estiva ID ceiling, so it is not blocked on anything. I will do it once ship#37 merges, and verify by reading the `31990` event back off the relay rather than by the script exiting 0.

**Rehearsed 2026-08-27 against a production-shaped database. Nothing refused. Production was read, never written. Estimated outage window: seconds.**

Relay built from CAT-4s merge commit `b09aeba7f` (702 commits of upstream), run in an isolated docker stack — throwaway Postgres 17.10 + Redis + MinIO on their own network, ports 3100/deliberately not 3000.

## The database, and that it really is production-shaped

Read-only `pg_dump` of **buzz only** — no `.env`, no MinIO, no secrets — restored with **zero errors**. Verified against the numbers I measured directly on production earlier the same day:

| | restore | production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| schema version | 24 | 24 |
| channels | 61 | 61 |
| `events` partitions | 8 | 8 |
| `kind:39002` rosters | 64 | 64 |
| global `kind:30850` | 11 | 11 |
| `workflow_runs` | 0 | 0 |
| events | 1324 | 1275 (hours earlier) |

**`kind:30078` went 0 → 3 between the two reads.** This ticket warned that "a copy with no `30078` rows at all would pass and prove nothing" — so the copy is now *better* shaped than it would have been this morning. The three rows are `estiva-peek:stars:v1`, Peeks app-private storage (CRO-11s convention), **not** read-state: none matches the `read-state:` d-tag pattern, none carries the `t: read-state` tag, and **0 have the ambiguous `d` cardinality** the known refuser looks for. So CAT-3s conclusion stands, now on evidence rather than absence — and note its premise expired within a day.

## Every migration, in order, with timings

Ten, not eight — `0033` and `0034` arrived with upstreams next 77 commits. Applied to the production-shaped copy, each in its own transaction as sqlx does. Against a measured **~127 ms** `docker exec`+psql baseline (3 samples: 131/122/130), net SQL time:

    0025 relay_invites                 ~9 ms
    0026 replica_heartbeat             ~0 ms
    0027 channels_id_lookup_index      ~0 ms
    0028 long_reaction_payloads       ~10 ms
    0029 community_deletion           ~67 ms   <- heaviest
    0030 community_deletion_recovery  ~26 ms
    0031 workflow_run_error_codes      ~0 ms
    0032 channel_roster_snapshot_fence ~7 ms   <- the one I had flagged
    0033 private_managed_agent_fts   ~116 ms
    0034 replica_heartbeat_vacuum      ~0 ms
    ------------------------------------------
    total                            ~235 ms

**Nothing refused. Nothing destructive.** 1324 events and 61 channels preserved; floor guard and roster fence both on 9 relations (parent + 8 partitions).

**0032s missing `lock_timeout` is confirmed as a tail risk, not a cost.** ~7 ms of work at this scale. It remains worth adding one line, because the exposure is an unbounded *wait* behind a conflicting lock, not duration.

## The real startup path, not just the SQL

A second fresh restore, migrated by **the relay itself** with `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=true`. `_sqlx_migrations` went **24 → 34|34**, and every gate reported in its own words:

    Database migrations complete
    partition range already covered by an existing partition   (x8)
    Community deletion serving fences verified
    git object-store backend admitted: A3 conformance probe passed
    Channel roster fence verified

**Relay reached "TCP listening" in 8.8 s** from container start, migrations included. So the restart dominates the migration by ~40x, and the outage window is **seconds** — CAT-7 should add image-pull time, which cannot be measured from here.

## Schema version before and after

**24 → 34**, by sqlx, recorded in `_sqlx_migrations`.

## The relay serves a read and a write afterwards — PASS

Published a real signed `kind:30851` into a fresh Folder and read it back by `#h` filter through `@estiva-app/protocol`; id matched byte-for-byte. With a **negative control** — the same query against an unknown folder returned 0 events — so "returned something" is distinguishable from "returns everything regardless of filter".

## 0032s runtime constraint, which my CAT-3 comment said this ticket must test

Tested directly against a real channel with 3 active members:

- a roster whose `p` tags **match** canonical membership → **accepted**
- a roster with **one bogus extra member** → `ERROR: kind 39002 roster does not match canonical channel membership`

So the trigger enforces what it claims and is not a blanket block on `39002` writes.

Then the tool itself, which is what I was actually worried about. `buzz-admin reconcile-channels --channel <id>` on a 4-member production channel: **"Reconciled 1 channels"** — the emitted roster passes the trigger. Full reconcile across the community: **"Reconciled 0 channels (60 already had events, 60 total)"** — no channel is missing discovery metadata, and nothing violated the fence. **That risk is retired.**

## The backup trap — answered, and it needs a human

`~/estiva-backups` **does** cover the relays Postgres: `/opt/backup/backup.sh` dumps `buzz.sql` (events, channels, memberships) alongside `estiva-id.sql`, both `.env` files and a MinIO tar.

**But I could not verify that it restores.** Everything is encrypted to an age public key whose private half is deliberately **not on the box** — it lives in a password manager. The archive also bundles `BUZZ_RELAY_PRIVATE_KEY` and `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEK`, which is material I should not be decrypting regardless. So "a backup nobody has restored is a hope" is still true, and **retiring it is a human task**: decrypt one archive with the password-manager key and restore `buzz.sql` into a throwaway.

Two things worth knowing meanwhile: the boxs backups are **current and healthy** — daily timer, todays at 03:34, 3.2 MB and growing week over week. The copies in `~/estiva-backups` are **three weeks stale** (37 KB, 2026-08-07) and are not what a restore should be tested against.

## Also found here — a correction to my own CAT-3 comment

I wrote that migrations "run automatically at relay startup". They run **only when `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE` is set**. Production has it `true`, so the claim holds there, but it is conditional: without it the relay logs `Skipping database migrations because BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE is not enabled` **and starts anyway**. A rehearsal that forgot it would have looked clean and tested nothing.

And two startup gates that were not in my list of three, both found by the relay refusing to boot: the **community-deletion serving-fence** check, and a **git object-store conformance probe** that requires a reachable S3 backend. Both fail closed before the relay listens, so a deploy missing MinIO presents as a relay that never comes up rather than a degraded one. **CAT-7 needs MinIO reachable before the relay restarts.**

## Nothing filed against M5

No migration refused, so per the done-when there is no blocking ticket to open before CAT-7. The residual items are one-liners, not blockers: add `lock_timeout` to 0032, and have a human verify the backup restores.

## The blocker: a third gate nobody had checked

A `kind:30850` with no `h` is refused by production:

```
200 {"accepted": false, "message": "invalid: channel-scoped events must include an h tag"}
```

Buzz lists `KIND_LL_PROJECT` in `requires_h_channel_scope` (`buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:494`), next to `KIND_LL_ISSUE` and `KIND_LL_CHANGE`. Measured against the relay, not read off the source, and probed in three shapes — with `buzz-channel`, without it, and a control with `h`. The first two get the message above; the control gets past it.

This ticket says "Estiva ID's ceiling is unchanged; 30850 is already granted." True, and never the binding constraint. **The relay's h-requirement is a separate gate**, and the ticket did not name it.

Unblocking is one entry removed from that list plus a relay deploy. Issues and changes stay on it — only the record goes global. The comment justifying the list says the Folder is required because it is "both how objects are grouped and how access is enforced", which is exactly right for an issue and is the thing this ticket argues is wrong for a *record*.

So: **reader landed, writer parked.** `src/events.ts` carries the whole diagnosis next to `buildProject`, including the tag array it will emit, so the flip is a one-builder change when the relay moves.

---

## 1. Does global discovery fix the unreachable-record problem?

**No. Something else causes it, and global discovery fixes none of it.**

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reachable | 80 | 80 |
| unreachable | **13** | **13** |
| total | 93 | 93 |

Root cause of all 13, measured one at a time:

| cause | count |
| --- | --- |
| parent project record **deleted** — does not resolve by `#d`, by bulk query, or by any route | 12 |
| no `a` tag naming a project at all | 1 |
| access-gated project record | **0** |

And the part that settles it: **all 13 sit in folders this reader can already see.** Every one of the 13 `h` values resolves to a `kind:39000` the reader gets back. There is no access problem to fix.

The ticket's premise — "discovery runs through access-gated project records" — is half right. Discovery does run through project records. On this workspace they fail to resolve because they were **deleted**, not because they were gated. A deleted record cannot be discovered by making records discoverable.

Worth adding, from the §5.2 probe done alongside this: **every one of production's 50 channels is `open`**, and a reader who is a member of none of them reads all 50. So on this relay, as configured today, channel gating never bites for Ship at all. It would bite the moment somebody made a Folder private — the fix is real for the future, it just is not the fix for these 13.

**What would actually fix them:** discovering issues directly rather than only through their parents — `{kinds:[30851]}` with no scoping, which is precisely what `coverage()` already does to *count* them. That is a discovery-model change in `loadAll`, not a record-shape change, and it is a different ticket. Not done here, deliberately.

## 2. What breaks when a record's name becomes world-readable?

Nothing breaks mechanically. What changes is what leaks, and the honest answer is **less than it first appears, because the people are already public.**

The §5.2 probe measured this: an open channel's **full `kind:39002` member roster is already world-readable** to any relay member. `get_accessible_channel_ids` is *member of* `UNION` *every open channel*, and `39002` rides the same rule — 50 of 50 rosters read by a key in none of them. A Ship Folder is created `open` by `ensureFolder`, for stated reasons. So today, for any Ship project: who is in it is public, its issues are public, its conversation is public. Only the project record's own metadata was behind the channel, and only incidentally.

So the trade is narrower than the ticket implies: the *name* joins a set of things that were already exposed. It is still a real trade — a project called "Acquisition of X" would leak, and that must be said before shipping. Anything needing a private name wants RFC 0.3's private-folder model, and RFC 0.3 §4.2's stub/detail split exists for exactly this.

Two second-order effects worth knowing:

- **`resolveObject` fails silently on a global record.** It found the event, looked for `h`, found none, returned `null` — which the app reports as "you may not have access to its Folder". A lie, about the record type most likely to be public. Fixed in the PR; it would have been invisible.
- **`loadFolder`/`loadFolders` stop seeing the record**, because they filter by `#h`. Correct rather than broken — a global record is in no Folder — but it means "read this one container" and "read everything" stop agreeing about what a project is. `loadAll` is the one that sees everything.

## 3. How does the fold cope with two shapes coexisting?

Cleanly, and it turns out to be **three fallbacks, not one**, because the tags move independently: a record can carry `name` with `h`, or `title` with `buzz-channel`.

- `projectFolder` — `h` ?? `buzz-channel`
- `projectName` — `name` ?? `title`
- `projectDescription` — `description` tag ?? `.content`

Three decisions that were not obvious until written:

- **`h` wins when both are present.** A record carrying `h` really is filed under a channel, whatever else it claims. Reading `buzz-channel` first would describe a channel-scoped record as global.
- **An empty `description` tag beats leftover `.content`.** Absent and empty are different: clearing a description must not resurrect prose somebody thought they had removed.
- **`originFolder` kept its name and its callers.** For a global record it is the `buzz-channel` — still where a `kind:1851` about that project must be addressed, because changes stay channel-scoped whatever the record does. `apps/ship/` needed no change.

**Coexistence is permanent and the reason is worth recording precisely.** Not just the ±15 minute drift window: a replaceable event can only be rewritten by *its own author*, and rewriting stamps a fresh `created_at` that cannot be backdated. Interestingly `channel_id` is deliberately **not** part of the NIP-33 replacement key (`WHERE community_id AND kind AND pubkey AND d_tag`, `buzz-db/src/event.rs:718`), so an author republishing without `h` genuinely *would* replace their own channel-scoped record rather than duplicate it. The blocker on migration is losing `created_at`, not the mechanics. Reading both shapes forever is still right.

**Conformance is the evidence it costs nothing.** `fold-fixture.json` and `EVENTS_SHA256` are unchanged in both repos and the test passes — a fallback that only fires on tags no recorded event carries cannot alter a recorded fold. 11 new checks in `app.test.ts` cover both shapes, a record with both tags, the empty-description case, and a change still overriding a `name`.

## 4. How much work was it, really?

**The reader: about half a day, and 4 files — three of them comments.** `src/fold.ts` (three helpers, four call sites), `src/store.ts` (one `resolveObject` fallback plus doc corrections), `src/events.ts` (comment only), `scripts/app.test.ts` (11 checks). Mirrored to `estiva-agent` by copy; `diff -r` clean.

**The writer will be one builder** — `buildProject` emits a different tag array. Genuinely small.

**The relay change is one line and a deploy**, and that is the whole schedule risk. `~/buzz` is 625 commits behind upstream and the deploy is manual.

**What actually cost the time was none of the code.** It was finding the ingest gate — which only surfaced by publishing to production and reading the `accepted` field, exactly the trap the app's own relay client was written for — and then measuring the 13 issues rather than believing the ticket about them. Both findings are worth more than the diff.

### As a rehearsal for the folder decision (RFC 0.3 §10.1)

The scale claim holds: this is structurally the same move, and it was cheap. Three things it teaches that transfer:

1. **The reader must land first, and separately.** Not a nicety — with no migration available, two shapes coexist forever, and a folder model has the same property with more at stake.
2. **A relay change is on the critical path, and it will not be one line for folders.** §10.1 says the latest responsible moment for the upstream-versus-fork call is the first line of folder command or state code. This ticket says the relay's ingest gates are a thing to read *before* estimating, because they are invisible from the app and they fail as a 200.
3. **Check the defect a design change is justified by, before the change.** Global discovery was the right shape and the wrong fix for the bug attached to it. It stays worth doing on its merits — upstream alignment, discoverability, the private-Folder future — but the 13 issues were never its evidence.

RFC 0.3 §5.2/§5.3 were answered alongside this and both came back clean: [estiva-docs#3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/3).

Ship→Peek updates are not real-time and cannot explain themselves. Source ticket: PEEK-109.

## The actual diagnosis

There is no polling. Peek reads the relay **once per topic mount** and never again — `useTopicView.tsx` keys its sync effect on `[topicId, topicFolderId, relayUrl, convex]`, none of which change while you sit in a topic. "Replies take time to appear" is really "replies appear on remount", which is why a reload fixes it.

Four independent staleness sources, each matching a reported symptom:

1. **Messages/replies** — one fetch per mount (`useTopicView.tsx:144-159`). Reactions and deletions are additionally capped to the newest 100 messages per topic (`convex/nostr/sync.ts:41`), so an older message never picks up a reaction at all.
2. **Ship projects/issues in the sidebar** — `TopicProjectPanel.tsx:250-269` resolves once, keyed on a folder id that never changes. The file admits it: "the panel reflects the moment it resolved and does not live-update". A project created in Ship after the panel mounted never appears.
3. **Everything outside topics never syncs at all** — the only relay-read call sites are `useTopicView` (channel) and `AuthGate` (profiles). DMs, inbox, Desk and Screener have no read path.
4. **Auth failure is silent** — `useTopicView.tsx:150` calls `validToken()` and returns with no signal; relay failures below are `console.warn`. Silent refresh exists (PEEK-108) but it is a `setTimeout`, which browsers throttle in background tabs. The UI cannot distinguish "nothing changed" from "I stopped being able to ask".

## What is already true (verified live, 2026-08-21)

- `wss://estiva.estiva.app` accepts a WebSocket upgrade through Cloudflare from Peek's origin and immediately sends `["AUTH","<challenge>"]`. Verified with curl; **pass `--http1.1`** or the same request returns NIP-11 JSON, because `Connection`/`Upgrade` are not HTTP/2 headers.
- NIP-11 reports `supported_nips` including 42, `auth_required: true`, `max_subscriptions: 1024`, `max_filters: 10`.
- **One subscription covers messages, reactions AND deletions.** `buzz-core/src/filter.rs:68-90` has an explicit `#h` fallback to `StoredEvent.channel_id` for events carrying no `h` tag (kind:7, kind:5, whose channel is derived at ingest). So `{"#h":[channelUuid]}` delivers messages + reactions + deletions + assertions in one REQ. The current HTTP path needs four sequential round trips to do less.
- **The projection is reusable unchanged.** PEEK-106 already split credential from projection: `importChannel` / `importReactions` / `importResolutions` take events, not tokens.
- **Convex is already reactive.** Once a row lands, every open view updates. The only missing link is relay→Convex.

## Two gates

**Gate 1 — Estiva ID must sign kind:22242 (blocking).** `estiva-id/src/db/seed.ts:79` gives Peek `[9,7,5,9007,27235,1851,9101,9002]` — no 22242, so Peek cannot answer the AUTH challenge and every REQ returns `auth-required`. The socket looks healthy and delivers nothing. Deploying needs a **manual re-seed**: `update.sh` runs `migrate`, never `seed`. Unlike PEEK-128 this is only one gate — AUTH never goes through `ingest.rs`, `Kind::Authentication` is built into `buzz-auth/src/nip42.rs:52`, so no Buzz change and no relay deploy.

**Gate 2 — one subscription per channel (silent trap).** `buzz-relay/src/handlers/req.rs:1013` returns `None` when filters name more than one distinct `#h`; `subscription.rs:84-113` then registers the subscription as *global*, and `fan_out_scoped:273-288` consults only the channel indexes for channel-scoped events. The invariant is stated at `subscription.rs:321-325`. A multi-channel subscription returns correct history at EOSE and then receives **zero** live events. One REQ per channel; 1024 per connection is no practical ceiling.

## Why the socket stays in the browser

`convex/nostr/sync.ts:18-20` proposes an external consumer holding the socket. An identity is obtainable — `estiva-id/src/domain/roles.ts` has role identities with a client-credentials grant. But Buzz gates reads **per channel**: `handlers/event.rs:181-196` filters live fan-out through `is_member_cached(community, channel, pubkey)` and fails closed on private channels. A service identity would need membership in every topic — a product decision (a bot in every conversation), not an implementation detail. `convex/crons.ts` already reached this conclusion. Convex keeps the projection; only the socket moves.

## Shape of the fix

One shared WebSocket per tab. One subscription per open channel. Live events routed into the existing Convex import actions. Convex reactivity carries it to the UI. The HTTP path stays as the backfill on subscribe (it owns the `since` cursor and paging) and as the fallback when the socket is down — so the change is additive and a WS failure degrades to today's behaviour rather than to nothing.

Ordering caveat to design for: `created_at` is in seconds and several events routinely land in the same one (SPEC §6.2). Imports are idempotent by event id and `nostrSyncedAt` only moves forward (`convex/nostr/data.ts:523`), so live and backfill can overlap safely.

## Milestones

- **M1 — Un-gated relief.** Refetch on focus/visibility plus a short interval, in both the topic sync and the project panel; TTL the profile cache. Turns "until remount" into "within 30 seconds" and probably clears most reported symptoms. Nothing blocks this.
- **M2 — Open the 22242 gate.** Add it to Peek's allowed kinds, scoped by `relay` tag, deploy, **re-seed**, verify the row.
- **M3 — The live socket.** WS client with NIP-42 AUTH and reconnect; refcounted per-channel subscription manager; live events into the Convex projection; `useTopicView` subscribing with HTTP as backfill and fallback.
- **M4 — Honest state.** One derived connection state surfaced once, and relay read failures made visible instead of swallowed.
- **M5 — Beyond topics.** Subscriptions for the inbox, Desk and DMs, which have no relay read path at all today.

**Filed 2026-09-02 from a request to "add the rich text field to the project description as well".** Worth correcting first, because it changes what this ticket is:

> **Rendering already covers both.** RIC-6 shipped it for the issue description (ship#80) and for the project description (ship#82) — the second only because opening the page showed 49 literal `**` and `#` markers still on screen after the first. Both surfaces now draw headings, lists, quotes, fences and code spans from a real production body.

What is **not** done, and is the same on both surfaces: **Ship only ever reads a rich text field. It never writes one.** Every description in the workspace is still §13.2 marker text typed into a `<textarea>`, and the block model that RIC-5 shipped has no producer.

## Why this was held back rather than folded into RIC-6

A published event cannot be unpublished. Once Ship writes a block document the corpus starts gaining JSON permanently, so the read path should be seen working on production first — which it now has, on 157 root descriptions and 26 change-carried ones.

## What to build

- **Write a block document** with the `["content-format", "estiva-blocks-1"]` tag, on both the issue and the project description, for a new or edited body.
- **Preserve block ids across an edit.** `assignMissingBlockIds` (protocol 0.9.0) is the primitive and mints only what is missing; an editor that rebuilds the document per keystroke and re-mints detaches every anchored comment silently. RIC-7 binds to these.
- **An editor that produces blocks.** The field is a `<textarea>` today. This is the piece with real product surface in it, and the one to design rather than derive — Peek has TipTap, Ship has nothing, and SPEC §13 is deliberate that the *format* is shared and the *editor* never is.

## What must not break

- **A legacy untagged description still renders as marker text, permanently** (§13.4). 731 published bodies carry no tag and none can be given one.
- **The format is per event, not per object.** A description created as text and edited into blocks is an untagged root plus a tagged change; the fold already reads the tag from the event the value came from.
- **Peek must not regress.** Today it cannot: nothing Ship publishes has changed shape. The moment Ship writes JSON, a consumer that ignores `slots.body.format` renders a block document at a person. `contentFormatOf` and `ResolvedSlot.format` exist for this, and estiva-foundation#26's controls cover the read side — but a Peek check belongs in this ticket's done-when, not in an assumption.

## Done when

Ship writes a block document with the `content-format` tag from both the issue and the project description; a block's id survives an edit that does not replace it, checked rather than assumed; every existing untagged description still renders exactly as it does now; and **Peek is opened against a Ship object whose description is a block document** and shown not to render JSON at a reader.

**Unblocked by RIC-1.** This is the project's premise: the block model is proved in a field that exists today, with a second app already reading it, rather than in Leaf. It is also the escape from RFC 0.3's deadlock — Leaf should not start before §6 is answered, and §6 should not freeze before something can test it.

## What Ship does today

Every body goes through `textContent` in `apps/ship/ui.ts`'s `h()`, deliberately: *"no template strings holding user data — a project title goes through `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, because on a shared relay the titles are written by other people."*

**That position does not change.** [SPEC §13.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) makes it explicit that rendering a body as plain text stays conformant; what is forbidden is *interpreting* one as markup. Ship gains structure by rendering a parsed model through the same node construction, not by relaxing anything.

## What must keep working

Measured 2026-09-02, and none of it moves:

| corpus | bodies | carrying structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| root descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 157 | 135 (86%) |
| description changes (`kind:1851`) | 26 | 21 (81%) |

The change events are the easy ones to miss: **a description edited after creation lives in the `value` tag of a `kind:1851`, not in anyone's `content`.** RFC 0.4 §14.2 missed them and so did the first RIC-1 probe. §13.4's rule is per event, not per object — a description created as text and later edited into blocks is an untagged root plus a tagged change, and the fold must read the tag from the event it took the value from.

The shared `~/estiva-ship` checkout was **123 commits behind `origin/main`** on 2026-09-02, and the layouts differ: `CLAUDE.md` names `web/src/pages/IssuePage.tsx` while that checkout has `apps/ship/views/issue.ts`. Read `origin/main` from a worktree.
