**M3 · the cutover.** Last task in M3. Depends on publish, merge and the cache.

## Why do it in two steps

Read state is unusually forgiving to verify, and it would be a waste not to exploit that. The merge is a grow-only CvRDT: a wrong implementation **converges** rather than corrupts, and the worst outcome of a disagreement is a container that reads as unread when it should not. So the change can be run in parallel with the existing behaviour and compared on live data before anything is switched.

## Step 1 — dual-run

Compute both, use the existing one, log the difference:

- **A:** today's Convex-native read state (`readState.ts` written directly by `useMarkRead`)
- **B:** the merged NIP-RS state from the previous tasks

Render from **A**. Record where A and B disagree, with the context id, both timestamps and which is ahead. Leave it running long enough to cover a weekend — the horizon interacts with idle time, which is precisely when a bug would appear.

Expect and ignore two benign classes of disagreement:

- **B ahead of A** for anything read in another app or on another device. That is the feature working.
- **A ahead of B** immediately after a local read, until the debounced publish lands.

What to actually investigate: **A ahead of B persistently** (a publish is being lost, or a context id is being written under the wrong scheme), and any case where **B moves backwards** (a monotonicity violation, which is a bug in the merge and must be fixed before cutover).

## Step 2 — cut over

When the diff is quiet apart from the benign classes:

1. Render from the merged state (via the cache, per the previous task).
2. `useMarkRead` publishes a NIP-RS blob and updates the cache; it no longer treats Convex as authoritative.
3. Keep `readState` as the cache. **Do not drop the table or its fields.**

## Traps

- **Do not remove fields from the `readState` validator as part of this.** Removing a field from a table's validator fails the *entire* Convex push for every row that still carries it, and it fails at deploy time — not at `tsc -b`, not in the test suite. If anything must go, ship a sweep first, run it, confirm zero, then remove.
- Do not delete `useMarkRead`'s local write. The cache update is what keeps the UI instant; the publish is asynchronous and debounced.
- Keep the dual-run logging behind the existing debug surface rather than `console.log`, so it can be left on.

## Done when

The sidebar and Desk render from merged state, marking read still feels instant, and the dual-run diff shows nothing outside the two benign classes over a multi-day window. Confirm against the actual UI, not just the logs.

**Unblocked by RIC-1, and this is the one the rest exists for.** RFC 0.4 §6 (Component anchoring) was open question 2, frozen in 0.3 because it *"needs a real editor to choose against"* and unfrozen in 0.4 once Ship's description field was named as the test bed instead of Leaf.

> **Miky, 2026-08-24** — "You will be able to comment on specific blocks in Leaf." … "You will be able to reference in Peek or Ship conversation not just whole Leaf document, but just specific block like a table or paragraph."

Nothing addressable exists below a document today.

## The shape

An anchor is the object's address plus a block id — the id [SPEC §13.3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) requires to be unique in the document and stable across edits that do not replace the block. A `kind:1111` comment already scopes to an address; the block id is what it gains.

**Depends on the block model ticket.** If ids are generated at render time rather than persisted, there is nothing here to bind to and this ticket cannot start.

## The hard part is not the happy path

An anchor outlives the thing it points at. A block can be deleted, split, or merged by someone who never saw the comment, and the description is replaced wholesale each edit — so the anchor has to fail *visibly*. **A comment that silently detaches and shows as unanchored is the failure mode**, because it looks identical to a comment that was never anchored, and nothing reports it.

That is the same shape as §7.5's widget fallback chain terminating in a closed type: an object that is present but blank is indistinguishable from one you may not be allowed to see.

## Done when

A comment in Ship anchors to one block; the anchor survives an edit that does not replace that block; an anchor to a block that no longer exists **degrades visibly rather than silently**; and **Peek can read the anchor through the projection layer** — one app anchoring and reading its own comments proves nothing about the protocol, which is the whole reason this is being built in Ship rather than in Leaf.

**Merged: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/65 → `183d036`. Live on peek.estiva.app and confirmed working in two browsers.**

M3's first desired outcome is met: a topic open in one window updates from another within a second or two, over the socket, with no interval involved.

## Verified against the bytes production is serving, not the image id

The container started 37 seconds after the publish job finished, which is close enough to be worth checking properly rather than inferring. The served bundle was fetched and grepped:

```
assets/index-C9eB-FYh.js
  "live topic subscription unavailable"  ✓   the effect's guard
  "not a channel uuid"                   ✓   PEE-6's channel-key guard
  "auth-required"                        ✓
  "22242"                                ✓
```

An image id matching a local tag would not have proved this; the strings do.

## What the ticket asked for that does not exist

**There is no M1 interval to idle.** PEE-1/2/3 are unstarted, so today's behaviour is one sync per topic open and there is no focus/visibility/interval refetch to keep active or idle. The fallback is therefore the unconditional mount backfill plus a **backfill on every reconnect**, which is strictly better than what was there.

That reconnect backfill is not in this ticket and is the half the socket cannot cover: while the connection is down, events are missed, and the restored subscription then delivers only what is new. Without it the gap would be invisible and permanent — a topic quietly missing whatever was said during an outage.

`relayState` is returned from `useTopicView` rather than rendered. **PEE-9 should consume that rather than deriving its own**, and PEE-1 should idle its interval against it. Either opening a second socket would double the AUTH round trips for nothing.

## Two design points worth keeping

**One connection per tab, as a module singleton.** A client created inside a component is one per mount, and StrictMode mounts everything twice in development. A module instance is built once and *watched* twice — which is exactly what PEE-6's refcounting handles, so the double mount needed no special case anywhere.

**The late-backfill trap is avoided structurally, not with a cancellation flag.** Every import is keyed by `topicKey` and nothing in this path touches component state, so a run landing after `topicId` changed writes the previous topic's history to the previous topic. Said in the code so nobody adds ceremony for it later.

## What was observed, and what was not

Confirmed by hand: live delivery between two browsers, and a clean console — no reconnect chatter, no listener errors.

**Not separately reported: the offline/online leg** — that the app keeps working with the socket down and resumes live delivery without a reload. It is unit-covered (reconnect restores every channel with a live refcount) and the reconnect path itself was exercised against production in PEE-5, but nobody has watched this specific cycle in the app. Worth a moment during PEE-9, which will be rendering exactly that transition.

## The gate that keeps earning its keep

`npm run test:run` is the only PR gate here; `tsc -b` runs solely on a push to main. It failed twice on this ticket while 478 tests passed — a missing `ViewSlots` field and an early-return path that did not carry it. Third ticket in a row. **Run `npm run build` before merging anything in this repo.**

**A documented guardrail that has never run.** Found while adding RFC 0.4 to the docs site; incidental to SHA-9 rather than caused by it.

`estiva-docs/package.json` declares:

```json
"check": "node site/check.mjs"
```

**`site/check.mjs` does not exist.** `git ls-tree origin/main site/` returns `build.mjs`, `nav.mjs`, `search.js`, `serve.mjs`, `styles.css` — and nothing else. Running `npm run check` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, so the script has never worked in this repo's history.

## Why it matters more than a missing file usually would

`site/nav.mjs` documents the guarantee this script was supposed to provide, in a comment above the unpublished-pages set:

> A link to a file that is NOT published must not silently 404. `build.mjs` turns those into plain text with a marker, and **`check.mjs` fails the build if a published page links to an unpublished one** — otherwise the split above leaks as a trail of dead links pointing at documents nobody outside can read.

So the repo **states** that a published page linking to an internal document is a build failure. It is not. `build.mjs` still does its half — degrading the link to marked plain text — but nothing enforces the rule, and nothing reports when it is broken.

This is the shape `operations/SILENT-FAILURES.md` collects: a safety mechanism that is described where people will read it, believed to be running, and absent.

The unpublished set is not small — both ADRs, `FILES_ARCHITECTURE.md`, `NIP-FC.md`, and now RFC 0.3 and RFC 0.4 — so there is real surface for a published page to link into.

## Two possible resolutions, and they are genuinely different

1. **Write `check.mjs`.** Walk the published pages, resolve every internal link against `BY_FILE`, fail on any that resolves to a member of the unpublished set. This is what the comment promises.
2. **Delete the `check` script and the sentence in `nav.mjs`**, and rely on `build.mjs`'s marker alone.

Either is defensible. What is not defensible is the current state, where the comment describes a check that does not exist — a reader has no way to tell which of the two is true.

## Done when

Either the check exists and fails a deliberately-introduced bad link, or the claim is removed from `nav.mjs` so the repo stops describing a mechanism it does not have. **Verify by introducing a link from a published page to an unpublished one and confirming the build's actual behaviour** — not by reading the script.

**M3 · the payoff.** Depends on the previous three tickets. After this, the ticket's first desired outcome is met.

## Why

`peek-app/src/components/views/useTopicView.tsx:144-159` currently owns the whole read path for a topic. This ticket makes the socket the primary path and demotes HTTP to two specific, still-necessary jobs.

## What to change

In `useTopicView`, alongside the existing Folder resolution:

1. **Subscribe** to the topic's `channelUuid` on mount, release on unmount. The uuid comes from `api.nostr.sync.syncPlan`, which already returns `{ channelUuid, since }` for the viewer's topic.
2. **Backfill once on subscribe** via the existing `syncTopicFromRelay`. Do not try to make the socket do history — the HTTP path already owns the `since` cursor, the `PAGE_LIMIT` paging, and the resolution read that is deliberately *not* cursored (an assertion about an old message can be made at any time, so a cursored read would miss it).
3. **Fall back to HTTP** when the socket is not `live`. Keep the M1 focus/visibility/interval refetch active in that state and idle when the socket is live.

The result is additive: a WS failure degrades to today's behaviour rather than to nothing.

## Traps

- **Keep the mount-time backfill unconditional.** A subscription only delivers what arrives *after* it is registered. Opening a topic must still read history.
- **Do not delete the HTTP path.** It is the fallback and the backfill. `convex/nostr/sync.ts` and `src/nostr/sync.ts` both stay.
- **`validToken()` per run, not captured** — same trap as the M1 ticket. The existing comment explains why a module-load snapshot breaks sync for a whole session.
- Cancel or ignore a backfill that lands after `topicId` changed, or the previous topic's history writes while the next topic is on screen.
- Do not move the relay read into a Convex action to simplify this. The token is the credential and the browser is the only place it belongs — Convex surfaces function arguments in its dashboard logs, which is why PEEK-106 moved these reads out.

## Done when

Two browsers on the same topic, both idle and focused. A reply, a reaction, a deletion and a status change from Ship each appear in the other **within a second or two**, with no interval involved — confirm by watching for the absence of periodic `POST /query` traffic while the socket is live. Then kill the socket and confirm the app keeps working on the M1 timer, and that reconnecting resumes live delivery without a reload.

**M4.** Small, and it is the cheapest single win for the trust problem in the source ticket. Can land before or after the connection-state ticket.

## Why

Every relay read failure in Peek currently ends in `console.warn` and a silent `return`:

- `src/components/views/useTopicView.tsx:159` — `.catch((error) => console.warn('[nostr] viewer sync failed:', error))`
- `src/nostr/sync.ts` — three separate `console.warn` sites for a failed read, a failed `importChannel`, and failed `recordProfiles`
- `src/nostr/foreign.ts` — a failed resolve returns `null`, which the panel draws as "no project here", the same as success-with-nothing
- `src/auth/AuthGate.tsx:97` — profile sync failure is warned and ignored

Swallowing was the right call when each of these was added: a relay that is down must leave the app working off its Convex rows. That reasoning is still correct. **What is missing is that the person cannot tell it happened.** An empty panel that means "refused" looks exactly like an empty panel that means "nothing here", and that ambiguity is what makes the app feel untrustworthy rather than merely slow.

## What to change

Keep swallowing — keep the app working — but **record** the failure and let the UI say so:

1. Give the sync and resolve paths a way to report a failed attempt (reason plus timestamp) instead of only logging it.
2. Feed that into the connection state, so `polling` can carry "last successful sync 40 minutes ago" rather than implying freshness.
3. In `TopicProjectPanel`, separate the two empty states: **"no project in this Folder"** (a normal state, already drawn) from **"could not read the Folder"**. The `onAct` path already models this correctly with its per-object `errors` map — extend the same idea to the initial resolve.

## Traps

- **Do not convert these into thrown errors or toasts.** A relay blip must not interrupt someone mid-sentence, and a toast per failed poll on a flaky connection is worse than silence.
- `relay_membership_required` on a channel read is **not** an error — it means the viewer is not a member of that channel, which is a real answer. `src/nostr/sync.ts` says so. Classify it as such, not as an outage.
- `resolveObjectAsViewer` returning `null` for an unresolvable reference is deliberate: a broken reference degrades to plain text rather than breaking the message. Do not turn that into a visible error.

## Done when

Point Peek at an unreachable relay origin. The app still works off Convex rows, nothing throws, nothing interrupts — and the UI states plainly that it is not current, with when it last was. Then restore the relay and watch it clear itself.

**M3 · fixes a live defect and aligns with upstream at the same time.** Independent of RFC 0.3's undecided parts.

## Why — there is a real bug here, not just a divergence

Ship's project event (`kind:30850`) carries an `h` tag, so the relay files it under a channel and gates reads by membership. Consequences, both live:

- **13 of 65 issues on production are unreachable.** `loadAll` discovers from projects and widens into their Folders, so an issue whose project record does not resolve is invisible — to the CLI and to `ship.estiva.app` alike. The `coverage` block in the agent's own output reports this on every read.
- A project cannot be discovered by anyone who is not already in its channel, which makes "browse the workspace" impossible by construction.

Upstream solved the same problem differently and better: their project (`kind:30621`) is a **global** addressable event that *references* a channel via a `buzz-channel` tag. Global means discoverable by `kinds`+`authors` alone; the channel still gates the conversation.

RFC 0.3 §4.2 shows the same reasoning generalised — three of four required container properties are impossible under `h`.

## What to change

Publish `kind:30850` **without** an `h` tag, carrying the channel as a tag instead, and adopt upstream's vocabulary while touching it:

| today | change to |
| --- | --- |
| `["h", "<folder-uuid>"]` | `["buzz-channel", "<folder-uuid>"]` |
| `["title", "…"]` | `["name", "…"]` |
| description in `content` | `["description", "…"]` tag |
| `["d", "<uuid>"]` | unchanged — keep the uuid, **do not** move to a slug |
| `["lead", "<pubkey>"]` | unchanged, Estiva-specific |

Keeping `d` as a uuid is deliberate: RFC 0.3 §4.3 explains why a human slug in an address leaks a name you may later want private, and an address is immutable.

## Traps

- **Read both shapes.** Existing project records have `h` and `title`; new ones will not. The fold must accept either, indefinitely — republishing is barred by the ±15 minute drift window.
- **A global event is world-readable.** A project's *name* becomes public even to non-members. That is the intended trade for discoverability, but say it out loud before shipping — a project called "Acquisition of X" would leak. If any project needs a private name, it needs the RFC 0.3 private-folder model and does not belong in this ticket.
- Issues keep their `h` and stay channel-scoped. Only the project *record* goes global. Do not remove `h` from `30851`.
- `Store.loadAll` widens from projects into Folders. Global projects change discovery from "channels I can see" to "projects I can see" — verify the 13 unreachable issues actually become reachable rather than assuming, and record the before/after count on this issue.
- Estiva ID's ceiling is unchanged; `30850` is already granted.

## Done when

A project is discoverable by a relay query with no channel membership, its conversation is still gated, old project records still fold correctly, and the unreachable-issue count is measured before and after and recorded here.

**M5 · the last ticket, and the one that says whether this worked.** Blocked by the deploy.

## Why a separate ticket

The deploy ticket verifies the *relay*. This one verifies the **ecosystem**, because that is what a person actually experiences and it is the thing 625 commits of change could break in ways no relay-side check would notice.

Verify the user-facing action, not the mechanism. A green build, a matching image id and a healthy endpoint are all compatible with Peek being broken.

## What to exercise, by hand, against production

**Peek**
1. Sign in with Estiva ID — exercises NIP-98 and the token path.
2. Open a topic with history — exercises the channel read path and membership gating.
3. Post a message — exercises `kind:9` publish and the `accepted` field.
4. React to something — `kind:7`, whose channel is *derived* from its target rather than carried, so it exercises a path that is easy to break.
5. Confirm a Ship project widget still renders in the sidebar — exercises `naddr` resolution and the NIP-89 manifest path across apps.

**Ship**
6. List projects and open one — exercises `30850`/`30851` reads and the fold.
7. Comment on an issue — `kind:9` with an `about` tag, or `kind:1111` if REW-10 has landed.
8. Change a status and an assignee — `kind:1851` change events.

**The agent**
9. `npx tsx scripts/agent.ts ship projects` from `estiva-agent` — exercises the client-credentials grant, `/sign`, NIP-98 and `/query` in one command. It is the cheapest end-to-end check in the ecosystem and it fails loudly.

**Cross-app**
10. Create an issue in Ship, confirm it becomes visible in Peek. This is the interop claim the whole suite rests on.

## Traps

- **Use a real identity, not a fresh one.** History, membership and profile resolution only exist for an account with a past.
- If something is broken, the useful question is *which layer* — the probe (M3) already proved kinds, so a failure here is projection, auth, or an app-side assumption, not the registry.
- Watch the relay logs during this, not after. `docker logs`, not journalctl — history stops at container start and a journalctl grep returning nothing proves nothing.
- A partial pass is a fail. Ten checks, ten results recorded.

## Done when

All ten pass and are recorded on this issue. If any fail, this issue carries what broke and what was measured — and the rollback decision belongs here, not in a separate conversation.

**M3 · alignment, cheap.** Independent of RFC 0.3's undecided parts — do not wait for them.

## Why

Ship posts a comment as a `kind:9` message into the project's Folder carrying a custom `about` tag pointing at the issue address (`Store.postMessage`). The pattern is right; the tag is not standard.

**NIP-22 `kind:1111` is the standard version of exactly this idea.** From Buzz's own kind registry:

> a threaded comment scoped to any event, address or external identifier. Uppercase `A`/`E`/`I`/`K`/`P` tags name the thread root, lowercase the immediate parent. The point of NIP-22 over a bare kind:1 reply is that it can scope to an **addressable** event, which is what lets two different apps comment on the same object without either owning the comment kind.

Three reasons this is worth doing inside the rewrite:

1. **Upstream plans `1111` for issue comments too** (`VISION_PROJECTS.md`: *"Threaded comments use NIP-22 kind:1111"*). Their issue layer is designed and not built, so matching now costs nothing and buys interop later.
2. **Our relay already accepts it** — commit `ffeb41606` added `1111` to the kind registry. No gate, no re-seed, no relay deploy.
3. RFC 0.3 makes NIP-22 the conversation mechanism for *every* file type. Ship is the cheapest place to prove it, because Ship already has the one-channel-many-anchored-threads shape in production.

## What to change

- Publish comments as `kind:1111` instead of `kind:9`+`about`.
- Root tag: uppercase `A` = the issue's address (`30851:<pk>:<d>`). Parent: lowercase `a`/`e` for a reply to a reply.
- Keep the `h` tag on the project's Folder — that is what gates who can read the thread, and it is unchanged.
- Read both: fold `1111` **and** existing `kind:9`+`about` messages, so history stays visible.

## Traps

- **Do not migrate old comments.** The relay rejects `created_at` outside roughly ±15 minutes of its own clock, so republishing history would stamp every comment with today's date. Read both shapes instead, indefinitely.
- Peek renders a Ship issue widget above a conversation because the message carries `about`. If Peek reads `about` specifically, `1111` comments will lose the widget until Peek is taught the new tag — check `convex/nostr/projection.ts` before assuming, and file a Peek ticket if so.
- Estiva ID must be allowed to sign `1111`. Verify with the `allowed_kinds` query before starting; the app ceiling is separate from the relay's registry.
- `1111` is channel-scoped when it carries `h` and global otherwise. Always carry `h` — a global comment thread on a private issue would be a leak.

## Done when

A comment posted from Ship is a `kind:1111` anchored at the issue address, readable by another participant, invisible to a non-member of the Folder, and old `kind:9`+`about` comments still render in the same thread.
tags: Comments as NIP-22 kind:1111 instead of kind:9 with an about tag

**M3.** Depends on DM messages being published. This should be a second caller, not a second projection.

## Why it should be nearly free

The relay stores each DM message with the DM channel's `channel_id`, exactly as it does a topic message. So every read-path mechanism Peek already has works on a DM channel with no new logic:

- `syncPlan` → returns `{ channelUuid, since }` for a container
- `importChannel` / `importReactions` / `importResolutions` → take events, not tokens
- the `since` cursor and `nostrSyncedAt` monotonic advance (`convex/nostr/data.ts:523`)
- reaction and deletion handling, including the `#h` fallback for kinds that carry no `h` tag
- the live WebSocket subscription from *Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates*, which subscribes per channel

If this task ends up large, that is the signal something is being reimplemented rather than reused.

## What to change

- `syncPlan` currently resolves only `topics` rows. Teach it to resolve a `dmConversations` row too, returning that channel's uuid and cursor. Keep the existing lookup shape — it scans and matches on `_id` or `seedKey` because `topics` has no `seedKey` index.
- The projection writes messages with `parentKind`/`parentId`. For a DM channel those must resolve to `'dm'` and the `dmConversations` id.
- Whatever triggers a topic sync should trigger a DM sync on the same terms — the mount-time sync, the focus/visibility refetch, and the live subscription.

## Traps

- **Do not create a parallel `dmSync.ts`.** One projection, two container types. Two projections will diverge, and the divergence will be silent because each is self-consistent.
- **`resolveExternalUser` matters more here.** A DM's other participant may have no Peek user row. The projection already mints one from a pubkey (`internal.nostr.data.resolveExternalUser`); make sure the DM path uses it rather than dropping messages from unknown authors.
- Participants come from the relay's participant set, not from an `h`-tagged member list. Do not infer membership from who has spoken.
- Do not let a DM sync mark anything read.

## Done when

A DM sent from one identity appears in the other's Peek without a reload, projected through the same code path as a topic message. Confirm by checking that the diff for this task adds callers and arguments, not a new projection.

https://github.com/estiva-app/ship/pull/53 — a status now declares what it *means*, not only what it is called.

Review feedback corrected my scope call, and the existing code argued for it better than I did. Peek decided open-vs-done with a hardcoded English word set matched on lowercased labels, and **its own comment admitted** *"an app whose statuses are spelled differently shows an empty section until its values are added here — the failure worth having"*. For a layer whose purpose is making the third app cheap, that is PEE-10: blank reads as "that app is broken".

So the owning app declares it: `stage: open | started | done | dropped`.

**`dropped` is the one that earns its place.** A cancelled ticket is neither open nor done — counted as open a finished project sits at 3/4 for ever; counted as done it claims abandoned work. Only the owner knows which statuses have that shape.

"1/3" vs a progress bar vs nothing stays the consumer's call — an owner that could set that would be designing another app's UI, which is §13.1's iframe objection. Declaring meaning is the inversion working; declaring layout would be it breaking.

**REW-11 just ran this exact shape of change end to end. Three things transfer directly.**

This ticket swaps `kind:9` + a custom `about` tag for NIP-22 `kind:1111`. That is the same move REW-11 made on the project record: a wire-format change to a kind already in production, with old events that cannot be rewritten.

**1. Land the reader first, as its own PR.** There is no migration — a `kind:9` comment is not replaceable at all, so unlike the project record it cannot even be rewritten by its author. Every existing comment stays `kind:9` + `about` **forever**, and a fold that only understands `1111` loses the entire existing conversation history. Teach the fold both shapes, merge that, then flip the writer separately. REW-11 split this way and the writer flip was a one-builder diff with no coordination needed.

**2. Check the relay accepts the shape *before* estimating.** REW-11 was blocked for a full cycle by `requires_h_channel_scope` — a list nobody knew about, which is separate from the kind allowlist, and which refuses with `200 {"accepted": false, …}`. `kind:1111` is registered (commit `ffeb41606`), but registered is not the same as *accepted in the shape you intend to write*. Publish one and read the `accepted` field before planning the work. NIP-22 uses uppercase `A`/`E`/`K`/`P` for the root and lowercase for the parent, and whether Buzz gates on an `h` alongside those is exactly the sort of thing that is invisible from here.

**3. Expect the fold to need more fallbacks than the table suggests.** REW-11 looked like one swap (`h` → `buzz-channel`) and needed three, because the tags moved independently and a record could carry either combination. Comments will be worse: `about` versus `A`, `e` versus `E`, and threading semantics that differ rather than merely rename. Budget for reading both shapes in every field, not just the one the ticket names.

Conformance is the cheap proof it costs nothing: if the fixture and its checksum are untouched and the test still passes, the fallbacks provably cannot alter any recorded event.

**A short amendment to the decision record that owns package decisions.**

The rule agreed for the projection layer, rich text and the conversation standard: **functionality lands in a real app first and is packaged afterwards.** Extraction with no consumer produces a package shaped like nothing — SHA-7's lesson, where the live socket went into `@estiva-app/protocol` as a single implementation with a single caller that no second consumer ever pushed back on.

But *"we will extract it later"* is exactly how `liveTopics.ts` became a ticket. So the intention has to be **checkable while the code is being written**, not asserted afterwards:

1. **No imports from the app's data layer, store or config.** The dependency runs one way.
2. **Every environment touch is an injected parameter** — query function, signer, clock. Never a module-level global.
3. **Its tests run with no app.** If a test needs a deployment or a browser, the package cannot carry that test, and untested code does not travel.
4. **Put it where it is going.** A path that lies about what a file is, is how a thing quietly grows app-shaped.

## Both outcomes are already in the tree, which is why this is worth writing down

- **`projection.ts` passes all four** and is extractable today. Its own header: *"takes a query function and knows nothing about Convex."* It fails only (4) — it lives under `convex/`.
- **`textParsing.ts` fails (1)** — it imports Peek's own `PEOPLE` and `TOPICS` fixtures, so the parser needs Peek's directory to run and cannot leave the building.
- **`liveTopics.ts` failed (2)** — module singleton, credential provider, `navigator.onLine`, all of which SHA-7 now has to relocate.

## Why ADR 0002 rather than the roadmap

ADR 0002 owns where packages live, how they publish, and who owns a breaking change. This is the same class: a decision about packages that is not an implementer's to make case by case.

## Done when

ADR 0002 carries the four constraints and the three worked examples, and the projection layer's extraction ticket cites it.

**Part 1 of 2 open: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-foundation/pull/10** — `@estiva-app/protocol` 0.2.0. The package half; the consumer half follows once it publishes.

## What it adds

- **`RELAY_PAGE_CEILING`** — the number, in the one place that talks to the relay for a living, instead of copied into four call sites that cannot know when the relay changes it.
- **`Relay.queryAll(filters, { pageSize, maxPages })`** — every matching event, paged on the `until` cursor, rather than the first page.

## The decision worth recording, because the obvious version is wrong

Paging until a page comes back smaller than the page size **reintroduces this bug**. It trusts `RELAY_PAGE_CEILING` to equal the relay's real limit; if the relay's were ever *lower*, every page would look short and the first would be mistaken for the whole set.

So the termination rule is **whether the `until` cursor still advances**, which holds whatever the true ceiling is, at the cost of one extra round trip at the end. Pinned by a test where the fake relay clamps to **40** while the caller asks for **500** — all 200 events still return.

Two more, both learned by getting them wrong first:

- **Dedup by id is not the termination signal.** Under two filters matching the same events, a page of already-seen ids means "these filters overlap", not "stop". The first draft conflated them and **its own test caught it** — the shared `seen` set was doing double duty for the returned union and for deciding when to stop.
- **It throws where no correct answer exists.** If the cursor cannot advance and the page is full, more than `pageSize` events share one `created_at`; no value of `until` reaches past them without skipping some. Better to say so than return a plausible subset.

## Verification

145 tests pass, typecheck clean, and **this repo actually has working CI** — unlike buzz, the PR gets an independent check rather than "no checks reported".

## Versioning, deliberately

**Minor, not patch.** Consumers pin `^0.1.0`, which excludes 0.2.0, so nothing picks this up silently. That is the intent: they have to change anyway to stop naming a page size, and an accidental upgrade would be worse than an explicit one. `PROTOCOL_VERSION` and `package.json` moved together — the drift test in `runtime.test.mjs` covers it.

## Still to do

1. Merge #10, then publish by pushing the tag `@estiva-app/protocol@0.2.0` (release fires on `*@*`).
2. Consumer PRs: replace the four `limit: 2000` literals in `estiva-agent` (`apps/ship.ts`, `apps/peek.ts`, `manifest-reader.ts` ×2) with `queryAll`, bump the range to `^0.2.0`, and do the same for `estiva-ship`'s copies. The three `limit: 500` sites are the same class and should go the same way.

Unrelated observation from the worktree: `package-lock.json` on `estiva-foundation` `main` is **stale for identity 0.1.1** — `npm install` corrects it to `0.1.1`. Kept out of this PR to avoid mixing changes; worth a one-line commit.

**This is the ticket that makes the extraction trustworthy**, and it should be treated as a requirement of the extraction rather than a follow-up to it.

SHA-7 exists because `createLiveRelay` went into `@estiva-app/protocol` as a single implementation with a single caller: *"no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API."* Every line of the projection consumer runtime is in that same position today, and it is a larger surface.

## What to build

Ship resolves a `nostr:naddr…` reference to a Peek Topic or Message inside a project or issue description and renders it through the manifest — its own tokens, its own design language, zero lines that know what Peek is.

## What this specifically tests

- **The fallback chain**, because a Message is not one of the four closed widget types
- **The `list` slot**, because a Topic carries one
- **Ship's plain-text discipline** meeting a body that may carry structure — see the *Rich text and blocks* project, and do not quietly start rendering markup here
- **A relay-signed author**, which Ship has never had to attribute

## Done when

Ship renders a real Peek Topic and a real Message from production, and **whatever the second consumer forced to change in the runtime is written on this issue — including "nothing"**, which is the answer that retires SHA-7's worry rather than deferring it.

Only after this should the runtime be published as a package.

Found while measuring SHI-12. After the workspace read, this is the largest per-tick cost, and the only one that scales with what is on screen.

ForeignReferences.tsx bumps a nonce on useRefresh, and the effect re-runs resolveForeign for every naddr in the open issue's description. Measured against production: 4 requests per reference, ~600ms, identical on a second resolve — nothing is cached, and no request is conditional on anything having changed.

Per tick, on an issue with N references, on the 10s cadence: 4N requests, 24N a minute. The whole tab has 300 a minute (human_api_calls_per_min, api/bridge.rs). The workspace read is 34 and read state is 1, so ~210/min is spent before references; N=3 is 72 more and the headroom is gone. Confirmed at 244 req/min with N=2.

PRO-10 made this re-resolve for a good reason and the reason still holds: resolving once made the widget a screenshot with a timestamp nobody can see, and the demo claimed liveness. So the fix is not to stop refreshing.

What is missing is a reason to skip. Candidates, cheapest first:
1. Hold the resolved object and re-resolve only when the reference set changes — wrong on its own, that is the screenshot again.
2. Cheap liveness check: one query for the referenced address's latest created_at, refetch the rest only if it moved. 4 requests becomes 1 in the common case.
3. Share one cache across widgets, keyed by address, so the same project referenced from three issues resolves once.

2 and 3 compose. 2 is the one that changes the arithmetic.

Done when: an issue showing three references costs no more than one request per reference per tick while nothing changes, the widget still updates within one tick when the referenced object does, and both are measured against production rather than reasoned about.

**Unblocked by RIC-1.** [SPEC §13.3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) specifies a rich text field as a JSON block document. Nothing writes one today — this is the first implementation, and §13.3 was written ahead of it deliberately.

## What a block document is

```jsonc
{ "type": "doc", "content": [
  { "type": "paragraph", "id": "b1", "content": [ … ] }
] }
```

Block types: `paragraph`, `heading` (level 1–3), `bulletList`, `orderedList`, `listItem`, `blockquote`, `codeBlock`, `table`, `horizontalRule`, `attachment`, and `widget` — which names a §7.5 widget and inherits that section's fallback chain.

## The `id` is the whole reason this is JSON

**Every block carries an `id` unique within the document, stable across every edit that does not replace the block.** That is what a comment anchors to, and it is the only thing JSON buys over text. An implementation that generates ids at render time has built a tree and not an addressable one — the anchor ticket then has nothing to bind to.

## What to build

- parse, serialise and **validate** a block document in `@estiva-app/protocol`
- id generation and preservation across edits
- write `["content-format", "estiva-blocks-1"]` on publish; **honour its absence on read** (§13.4)
- an unknown block type renders its inline text and is never dropped silently

**Moved here from RIC-4 (2026-09-02):** the **inline JSON node parser and serialiser** — §13.1's right column, `{"type":"bold"}` and friends. RIC-4 shipped the marker-text serialisation and stopped there deliberately: its own words for this item were *"for the block model to consume"*, and until this ticket exists there is no consumer to design it against. It is a small symmetrical addition to `content.ts`, and it is needed here on day one, because a block's inline content is exactly these nodes.

So this ticket owns the block layer **and the inline layer's second serialisation**. What stays shared with messages is the *vocabulary* — the same six marks, the same meanings — not the encoding.

## Done when

The package round-trips §13.1's inline JSON nodes against the marker text of the same content, so the two serialisations provably carry the same marks; the package can round-trip a block document; ids survive an edit that does not replace the block; a document containing an unknown block type still yields its text; **the absence of a `content-format` tag is treated as marker text on read**; and **a legacy description that begins with `{` is still read as marker text** — §13.4 forbids deciding by sniffing, and that is the case which proves it.

*Amended on closing, 2026-09-02.* The original clause also said the tag is **written on publish**, which nothing in this ticket's scope can do — the package has no publisher, and RIC-6 is the first writer of a block document. That half was already stated verbatim in RIC-6's done-when, so it is dropped here rather than duplicated into a clause this ticket could never satisfy.

## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.7.0` — `blocks.ts` and the inline layer's JSON serialisation. estiva-foundation#27.
- The read half of §13.4 is met by `contentFormatOf` in `@estiva-app/interop` (#26, another session, landed mid-ticket), not by this package. `behaviour.test.ts:1502` is the no-sniff control; the protocol side adds the matching case — a `{`-leading legacy body parses as marker text and `parseBlockDocument` refuses it.
- 227 tests, with controls: dropping `code` from the JSON encoding fails 4, re-minting ids unconditionally fails 2.

**Note for RIC-6: 0.7.0 is merged but not yet published.** The registry serves 0.6.0 until somebody pushes the `protocol@0.7.0` tag.

**List 4 closed — read from production 2026-08-27, read-only SELECTs, nothing written. Two of my earlier verdicts change.**

**Schema version 24**, read not assumed. 24 migrations applied, none failed. So the eight new ones are `0025`–`0032` exactly as the checkout predicted.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `channels` | **61** |
| `workflow_runs` | **0** |
| `events` | **1,275** |
| `events` partitions | **8** |
| `kind:30078` rows | **0** |
| `kind:39002` rows | **64** |

**Downgrade: 0032 is no longer "the one to plan around".** At 1,275 events across 8 partitions the trigger creation is milliseconds of work. The missing `lock_timeout` is still a real defect but it is a **tail risk, not an expected cost**: the danger is an unbounded *wait* if another transaction happens to hold a conflicting lock on `events`, and because migrations run at startup that would present as a relay which never becomes ready. Add `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 5s` locally and it is gone. I overstated this before I had the row counts.

**The partition-cloning assumption is now proven, not inferred.** Every parent trigger on `events` sits on exactly **9 relations** — the parent plus all 8 partitions:

    events_created_at_floor                     9
    events_enqueue_push_match                   9
    events_refresh_channel_ttl                  9
    trg_events_guard_nip_rs_hard_delete         9
    trg_events_nip_rs_watermark                 9
    trg_events_purge_soft_deleted_nip_rs        9

So 0032s trigger will reach all 9 the same way, and `verify_channel_roster_fence_catalog` — the one genuinely new fail-closed gate — will pass. `trg_events_guard_channel_roster_snapshot` is correctly absent today, which is the negative control for that reading.

**The NIP-RS refuser is doubly inert.** Version 24 is above the gates `>= 7` early return, **and** there are zero `kind:30078` rows for it to find. Note for CRO-2: even once read-state rows exist, this gate still cannot fire at version 24.

**Upgrade: the part of 0032 that actually matters is the runtime rejection, not the lock.** Production already holds **64 `kind:39002` rosters across 61 channels**, so the relay is actively emitting them. The trigger is `BEFORE INSERT`, so it does not validate the 64 existing rows — but every future roster snapshot must match `channel_members` exactly or raise `23514`. That is live traffic meeting a new constraint, and `buzz-admin`s "emit 39000/39002 for channels missing them" command is the most likely thing to trip it. **CAT-6 should exercise that command specifically**, not just run the migrations.

**Revised plain answer:** deploying upstream today would not break, block or silently change production data. 0025–0031 are all effectively instant at this scale. The residual risks are one missing `lock_timeout` and one new runtime constraint on a kind we already write — both cheap to handle, neither a reason to delay.

Pairing writes one change, into the Folder the project record lives in. The Folder being paired therefore holds no trace of the pairing: the project keeps the h it was born with, and so does that change, so nothing carrying the topic's h names the project.

Measured on production. Folders 1a0163b1... and 2a059a2a... held 10 and 11 Ship issues and no project event, and Peek's sidebar said 'No project linked to this topic' about both. Peek now infers the pairing from the issues (estiva-app/peek#54, merged and live), which works and has the hole you would expect: a Folder paired before any issue is filed in it contains nothing to infer from.

Fix: publish the same folder change again into the Folder being paired. Identical field and value rather than a new vocabulary - it folds to the same state, so a reader that already understands folder needs no change, and one that loads both Folders folds the repeated value once.

@Katerina Kelepouri Miky asked me to write this up for you. Two things — the Desktop one is already fixed, and the VS Code one now exists.

## First: you do *not* need to delete your bot

The error you got was my bug, not anything you did — new bots were being created without permission to reach the relay, so they could sign in and then read nothing.

I repaired your existing bot directly, so **the credential you already typed into Claude Desktop is still the right one**. No deleting, no re-entering. Just ask it something again and it should answer.

(Miky's message above about creating a new one was written before the repair — it would work, but it's extra work you don't need.)

## Now: using it in VS Code

You'll need VS Code with the **Claude Code** extension installed.

### 1. Make a second bot

Not because the first one is broken — because **the secret is only shown once**, and yours is already in Desktop. There's no way to look it up again, and asking for a new secret would stop Desktop working. Two bots is the normal way to do this: you can have five, roughly one per app or machine.

- Go to **id.estiva.app** → your account → **Your bots**
- Under *What is it for?* type something like `VS Code`
- Click **Make a bot**
- **Copy the secret straight away** — it disappears when you close that panel. Copy the client id too (there's a button).

### 2. Install the plugin

In Claude Code — either the panel in VS Code or the terminal — type these two, one after the other:

`/plugin marketplace add estiva-app/estiva-agent`

`/plugin install estiva@estiva`

If it tells you to reload, run `/reload-plugins`.

### 3. Give it your credential

Unlike the Desktop extension there's no settings dialog, so it reads a small file in your home folder. **The easiest way is to let Claude write it for you** — paste this into Claude Code, with your two values swapped in:

> Create a file at ~/.estiva-agent.env containing ESTIVA_ID_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id and ESTIVA_ID_CLIENT_SECRET=your-secret, and make it readable only by me.

Then reload with `/reload-plugins`, or just restart VS Code.

### 4. Check it

Ask it:

> Is the Estiva connection working?

That runs a four-step check and tells you which step failed, if any. Then try something real — *what Ship issues are open?*

You get the same twelve things Desktop has: read and comment on Ship issues, set status, assign, create issues and projects, and read and reply in Peek topics.

## If it misbehaves

- **The plugin installed but there are no Estiva tools** — type `/plugin`, open the **Errors** tab, and send me what it says.
- **An error mentioning `node`** — the plugin is a small Node program and yours may not have it. Tell me and I'll sort it.
- **`invalid_client`** — usually the Desktop bot's secret used by mistake, or a character lost in copying. The new bot's secret is the one you want.
- **Anything else** — paste the exact message here. That's genuinely more useful than a description.

One honest caveat: I couldn't run those two install commands myself to check them — there's no Claude Code where I run. Everything after them is tested, but if step 2 does something unexpected, you're the first person to see it, and I'd like to know exactly what.

`main` carries a Revert that `nfb-demo-kinds` does not. Branching from `main` and rebasing **silently proposes deleting the members API and the relay-image workflow** — a diff that looks like a clean catch-up and is a feature deletion.

Found while measuring SHA-14. Concurrency fixed latency; this is the volume, and it is the one that bites.

Buzz meters every POST /query against human_api_calls_per_min — a fixed 60s window, default 300, and enforce_http_admission (api/bridge.rs) reads the HUMAN limit unconditionally whatever tier the caller is. Ship's loadAll is 66 requests, so 22% of a minute's whole allowance per read, and no client gets more than ~4.5 workspace reads a minute.

Ship polls every 5s. At a 9s read that is ~6 reads/min = ~396 req/min. Already over 300. I hit 'rate-limited: quota exceeded; retry in 10s' on the published serial client while measuring, so this is live now.

With SHA-14 merged a read is 1.6s, so the poll gets ~12 reads/min = ~792 req/min — 2.6x over. Faster reads must not be taken as headroom to poll harder.

Why 66 and not 33: queryAll spends one extra confirmation round trip per filter. A filter whose whole result fits in one page still asks twice, because a short page is not trusted to mean 'complete' — the relay's real ceiling may be lower than the requested pageSize, and NIP-01 has no truncation signal. That distrust is correct and has a test.

The way out is to stop guessing: the relay advertises limitation.max_limit in NIP-11. Read it once per Relay, cache it, and a page shorter than the ACTUAL ceiling is conclusively the end — 66 requests becomes 33, plus one NIP-11 fetch. Ship then fits inside the budget at a 5s poll.

Not the only option; slowing the poll or scoping the read would also work, and are Ship-side. This one is in the package and helps every consumer.

Done when: a Ship loadAll costs one request per filter, the paging tests still pass unchanged (including 'paging does not trust RELAY_PAGE_CEILING'), and a measured read against production stays under the quota at a 5s poll.

**Merged: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/62 → `089faa3`.** The protocol is proven end to end against production.

```
<- AUTH  dae4262d1e05f9f997efd62c8ce46868…
<- OK    4df660dbe510c647bbe524247777a348  true
AUTHENTICATED — subscribing
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  91044c77…
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  51b5635d…
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  c48fbd49…
<- EOSE  probe
```

Challenge → signed 22242 accepted → REQ answered with real events and an EOSE, on one socket, from a signed-in browser. This also closed **PEE-4**'s last unproven leg, which was the same observation from the other side.

## What is proven, and by what — the distinction matters for PEE-7 and PEE-8

**The protocol sequence and the grant** are confirmed against production, exactly as implemented here: the same frames, the same `relay` tag (`wss://estiva.estiva.app`, an origin), the same ordering.

**The module's own behaviour** — reconnect with backoff, re-issuing every live subscription afterwards, routing events per subscription, treating a poisoned socket as fatal — is covered by 22 tests against a fake relay built to match `crates/buzz-*`, not by production. That is the honest split.

**What has not happened is `liveRelay.ts` itself running inside the app**, because nothing imports it yet. It is unconsumed code until PEE-7 routes its events into the projection and PEE-8 wires `useTopicView`. **PEE-8 is where "the socket reaches `live` in the real app" actually gets observed**, and it is worth doing deliberately there rather than assuming it follows — the module is correct against a fake and against a hand-run protocol, which is not the same as correct inside React's lifecycle.

The specific thing to watch for at PEE-8: this creates **one connection per tab**, and a component mounting twice under StrictMode must not open two. That is a wiring concern, not a client concern, so it is not solved here.

## Carried forward

- **±60s clock tolerance** (`RELAY_AUTH_TOLERANCE_SECS`) — a browser more than a minute out signs a valid event that is refused every time, and lands in the poisoned-open state. PEE-9 should be able to say so rather than showing a generic disconnect.
- **`failed` is terminal and means auth, not availability.** A relay that is down stays `reconnecting` forever, by design. PEE-9 should render those two differently — one is "wait", the other is "this will never work".
- The connection-state values are `connecting | authenticating | live | reconnecting | failed`, surfaced through `onState`, with nothing rendered here.

**M3.** Blocked by the merge. This is the ticket that catches a misresolved list.

## Why a build passing is not enough

`ALL_KINDS` is a list, and a merge that drops an entry compiles cleanly. The failure appears in production as `restricted: unknown event kind` when Peek or Ship publishes — long after the merge looked fine.

So ask the relay itself, in its own words, rather than reading the source and believing it.

## What to run

`estiva-ship` has a probe built for exactly this: `npm run probe` (`scripts/probe-kinds.ts`). It asks the relay one kind at a time whether it would accept an event, and its header says why it exists:

> Run before and after patching Buzz. Before, every Estiva Ship kind should come back `restricted: unknown event kind`; after, every one should be accepted. The point is to have the relay's own words rather than an assumption about what the allowlist contains.

Point it at a **locally built relay** from the merged branch, not production:

```bash
PROBE_SECRET_KEY=<hex> RELAY_URL=http://localhost:3000 npx tsx scripts/probe-kinds.ts
```

## Traps

- **A closed relay needs the probe key admitted.** If the local relay runs with `BUZZ_REQUIRE_RELAY_MEMBERSHIP=true`, a key invented at runtime can never be a member. Admit it with `buzz-admin add-member <pubkey>` and remove it afterwards — a standing member that exists only to run tests is its own problem.
- **`/query` requires NIP-98 auth**, so a bare curl returns 401 and is indistinguishable from a refused kind. Use the probe; do not hand-roll.
- The probe publishes into a throwaway Folder it creates. Safe to repeat, but point it at localhost — running it against production writes to production.
- Extend the probe if it does not already cover all eleven of our kinds. It predates some of them.

## Done when

Every Estiva kind is accepted by the locally built relay, with the relay's own response recorded on this issue. Any refusal is a merge defect, not a probe defect — fix the merge.

events.content:
**M2 · the ticket that gives SHA-4 its seam.** The most valuable ticket in this project for the ecosystem, and an upgrade for Ship rather than a port.

## Why this is not a port

Ship's `lib/auth/estiva-id.ts` (358 lines) and Peek's `src/auth/estivaId.ts` are two independent implementations of the same PKCE flow against the same identity service — converged in behaviour, diverged in naming:

| Peek | Ship |
| --- | --- |
| `refreshAccessToken` | `renewAccessToken` |
| `takeReturnTo` | `restoreRoute` |
| `stashShellReason` / `takeShellReason` | **missing** |

**Ship is behind.** It has no shell-reason vocabulary, which means it cannot distinguish the states Peek learned to distinguish the hard way. So: adopt `@estiva/identity` (SHA-4), do not port Ship's file.

## Ship is the second consumer, and that is the point

SHA-4 cannot be extracted safely from Peek alone — a library pulled from one app comes out shaped like that app. The specific risk: `peek-app/src/auth/useEstivaIdAuth.ts` is the `ConvexProviderWithAuth` adapter, and if it ends up in the package, Ship and Leaf inherit a Convex dependency to work around.

**Ship needs no adapter at all.** It hands the token straight to its relay client. If wiring Ship reveals that the package assumes a data layer, that is the finding SHA-4 exists to surface — record it there rather than working around it here.

## What must work

- Sign-in through Estiva ID, with `client_id` `estiva-ship` and a `redirectUri` matching a seeded entry **exactly** (Estiva ID compares exact strings; a trailing slash is a refused sign-in).
- Silent renewal before expiry.
- The auth shell — try to enter on its own, ask only when it genuinely cannot. Ship has its own version today (`scripts/auth-shell.test.ts` exists), so there are already two.
- Sign-out that actually signs out: navigating to `/logout` with `client_id` and `post_logout_redirect_uri`. Clearing the local token is not signing out, because the `estiva_id_session` cookie on the identity origin survives it and the next silent probe puts the person straight back in.
- Signing through `estivaIdSigner`, keeping the `expectedPubkey` guard — `/sign` signs as the token's subject regardless of what it is handed, so a mismatch returns HTTP 200 with an event authored by somebody else.

## Traps

- An empty `ID_BASE` means sign-in is not offered at all. Preserve that: the anonymous-only build is a real mode, not a broken one.
- Do not unify token storage without thinking about lifetime. If CRO-4 lands here too, NIP-RS slots need `localStorage` because they must survive a restart, while the access token does not.
- `scripts/auth-shell.test.ts` covers Ship's current shell. Whatever replaces it must be covered too — deleting a test because the code it tested moved into a package is how a package arrives untested.

## Done when

Ship signs in, renews silently across an expiry, drops to the shell on a failed renewal with an honest reason, and signs out such that a reload does **not** let you straight back in. All four by hand, against production Estiva ID. And `@estiva/identity` carries no Convex import — verify by reading the package's dependencies, not by it happening to work.

`truncate` is a plain-text operation and MUST NOT be applied to a structured field. RFC 0.4 §13.3:

- `subtitle` carries a **plain-text summary**
- `body` carries **structure**

An app whose description is structured owes the consumer a plain-text summary rather than expecting the consumer to flatten markup it does not know the grammar of.

The `body` slot, and the content-format decision — a summary can only be derived automatically once the format is specified. **In the meantime the honest fix is not to declare a `truncate` on a field that carries structure**, which is a one-line manifest change and strictly better than what is rendered today.

## What the ticket set out to answer

1. **Does global discovery fix the unreachable records?** No — 13 before, 13 after, measured twice: by diagnosing each of the 13 before building, and again with a global record live. Twelve have a *deleted* parent, one never had an `a` tag, all thirteen sit in Folders the reader can already see. Filed as SHI-7.
2. **What breaks when a name becomes world-readable?** Nothing mechanically; the exposure is the point and it is narrower than it looked, because an open channel's member roster was already world-readable on the same rule. Two silent things did break and are fixed: `resolveObject` returned `null` for a global record (reported to the person as "you may not have access"), and `loadFolder`/`loadFolders` stop seeing the record, which is correct and now documented.
3. **How does the fold cope with two shapes?** Three fallbacks, not one, because the tags move independently. `h` beats `buzz-channel` when both are present; an empty `description` tag beats leftover `.content`. Conformance passing untouched is the evidence it costs nothing.
4. **How much work, really?** The code was half a day and four files. What cost the time was finding the relay's `h` gate — invisible from the app, and it fails as a `200` — and measuring the 13 rather than believing the ticket about them.

## As a rehearsal for the folder decision (RFC 0.3 §10.1)

Three things that transfer, all in the RFC now:

- **Reader lands first, and separately.** With no migration available the two shapes coexist forever; a folder model inherits that and §4.2's stub/detail pair doubles it.
- **Read the relay's ingest path before estimating.** One line here; it will not be one line for folder command and state kinds.
- **Measure the defect a design change is justified by, before the change.** This one was justified on a bug it does not fix.

Housekeeping: verification wrote three project records and one issue to production across the run. All archived or cancelled — `kind:5` stays refused for this identity, so none could be deleted.

**M1 · blocking prerequisite for M3.** Nothing in the NIP-RS client can be written until this exists.

## Why

NIP-RS requires the read-state blob's `content` to be NIP-44 ciphertext, with the conversation key computed as `nip44_conversation_key(user_privkey, user_pubkey)` — the user encrypting to themselves. That needs the user's **private** key.

Peek holds no keys by design (PEEK-40/41), and Estiva ID exposes `/sign` and nothing else. Enumerating `estiva-id/src/http/routes/` gives: auth, authorize, tokens, refresh, invites, recovery, roles, directory, profile, logout, admin, sign. There is no encryption endpoint of any kind.

## What to build

Two endpoints in `estiva-id/src/http/routes/`, mirroring `sign.ts` in shape — bearer token in, operation performed as the token's subject, no key ever leaving the service:

- `POST /nip44/encrypt` → `{ plaintext }` ⇒ `{ ciphertext }`
- `POST /nip44/decrypt` → `{ ciphertext }` ⇒ `{ plaintext }`

## Scope it to SELF-encryption only — this is the important part

**Do not accept a peer pubkey.** Both endpoints operate on `nip44_conversation_key(own_priv, own_pub)` and nothing else.

The reason is the difference between two very different security postures. A *general* `/decrypt` is a decryption oracle: any app holding a token could read anything ever encrypted to that user. A **self-only** `/decrypt` can read only what the user encrypted to themselves — today, read-state blobs. That is still sensitive (it reveals what you have read and when, which is behavioural data) but it is bounded.

Build the narrow version. Widening later is a deliberate decision with its own review; starting general and narrowing later does not happen in practice.

## Also required

- **Rate limit both endpoints** and emit **audit entries**, from the start. Read positions are behavioural data about a person.
- Follow the existing policy seam: `src/domain/policy.ts` is where `/sign` decides what is permitted. Encryption has no kind to check, but the `app.status !== 'active'` gate and the same refusal vocabulary should apply — a disabled app must not be able to decrypt.
- NIP-44 v2 specifically (ChaCha20 + HMAC-SHA256, padded). Use an audited implementation rather than hand-rolling the padding scheme; `@noble/*` is already in the dependency tree.

## Traps

- `/sign` deliberately ignores any pubkey it is handed and signs as the token's subject. Keep that principle: these endpoints must not accept an identity argument at all, so there is nothing to get wrong.
- Do not log plaintext or ciphertext. Estiva ID's own audit table records *that* an operation happened, not its content.
- NIP-44 is not interchangeable with NIP-04. Do not fall back to NIP-04 for any reason.

## Done when

A Peek browser session can round-trip a string through `/nip44/encrypt` then `/nip44/decrypt` and get it back, an attempt to pass a peer pubkey is refused, a disabled app is refused, and both calls appear in the audit log without their contents.

The done-when asks that `/sign` accept the kind. `/sign` authorises against the **calling credential**, so proving it requires holding `estiva-peek`'s or `estiva-ship`'s client secret — which is a browser session belonging to a person, not something this identity can borrow. The agent's own credential is a different row and is not granted these kinds, so signing with it would prove nothing about either app.

What *is* verified, from the row rather than the seed file:

    estiva-peek   {9,7,5,9007,27235,1851,9101,9002,9008,1111,30078,41010,41011,41012}
    estiva-ship   {30850,30851,1851,9,5,9007,31989,27235,1111,30078}

And the mechanism behind the done-when is no longer in doubt in general: the same ceiling was exercised end to end for `kind:1111` on `claude-agent` this session — refused before the grant, accepted after, with `5` and `31990` held as controls to show the grant was exact. There is no reason to expect these kinds to behave differently; there is simply nobody to sign as.

**Left `in_progress` rather than closed.** It is one browser action away, and the honest state is "granted and unproven from this side" rather than done.

**Through MCP, every Ship listing is 13 issues short — and the field whose job is to warn about that reports the wrong reason for it.**

Measured this morning, same identity, same relay, minutes apart:

| read path | coverage |
| --- | --- |
| `mcp__estiva__ship_list_issues` | `reachable 95, unreachable 13, total 108`, plus the note *"Do not describe this list as complete"* |
| `ship issues` from a worktree at `origin/main` | `reachable 108, unreachable 0, total 108` |

`estiva_ping` rules out the boring explanations: the server signs as `b38fd268…` from `/home/miky/.estiva-agent.env` and reads `https://estiva.estiva.app` — the same credential, identity and relay the CLI used.

## The cause is which code is running

`scripts/mcp-server.sh` does `cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."` and then `exec node node_modules/tsx/dist/cli.mjs scripts/mcp-server.ts`, so a session gets whatever is checked out in `~/estiva-agent` at the moment its server starts. That checkout has been parked on `peek-161-claude-code-plugin` (`3f8cbbb`) since 2026-08-24 22:47. The three server processes alive right now started 2026-08-28 at 01:34, 07:20 and 10:02 — all three from that revision, six commits behind `origin/main`.

`loadAll` lives in `src/store.ts`, one of the six files that differ. On `3f8cbbb` discovery is `relay.query([{ kinds: [KIND.PROJECT], limit }])` and widens into project Folders only; on `origin/main` it asks for `{ kinds: [KIND.ISSUE] }` in the same round trip and widens into each issue's own Folder. That is SHI-7, and it is not in the running server.

**It is not a stale data cache**, which is worth stating because it is the first guess: the same server returned SHA-7 within seconds of it being filed. Only the code is old.

## Why this is worse than a stale CLI

`CLAUDE.md` can tell a person to read from a worktree at `origin/main`. Nothing can tell an agent, because the answer carries no revision — `estiva_ping.runtime` reports platform, WSL, node, entry path and client, and no commit.

And the failure is silent and authoritative at once: a list that is 13 short, plus a note asserting the shortfall is a known limit of the *workspace* rather than of the binary. An agent following the tool description exactly will report the wrong thing confidently, which is the failure mode `coverage` exists to prevent.

## Two changes, independently worth having

1. **Report the revision in the answer.** `estiva_ping.runtime` gains the git revision and a dirty flag for the tree it is running from. This is the one that turns any future instance of this into a one-call diagnosis instead of an afternoon.
2. **Stop launching from a mutable working tree.** AGE-1 covers the committed `plugin/server/index.js` bundle going stale through a merge; this is the other half — the `mcp-server.sh` entry runs whatever branch a peer left checked out, and the shared checkout is routinely on somebody's branch. A pinned worktree, a built artifact, or the plugin path AGE-1 is fixing would each do it. **Not an implementer's choice to make silently:** it decides whether a local edit to the agent is testable by restarting a session, which is the reason the current shape exists.

## Done when

A freshly started session's `ship_list_issues` reports `unreachable: 0` for the workspace as it stands, and the revision that produced that answer is readable from the answer itself.

**Keep the negative control.** The number must still rise above zero for an issue genuinely sitting in a Folder this reader cannot see — the field is not being removed, it is being made trustworthy. Verify by reading a listing, not by reading the diff.

It reads back by `#a` and by `#h`, and Ship's merged fold attaches it to the right issue through the uppercase `A`. Every reader was in place before the first one was written, which is the payoff of doing them in that order.

## What is left is one commit in Ship

1. `buildConversationMessage` emits `kind:1111`: uppercase `A`/`K`/`P` for the thread root, lowercase for the parent, **`h` always present**. The relay accepts a global `1111` perfectly happily — measured — so a missing `h` is world-readable however private the issue. Test it rather than comment it.
2. `src/manifest.ts` → `emits: { kind: 1111, scope: "address", alsoRead: [9] }`. **Both parts, same commit.** Peek publishes under `kind` and reads the union, so omitting `alsoRead` silently undoes PEE-10, and flipping the manifest in a different commit from the writer makes Peek publish a kind Ship is not yet writing.
3. Nothing else. Ship's reader, the agent's reader and both Peek surfaces are already merged.

Worth keeping in view while doing it: Ship's manifest does not describe Ship, it instructs Peek. That is why 1 and 2 are one commit and not two.

Found while surveying CAT-1/2/3 on 2026-08-27. **This is not a merge risk.** Both halves are already on `nfb-demo-kinds` at the upstream merge-base, so the defect is live on the branch today and the catch-up neither causes nor fixes it.

## The contradiction

`6e5db342a` (#6) replaced the hard-coded `MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS = 900` in `crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs` with a configurable `BUZZ_MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS`, so an operator can widen the ingest window for a history import. Its own commit message gives the reason: Peek is migrating four months of real messages off an old Convex deployment, and restamping them to `now` would corrupt the shared record for every other app reading the relay.

Migration `0021_created_at_fence_floor.sql` enforces a **commit-time** floor instead, `CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS = 960` in `crates/buzz-db/src/replica_fence.rs`, armed by the writer pool on **every** connection via the `after_connect` hook in `crates/buzz-db/src/lib.rs`. It is a `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` constraint trigger, so it fires during COMMIT and re-evaluates `clock_timestamp()` rather than `now()`.

The two do not agree, and nothing reconciles them. `CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS` even documents the assumption it is built on — that the ingest envelope is 900 — which stopped being true when #6 landed.

## What happens

For any event carrying an `h` tag, which is every Issue, Change, comment and message, `channel_id` is NOT NULL and the guard applies. So with the window widened:

1. Ingest accepts the event. The client is told `accepted: true`.
2. The insert succeeds.
3. The transaction **aborts at COMMIT** with `check_violation`, because `created_at` is more than 960 s before commit time.

The usable range for channel-scoped events is therefore `900 < x <= 960`, not whatever is configured. The knob still works for global kinds — `channel_id IS NULL` is the one structural exemption, which covers profile and discovery snapshots — so it is not inert, just unusable for the case it was written for.

Migration 0021 states the intent plainly: there is *deliberately NO in-band bypass* for channel-bearing rows, and any operational backfill of them must run on a connection outside the relay writer pool, with the replica breaker held closed from before the transaction begins until its WAL is replayed. That is a real procedure, and it is not what #6 built.

## Verified against production, 2026-08-27

Read-only, nothing written:

- The guard is fully installed and enabled: `events_created_at_floor` exists on **9 relations** — the `events` parent plus all 8 partitions. The enforcement half is live.
- `BUZZ_MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS` is **not set** on the box and not in the relay container env, so the window is the default 900 and sits inside the 960 floor. **There is no live impact right now.** The defect bites the next time somebody sets the knob for an import and believes the `accepted: true` they get back.

**Not verified:** the accept-then-abort sequence itself. Proving it needs a real signed event with an old `created_at` published through the writer pool, and that is a write to production. It belongs on a throwaway — see CAT-6, which is already standing up a production-shaped database.

## Why this is worth an issue rather than a comment

It is the exact failure shape this ecosystem keeps producing: every local signal agrees, the client is told the write succeeded, and the row never lands. A future operator reaching for this knob during a migration has no reason to suspect the relay will take the event and then drop the transaction, and the 200-with-`accepted` idiom means nothing obvious surfaces.

## Done when

Either the floor is derived from the configured ingest window rather than a hard-coded 960 — which is the change that makes the knob mean what it says, and needs the replica-fence proof re-examined because the fence subtracts the same constant — **or** the knob is documented as global-kinds-only and the channel-scoped history import gets the outside-the-pool, breaker-closed procedure written down where an operator will find it. Whichever is chosen, one test must publish a channel-scoped event older than the floor and assert the outcome, so the accept-then-abort path can never be silently reintroduced.
