**Audit done 2026-08-27, read-only. Three of the four lists are complete; list 4 needs production and I could not reach the box from this session — see the end. Not marking this done.**

**Plain answer: deploying upstream today would not break or silently change production data. The one thing it could do is BLOCK, and the blocker is migration 0032, on a lock rather than on data.**

**1. The list.** Fork ships 24 migrations (`0001`–`0024`), upstream 32. **Eight new: `0025`–`0032`.** Purely additive — 841 insertions, **zero deletions, and all 24 existing files byte-identical**. That last point matters more than the eight: sqlx keys `_sqlx_migrations` on a checksum, so a *modified* old migration would refuse the whole run with `VersionMismatch` before applying anything. **That failure mode is ruled out.** The fork adds no migrations of its own, so there is no numbering collision and nothing of ours to preserve — the direction is one-way.

| | what | risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0025 | `relay_invites` table | new table, none |
| 0026 | `replica_heartbeat`, single row | none |
| 0027 | index on `channels`, no `CONCURRENTLY` | ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on `channels`; duration ∝ channel count |
| 0028 | `reactions.emoji` → `VARCHAR(66)` | varchar *widening* is catalog-only, no rewrite |
| 0029 | community deletion: +3 cols on `communities`, many new tables/triggers | `NOT NULL DEFAULT` with a constant → no rewrite on PG11+; touches nothing on `events` |
| 0030 | drop/add constraints on `community_deletion_requests` | table created empty in 0029, so CHECK validation passes trivially |
| 0031 | `+workflow_runs.error_code` (nullable) **+ a backfill UPDATE** | duration ∝ `workflow_runs` rows |
| 0032 | **`BEFORE INSERT ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger on the partitioned `events` table** | **the real one — see below** |

**2. The refusers.** The important finding: **the refusal risk is not mainly in the migrations.** `run_migrations` wraps `MIGRATOR.run` in an exclusive advisory lock and three fail-closed gates, and migrations run **automatically at relay startup** — so a refusal is a relay that never becomes ready, not a crash-loop.

- `reject_legacy_nip_rs_cardinality_ambiguity` — the one this ticket quotes. **Inert for us.** It early-returns when `max(version) >= 7`; we are at 24. It cannot fire regardless of what `kind:30078` rows exist, so CRO-2 landing does *not* give this ticket's answer a shelf life. That premise in the description is wrong.
- `verify_floor_guard_catalog` — requires migration 0021's trigger on `events` **and every partition**. **Already on the fork and already passing in production**, since the running relay calls it at startup (`buzz-db/src/lib.rs:453`). So production's partition topology already satisfies a parent-created trigger cloned across all partitions — a useful positive.
- `verify_channel_roster_fence_catalog` — **new with the merge.** Same shape, for 0032's trigger, across `public.events` and every partition, requiring it enabled and exact-shaped. Materially de-risked by the line above, because the same topology assumption is already proven for the floor guard.

**3. The irreversibles: none.** Nothing drops or rewrites a column. 0028 widens a varchar (no rewrite); 0030 drops *constraints* on a table that 0029 created empty. A backup before CAT-6 is still worth taking, but no migration here forces it.

**Why 0032 is the one to plan around.** It installs a row-level `BEFORE INSERT` trigger on `events` — the monthly range-partitioned table holding everything — and it is the **only one of the four DDL migrations with no `lock_timeout`** (0029, 0030 and 0031 each `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 5s`). So it waits indefinitely for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on `events` and, while waiting, queues every insert behind it. On a live relay that is the classic Postgres migration stall. Mitigation is operational, not a code change: quiesce writes, or add a local `lock_timeout` and retry.

It also adds a **new runtime rejection path**: a `kind:39002` roster whose `p` tags do not exactly match `channel_members` now raises `23514`. Note our `buzz-admin` has a command that emits `39000`/`39002` "for channels missing them" (`buzz-admin/src/main.rs:568`) — post-merge those snapshots must match canonical membership exactly or the insert is refused.

**4. Row counts that matter — OUTSTANDING.** SSH to the box is blocked from this session, so I did not read production and am not guessing. Three reads decide the remaining risk, all read-only:

```
select max(version) from _sqlx_migrations where success;
select count(*) from channels;                 -- 0027 index build
select count(*) from workflow_runs;            -- 0031 backfill UPDATE
select count(*) from pg_inherits where inhparent = public.events::regclass;  -- 0032 trigger fan-out
```

Expectation, to be falsified rather than assumed: version 24, channels in the low hundreds, `workflow_runs` **empty** (Estiva ships no workflows), and one partition per month of operation. If that holds, 0025–0031 are all sub-second and the entire decision reduces to scheduling 0032's lock.

**Separate finding, not a migration risk — a live defect on `nfb-demo-kinds` today.** `BUZZ_MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS` (#6) widens the *ingest* window, but migration 0021 enforces a **commit-time** floor of `CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS = 960`, armed by the writer pool on every connection. Both are already on the branch at the merge-base, so the merge does not cause this. For any event carrying an `h` tag (→ `channel_id NOT NULL`), widening past 960s means **accepted at ingest, then the transaction aborts at COMMIT**. Usable range is effectively `900 < x <= 960`; Peek's four-month Convex import — the stated reason the knob exists — cannot work through the relay. 0021's own comment says there is "deliberately NO in-band bypass" and that such backfills must run outside the writer pool with the replica breaker closed. Code read across four files, **not live-verified.** Filing separately if you agree.

https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/87

Correction to the premise: Peek already had path routing, `/topics/:id`, and the nginx index.html fallback. What was missing is that the id in the URL was a Convex `seedKey` — Peek-private. Canonical URL is now §7's `/topic/<slug>-<channel-uuid>`; legacy links upgrade in place.

Verified on production: a deep `/topic/…` path returns 200 (404 on a missing asset as the negative control), and all 40 topics have a v4 uuid folder. Manifest `urls`/`web` (§7.5) deliberately left out — that file is PRO's right now.

`estiva-app/buzz` is **625 commits behind `block/buzz`** and 4 ahead (measured 2026-08-24). The gap grows weekly, and the four commits we carry are all narrow kind-registry additions — so the fork is nearly pure upstream with a thin seam, which is the best possible position to catch up from and the worst one to let rot.

## Why now, and why not all of it now

The survey is cheap and informative and should happen soon. **The merge and deploy are neither, and should wait for a reason.**

That reason will come — the RFC 0.3 folder decision wants to know what shape upstream's forge layer settles into, and there is real value sitting in those 625 commits (NIP-MP projects, NIP-34 git statuses `1630`–`1633`, the NIP-FI federated-identity family, presence snapshots). But deploying 625 commits of relay change against the database that Peek and Ship both depend on is not something to do because the number is annoying.

So: **M1 immediately, M2 onward on a trigger.** Doing the survey first is also what makes the trigger legible — right now nobody can say what catching up would cost.

## What we carry

Four commits on `nfb-demo-kinds`, all additions to the kind registry and its scope mapping:

```
d207a1148  accept Linear-lite Projects, Issues and Changes (30850/30851/1851)
ffeb41606  accept NIP-22 comments and NIP-89 handlers (1111, 31989/31990)
70f75609b  accept NIP-FC Files and Components (30840/30841)
e8b0dab5b  accept NIP-84 highlights (kind:9802)
```

They touch `crates/buzz-core/src/kind.rs` (constants and `ALL_KINDS`) and `crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs` (`required_scope_for_kind`). Both files have been edited heavily upstream across 625 commits, so **that is where the conflicts will be** — and they are conflicts in a list, which resolve easily and misresolve invisibly.

Verified 2026-08-24: none of `30850`, `30851`, `1851`, `9101`, `30840`, `30841`, `9802` is claimed upstream. **Re-verify at merge time** — upstream allocates numbers continuously, and NIP-MP's own allocation note says both external kind registries are advisory rather than authoritative.

## The traps, in the order they will bite

**1. `main` and `nfb-demo-kinds` have diverged by a Revert.** `main` carries a revert that `nfb-demo-kinds` does not. Branching from `main` and rebasing **silently proposes deleting the members API and the relay-image workflow.** Merge into `nfb-demo-kinds`; do not route through `main`.

**2. `nfb-demo-kinds` is not rustfmt-clean.** Running `cargo fmt` reflows unrelated comments, burying the real diff in noise. Do not format as part of this.

**3. The relay image is built from `nfb-demo-kinds`, not `main`.** `relay-image.yml` produces `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb`. That workflow is ours — a careless merge is exactly what trap 1 proposes deleting.

**4. Only one workflow is enabled.** The other twelve upstream workflows are `DISABLED_MANUALLY` to save minutes. That is a **repo setting**, not a file, so a merge does not re-enable them — but confirm afterwards rather than assuming, because 625 commits may have added new ones that arrive enabled.

**5. Database migrations are the real risk.** 625 commits include schema migrations that run against the production Postgres on startup. At least one is known to *refuse* rather than migrate — `buzz-db/src/migration.rs` blocks the NIP-RS pre-0007 path if existing `kind:30078` rows have ambiguous `d`/`t` tag cardinality. Assume there are others. **This is the part that needs a throwaway relay, and there is no staging.**

**6. The relay has no update timer.** Every other service has one; Buzz does not. Deploy by hand, and pull only the relay:

```bash
cd /opt/buzz && docker compose pull relay && ./run.sh restart
```

`run.sh pull` also pulls postgres, redis and minio.

**7. Verify by image id, never by health.** A healthy relay serving a stale image is precisely the state this project can produce. Compare the running image id to `:nfb`.

## Blast radius

The relay is the only shared dependency in the ecosystem. Peek and Ship both read and write it; Estiva ID signs for it; the agent CLI and the MCP server read through it. A bad relay deploy takes down everything at once, and there is no staging workspace to rehearse against.

That is not an argument against doing this. It is an argument for M3 and M4 being real work rather than a formality.

## Milestones

- **M1 · Survey (do this soon).** What is in the 625 commits that matters; which of our four conflict and how badly; which migrations would run and whether any would refuse; whether any upstream kind now collides with ours. Output is a written answer and a cost estimate, no merge.
- **M2 · Merge into `nfb-demo-kinds`.** Resolve conflicts, keep all four of our commits' behaviour, do not reformat, do not lose the relay-image workflow. `cargo build` and the test suite green.
- **M3 · Prove the kinds still work.** `npm run probe` from estiva-ship against a locally-built relay — every Estiva kind accepted, with the relay's own words rather than an assumption.
- **M4 · Prove the migrations on a throwaway.** A relay instance with a copy-shaped database, not the production one. This is the milestone that exists because there is no staging.
- **M5 · Deploy and verify.** Build `:nfb`, pull on the box, restart, compare image ids, then exercise Peek and Ship against it — a read and a write each.

## Out of scope

- **Merging to `main`.** `main` is not what builds the image. Leave the Revert divergence alone unless a separate ticket says otherwise.
- **Adopting anything new from upstream** — NIP-MP, git statuses, NIP-FI. Catching up makes them *available*; using them is a decision per feature, and NIP-MP specifically is entangled with RFC 0.3's deferred question.
- **Contributing anything upstream.** Separate, and deferred — see RFC 0.3 §10.1.

## Notes

- `upstream` is already configured with **push disabled**, which is the right guard. Keep it.
- Rebasing our four onto upstream is the alternative to merging. Rebase gives a cleaner history and replays each conflict separately; merge is one resolution and preserves what actually happened. With four commits either is defensible — decide in M1 and record why.

**A reading session and a decision, like SHA-10 — and a cheaper one.**

[RFC 0.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/RFC-0.5-ASSOCIATION.md) specifies how files in different apps relate. It exists because RFC 0.4 lets a Folder hold several files of one kind, so **the container can no longer be the relationship** — a project's conversation used to *be* a topic because they shared one channel.

## What accepting settles

- **Three tiers** — none, basic (one file names another, shown in a panel, shared not personal), facet (files are perspectives on one thing and their conversations merge).
- **Facets merge, and never copy.** One comment, two views, ordered by time, origin unlabelled.
- **Declaration is one-sided, effect two-sided** — forced, because a `kind:39000` topic is relay-signed and Peek can never tag it.
- **The access-compatibility invariant** — a facet may not merge conversations that are not equally readable.
- **The two change cases**: removing a facet splits the thread *list* and never a thread; deleting an object never deletes its comments.

## Why it is cheaper than 0.4's acceptance

**No new kind and no Buzz change.** A facet is a tag on a file record, signed by that file's author — so authorization falls out of who holds the key rather than needing a permission model. The expensive relay-maintained version stays available for when the trigger fires.

## What it does not settle

Deliberately deferred with triggers in §8: who may create a facet beyond "you can sign the file", relay enforcement of the invariant (a read rule does it today), and whether a merged view labels which facet a comment was written against.

## The one thing worth arguing about

**§4, the invariant.** It is the only clause that forbids something people will want — faceting a private discussion onto a public object. The argument for it is that the failure is not disclosure (the relay still gates content) but **context collapse for the one person who can see both sides**, who then answers privately in what looks like a public place. If that argument does not hold, the invariant should go rather than be quietly ignored.

## Done when

Accepted or amended, and if amended, what changed and why is on this issue. Association and facet tickets get filed only after that — per rule 2, nothing is filed against the undecided parts.

---

## §7 Addressing was added 2026-08-31, and it is part of this decision

RFC 0.5 gained a section on **what a link looks like**, because the question
turned out to be protocol rather than per-app taste: *people copy the address
bar*, so the URL an app puts there has to be resolvable by a different app. That
is wire-visible under SPEC §10's test — two apps can disagree and a user sees it.

**The grammar:**

```
https://<app>.estiva.app/<type>s                  a directory of that kind
https://<app>.estiva.app/<type>/<slug>-<d>        one object
```

- the **`d` is the whole identity, untruncated** — a consumer resolves
  `{kinds:[<type>], "#d":["<uuid>"]}`, one query, no index and no service that
  can go down and take every link with it
- the **kind comes from the path segment**, so `/project/` means 30850
- the **slug is decorative** — renaming changes it and the link still resolves

**Two findings behind it, both measured rather than assumed.**

*An naddr cannot be the suffix.* It is bech32 over `(kind, pubkey, d, relay
hints)` **plus a checksum over the whole string**, so a slice of it is checksum
bytes rather than the `d` and resolves to nothing without an index. It is also
not stable for one object — relay hints are part of the encoding, and both forms
are live today: Ship's `referenceFor` passes a hint, the runtime's `buildObject`
passes none.

*The pubkey does not need to be in the URL.* `d` is a v4 uuid (0.4 §4.3), so
`(kind, d)` is unique. Measured on production: 235 records across 30850/30851/
39000, **zero** non-uuid `d`, **zero** `(kind, d)` shared by more than one
author. This gives §4.3's existing MUST a second and quieter reason — an app
using a readable `d` would not fail loudly, it would collide and resolve to the
wrong object.

**A consumer resolves an app it has never met** by matching a pasted URL against
the patterns every app publishes in its manifest (`urls`, alongside `web`).
`kind:31990` is global, so this needs no per-app integration and no registry.

## What §7 additionally requires

- **Paths, not hashes.** Ship uses hash routing because it is static files with
  `try_files … =404`. Path URLs need an index.html fallback per app.
- **Peek has no object URLs at all** — no routing, no per-topic path. That is
  the prerequisite, and it is filed separately because it does not depend on
  this decision.
- **Messages still have no URL.** A `kind:9` has no `d`, so it has no place in
  the grammar — the same gap §13.6 records for projections, and PRO-11's.

Split out of PRO-2, whose other two slots (list, body) are delivered. Filed rather than left as a comment because it is blocked on something outside this project.

Measured on production 2026-09-02, scanning every tag name on the addressable kinds and on profiles:

kind:39000 Topic     70 events   image-ish tags: 0   (about, closed, d, name, public, t)
kind:30850 Project   15 events   image-ish tags: 0   (buzz-channel, d, description, h, name, title)
kind:30851 Issue    100 events   image-ish tags: 0   (a, d, h, ref, title)
kind:9 / kind:1111  200 events   image-ish tags: 0
kind:0 Profile        7 events   picture: 3

So the only image data in the workspace belongs to a *person*, and that path is already covered without this slot: interop resolves authors into object.people with a picture, and Peek renders an Avatar for any slot declared as: pubkey (ForeignObjectWidget). An image slot would add nothing there.

SPEC §7.2 lists image as 'an avatar, thumbnail or cover, as a URL' for an *object*. Nothing in the ecosystem has one. Declaring it against a person's avatar would be wrong twice: the value is not the object's, and it would duplicate a rendering that already works.

This is the same shape as SPEC §13.3, which is specified ahead of an implementation and says so. The difference is that §13.3 has RIC-5 behind it and this has nobody.

Done when: either an app grows a real image field and declares it — a Topic cover or a File thumbnail are the plausible ones — or SPEC §7.2 records that image is reserved and unproduced, so the next person reading the closed slot set does not assume a consumer is missing something. Whichever, do not implement a consumer for it first: an unproduced slot cannot be verified against anything.

**Publish from a second identity, not a second window.** Track A learned this the expensive way: two windows on one account prove nothing, because both are served by the same Convex deployment and the reply arrives by reactivity alone.

Fixed and proven, not yet merged: estiva-app/buzz#8, branched from nfb-demo-kinds.

THE FIX

Delete the !require_relay_membership guard at both call sites rather than invert it. extract_nip_oa_owner verifies a Schnorr signature over a preimage naming the presenting pubkey and returns None for an absent or invalid tag, so relay membership has no bearing on whether the signature is true. api/mod.rs already says as much, and the ban cascade twenty lines above the auth.rs site already extracts the owner unconditionally for that exact reason. The guard was the anomaly.

PROVEN AGAINST A BUILT BINARY

PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-id/pull/55 — batched with PEE-4 as one Gate 1 deploy. Not done until it is verified against production.

## Built as specced, with two deliberate additions

Both endpoints are self-encryption only, as required. One thing the ticket left open that turned out to matter: the request schemas are **`.strict()`**, so a caller sending `pubkey` or `peer` gets a `400` rather than having it ignored.

The ticket suggested following `/sign`, which "deliberately ignores any pubkey it is handed". That is right for `/sign` — the authoritative answer there is unambiguous, you always want your own signature. It is **wrong here**, and the difference is worth recording: an app that believed it was encrypting to a colleague would receive a blob only the user can open, succeed, publish it, and the mistake would surface as an undecryptable message on the far side days later. Refusing says so at the call. "Nothing to get wrong" is stronger when the wrong thing is rejected rather than silently discarded.

Second: **every decryption failure returns one answer**, `detail.reason: undecryptable`. The underlying `Nip44Error` distinguishes a bad MAC from bad padding and that distinction is kept — in the audit row, not the response. A caller that can tell them apart has a padding oracle. (The MAC is checked before unpadding, so the exposure was narrow, but the response shape should not depend on that ordering staying true.)

## On "use an audited implementation rather than hand-rolling the padding"

Taken seriously, and the resolution is not quite what the ticket assumed. `@noble/*` is in the tree, but @noble provides *primitives* — there is no NIP-44 in it. What exists is ChaCha20 (added `@noble/ciphers`, zero dependencies, no conflict with the `@noble/hashes` 1.x already present), HKDF, HMAC and secp256k1 ECDH.

So the composition is ours, which means the padding scheme is ours, which is the exact thing the ticket warned about. The answer is to be **judged by somebody else's expectations**: the reference vector suite from `paulmillr/nip44` is vendored and all **108 vectors** run, valid and invalid. This is the same pattern `nip-oa.test.ts` already uses against Buzz's Rust vector, and it is stronger than a round-trip test in a specific way — 10 of the vectors supply the nonce and pin **our ciphertext byte-for-byte against theirs**, which is the only way to catch a padding or HKDF divergence that round-trips perfectly against itself and interoperates with nothing.

The invalid half earned its keep immediately. Node's `Buffer.from(s, 'base64')` silently skips characters outside the alphabet, so the "invalid base64" vector decoded to *something* and would have failed later as a misleading MAC error. Strict base64 validation is in because a vector said so, not because it was foreseen.

Two more that would not have been written from prose: `calc_padded_len` uses `31 - Math.clz32(n)` rather than `Math.floor(Math.log2(n))`, because a float log is one ulp from the wrong integer at exact powers of two — the resulting bug would have been a padded length that differs from every other implementation only for certain message sizes. And the 1..65535 bound counts **bytes of UTF-8**, not characters; a naive `plaintext.length` check admits an over-long multi-byte message, which is now a test of its own.

## Rate limiting — sized, and with a limitation worth knowing

120 operations per minute, shared between encrypt and decrypt, keyed on (clientId, pubkey). One budget because the pair is one capability — a decrypt limit that reset whenever encrypt was idle would bound nothing.

**It is a per-process counter.** Estiva ID runs as one container on one box, so that is a per-deployment limit today. It is not that under two replicas: each would keep its own window and the effective limit would be N×. Anything that scales this service out has to move the counter to Postgres or Redis first, and `src/http/rate-limit.ts` says so where somebody will find it.

## Audit

`nip44.{encrypt,decrypt}.{granted,refused}` rows. Neither plaintext nor ciphertext is recorded — **and neither is their length**, which was a judgement call: a length is not content, but it is a hint about a read-state blob, and the ticket's bar is "that an operation happened".

The test asserts this by dumping the **whole `audit_events` table as text** and searching it, not just the `detail` column — a length or a prefix leaking through some other field would pass a narrower check.

## What is proven, and what is not

530 tests pass across the repo, 21 of them new here — including one that encrypts a blob **outside the service** under `conversation_key(own_priv, own_pub)` and decrypts it through the endpoint. That is the strongest available statement of "self-encryption": it is the key NIP-RS specifies, not merely one that is internally consistent.

Verified against production before merging, as the deploy's negative control: `POST /nip44/encrypt` currently returns **404 No route**.

**The done-when says "a Peek browser session".** That specific path stays unproven — no Peek session is mintable from here. What *will* be run against production after the deploy is a full `/nip44/encrypt` → `/nip44/decrypt` round trip using the `claude-agent` service credential, which exercises the identical server path end to end. The browser half is CORS, which in-process tests cannot check at all (`http/cors.ts` says so) and CRO-4 will be the first thing to actually exercise.

**Merged: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/63 → `180651f`. Done-when met live.**

Two channels, two REQs, one socket, from a signed-in browser — and the events were the two comments posted onto this ticket and onto CRO-4, so no synthetic data was involved:

```
subscribed — chanA, chanB, and BOTH-control (multi-#h)
CLOSED BOTH-control  restricted: p-gated events require #p matching your pubkey
15:36:48  EVENT on chanA  kind 1111
15:36:51  EVENT on chanB  kind 1111
```

Both channels received simultaneously. The multi-`#h` control did not. That is the case this ticket exists to prevent, demonstrated rather than cited.

## The trap fails two ways, and this ticket describes only one

**The control was refused outright**, not silently starved. That is a correction to the ticket's premise and it is worth having exactly right, because the two arms behave oppositely.

`p_gated_filters_authorized` (`handlers/req.rs`) gates every subscription that resolves to `channel_id: None`. Its first test:

```rust
let can_match_p_gated = filter.kinds.as_ref().is_none_or(|ks| …);
if !can_match_p_gated { return true; }
```

| multi-`#h` filter | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| **kindless** — `{"#h":[a,b]}` | `is_none_or` → could match a p-gated kind → no `#p` → **CLOSED, loudly** |
| **kinded, ordinary** — `{"#h":[a,b],"kinds":[9]}` | returns early as authorized → registers globally → **silently receives nothing** |

Our control was kindless, so it hit the loud arm. **The silent arm is still real, and it is the more likely one to be written** — somebody optimising "one subscription for messages across all my channels" writes `kinds:[9]`, passes the gate, gets correct history and no live events. So the ticket's warning stands; the loud gate is simply a newer layer in front of the failure it describes, not a replacement for it.

I have corrected the same overstatement in my own PR: I had called the non-uuid key an "identical silent death". Since this module always builds a kindless filter, a bad key lands on the loud arm. It is still a subscription that never delivers, and still an asynchronous `CLOSED` the app has to interpret, so the throw at the call site still earns its place — but "silent" was wrong.

## Two things confirmed as a side effect

**The kindless filter picks up kinds nobody enumerated.** The events that arrived were **kind:1111**, not kind:9 — Ship comments moved to NIP-22 with REW-10. Nothing in this manager mentions 1111, and it delivered anyway, which is the wildcard-index behaviour working as read.

**A Ship folder uuid is the channel uuid** — `fold.ts` maps `folder: tag(event, 'h')`. That is what made a zero-pollution live test possible, and it is worth knowing for PEE-7.

## For PEE-7 and PEE-8

The manager is keyed on channel uuid and refuses anything else, per the RFC 0.3 note. Reconnection is delegated to `liveRelay` rather than reimplemented. What has still never happened is either module running **inside the app** — PEE-8 remains where that gets observed, and the StrictMode double-mount caution from PEE-5 still applies.

Everything this ticket changes lives in `src/events.ts` (`buildProject`), `src/store.ts` (`createProject`, `loadAll`) and `src/fold.ts` — the shared code REW-1 explicitly says **not** to move, because `estiva-agent` vendors it at identical paths. **1. It fixes a live defect.** 13 of 65 production issues are unreachable because discovery runs through access-gated project records. That is not waiting for a rewrite to be worth fixing, and every read the agent does reports it in the `coverage` block.

**2. It is a rehearsal for the folder decision, which is the decision blocking the most.**

- does global discovery actually fix the unreachable-record problem, or does something else cause it?
- what breaks when a record's name becomes world-readable?

## Closing, and what it cost

Four production records rendered untitled in Peek, one of them real. The cause was REW-11 renaming a tag and not the projection that reads it, and it survived because the tool that checks exactly this had been broken by the same change — one bug hiding the other's damage.

Two smaller things fell out and are fixed with it: the manifest's "open in Ship" links pointed at `localhost:5190` on two republishes (a green line printed the wrong value and I read past it twice), and `publish-manifest.ts` had been leaving a real project on production every run since long before today — four had accumulated, all now deleted, and it cleans up after itself.

The general lesson, which is going into the docs rather than only here: REW-11 verified the record shape, the fold and the relay's acceptance, and never verified **the other app's rendering** — the one thing the change existed to serve.

**A reading session and a decision, like SHA-10 — and a cheaper one.**

[RFC 0.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/RFC-0.5-ASSOCIATION.md) specifies how files in different apps relate. It exists because RFC 0.4 lets a Folder hold several files of one kind, so **the container can no longer be the relationship** — a project's conversation used to *be* a topic because they shared one channel.

## What accepting settles

- **Three tiers** — none, basic (one file names another, shown in a panel, shared not personal), facet (files are perspectives on one thing and their conversations merge).
- **Facets merge, and never copy.** One comment, two views, ordered by time, origin unlabelled.
- **Declaration is one-sided, effect two-sided** — forced, because a `kind:39000` topic is relay-signed and Peek can never tag it.
- **The access-compatibility invariant** — a facet may not merge conversations that are not equally readable.
- **The two change cases**: removing a facet splits the thread *list* and never a thread; deleting an object never deletes its comments.

## Why it is cheaper than 0.4's acceptance

**No new kind and no Buzz change.** A facet is a tag on a file record, signed by that file's author — so authorization falls out of who holds the key rather than needing a permission model. The expensive relay-maintained version stays available for when the trigger fires.

## What it does not settle

Deliberately deferred with triggers in §7: who may create a facet beyond "you can sign the file", relay enforcement of the invariant (a read rule does it today), and whether a merged view labels which facet a comment was written against.

## The one thing worth arguing about

**§4, the invariant.** It is the only clause that forbids something people will want — faceting a private discussion onto a public object. The argument for it is that the failure is not disclosure (the relay still gates content) but **context collapse for the one person who can see both sides**, who then answers privately in what looks like a public place. If that argument does not hold, the invariant should go rather than be quietly ignored.

## Done when

Accepted or amended, and if amended, what changed and why is on this issue. Association and facet tickets get filed only after that — per rule 2, nothing is filed against the undecided parts.

## The distinction that shaped the change

Not every `limit` literal was the bug. Two categories, and conflating them would have broken things:

**Page sizes standing in for "everything"** — 9 in the agent, 1 in Ship. All moved to `queryAll`: channels, messages in a folder, all messages for per-folder counts, **issues (the `loadAll`)**, folders, manifest records, changes, profiles, and Ship's discovery check.

And `cli.ts`'s connectivity probe reads whatever one request gives, which is the point of a probe.

**`src/store.ts` needed no change** — its limits are all `limit: 1`. That is fortunate: it is the copy vendored at identical paths in both repos, so not touching it keeps them byte-identical and avoids the cross-repo drift `conformance.test.ts` exists to catch.

## One site that was neither

`peek read --limit` is **user-supplied**, default 200. Above the relay's ceiling it was silently clamped, so someone asking `--limit 5000` got 1000 and was told nothing — the same failure reaching a person directly. It now pages and trims above the ceiling and stays a single request below it.

Creating the issue elsewhere solves the typing and not the knowing. The thread has to end up carrying the thing that was created.

## What it does

After a successful publish, post a message into the conversation carrying a reference to the new object. It renders through the object's own projection — so a Ship issue looks like a Ship issue, drawn in Peek's design language, live rather than a screenshot.

The end state is already designed: Katerina's Storybook covers *"a reply carrying the new issue as a reference widget."*

## Why it is its own ticket

The publish and the trace are separable, and the trace is the half that changes behaviour. A version that creates the issue and says nothing in the thread is worse than useless — it is the current context switch with an extra step.

## Watch

The widget has to survive everything a foreign object can do: the person reading it may not have access, it may be deleted later, it may be a kind this build of Peek does not know. Those states are already specified — see the design guide's *Something from another app, inside yours*.

Creating an issue from a thread leaves a message in that thread which renders the issue live, and a person who cannot read the issue sees the absence honestly rather than a blank card.

**Follow-up: the signing half is now proven from a browser, and the scope with it.**

This closed on the row. It no longer has to. From devtools on a signed-in `https://peek.estiva.app`, cross-origin to the live `https://id.estiva.app`:

```
22242  relay=wss://estiva.estiva.app   200  signed
22242  relay=wss://evil.test           422  {"reason":"relay_auth_relay_not_allowed"}
```

**The second line is the ticket's actual subject.** The grant was never the risky part — the scope was, and this is it refusing a relay Peek has no business authenticating to, with the real credential, from the real origin. That is the widening the ticket existed to prevent, demonstrated rather than argued. Both bounds are in play: the deployment's `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` and the row's `relay_auth_urls`, ANDed.

It also settles a question in-process tests cannot touch. The 422 body was **readable by the browser**, so the refusal arrives as `policy_violation / relay_auth_relay_not_allowed` rather than a generic network error. That is PEEK-93's failure mode checked from the far side, and it matters for PEE-5: when a challenge is refused, the reason will be legible in the console instead of looking like a dropped connection.

## What is left, now much narrower

Still unproven, and still PEE-5's to observe: **that the relay accepts one.** The challenge above was fabricated by hand, not issued by a socket, so nothing has yet round-tripped a real AUTH. The remaining unknowns are on the relay's side of the wire, not Estiva ID's:

- the relay accepting the challenge response it issued
- a REQ on that connection returning events rather than `auth-required`

If either fails, it is now almost certainly **not** this ticket — the ceiling, the scope, the deployment bound and browser signing are all confirmed against production. Look at the challenge round trip and the socket, and note that the relay wants `--http1.1` on the upgrade or it answers with NIP-11 JSON instead.

Checked how Peek does it when a human edits, since that should be the model. It is not a Nostr mechanism at all.

convex/messages.ts editBody is a ctx.db.patch on Peek's own row. Nothing is published. The action beside it, deleteMessage, does publish — publishDeletions sends one kind:5 per target. Peek publishes messages, replies, reactions, resolutions and deletions outward; edits are the one thing it keeps local.

Two consequences. The agent cannot copy Peek's approach: it has no Convex, only the relay, so there is no convention to follow because none exists on the wire. And more importantly this is not only an agent problem — when a human edits in Peek, the relay keeps the original body, so Ship's conversation view and every other reader show the old text indefinitely with nothing announcing the divergence.

So this ticket cannot be satisfied in a way anybody else would see. The decision is upstream of the agent: either Peek publishes edits as a convention that keeps the event id and readers honour it, or edits stay Peek-local and the agent's version is honestly out of reach. Worth deciding there first.

Note Peek's buildDeletion takes targetEventId and emits an e tag — the same shape measured working here yesterday.

events.content:
**M2.** Depends on the DM channel existing. This is the smallest task in the project, and that is the point.

## Why it is small

A DM message is an ordinary `kind:9` against the DM channel's `h`. That is the same event Peek already publishes for topic messages. The existing `unsignedMessage` query in `convex/nostr/outbox.ts` refuses it only because of one guard:

```ts
// Only topic messages publish: DMs need NIP-17 gift wrap and huddles have no Buzz container.
if (m.parentKind !== 'topic') return { ok: false, reason: 'not a topic message' }
```

That comment describes NIP-17, which this project decided against. With DM channels the refusal no longer applies to DMs — only to huddles.

## What to change

Widen `unsignedMessage` (and `unsignedReply`) to accept `parentKind === 'dm'`, resolving the channel uuid from the `dmConversations` row instead of the `topics` row. Keep the huddle refusal, and **update that comment** — leaving it in place would tell the next reader that DMs need gift wrap, which is now false and is exactly the kind of stale comment that sends someone down a three-day path.

Everything else in the function already applies unchanged and should be kept: the idempotency check (`if (m.nostrEventId) return ... 'already published'`), the author check, the drift-window check, and the "channel must exist" check.

## Traps

- **Keep the drift-window check.** The relay rejects `created_at` outside roughly ±15 minutes of its own clock. The existing code checks this *before* signing so an old row costs nothing and the reason is legible rather than arriving as a generic relay rejection.
- **Keep first-publish-wins idempotency.** A row with a `nostrEventId` must never publish twice.
- `unsignedReply` refuses when the parent is unpublished, because Buzz rejects a reply to an event it does not know. That rule is unchanged for DMs.
- Reactions and deletions need no work at all: `buzz-core/src/filter.rs` derives a kind:7 or kind:5's channel from its target at ingest, so they follow the DM channel automatically.

## Done when

A DM sent in Peek appears on the relay as a `kind:9` with the DM channel's `h`, and is readable back by the other participant but not by a third identity. Verify the last part — it is the privacy boundary this whole design rests on.

**Writer half open: ship#33 + estiva-agent#6.** The relay change (CAT-9) is deployed, so the shape is accepted. Staying `in_progress` until both merge — an unmerged PR is not done.

## The done-when, measured against production through the new writer

The claim worth testing is not "the relay accepted it" — that is CAT-9. It is that the record is **global**, not filed under the channel it names. The observable is an `#h` query:

| check | result |
| --- | --- |
| `{kinds:[30850,30851],"#h":[folder]}` returns the issue but **not** the project record | ✅ returned kinds `[30851]` only |
| unscoped `{kinds:[30850]}` returns the record | ✅ |

| `resolveObject` returns it with its Folder | ✅ — this returned `null` before the reader half |
| its issue is attached and still channel-scoped | ✅ |
| the 14 pre-existing `h`/`title` records still fold | ✅ |

So: discoverable without channel scoping, conversation still gated, old records still fold. Three of the four done-when clauses.

Unreachable-issue count with a global record actually live: **13 before, 13 after** (84/13/97 now, 80/13/93 when first measured — the totals moved because the workspace grew, the 13 did not). Twelve have a deleted parent record, one never had an `a` tag, all thirteen sit in Folders the reader can already see. Filed as SHI-7.

`createProject` still bails when `ensureFolder` fails, and the reason narrowed rather than disappeared. The record no longer needs the channel to exist — but every issue, change and message filed into it does. Publishing the record anyway would advertise a container that does not exist, and now it would advertise it **globally**, to everyone, instead of failing in front of the one person who tried. **Planned, not started.** Eleven issues filed in implementation order: DMS-1 → DMS-11.

**Decision recorded: DM channels, not NIP-17 gift wrap.** This is business software, not a second Signal — end-to-end encryption prevents search, retention, offboarding and admin recovery, and the relay operator is the organisation. Three things confirm the platform already assumes this: the relay sends DMs itself for moderation notices (`moderation_notices.rs:102` calls `open_dm`), NIP-IA identity archival exists for offboarding, and NIP-50 search is advertised live — gift-wrapped content is invisible to all three.

**What that decision bought.** Both blocking prerequisites disappeared. `ingest.rs:1498` restricts only gift wrap and presence to WebSocket, so DM commands publish over the HTTP bridge Peek already uses — no dependency on the WebSocket work in *Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates*. And plaintext `kind:9` messages need no encryption, so no dependency on the Estiva ID NIP-44 service either. This project is independent and can run in parallel with *Cross-app read state*.

It also means DMs reuse machinery Peek already has: the relay knows each DM message's `channel_id`, so the existing projection, cursor, reaction and deletion handling and live subscription all work on a DM channel unchanged. DMS-5 should add callers, not a projection.

**Next logical step.** DMS-1 (grant `41010`/`41011`/`41012`, and deliberately *not* `30622` — it is relay-signed) followed immediately by DMS-2, the probe. DMS-2 exists to verify the assumption this project's independence rests on: that `41010` is accepted over HTTP. If it is not, this project needs the WebSocket publish path and the plan changes shape — so run it before anyone starts M2, not after.

**The cost to own.** DMs will be private by membership, not by encryption; the relay stores them in plaintext. DMS-11 makes sure nothing in the UI implies otherwise. DMS-7 is a decision task, not a migration — the relay's ±15 minute drift window means republished history cannot carry its original timestamps, so "migrate the old DMs" is not the free option it looks like.

**Anyone installing the Claude Code plugin today gets an agent that silently misses 13 issues.** `origin/main`'s committed bundle does not match `origin/main`'s source.

## The state

Rebuilding a pristine `origin/main` leaves `plugin/server/index.js` dirty by 198 insertions and 187 deletions. The committed bundle is missing SHI-7's issue-Folder widening, so a plugin install folds discovered issues without their `kind:1851` changes — the exact failure SHI-7 was careful to avoid, shipped by a different route.

A plugin runs **no install step**. There is no `npm ci`, no build, nothing that would notice. What is in the repo is what runs.

## Why CI did not catch it, which is the part worth fixing

`.github/workflows/check.yml` has the right check:

    - name: The committed plugin bundle is current
      run: git diff --exit-code -- plugin/

But it validates **the branch, not the merge result**. The sequence:

1. `plugin/` was added in #8.
2. SHI-7's mirror (#7) was cut from a `main` where `plugin/` did not exist yet, so `git diff -- plugin/` had nothing to diff and the step passed **vacuously**.
3. #8 merged, then #7 merged. Neither PR was ever red, and `main` ended up behind its own source.

This is a property of any generated file kept in the tree, not a one-off: whenever two PRs are open at once and only one of them regenerates, green-when-you-opened is not green-when-you-merge.

## Options

- **Require branches to be up to date with `main` before merge** (a GitHub branch-protection setting). Cheapest, and catches every instance of this shape, not just this file.
- **Run the check on `main` after merge** as well as on PRs, so a stale bundle is at least loud rather than silent.
- **Stop committing the artefact** and build it at package time — biggest change, removes the class entirely, and loses the property that the plugin needs no install.

The first is probably enough and costs a checkbox.

## Immediate

ship#36's companion, estiva-agent#9, rebuilds the bundle and so fixes the current staleness as a side effect. That does not fix the mechanism.

## Done when

`git diff --exit-code -- plugin/` passes when run against `origin/main` itself, and something prevents a stale bundle reaching `main` again rather than relying on whoever opens the next PR to notice.

**M5 · last.** Do this after the topic path is proven end to end. It is the same machinery pointed at more surfaces, and it closes the gap the source ticket hints at without naming.

## Why

**Only topics sync at all today.** The complete set of relay-read call sites in Peek is two:

- `src/components/views/useTopicView.tsx` — one channel, on mount
- `src/auth/AuthGate.tsx` — profiles, once at sign-in

DMs, the inbox, Desk and Screener have **no relay read path whatsoever**. Not a slow one — none. So a Ship-side change that should surface in the inbox has no route in, and no amount of work on the topic path will make it arrive. That is why the source ticket's "status updates and new issues created in Ship can take time to appear" is only half explained by the topic-sync gap: for anything outside an open topic, "take time" means "never, until you open the topic it lives in".

## What to build

Extend the refcounted subscription manager beyond the currently-open topic:

1. Decide the working set. The obvious candidate is the channels behind whatever the inbox and Desk are showing — the topics a viewer has unread state in, not every channel they are a member of.
2. Subscribe to that set, one REQ per channel (see the subscription-manager ticket — a multi-`#h` subscription silently receives no live events).
3. Keep the refcount honest: a channel in the inbox working set *and* open on screen is one subscription with two holders.

## Traps

- **Bound the working set.** `max_subscriptions` is 1024 per connection (production NIP-11), which is not a licence to subscribe to everything — each subscription costs a relay-side index entry and a fan-out check per event. Subscribe to what is being displayed, and say in the code what the bound is and why.
- **Do not put this on a cron.** `convex/crons.ts` documents why background work has no identity that can see anything: reads happen as the signed-in viewer because only they are a member of their own channels. That reasoning is unchanged by any of this work.
- DMs may need a different filter shape than `#h` — check how DM events are addressed before assuming the channel subscription covers them. `filter.rs`'s `#h`→`channel_id` fallback covers kinds that derive their channel from a target; verify rather than assume it covers gift-wrapped DMs.
- Watch for the read-state interaction: syncing a channel nobody is looking at must not mark anything read.

## Done when

A Ship-side change to a topic that is **not** currently open shows up in the inbox unread state without opening that topic and without a reload. Then confirm the subscription count stays bounded as the viewer's topic list grows — take a count against a workspace with more channels than the working-set bound and confirm it holds.

Found by PRO-4, and the half that RFC 0.4 §13.9 deliberately left open.

An issue created from Peek arrives with no display key. That is correct: a ref is the project title plus a count of its siblings, so only Ship can compute one, and Ship's manifest rightly declares add-issue with just a title. §13.9 records the rule that follows — a property the owner derives must live in the change stream, because a NIP-33 address is (kind, pubkey, d) and the owner cannot rewrite a root it did not sign.

What is missing is a way for the manifest to SAY so. A consumer holding the object cannot tell 'you may not set this, the owner will' from 'this is simply absent'. Both render as a blank.

Today that is cosmetic. It stops being cosmetic when an agent fills these forms from context, which is §13.4's second caller and the reason object-creating actions were made renderable at all. Nothing tells it not to invent an issue number, and a made-up PRO-15 is indistinguishable from a real one. That is the driver: a label saying 'this field is mine to fill in' is the difference between an assistant leaving it alone and confidently making one up.

Three shapes, researched:

1. INFER. A field is settable iff some action's input.properties names it. Ship's status and assignee have actions; ref has none, so the inference picks out exactly the right field today. Free, no manifest change. But it cannot tell 'the owner will assign this' from 'nobody can set this and nobody will', and those want opposite renderings — pending versus absent.

2. ON THE SLOT — {tag: 'ref', derived: true}. Sits where a consumer is standing when it needs the answer: a blank slot is the moment you choose between drawing a dash and drawing 'not yet assigned'.

3. ON RECORDS — records.derived: ['ref']. Coherent, since the rule is 'derived fields live in the change stream' and records describes the change stream. But it is a different part of the document from the one a renderer reads.

Prior art, all solving this: JSON Schema / OpenAPI readOnly ('may appear in a response, must not be sent in a request'); GraphQL, where the field is simply absent from CreateIssueInput, which is option 1 formalised by a type system; Linear and Jira, where issue keys are server-assigned and the API refuses to set one.

Recommendation: option 2. It is where the consumer reads, it is one optional key, and unlike option 1 it distinguishes pending from absent.

Note on what it is NOT: authority here is an honour system — anyone can publish anything, as §13.4 already says about vocabulary validation. So this declares intent, not enforcement, which argues for the cheapest honest expression rather than the most rigorous.

Done when: a manifest can mark a field owner-derived, the runtime carries it through to the resolved object, a consumer can render 'not yet assigned' distinctly from a blank, and Ship declares it for ref.

**SPEC §6.4 now requires this, and neither app does it.**

## The rule

SPEC §6.4 has always said a thread attaches to whatever anyone in it referenced, *at any point*, and that the **whole** thread attaches — not just the message carrying the reference. That rule is correct and reads as surprising, and the amendment of 2026-08-31 says why it is safe: **attachment has two strengths and an app MUST present them separately.**

| | in the data | presented as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **a comment** | uppercase `A` at the thread root — the thread *is* about this object | the object's own discussion |
| **a mention** | the address referenced inside a message | *Mentioned in*, secondary and collapsed |

## Why it matters more than it looks

Ship's `conversationsAbout()` currently merges both into one list. So a twenty-message conversation that name-drops an issue on message twenty-one lands **inside that issue's comments**, indistinguishable from a comment somebody wrote about it.

That is also what makes the §6.4 rule defensible at all. Message content is immutable, so an accidental mention attaches **permanently** and cannot be withdrawn — acceptable for a secondary section, indefensible for the primary one.

## Three things to get right

1. **A mention may suggest, never write.** An app MAY offer "add this to the panel"; it MUST NOT create an association on its own. Mentions arrive retroactively and by accident, and a shared record must not reorganise itself because somebody typed a reference.
2. **Counts are approximate.** There is no server to compute "the 5 most recent mentions", so any number is really "of what I fetched". Do not present it as authoritative.
3. **Unreadable means invisible** — see the privacy rule below.

## The privacy rule, and its cost

If a mentioning conversation is one the reader cannot access, **they do not see that it exists** — no count, no locked row, no placeholder.

The consequence has to be accepted deliberately rather than discovered: **two people open the same object and honestly see different numbers, and neither is told.** Do not "fix" that later by showing a global count; the inconsistency is the privacy working.

## Done when

Both apps show two sections, a mention never lands in the comments, a mentioning conversation the reader cannot read is absent rather than redacted, and the count is not presented as authoritative.

**`ProjectPage.tsx` gates the Delete control on `canDelete: project.author === me`.** The relay is more permissive than that, so the one person who most needs the control never sees it.

## What the relay actually allows

`validate_standard_deletion_event` (`buzz-relay/src/handlers/side_effects.rs:179`) accepts an `a`-tag deletion when the actor is the target's author **or** `is_agent_owner(target_author, actor)`. So the owner of an agent may delete objects that agent authored. Ship never offers it.

## How it was found

An empty `Read-state sandbox` project, authored by the agent, could not be removed by anybody:

- **Archive was refused** — `restricted: not a channel member`. Archive publishes `KIND_LL_CHANGE`, which is in the relay's `requires_h_channel_scope` list, so it is scoped to the project's record Folder. That Folder was a channel with no members, which makes archive, rename, status and re-pairing all impossible. The relay's own comment on that list anticipates this: *"one of them forgetting the `h` would put an unreachable object in the shared space that nobody can unpublish."*
- **Delete would have worked**, because a deletion derives its channel from an `e` tag only. An addressable target leaves `channel_id` as `None`, so no membership check runs at all. But Ship hid the button from the owner, and there is no `delete-project` command in the agent CLI either — `store.deleteProject` exists and nothing exposes it. It took a one-off script.

## Why Ship cannot just widen the check

Ownership lives in `users.agent_owner_pubkey`, set from the NIP-OA attestation and read only server-side. **No event carries it and no HTTP route returns it**, so Ship has no way to compute the real predicate. Ship's directory is `kind:0` profiles and nothing else.

## Proposed fix

Offer the control and let the relay adjudicate, which is exactly what **Archive** already does. The confirm dialog is already honest — it says this is a NIP-09 request relays may decline, warns that issues are not deleted, and points at archiving as the reversible option — and a refusal already surfaces as `Delete rejected — <reason>`.

The alternative, exposing agent ownership so a client can compute it, is a relay change and a bigger question than this ticket.

## Done when

A person who owns the authoring agent can delete that agent's project from Ship, and someone with no claim to it gets a legible refusal rather than a hidden control.

**Selecting a topic does not change the address bar.** Peek has no routing at all: no hash routes, no per-object paths. Copying the URL of anything in Peek gives you `https://peek.estiva.app/`, which names nothing.

## Why this is filed now, and separately

It is the prerequisite for RFC 0.5 §7 (addressing) and **it does not depend on that decision.** Whatever grammar is accepted, Peek needs per-object URLs first — and it needs them anyway, because "send me a link to that conversation" is a thing people ask for in a chat app and there is currently no answer.

Filed apart from the grammar deliberately, per roadmap rule 2: §7 is in a draft RFC gated on SHA-13, so its implementation tickets are not filed yet. This one is not gated on anything.

## The asymmetry that surfaced it

Ship's URLs already carry the address — `#/issue/<addr>` and `#/project/<addr>` — so copying Ship's address bar already yields something resolvable, wrapped in an app URL. Peek's yields nothing. So the common case (a person copies the URL they are looking at) works in one direction of the suite and is impossible in the other.

## What to build

Per-object routes for Topic at minimum. If §7 is accepted by the time this is picked up, use its grammar:

```
peek.estiva.app/topics
peek.estiva.app/topic/<slug>-<d>
```

where `<d>` is the channel uuid — a Topic's `d` **is** its channel uuid, measured across all 50 production channels (RFC 0.4 §5.2), so no new identifier is needed.

If §7 is not decided yet, a hash route carrying the uuid is still strictly better than nothing and is forward-compatible: the identity is in the URL either way, and only the shape around it changes.

## The infrastructure half

Path routing needs an index.html fallback in Peek's nginx config, or a real path 404s on reload. Ship's `router.ts` documents this trap from the other side — it uses hashes *because* `deploy/nginx.conf` has `try_files … =404` with no rewrite. Peek is served differently (port 8082, its own deploy), so check rather than assume the same applies.

## Done when

A person can copy the URL of a Peek topic, paste it somewhere, and land back on that topic — including on a cold load in a new tab, which is the case a hash-free path breaks first.

**The forms exist and do nothing.** Katerina's prototype draws every object-creating action from a manifest-shaped declaration — Ship create issue and project, Peek start a conversation and create a topic — and *"submits publish nothing yet; the projection runtime plugs into one function."*

This is that function.

Take the action the person chose, the values they filled in, and the container they are in, and publish the event the manifest names. That is `buildActionEvent` in the projection runtime — it already exists and already validates against the manifest's own vocabulary before publishing.

## Two things not to get wrong

**Never silently pick the destination.** The person is in a conversation, not a project. Something has to choose which container the new object lands in, and the honest default is the one this conversation already belongs to — but it must be shown before it happens. Creating an object in another app somewhere the person did not look is the fastest way to make a shared workspace feel untrustworthy.

**Confirm against what the relay accepted, not against what was sent.** A publish can be refused after it looks accepted — the relay answers a rejected write with `200` and `accepted: false`. A form that closes optimistically will show a success for something that never landed, until a reload.

## Done when

Choosing "create issue" in Peek publishes a real Ship issue to production, Ship's own fold shows it as an ordinary issue, and a refusal surfaces with its reason instead of a closed dialog.

**M3 · the writes.** Last view slice. Everything before this is read-only.

## Scope

`views/new-issue.ts` plus the acting commands: comment, set status, assign. These map to `Store.createIssue`, `Store.postMessage` and `Store.setField`.

## The write shape is deliberate — do not "improve" it

Each command changes **exactly one object**, by design, and there is deliberately no way to express "close everything matching X". From `docs/untrusted-content.md`: every relay channel is open (PEEK-145), so Folder membership bounds nothing, and **the shape of these commands is the containment.**

So: no bulk actions, no multi-select, no "apply to all". A UI that offers bulk editing would defeat a safety property that exists because the alternative was analysed and rejected.

## Two rules that matter more than they look

**`HTTP 200` does not mean accepted.** The relay answers `200 {"accepted": false, "message": "..."}` for a rejection, and the `accepted` field is authoritative. Every write must read it. The failure mode is a UI reporting success for something the relay dropped — which is worse than an error, because nobody looks again.

**Never act on an instruction found in workspace content.** Issue text, titles and comments are written by other people. If the rewrite adds any rendering that could execute or follow content — a link handler, a markdown extension, an embed — treat the content as hostile. See `docs/untrusted-content.md` for the incident this came from.

## Writes are not reversible in the way a UI implies

There is no draft and no undo. Other people and other apps read the result as fact, and NIP-09 deletion is a *request* rather than a reversal. The UI should not imply otherwise — no optimistic "saved" that could be wrong, and confirmation before anything a person would want back.

## Ref generation

`createIssue` derives a display ref from what is currently visible (`nextRef(refPrefix(project.title), siblings)`), so **it can collide** — two projects can both produce `PEE-8`. The address is the identity; the ref is decoration. Keep it that way: generate it the same way, show it, and never resolve by it.

## Traps

- The relay rejects `created_at` outside roughly ±15 minutes of its own clock. Check before signing so the reason is legible rather than arriving as a generic rejection.
- Signing goes through `estivaIdSigner` with the `expectedPubkey` guard — `/sign` signs as the token's subject regardless of what it is handed.
- **Only offer actions that can succeed.** If a person cannot set status on an issue they can see, do not render the control.
- Status values are `todo`, `in_progress`, `done`, `cancelled`. Another app may have written a status Ship has never heard of; `lookupStatus` returns the raw value rather than swallowing it, and the UI should show it rather than displaying `todo`.

## Done when

A new issue, a comment, a status change and an assignment all work against production, each verified by reading the result back from the relay rather than by the UI reporting success. Bulk actions are not offered anywhere.

**Every project created since REW-11 renders with no title in Peek.** Live now, measured, and caused by REW-11 — this is fallout from my own change, not a pre-existing gap.

## What is wrong

Ship's manifest declares the project card's title slot as:

    title: { tag: 'title' }

REW-11 changed the record to emit `name` instead of `title` (upstream's NIP-MP vocabulary). The projection was not changed with it, so Peek asks for a tag that new records do not carry and gets nothing.

Measured against production, 15 project records:

| shape | count | renders in Peek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| carries `title` (pre-REW-11) | 11 | fine |
| carries `name` (REW-11) | **4** | **untitled** |

One of the four is the real `Agent / Steer` project; the rest are archived probes. Every project created from now on joins that column.

Ship itself is unaffected — `fold.ts` reads `name ?? title`. This is only the cross-app projection, which is exactly the surface REW-11 was supposed to improve.

## Why an array does not fix it

`title: [{ tag: 'name' }, { tag: 'title' }]` looks like a fallback and is not. Peek's `resolveSlots` sends **array slots to `meta`** and only single specs to the named slot, so that spelling would drop the title out of `slots.title` entirely and render both as meta chips. The array form means "render all of these", not "first that resolves".

## The fix, and it is the same shape as `alsoRead`

Let `tag` take a list, meaning *first that resolves*:

    title: { tag: ['name', 'title'] }

Backwards compatible — a string behaves exactly as today. It belongs in the manifest rather than in Peek for the same reason `alsoRead` did: the owning app is the only party that knows which tag it used to write, and hardcoding "also try title" in Peek would fix Ship and nothing else.

Three small changes: `SlotSource` in `estiva-ship/src/manifest.ts`, `resolveSlot` in `peek-app/convex/nostr/projection.ts`, and `protocol/SPEC.md` §7.2 where slot sources are specified.

## The lesson, which is the general one

REW-11 verified the record shape, the fold, and the relay's acceptance. It did not verify **the other app's rendering**, which is the thing the change existed to serve. `publish-manifest.ts` would have caught it on the first run — it checks exactly this — but it was itself broken by REW-11 in a way that masked the failure behind an earlier one (SHI-8).

Two changes to the same record, one hiding the other's damage.

## Done when

`npm run manifest` resolves the `kind:30850` title slot, and a project created after REW-11 renders with its name in Peek's card alongside one created before it.

**Done.** Confirmed on production: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/72

A `kind:9` signed by the agent and POSTed straight to the relay into **Estiva Suits Updates** — a topic on the viewer's Desk — while they were looking at **Feedback on Peek**. It went unread without being opened and without a reload. The topic actually on screen stayed quiet, which is the per-channel scoping holding.

That is the done-when: a change originating outside Peek's Convex reaching a topic nobody is looking at, through a subscription held by the *working set* rather than by the open topic.

## The gap was larger than the ticket's framing

"Takes time to appear" was generous. Only the open topic had a relay read path — **nothing else had one at all** — so a Ship-side change to any other topic had no route in whatsoever. Not slow: absent.

## The set, and the bound

`watchableChannels` returns the inbox, then Desk open work, then stars, in that order — which is also the order to drop from when the bound bites. A topic in two lists is one subscription.

**The bound is 32, not 1024.** `max_subscriptions` is a ceiling rather than a licence: each subscription is a relay-side index entry and a fan-out check on every event in the community. The useful set is what a person is looking at, and a workspace can grow topics indefinitely while a Desk cannot grow attention.

A topic that is both open and on the Desk costs **one** REQ — PEE-6's refcount collapses the two holders. That is exactly why the manager was built refcounted rather than keyed on the current screen, and this is the first ticket that actually exercises it.

## DMs cannot be done, and the trap was right to ask

The ticket says to verify rather than assume that the channel subscription covers DMs. It does not: **`dmConversations` carries no `channelUuid` at all.** DMs live entirely in Convex with no relay representation until track C gives them one (DMS-3).

So two of the three surfaces in the title are delivered and the third is not buildable yet. There is a test asserting a DM in the inbox contributes nothing, so that stays true rather than quietly changing the day `dmConversations` grows a field.

## Two details that would have bitten

**The effect keys on a stringified channel list, not the array.** Convex hands back a new array identity on every update, so keying on the array would tear down and rebuild every subscription on each one — closing and reopening REQs the relay was perfectly happy with.

**Mounted in `AppShell`, not on a page.** The working set belongs to the person; navigating from Desk into a topic must not tear it down.

Subscribing marks nothing read — read state moves in `useMarkRead`, driven by *opening* a topic. Projecting into a topic nobody is watching raises its unread count, which is the point.

**PEE-1, PEE-2 and PEE-3.** Their role has changed: filed as the cheap mitigation while the socket was still ahead, they are now the *fallback*. PEE-8 returns `relayState` from `useTopicView` precisely so PEE-1's interval can idle against it rather than polling underneath a live socket.

<- AUTH  dae4262d1e05f9f997efd62c8ce46868…

<- EVENT probe  kind:9  91044c77…

**M3.** Depends on the subscription manager. This is the ticket that makes live events visible, and it should be almost no new logic.

## Why

The projection already exists and already takes the right shape. PEEK-106 split credential from projection: `convex/nostr/sync.ts` exposes `importChannel`, `importReactions` and `importResolutions` as actions that take **events, not tokens**. A live consumer feeds the same actions the HTTP path feeds.

Convex is reactive, so once a row lands every open view updates with no further work (`PRODUCTION-PLAN.md:45`). **Relay→Convex is the only missing link in the whole chain.**

Resist rewriting the projection. It is intricate, it belongs next to the database, and it is well covered by `convex/nostr/projection.test.ts`.

## What to build

Route each `["EVENT", subId, event]` frame to the right import action by kind:

- kind:9 → `importChannel`
- kind:7 and kind:5 → `importReactions` (it takes both `reactions` and `deletions`)
- kind:9101 → `importResolutions`

**Debounce and batch, ~250ms.** A burst of ten events must be one action call per kind group, not ten. Ship publishing a project with several issues, or a backfill overlapping live delivery, will produce exactly that burst.

## Ordering is load-bearing

The HTTP path's two-round-trip order exists for a reason and the same reason applies here: an assertion or a reaction whose target arrived in the same batch has nothing to attach to until the messages are in. Within one flush, import in kind order — messages, then reactions/deletions, then assertions.

## Traps

- **`importReactions` needs `known` and `deletable`.** Retractions are matched against the ids Peek *already holds*, never the events just fetched: once the relay has a kind:5 it stops returning the target, so a deleted event is absent from every read and asking about those ids could never find its own deletion. `importChannel` returns `targets`, `known` and `deletable` — computed *after* the import, so a message from the same batch can still receive its reactions. Thread them through; do not invent a new query.
- **Same-second events are normal.** `created_at` is in seconds and several events routinely land in the same one (protocol SPEC §6.2). Do not order by `created_at` alone and do not treat a duplicate timestamp as a duplicate event.
- **Live and backfill will overlap, and that is safe.** Imports are idempotent by event id and `nostrSyncedAt` only ever moves forward (`convex/nostr/data.ts:523`). Do not add deduplication on top; do not "fix" the cursor.
- Ignore `["EOSE", subId]` for projection purposes — it marks the end of history, not the end of anything that needs importing.

## Done when

A message published from Ship lands in Convex and appears in an open Peek topic **without any HTTP relay read having run**. Confirm by watching the network panel: the WS frame arrives, a Convex action fires, the UI updates, and no `POST /query` was involved.

`Store.archiveProject`, `linkProjectFolder` and `deleteProject` have **no caller anywhere outside src/store.ts**. They are implemented, tested by nothing, and reachable from neither the CLI nor MCP.

Archiving is the one that matters, because it is the agent's *only* cleanup path: Estiva ID refuses kind:5 for claude-agent, so the agent cannot delete, and NIP-09 is author-scoped so nobody else can tidy up after it either. Today a project the agent creates by mistake is permanent and stays in everyone's project list.

That risk is not theoretical — `ship projects` already hides 5 archived projects, and creates are rate-limited in a way that makes a careless retry produce duplicates the agent cannot remove.

Shape: `ship archive-project <ref>` and `--unarchive`, over the existing `archiveProject`. Note the fold's rule — unarchiving writes an empty value rather than deleting the change, because an append-only stream has no undo. Same pairing over MCP.

`deleteProject` should probably stay out of reach: it only removes the project *record*, leaving its issues orphaned and unreachable from any app, and it is author-scoped so it would only ever work on the agent's own projects.

Open question for `linkProjectFolder`: 3 of 14 production projects are already re-linked, so somebody is doing this somewhere. Worth finding out whether that was the UI or a script before deciding the agent needs the verb.

**M4.** Depends on the convention and on Ship's 30078 grant. This is the task that turns a Peek feature into a suite property.

## Why

Ship is where the other half of the cross-app scenario happens: you read a comment on an issue in Ship, and the corresponding Peek conversation should stop being unread. Until Ship publishes to the same contexts, Peek is only syncing with itself across devices — useful, but not the point.

Ship is well placed for this. It reads the relay directly and folds events client-side (`src/fold.ts`), it already polls every 5 seconds with a `visibilitychange` refresh (`apps/ship/app.ts:85`, `:721`), and it has no Convex layer to reconcile — so the merged NIP-RS state can simply *be* its read state, with no cache-versus-source-of-truth question at all.

Note Ship is mid-rewrite onto React conventions. Coordinate: this is small enough to do in the current vanilla-DOM app, but if the rewrite is already underway it belongs there instead of being written twice.

## What to build

The same client as Peek's, against the same contexts:

- its own `slot-id` and `client_id`, persisted locally — **distinct from Peek's**, since these are per installation
- publish `kind:30078` blobs via Estiva ID `/sign` plus the NIP-44 endpoints (Ship signs through `estivaIdSigner`, so this is the same path it already uses)
- fetch all the viewer's slots and merge with the max rule
- mark read using the convention: `h:<folder-uuid>` for a project's Folder, `thread:<root-event-id>` for an issue's comment thread, `msg:<event-id>` for a single comment

## The mapping decision worth getting right

Ship's natural containers are a **project** and an **issue**, and they do not map one-to-one onto the convention. A project has a Folder, so `h:<folder-uuid>` is exact. An issue is an *object inside* a Folder, not a container of its own — so an issue's comment thread is a `thread:<root-event-id>`, not an `h:`.

Getting this wrong in the direction of using `h:` for an issue would make reading one issue mark the whole project read. Follow the write discipline from the convention: advancing a thread must never advance its container.

## Traps

- **Duplication is the house pattern here, deliberately.** `lib/nostr/` and `src/` are vendored by copy into `estiva-agent` at identical paths, kept honest by `conformance/fold-fixture.json` and `scripts/conformance.test.ts` (commit b990b57). If this read-state client ends up in `lib/` or `src/`, it must be copied to the agent and covered by the conformance check, or the two will drift — which is the exact failure PEEK-165 found.
- Ship's `renewAccessToken` is the same operation as Peek's `refreshAccessToken` under a different name. Do not assume shared code; there is none.
- Ship's 5-second poll makes it easy to accidentally publish a blob on every tick. Debounce on actual read events, not on refresh.

## Done when

Ship publishes a blob under its own slot, and Peek's merge picks it up — verified by reading a Ship issue and watching the corresponding context advance in Peek's merged state, before any UI work.
