**This is the ticket that makes the extraction trustworthy**, and it should be treated as a requirement of the extraction rather than a follow-up to it.

SHA-7 exists because `createLiveRelay` went into `@estiva-app/protocol` as a single implementation with a single caller: *"no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API."* Every line of the projection consumer runtime is in that same position today, and it is a larger surface.

## What to build

Ship resolves a `nostr:naddr…` reference to a Peek Topic or Message inside a project or issue description and renders it through the manifest — its own tokens, its own design language, zero lines that know what Peek is.

## What this specifically tests

- **The fallback chain**, because a Message is not one of the four closed widget types
- **The `list` slot**, because a Topic carries one
- **Ship's plain-text discipline** meeting a body that may carry structure — see the *Rich text and blocks* project, and do not quietly start rendering markup here
- **A relay-signed author**, which Ship has never had to attribute

## Done when

Ship renders a real Peek Topic and a real Message from production, and **whatever the second consumer forced to change in the runtime is written on this issue — including "nothing"**, which is the answer that retires SHA-7's worry rather than deferring it.

Only after this should the runtime be published as a package.

---

## What PRO-6 established, 2026-08-31

Peek's manifest is written and merged, so the shape of this ticket is no longer
guesswork. Three things below were **not** knowable when it was filed, and two
of them are larger than anything in "What to build".

### 1. A Message is not addressable, and every resolver here starts from an address

Confirmed against production: a `kind:9` carries **no `d` tag**. It is a regular
event, referenced by event id, never by `kind:pubkey:d`.

`resolveForeignObject` takes an `naddr`, `referenceToPointer` returns an
`AddressPointer`, and the root is fetched with `{kinds, authors, '#d'}`. None of
that reaches a message. **Resolving a Message needs a second entry point keyed
on event id** — `nevent`/`e` rather than `naddr`/`a` — and that is the larger
half of this ticket. Note the knock-on: comments and changes are fetched by
`#a`, which a non-addressable root cannot be the target of either.

### 2. The `list` slot does not resolve for an object reached by address

`list` was implemented in PRO-2 down the *folder* path, where containment is
discovered from the Folder's contents. `resolveForeignObject` never resolves
it: `rawSlotValue` returns undefined for a `children` spec, so the slot is
dropped.

Measured: 5 of 5 real production Topics resolve by address through Peek's
manifest and render **title and subtitle and no messages**. So "a Peek
conversation inside a Ship issue" does not fall out of the manifest as filed —
wiring `list` into the by-address path is work this ticket owns.

### 3. A Topic carries no `h` tag — it *is* the container

So `resolveFolderProject` cannot find one, and a Topic is reached by address:
`39000:<relay pubkey>:<channel uuid>`.

### Still true, and now with detail

- **The fallback chain** — Peek declares `widget: ["message", "card"]`. Nothing
  consumes a chain yet; a consumer reading `widget` as a string sees an array.
  That is PRO-3's, and this ticket is its first caller.
- **The relay-signed author** — a `39000` is signed by the relay, so "who wrote
  this" resolves to the relay's pubkey. Any attribution slot must not render it
  as a person.
- **Ship has no consumer runtime at all.** It is a producer only: `src/manifest.ts`
  and `scripts/publish-manifest.ts`, no `ForeignObjectWidget`, no resolver. The
  second consumer is being built from nothing, not adapted.

### Blocked on

**Peek's manifest is written but unpublished.** Publishing `kind:31990` is
refused at two of SPEC §8's three gates — a fresh key gets
`relay_membership_required`, and Estiva ID refuses to sign for `claude-agent`
(`App claude-agent may not sign kind 31990`). Neither `estiva-peek` nor
`estiva-ship` carries 31990 in `allowed_kinds`; Ship publishes from a raw key
registered as a relay member. Until an identity is settled, Ship can only
resolve Peek's manifest from a local copy, which tests the runtime and not the
discovery. See PRO-6.

### What actually changed in the runtime, for the "including nothing" answer

PRO-6 already forced four changes, so that answer will not be "nothing":
`match: 'address' | 'identifier'` on `children`, `field: 'pubkey'` as a slot
source, `records` made optional in both resolvers, and the discovery that a
kind is `u16` so an unmatchable-filter trick is refused by the relay. Those came
from the *producer* side. This ticket collects what the consumer side forces.

events.content: Unassign

**Do this as part of the Ship rewrite, with Ship as the second consumer.** Depends on the publishing decision and on `@estiva/protocol`. Higher risk than either, because the seam is a judgement call rather than a diff.

## Why

Both apps already implement the full Estiva ID client, independently, converged in behaviour and diverged in naming:

| Peek (`src/auth/estivaId.ts`) | Ship (`lib/auth/estiva-id.ts`, 358 lines) |
| --- | --- |
| `refreshAccessToken` | `renewAccessToken` |
| `takeReturnTo` | `restoreRoute` |
| `beginSignIn` / `completeSignIn` | `beginSignIn` / `completeSignIn` |
| `stashShellReason` / `takeShellReason` | — **missing** |

Two hand-written PKCE clients against one identity service, one of them behind on the shell vocabulary. Ship's rewrite is the moment to collapse them, because a rewrite is going to touch this code anyway.

## THE SEAM DECISION: leave Convex out

`peek-app/src/auth/useEstivaIdAuth.ts` is the adapter `ConvexProviderWithAuth` reads. **It must not go in the package.** If it does, Ship and Leaf inherit a Convex dependency to work around, which is precisely the failure this project's sequencing exists to avoid.

The split:

- **In the package:** the PKCE flow, token storage and validity, silent renewal, sign-out, the returnTo/shell-reason vocabulary, and the auth-shell state machine.
- **In each app:** the adapter that hands a token to whatever that app's data layer is. Peek keeps `useEstivaIdAuth` for Convex. Ship needs no adapter at all — it passes the token to its relay client directly.

Getting this line right is the whole value of the ticket. Everything else is renaming.

## Hard-won behaviour that must survive — each of these is an incident

**Do not clear an in-flight sign-in when clearing a session (PEEK-167).** `clearSession` must touch only the token and the shell reason — never the verifier, state or returnTo. Those are credentials of an authorization request *currently in the air*, owned by the `beginSignIn` that wrote them. The failure path: a boot with an expired token calls `fetchAccessToken`, renewal fails, session clears, app drops to the shell, shell probes and writes a fresh verifier — then a *second* `fetchAccessToken` awaiting the same renewal resolves and clears again, deleting the verifier the probe just wrote. The code comes back to a tab with nothing to redeem it, `completeSignIn` refuses it before `/token` is ever called, and the identity service has **no record of a failure at all** because nothing was asked of it. Only `beginSignOut` clears both.

**`token_rejected` must never read as "session expired"** (`src/auth/shell/contract.ts:30`, asserted by `contract.test.ts:153`). Telling somebody their session expired when their token was refused for a configuration fault sends them to re-authenticate against a wall. Carry the whole reason vocabulary into the package, with its test.

**Refresh tokens are single-use, and a replay is treated as theft** — it revokes the whole chain. Peek guards this with a `refreshing` ref so two renewals cannot be in flight at once. The package must keep that guard; it is not an optimisation.

**Renew *before* expiry, not on failure.** The stored `expiresAt` is already 30s early (`tokenFrom` subtracts it), and a timer renews at that point so the person notices nothing. Note the timer is a `setTimeout`, which browsers throttle in background tabs — a known limitation worth documenting in the package rather than rediscovering per app.

**Clearing the local token is not signing out (PEEK-122).** The `estiva_id_session` cookie on the identity origin survives it, so the shell's silent probe succeeds on the next boot and puts the person straight back in. Real sign-out navigates to `/logout` with `client_id` and `post_logout_redirect_uri`.

**Silent renewal cannot use a hidden iframe.** The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax` and is withheld from one. The refresh-token grant exists because of this; do not "simplify" it back to an iframe.

## Also worth packaging

The **auth shell** (`src/auth/shell/`) — the state machine that tries to enter on its own and only asks when it genuinely cannot, with `markEntered` distinguishing a cold boot from an interruption (PEEK-123). Ship has its own version (`scripts/auth-shell.test.ts` exists), so there are already two.

Keep the *shell's rendering* per-app — it is a full-page surface and each app will want its own — but the state machine and the reason vocabulary are shared.

## Traps

- Each app has its own `client_id` registered in Estiva ID (`peek`, `estiva-ship`) with its own `redirectUris`. The package takes both as config; it must never hardcode either.
- `redirectUri()` must match a seeded `redirectUris` entry **exactly** — Estiva ID compares exact strings. A trailing slash difference is a refused sign-in.
- Do not unify token storage location without thought: Peek uses `sessionStorage` for the token. NIP-RS slots (CRO-4) need `localStorage` because they must survive a restart. Different lifetimes, different homes.
- Ship signs through `estivaIdSigner`; Peek signs through `signViaEstivaId`. Both call `POST /sign`, and both must keep the `expectedPubkey` guard — `/sign` signs as the token's subject regardless of what it is handed, so a mismatch returns HTTP 200 with an event authored by somebody else.

## Done when

Peek and Ship both authenticate through `@estiva/identity`, their local copies are deleted, the `token_rejected` test travels with the package, and both apps survive the four flows by hand: cold sign-in, silent renewal across expiry, a failed renewal dropping to the shell, and sign-out that actually signs out (confirm by reloading and *not* being let straight back in).

**Merged 2026-08-28 as `c8a4d521c`. Content verified. But the merge method defeated CAT-1's main reason for choosing merge, and the next catch-up must know it.**

**Content landed, verified against the branch rather than the merge report:**

## The problem: GitHub squash-merged a merge commit

    c8a4d521c parents -> e6766311e     (one parent, not two)

The PR head was a real merge commit with `upstream/main` as a second parent. **Squash collapsed it into a single-parent commit, so upstream's 702 commits are not in the ancestry.** Consequences, measured:

    git merge-base upstream/main origin/nfb-demo-kinds   b78a684cf   <- UNCHANGED
    is 69096c9a8 an ancestor of nfb-demo-kinds?          NO
    git rev-list --count nfb-demo-kinds..upstream/main   710

So git reports **710 behind** while the tree is level with `69096c9a8`. **CAT-1 chose merge over rebase precisely because "a merge commit preserves the merge-base, so the next catch-up is measurable" — squash removed that property.** The decision was right; the merge button undid half of it.

**Two ways this bites whoever does the next catch-up:**

1. A survey run the way CAT-1/CAT-2 were run reports ~710 behind and concludes nothing has been caught up.
2. **`git merge upstream/main` would try to re-apply all 702 commits' diffs to a tree that already contains them**, producing enormous spurious conflicts that look like a catastrophic divergence.

## Mitigation in place, and the better fix

Pushed a marker tag — safe, `relay-image.yml` triggers on branches only, so no rebuild:

    upstream-merged/69096c9a8 -> c8a4d521c

**So the real gap is `69096c9a8..upstream/main`, not `nfb-demo-kinds..upstream/main`.** Measure the next catch-up from the tag:

    git rev-list --count upstream-merged/69096c9a8..upstream/main
    git merge-tree --write-tree origin/nfb-demo-kinds upstream/main   # still correct for conflicts

**A stronger fix exists and was not done unilaterally:** an ancestry-only merge, `git merge -s ours upstream/main` pinned at `69096c9a8`, which changes no file but repairs the merge-base so every ordinary git command is right again. It needs a push to `nfb-demo-kinds`, which rebuilds the image for no content change. Worth doing before the next catch-up rather than during it.

**For next time: use a real merge commit, not squash, for an upstream catch-up.** Squash is right for a feature PR and wrong for this one — CAT-1's reasoning should say so explicitly.

**M5 · the honesty task.** Last one. It is a copy and product task, and it is the one most likely to be skipped — which is exactly why it is written down.

## Why

This project chose **DM channels** over NIP-17 gift wrap, deliberately: business software needs search, retention, offboarding and administrative recovery, and end-to-end encryption prevents all four. The relay operator *is* the organisation.

The consequence is unavoidable and must be stated: **DMs are private by membership, not private by encryption.** The relay stores them in plaintext. Anyone with relay database access can read every DM.

That is a defensible design. What is not defensible is a UI that implies otherwise. A lock icon, the word "encrypted", "private and secure", or even an unqualified "Private" next to a padlock sets an expectation the system does not meet — and in a tool for business organisations, that is the kind of misunderstanding that matters when someone decides what to type.

## What to do

1. **Audit existing copy** for anything implying end-to-end privacy — DM empty states, the composer placeholder, tooltips, settings, onboarding, marketing pages, and any lock or shield iconography.
2. **Decide what the product does say.** "Private" is accurate for membership-scoped, so it is not off-limits — but decide deliberately whether to say more, e.g. that DMs are visible to the workspace operator. This is a product and possibly a legal call, not a developer default. Bring it to whoever owns that.
3. **Write the decision down** in the repo, next to the DM code, with the reasoning. The next person to add a lock icon should find the argument before they ship it.

## Also worth deciding now, while it is cheap

The choice makes several things *possible* that are not in this project's scope, and they are easier to design for than to retrofit:

- **Export / legal hold / admin read.** Now feasible. Do not build them here, but do not accidentally preclude them.
- **Offboarding.** NIP-IA already exists (`9035` archive request, `9036` unarchive, relay-signed `8002`/`8003` deltas, `13535` list snapshot). Confirm archiving an identity does the right thing to its DMs, and record what it does.
- **Retention.** Buzz channels carry `ttl_seconds` and `ttl_deadline`. Whether DMs should ever expire is a policy question; note it and move on.

## Traps

- Do not overcorrect into alarming copy. "Your admin can read this" on every message is as wrong in the other direction — accurate, unusable, and it will just be turned off.
- Keep this out of the code-only bucket. If nobody who owns product copy has read the decision, the task is not done.

## Done when

No surface in Peek implies end-to-end encryption for DMs, the decision about what the product *does* say is recorded with its author, and the three follow-on questions above have written answers even if the answer is "not now".

**Do this as part of the Ship rewrite. Tokens before components, and keep the component set small.** Depends on the publishing decision. The highest-friction package in the project, and the one most likely to be resented if done greedily.

## Why

Ship's rewrite is moving it onto Peek's conventions — React, Vite, Tailwind, Peek's design tokens. Without a package that means copying `tailwind.config.js` and a handful of primitives into Ship, and again into Leaf. Three copies of a design system diverge faster than three copies of anything else, because every app makes small visual decisions weekly.

## Two things, and the order matters

**1. Tokens (do this first, ship it alone if necessary).** Peek's `tailwind.config.js` holds the custom design tokens; `src/stories/Swatches.tsx` enumerates them. Package the Tailwind preset and the CSS variables. That alone lets Ship and Leaf look like Estiva without inheriting a single component.

**2. Primitives (do this second, and sparingly).** The set Peek's own working rules name: **Avatar, AvatarStack, ListRow, Chip, IconButton.** Peek has 149 files under `src/components` — the overwhelming majority is product, not primitives, and must stay put. If this package grows past roughly a dozen components, it has become Peek's component library rather than Estiva's.

## The rule that makes this survivable

**Tokens are the contract. Components are a convenience.**

If Leaf needs a different `ListRow`, it must be able to build one from the same tokens without asking permission, and the result must still look like Estiva. Write this into the package README explicitly:

> Forking a component into your app is allowed and is not a failure. If you fork one, you owe nothing back. Tokens are the only thing you must not diverge from.

A shared component library people are afraid to deviate from becomes a tax rather than a gift, and the failure mode is not a debate — it is a quiet local reimplementation with slightly different padding.

## Carry the accumulated gotchas into the package, not into three apps

**The tw-merge pitfall, which is exactly the class of bug a shared library spreads.** From Peek's working rules: custom text classes like `text-btn-small` are *silently dropped* when followed by a `text-{color}` class in merged class lists. The mitigation is to use explicit arbitrary values (`text-[12px] leading-[12px]`) **in shared components**. That advice was written for Peek's own shared primitives; in a cross-app package it matters more, because the breakage appears in the consuming app and the cause is in the package. Encode it, and add a test or lint rule if one is possible.

**Menu and popover behaviour.** Peek's rules: stay open on hover, close on mouse leave, guard the parent hover state, close on outside click, close on Escape. Five rules, each individually forgettable, and a popover that fails one feels broken without anyone being able to say why. This is exactly the kind of thing worth having once.

**"Only offer actions that can succeed."** A product principle rather than a component one — an action appears only where it works, and the enabling surface advertises the capability. Worth stating in the README because it shapes what props a primitive should expose (a disabled state that explains itself, rather than a button that fails).

## Storybook

Peek has Storybook and a hardening plan, and its stories read fixtures from `@/api/fixtures`. Package primitives need stories that depend on **no app data at all** — if a primitive's story needs a fixture, the primitive is not a primitive.

Decide whether Storybook lives in the package (probably yes, it is the natural home for a component library) or stays per-app. Either way the package's stories must be runnable without Peek.

## Traps

- **Peek is the visual reference, and it is pixel-perfect by rule** — the prototype at `prototype-v1` is the source of truth. Extracting a primitive must not change how Peek renders. Screenshot-compare before and after, or the first thing this package does is regress the app it came from.
- **Do not extract anything with product knowledge in it.** A `ListRow` that knows what a topic is belongs to Peek. The test: could Leaf, which has documents and no conversations, use this unchanged?
- Peek uses design tokens and never raw hex, by rule. The package must make the right thing easy — if a consumer has to reach for hex, a token is missing.
- Ship is pre-rewrite and still vanilla DOM. Do not block this on Ship's rewrite finishing, but do not declare the seam settled until a React consumer other than Peek has used it.

## Done when

Ship's rewrite renders with `@estiva/ui` tokens, at least the five named primitives are consumed from the package by both apps, Peek's appearance is unchanged (verified by comparison, not by inspection), and the README states the forking rule and the tw-merge mitigation.
tags: Extract @estiva/ui — tokens first, then five primitives

projects.title: Catch up the Buzz fork
projects.description:
`estiva-app/buzz` is **625 commits behind `block/buzz`** and 4 ahead (measured 2026-08-24). The gap grows weekly, and the four commits we carry are all narrow kind-registry additions — so the fork is nearly pure upstream with a thin seam, which is the best possible position to catch up from and the worst one to let rot.

## Why now, and why not all of it now

The survey is cheap and informative and should happen soon. **The merge and deploy are neither, and should wait for a reason.**

That reason will come — the RFC 0.3 folder decision wants to know what shape upstream's forge layer settles into, and there is real value sitting in those 625 commits (NIP-MP projects, NIP-34 git statuses `1630`–`1633`, the NIP-FI federated-identity family, presence snapshots). But deploying 625 commits of relay change against the database that Peek and Ship both depend on is not something to do because the number is annoying.

So: **M1 immediately, M2 onward on a trigger.** Doing the survey first is also what makes the trigger legible — right now nobody can say what catching up would cost.

## What we carry

Four commits on `nfb-demo-kinds`, all additions to the kind registry and its scope mapping:

```
d207a1148  accept Linear-lite Projects, Issues and Changes (30850/30851/1851)
ffeb41606  accept NIP-22 comments and NIP-89 handlers (1111, 31989/31990)
70f75609b  accept NIP-FC Files and Components (30840/30841)
e8b0dab5b  accept NIP-84 highlights (kind:9802)
```

They touch `crates/buzz-core/src/kind.rs` (constants and `ALL_KINDS`) and `crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs` (`required_scope_for_kind`). Both files have been edited heavily upstream across 625 commits, so **that is where the conflicts will be** — and they are conflicts in a list, which resolve easily and misresolve invisibly.

Verified 2026-08-24: none of `30850`, `30851`, `1851`, `9101`, `30840`, `30841`, `9802` is claimed upstream. **Re-verify at merge time** — upstream allocates numbers continuously, and NIP-MP's own allocation note says both external kind registries are advisory rather than authoritative.

## The traps, in the order they will bite

**1. `main` and `nfb-demo-kinds` have diverged by a Revert.** `main` carries a revert that `nfb-demo-kinds` does not. Branching from `main` and rebasing **silently proposes deleting the members API and the relay-image workflow.** Merge into `nfb-demo-kinds`; do not route through `main`.

**2. `nfb-demo-kinds` is not rustfmt-clean.** Running `cargo fmt` reflows unrelated comments, burying the real diff in noise. Do not format as part of this.

**3. The relay image is built from `nfb-demo-kinds`, not `main`.** `relay-image.yml` produces `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb`. That workflow is ours — a careless merge is exactly what trap 1 proposes deleting.

**4. Only one workflow is enabled.** The other twelve upstream workflows are `DISABLED_MANUALLY` to save minutes. That is a **repo setting**, not a file, so a merge does not re-enable them — but confirm afterwards rather than assuming, because 625 commits may have added new ones that arrive enabled.

**5. Database migrations are the real risk.** 625 commits include schema migrations that run against the production Postgres on startup. At least one is known to *refuse* rather than migrate — `buzz-db/src/migration.rs` blocks the NIP-RS pre-0007 path if existing `kind:30078` rows have ambiguous `d`/`t` tag cardinality. Assume there are others. **This is the part that needs a throwaway relay, and there is no staging.**

**6. The relay has no update timer.** Every other service has one; Buzz does not. Deploy by hand, and pull only the relay:

```bash
cd /opt/buzz && docker compose pull relay && ./run.sh restart
```

`run.sh pull` also pulls postgres, redis and minio.

**7. Verify by image id, never by health.** A healthy relay serving a stale image is precisely the state this project can produce. Compare the running image id to `:nfb`.

## Blast radius

The relay is the only shared dependency in the ecosystem. Peek and Ship both read and write it; Estiva ID signs for it; the agent CLI and the MCP server read through it. A bad relay deploy takes down everything at once, and there is no staging workspace to rehearse against.

That is not an argument against doing this. It is an argument for M3 and M4 being real work rather than a formality.

## Milestones

- **M1 · Survey (do this soon).** What is in the 625 commits that matters; which of our four conflict and how badly; which migrations would run and whether any would refuse; whether any upstream kind now collides with ours. Output is a written answer and a cost estimate, no merge.
- **M2 · Merge into `nfb-demo-kinds`.** Resolve conflicts, keep all four of our commits' behaviour, do not reformat, do not lose the relay-image workflow. `cargo build` and the test suite green.
- **M3 · Prove the kinds still work.** `npm run probe` from estiva-ship against a locally-built relay — every Estiva kind accepted, with the relay's own words rather than an assumption.
- **M4 · Prove the migrations on a throwaway.** A relay instance with a copy-shaped database, not the production one. This is the milestone that exists because there is no staging.
- **M5 · Deploy and verify.** Build `:nfb`, pull on the box, restart, compare image ids, then exercise Peek and Ship against it — a read and a write each.

## Out of scope

- **Merging to `main`.** `main` is not what builds the image. Leave the Revert divergence alone unless a separate ticket says otherwise.
- **Adopting anything new from upstream** — NIP-MP, git statuses, NIP-FI. Catching up makes them *available*; using them is a decision per feature, and NIP-MP specifically is entangled with RFC 0.3's deferred question.
- **Contributing anything upstream.** Separate, and deferred — see RFC 0.3 §10.1.

## Notes

- `upstream` is already configured with **push disabled**, which is the right guard. Keep it.
- Rebasing our four onto upstream is the alternative to merging. Rebase gives a cleaner history and replays each conflict separately; merge is one resolution and preserves what actually happened. With four commits either is defensible — decide in M1 and record why.

projects.author: f3a38fa646debd4162125e0aed87b6d2393fb1ed9702b6875dcbc0c6529d64d1
projects.title: Shared foundation packages
projects.description:
**Start a new Estiva app with sign-in, the protocol, the design system and the app shell already working** — four packages you install, not four systems you rebuild.

---

# Context

## Source

> **Miky (2026-08-20)** — "I think it would be wise to have basic structure same for all those apps as it will be easier to maintain and keep updating."

> **Miky (2026-08-26)** — "Basically the plan has 4 shared foundational packages: @estiva-ui, @estiva/protocol, @estiva/identity, @estiva/platform."

> **Miky (2026-08-27)** — "The goal is to strip out from Ship and Peek couple of things and unify them: @estiva/identity → so the login/auth works same everywhere, @estiva/protocol → to unify how apps communicate with Buzz/nostr."

## Problem

Three apps had three copies of everything, and the copies **drift silently**. SHA-3 measured it: Peek's `buildMessage` grew an `about` parameter, Ship's copy could not emit one, the same logical message produced different bytes depending on which app sent it — and nothing failed, because each copy was self-consistent. A red build was never going to be the signal.

The customer is the next app's builder. **Leaf first**, and then, per the goals recorded 2026-08-18 — *"recruit engineers in the team"* and *"get a grant"* — an engineer who wants to try this without a week of setup.

## Usage scenarios

> **Miky and Katerina, 2026-08-26 to 08-27**
> Two people extracting shared code from two apps simultaneously, coordinating by hand to avoid collisions: *"I will work on those other 3 and steer AI to not create conflicts with your UI stuff"* / *"I'm not touching issues assigned to you or your claude."* Every hour of that coordination is the cost of the packages not existing yet.

> **Katerina, 2026-08-26** — "We touched peek and ship repos and created new one 'estiva-ui'."
> One shared component needed three repositories moving together.

*Scenario needed: an engineer outside the team starting an app from these packages. Nobody has tried it, so nothing yet proves the claim the project rests on.*

---

# Solution

Four packages on **public npm** under `@estiva-app`, built ESM plus type declarations, released through OIDC with no credential held in GitHub. `protocol`, `identity` and `platform` live in `estiva-foundation`; `ui` has its own repository.

Recorded in [ADR 0002](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/decisions/0002-foundation-packages.md).

## Options considered and rejected

- **One repository for all four.** Was the first answer and lost within hours — `ui` carries a 269-package toolchain the others have no use for, a different maintainer, and the fastest churn.
- **GitHub Packages.** Rejected: install auth on a new machine, which defeats "a third party installs exactly what we install".
- **Publish TypeScript source.** Rejected after it failed — green in Peek and red in Ship, because Ship's `noUnusedLocals` applied to the library's own source and `skipLibCheck` does not help when the files are not declarations.
- **A token in CI.** Rejected after `EOTP`: the account requires 2FA for writes, and npm removes direct publish from 2FA-bypass tokens in January 2027 regardless.

## The rule everything here is built under

Functionality lands in a real app first and is packaged afterwards — extraction with no consumer produces a package shaped like nothing. But *"we will extract it later"* is how the live socket became SHA-7, so the intention is checkable while the code is written: no imports from the app's data layer, every environment touch an injected parameter, tests that run with no app, and the file placed where it is going. SHA-11 records this in ADR 0002.

---

# Milestones

**MS1 — Framing & Shaping · complete.** ADR 0002, and Gate 2 closed 2026-08-27. `@estiva-app/protocol`, `identity` and `ui` are published and consumed by two apps each.

**MS2 — Internal Beta.** SHA-4 (finish the identity verification), SHA-2 (platform + PWA), SHA-7 (socket plumbing into platform), SHA-11 (the ADR amendment).

**MS3 — GA + GTM.** SHA-6, the scaffold template — **this is the GTM artifact, not a chore.** It is what an engineer being recruited actually starts from. Plus a quickstart that takes somebody from the scaffold to a working app end to end.

projects.author: f3a38fa646debd4162125e0aed87b6d2393fb1ed9702b6875dcbc0c6529d64d1
projects.title: Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates
projects.description:
Ship→Peek updates are not real-time and cannot explain themselves. Source ticket: PEEK-109.

## The actual diagnosis

There is no polling. Peek reads the relay **once per topic mount** and never again — `useTopicView.tsx` keys its sync effect on `[topicId, topicFolderId, relayUrl, convex]`, none of which change while you sit in a topic. "Replies take time to appear" is really "replies appear on remount", which is why a reload fixes it.

Four independent staleness sources, each matching a reported symptom:

1. **Messages/replies** — one fetch per mount (`useTopicView.tsx:144-159`). Reactions and deletions are additionally capped to the newest 100 messages per topic (`convex/nostr/sync.ts:41`), so an older message never picks up a reaction at all.
2. **Ship projects/issues in the sidebar** — `TopicProjectPanel.tsx:250-269` resolves once, keyed on a folder id that never changes. The file admits it: "the panel reflects the moment it resolved and does not live-update". A project created in Ship after the panel mounted never appears.
3. **Everything outside topics never syncs at all** — the only relay-read call sites are `useTopicView` (channel) and `AuthGate` (profiles). DMs, inbox, Desk and Screener have no read path.
4. **Auth failure is silent** — `useTopicView.tsx:150` calls `validToken()` and returns with no signal; relay failures below are `console.warn`. Silent refresh exists (PEEK-108) but it is a `setTimeout`, which browsers throttle in background tabs. The UI cannot distinguish "nothing changed" from "I stopped being able to ask".

## What is already true (verified live, 2026-08-21)

- `wss://estiva.estiva.app` accepts a WebSocket upgrade through Cloudflare from Peek's origin and immediately sends `["AUTH","<challenge>"]`. Verified with curl; **pass `--http1.1`** or the same request returns NIP-11 JSON, because `Connection`/`Upgrade` are not HTTP/2 headers.
- NIP-11 reports `supported_nips` including 42, `auth_required: true`, `max_subscriptions: 1024`, `max_filters: 10`.
- **One subscription covers messages, reactions AND deletions.** `buzz-core/src/filter.rs:68-90` has an explicit `#h` fallback to `StoredEvent.channel_id` for events carrying no `h` tag (kind:7, kind:5, whose channel is derived at ingest). So `{"#h":[channelUuid]}` delivers messages + reactions + deletions + assertions in one REQ. The current HTTP path needs four sequential round trips to do less.
- **The projection is reusable unchanged.** PEEK-106 already split credential from projection: `importChannel` / `importReactions` / `importResolutions` take events, not tokens.
- **Convex is already reactive.** Once a row lands, every open view updates. The only missing link is relay→Convex.

## Two gates

**Gate 1 — Estiva ID must sign kind:22242 (blocking).** `estiva-id/src/db/seed.ts:79` gives Peek `[9,7,5,9007,27235,1851,9101,9002]` — no 22242, so Peek cannot answer the AUTH challenge and every REQ returns `auth-required`. The socket looks healthy and delivers nothing. Deploying needs a **manual re-seed**: `update.sh` runs `migrate`, never `seed`. Unlike PEEK-128 this is only one gate — AUTH never goes through `ingest.rs`, `Kind::Authentication` is built into `buzz-auth/src/nip42.rs:52`, so no Buzz change and no relay deploy.

**Gate 2 — one subscription per channel (silent trap).** `buzz-relay/src/handlers/req.rs:1013` returns `None` when filters name more than one distinct `#h`; `subscription.rs:84-113` then registers the subscription as *global*, and `fan_out_scoped:273-288` consults only the channel indexes for channel-scoped events. The invariant is stated at `subscription.rs:321-325`. A multi-channel subscription returns correct history at EOSE and then receives **zero** live events. One REQ per channel; 1024 per connection is no practical ceiling.

## Why the socket stays in the browser

`convex/nostr/sync.ts:18-20` proposes an external consumer holding the socket. An identity is obtainable — `estiva-id/src/domain/roles.ts` has role identities with a client-credentials grant. But Buzz gates reads **per channel**: `handlers/event.rs:181-196` filters live fan-out through `is_member_cached(community, channel, pubkey)` and fails closed on private channels. A service identity would need membership in every topic — a product decision (a bot in every conversation), not an implementation detail. `convex/crons.ts` already reached this conclusion. Convex keeps the projection; only the socket moves.

## Shape of the fix

One shared WebSocket per tab. One subscription per open channel. Live events routed into the existing Convex import actions. Convex reactivity carries it to the UI. The HTTP path stays as the backfill on subscribe (it owns the `since` cursor and paging) and as the fallback when the socket is down — so the change is additive and a WS failure degrades to today's behaviour rather than to nothing.

Ordering caveat to design for: `created_at` is in seconds and several events routinely land in the same one (SPEC §6.2). Imports are idempotent by event id and `nostrSyncedAt` only moves forward (`convex/nostr/data.ts:523`), so live and backfill can overlap safely.

## Milestones

- **M1 — Un-gated relief.** Refetch on focus/visibility plus a short interval, in both the topic sync and the project panel; TTL the profile cache. Turns "until remount" into "within 30 seconds" and probably clears most reported symptoms. Nothing blocks this.
- **M2 — Open the 22242 gate.** Add it to Peek's allowed kinds, scoped by `relay` tag, deploy, **re-seed**, verify the row.
- **M3 — The live socket.** WS client with NIP-42 AUTH and reconnect; refcounted per-channel subscription manager; live events into the Convex projection; `useTopicView` subscribing with HTTP as backfill and fallback.
- **M4 — Honest state.** One derived connection state surfaced once, and relay read failures made visible instead of swallowed.
- **M5 — Beyond topics.** Subscriptions for the inbox, Desk and DMs, which have no relay read path at all today.

## Not yet verified

- The **live** `allowed_kinds` row for peek. `seed.ts` has no 22242; the read to confirm production matches was blocked. Run `docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U estiva_id -d estiva_id -tAc "select client_id, allowed_kinds from app_credentials"` before planning on it.
- No end-to-end 22242 signing test — needs a live user token.

Issues are filed in implementation order. Each is written to be picked up cold by Claude Code.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] A project description does not resolve object references the way an issue's does
issues.description:
**Found while checking whether the project description was missing anything the issue description has (2026-09-02).** It was, but not rendering — RIC-6 gave both surfaces that.

The asymmetry is PRO-7's behaviour, present on one and absent on the other.

| | `IssueView` | `ProjectHeader` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `nostr:naddr…` stripped from the prose | yes, `stripNaddrs(description)` | **no** |
| the referenced object drawn below | yes, `<ForeignReferences>` | **no** |
| rich text rendered | yes | yes (ship#82) |

So a project description containing a reference shows the reader a wall of bech32 *and* nothing that says what it names — which is exactly the outcome PRO-7 removed from the issue surface, on the argument that the bech32 is the half that means nothing to a person.

## It is latent, not biting

Measured on production 2026-09-02: **0 project descriptions and 0 issue descriptions currently carry a `nostr:naddr`.** So nothing is broken on screen today, and this is not urgent.

It is still worth filing rather than leaving to be rediscovered: a project description is the field this whole project chose as its test bed, it is the longest body in the workspace, and the first person to paste a reference into one gets the pre-PRO-7 experience with no indication that the issue surface behaves differently.

## What to build

`ProjectHeader` does what `IssueView` does: `display`/`displayNode` over `stripNaddrs(description)`, and `<ForeignReferences text={description}>` below. Both already exist; this is wiring, not design.

Worth deciding while doing it whether the pairing belongs in one component rather than being assembled correctly twice — that is the shape of defect this is.

## Done when

A project description containing a `nostr:naddr…` renders without the bech32 in its prose and with the referenced object below it, matching the issue surface; and there is a test, because this gap existed with every suite green.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] A description becomes a block document — written, not only read
issues.description:
**Filed 2026-09-02 from a request to "add the rich text field to the project description as well".** Worth correcting first, because it changes what this ticket is:

> **Rendering already covers both.** RIC-6 shipped it for the issue description (ship#80) and for the project description (ship#82) — the second only because opening the page showed 49 literal `**` and `#` markers still on screen after the first. Both surfaces now draw headings, lists, quotes, fences and code spans from a real production body.

What is **not** done, and is the same on both surfaces: **Ship only ever reads a rich text field. It never writes one.** Every description in the workspace is still §13.2 marker text typed into a `<textarea>`, and the block model that RIC-5 shipped has no producer.

## Why this was held back rather than folded into RIC-6

A published event cannot be unpublished. Once Ship writes a block document the corpus starts gaining JSON permanently, so the read path should be seen working on production first — which it now has, on 157 root descriptions and 26 change-carried ones.

## What to build

- **Write a block document** with the `["content-format", "estiva-blocks-1"]` tag, on both the issue and the project description, for a new or edited body.
- **Preserve block ids across an edit.** `assignMissingBlockIds` (protocol 0.9.0) is the primitive and mints only what is missing; an editor that rebuilds the document per keystroke and re-mints detaches every anchored comment silently. RIC-7 binds to these.
- **An editor that produces blocks.** The field is a `<textarea>` today. This is the piece with real product surface in it, and the one to design rather than derive — Peek has TipTap, Ship has nothing, and SPEC §13 is deliberate that the *format* is shared and the *editor* never is.

## What must not break

- **A legacy untagged description still renders as marker text, permanently** (§13.4). 731 published bodies carry no tag and none can be given one.
- **The format is per event, not per object.** A description created as text and edited into blocks is an untagged root plus a tagged change; the fold already reads the tag from the event the value came from.
- **Peek must not regress.** Today it cannot: nothing Ship publishes has changed shape. The moment Ship writes JSON, a consumer that ignores `slots.body.format` renders a block document at a person. `contentFormatOf` and `ResolvedSlot.format` exist for this, and estiva-foundation#26's controls cover the read side — but a Peek check belongs in this ticket's done-when, not in an assumption.

## Done when

Ship writes a block document with the `content-format` tag from both the issue and the project description; a block's id survives an edit that does not replace it, checked rather than assumed; every existing untagged description still renders exactly as it does now; and **Peek is opened against a Ship object whose description is a block document** and shown not to render JSON at a reader.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: add-issue declares only a title, so a capture from a conversation loses what was said
issues.description:
**A capture form with only a title is worse than the context switch it replaces.** `add-issue` declared `{title}` alone, so filing an issue from a Peek conversation had nowhere to put what was actually said.

> **Miky, 2026-09-02** — "we should add description to add-issue. Having only title is not good experience"

## Why it is not a one-line manifest edit

The runtime writes each declared property to a **tag of its own name**, so a foreign consumer's issue arrives with `["description", …]` and empty content. Ship's own composer does the opposite — body in `content`, no tag. Both of Ship's readers only knew about content:

- `fold.ts` — `fields.description ?? event.content`, so Ship's own UI would render it blank
- the issue projection's `body` slot — `{fold, field}` with no `tag`, so every *other* consumer would too

Declaring the input without both fixes publishes descriptions that are on the event, correct, and rendered nowhere. Nothing fails.

## Done when

Filing an issue from Peek's launcher with a description shows that description in Ship's own UI and in a foreign consumer's widget, a title-only capture still works, and the manifest has been read back off production rather than trusted.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The image slot has no producer, measured — it is specified ahead of any app that could fill it
issues.description:
Split out of PRO-2, whose other two slots (list, body) are delivered. Filed rather than left as a comment because it is blocked on something outside this project.

Measured on production 2026-09-02, scanning every tag name on the addressable kinds and on profiles:

kind:39000 Topic     70 events   image-ish tags: 0   (about, closed, d, name, public, t)
kind:30850 Project   15 events   image-ish tags: 0   (buzz-channel, d, description, h, name, title)
kind:30851 Issue    100 events   image-ish tags: 0   (a, d, h, ref, title)
kind:9 / kind:1111  200 events   image-ish tags: 0
kind:0 Profile        7 events   picture: 3

So the only image data in the workspace belongs to a *person*, and that path is already covered without this slot: interop resolves authors into object.people with a picture, and Peek renders an Avatar for any slot declared as: pubkey (ForeignObjectWidget). An image slot would add nothing there.

SPEC §7.2 lists image as 'an avatar, thumbnail or cover, as a URL' for an *object*. Nothing in the ecosystem has one. Declaring it against a person's avatar would be wrong twice: the value is not the object's, and it would duplicate a rendering that already works.

This is the same shape as SPEC §13.3, which is specified ahead of an implementation and says so. The difference is that §13.3 has RIC-5 behind it and this has nobody.

Done when: either an app grows a real image field and declares it — a Topic cover or a File thumbnail are the plausible ones — or SPEC §7.2 records that image is reserved and unproduced, so the next person reading the closed slot set does not assume a consumer is missing something. Whichever, do not implement a consumer for it first: an unproduced slot cannot be verified against anything.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Anchor a comment to a single block — the RFC 0.4 section 6 answer Leaf is waiting on
issues.description:
**Unblocked by RIC-1, and this is the one the rest exists for.** RFC 0.4 §6 (Component anchoring) was open question 2, frozen in 0.3 because it *"needs a real editor to choose against"* and unfrozen in 0.4 once Ship's description field was named as the test bed instead of Leaf.

> **Miky, 2026-08-24** — "You will be able to comment on specific blocks in Leaf." … "You will be able to reference in Peek or Ship conversation not just whole Leaf document, but just specific block like a table or paragraph."

Nothing addressable exists below a document today.

## The shape

An anchor is the object's address plus a block id — the id [SPEC §13.3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) requires to be unique in the document and stable across edits that do not replace the block. A `kind:1111` comment already scopes to an address; the block id is what it gains.

**Depends on the block model ticket.** If ids are generated at render time rather than persisted, there is nothing here to bind to and this ticket cannot start.

## The hard part is not the happy path

An anchor outlives the thing it points at. A block can be deleted, split, or merged by someone who never saw the comment, and the description is replaced wholesale each edit — so the anchor has to fail *visibly*. **A comment that silently detaches and shows as unanchored is the failure mode**, because it looks identical to a comment that was never anchored, and nothing reports it.

That is the same shape as §7.5's widget fallback chain terminating in a closed type: an object that is present but blank is indistinguishable from one you may not be allowed to see.

## Done when

A comment in Ship anchors to one block; the anchor survives an edit that does not replace that block; an anchor to a block that no longer exists **degrades visibly rather than silently**; and **Peek can read the anchor through the projection layer** — one app anchoring and reading its own comments proves nothing about the protocol, which is the whole reason this is being built in Ship rather than in Leaf.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Ship's issue description becomes blocks — the test bed, not Leaf
issues.description:
**Unblocked by RIC-1.** This is the project's premise: the block model is proved in a field that exists today, with a second app already reading it, rather than in Leaf. It is also the escape from RFC 0.3's deadlock — Leaf should not start before §6 is answered, and §6 should not freeze before something can test it.

## What Ship does today

Every body goes through `textContent` in `apps/ship/ui.ts`'s `h()`, deliberately: *"no template strings holding user data — a project title goes through `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, because on a shared relay the titles are written by other people."*

**That position does not change.** [SPEC §13.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) makes it explicit that rendering a body as plain text stays conformant; what is forbidden is *interpreting* one as markup. Ship gains structure by rendering a parsed model through the same node construction, not by relaxing anything.

## What must keep working

Measured 2026-09-02, and none of it moves:

| corpus | bodies | carrying structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| root descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 157 | 135 (86%) |
| description changes (`kind:1851`) | 26 | 21 (81%) |

The change events are the easy ones to miss: **a description edited after creation lives in the `value` tag of a `kind:1851`, not in anyone's `content`.** RFC 0.4 §14.2 missed them and so did the first RIC-1 probe. §13.4's rule is per event, not per object — a description created as text and later edited into blocks is an untagged root plus a tagged change, and the fold must read the tag from the event it took the value from.

## Moved here from RIC-4: the one safe renderer

**Moved 2026-09-02.** SPEC §13.5's *"one renderer that is safe by construction"* was RIC-4's third build item and shipped as neither — Peek got a React renderer of its own, and Ship still has nothing. It belongs here because **Ship is the app that needs it**, and building it in RIC-4 meant designing it against no caller.

One open question comes with it, and it is why this was not obvious: **Ship renders with vanilla `h()` and Peek with React.** "One renderer" therefore cannot mean one component. It has to mean the package emits a node tree — marks and blocks already resolved, nothing to interpolate — and each app maps that to its own DOM. That is what makes §13.5's guarantee structural rather than a convention every app has to remember.

Peek's `MessageBody` is the working reference for the mapping; it should not be the second implementation of the parsing.

## Before starting

The shared `~/estiva-ship` checkout was **123 commits behind `origin/main`** on 2026-09-02, and the layouts differ: `CLAUDE.md` names `web/src/pages/IssuePage.tsx` while that checkout has `apps/ship/views/issue.ts`. Read `origin/main` from a worktree.

The package emits a renderer-agnostic node tree and Ship maps it through node construction that cannot interpolate markup; an untagged legacy description still renders exactly as it does now; **Peek reading the same description does not regress**; and the check is run against a production description of each kind — a root, and one whose current value came from a `kind:1851` — rather than against a locally created issue.

*Amended on closing, 2026-09-02.* Two changes, both stated rather than quietly absorbed:

- **"Ship writes a block document with the `content-format` tag" moved to RIC-8.** Nothing in this ticket wrote one, and holding the write back was deliberate: a published event cannot be unpublished, so the read path should be seen working on production first. It now has been.
- **"the same `textContent` node construction it uses today"** was written when Ship rendered with a vanilla `h()`. ## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.9.0` — `toRenderTree`, one resolved tree for either content model, plus `contentFormatOf` moved down from interop so two folds could read a tag without depending on the projection layer. estiva-foundation#29, #30.
- `@estiva-app/ui@0.3.0` — `EditableText.displayNode`, because the component moved into the shared library mid-ticket. estiva-ui#4.
- Ship renders both descriptions: ship#80 (issue), ship#82 (project).
- The fold carries the format, identically in two repositories: ship#80 and estiva-agent#32, with the conformance fixture's `expected` re-recorded and its `events` and pinned checksum untouched.

## What the verification was worth

The browser check found what four green suites and three green CI runs did not: after ship#80, the **project** description — the longest real body in the workspace at 6,446 characters — still rendered 49 literal `**` and `#` markers. ship#82 fixed it, and `scripts/ric6-live-check.ts` is kept as the check that catches it next time.

**Peek cannot have regressed**, and it is worth saying why rather than asserting it: nothing Ship publishes changed shape. Every description is still the marker text it was. That stops being true the day RIC-8 lands, which is why a Peek check is in *that* ticket's done-when.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] The block model: a rich text field becomes an addressable tree
issues.description:
**Unblocked by RIC-1.** [SPEC §13.3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) specifies a rich text field as a JSON block document. Nothing writes one today — this is the first implementation, and §13.3 was written ahead of it deliberately.

## What a block document is

```jsonc
{ "type": "doc", "content": [
  { "type": "paragraph", "id": "b1", "content": [ … ] }
] }
```

Block types: `paragraph`, `heading` (level 1–3), `bulletList`, `orderedList`, `listItem`, `blockquote`, `codeBlock`, `table`, `horizontalRule`, `attachment`, and `widget` — which names a §7.5 widget and inherits that section's fallback chain.

## The `id` is the whole reason this is JSON

**Every block carries an `id` unique within the document, stable across every edit that does not replace the block.** That is what a comment anchors to, and it is the only thing JSON buys over text. An implementation that generates ids at render time has built a tree and not an addressable one — the anchor ticket then has nothing to bind to.

## What to build

- parse, serialise and **validate** a block document in `@estiva-app/protocol`
- id generation and preservation across edits
- write `["content-format", "estiva-blocks-1"]` on publish; **honour its absence on read** (§13.4)
- an unknown block type renders its inline text and is never dropped silently

**Moved here from RIC-4 (2026-09-02):** the **inline JSON node parser and serialiser** — §13.1's right column, `{"type":"bold"}` and friends. RIC-4 shipped the marker-text serialisation and stopped there deliberately: its own words for this item were *"for the block model to consume"*, and until this ticket exists there is no consumer to design it against. It is a small symmetrical addition to `content.ts`, and it is needed here on day one, because a block's inline content is exactly these nodes.

So this ticket owns the block layer **and the inline layer's second serialisation**. What stays shared with messages is the *vocabulary* — the same six marks, the same meanings — not the encoding.

## Done when

The package round-trips §13.1's inline JSON nodes against the marker text of the same content, so the two serialisations provably carry the same marks; the package can round-trip a block document; ids survive an edit that does not replace the block; a document containing an unknown block type still yields its text; **the absence of a `content-format` tag is treated as marker text on read**; and **a legacy description that begins with `{` is still read as marker text** — §13.4 forbids deciding by sniffing, and that is the case which proves it.

*Amended on closing, 2026-09-02.* The original clause also said the tag is **written on publish**, which nothing in this ticket's scope can do — the package has no publisher, and RIC-6 is the first writer of a block document. That half was already stated verbatim in RIC-6's done-when, so it is dropped here rather than duplicated into a clause this ticket could never satisfy.

## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.7.0` — `blocks.ts` and the inline layer's JSON serialisation. estiva-foundation#27.
- The read half of §13.4 is met by `contentFormatOf` in `@estiva-app/interop` (#26, another session, landed mid-ticket), not by this package. `behaviour.test.ts:1502` is the no-sniff control; the protocol side adds the matching case — a `{`-leading legacy body parses as marker text and `parseBlockDocument` refuses it.
- 227 tests, with controls: dropping `code` from the JSON encoding fails 4, re-minting ids unconditionally fails 2.

**Note for RIC-6: 0.7.0 is merged but not yet published.** The registry serves 0.6.0 until somebody pushes the `protocol@0.7.0` tag.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: interop was published four times with no CI workflow, and release does not run tests
issues.description:
Opening a PR against packages/interop showed "no checks". hello, identity and protocol each have a check-*.yml; interop never got one. release.yml builds and publishes on a tag without running npm test, so 0.3.0 through 0.6.0 shipped having run on nobody's machine but the author's.

An absent check reads like a repo that does not gate rather than a gap, which is why nobody noticed across four releases.

Fix in https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-foundation/pull/24 — a check-interop.yml mirroring check-protocol, plus a typecheck pass over test/*.test.ts, which node --test does not do. That pass immediately found seven assertions of the form assert.equal((found?.tickets).length, 10): the parens short-circuit the optional chain, so a regression throws a TypeError instead of failing the assertion by name. All seven were passing.

Done when: a PR touching packages/interop reports a check, a deliberate type error in test/ fails it while node --test stays green, and someone has decided whether release should gate on the package's own check rather than only on the tag.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] The inline vocabulary lands in @estiva-app/protocol
issues.description:
**Unblocked by RIC-1.** [SPEC §13.1](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) names six marks — bold, italic, underline, code, link, reference — and two serialisations of them: markers in a message, JSON nodes in a block document. This ticket is the one implementation.

## Why it belongs in the package

Wire-visible content, so SPEC §10's test applies: *would the relay notice if two apps disagreed?* It already does. Today there are **three producers and two renderers and no shared code** — Peek's `src/lib/textParsing.ts` is the only implementation of the marker dialect anywhere, and Ship has none on purpose.

## What to build

- **Marker text** (§13.2) — parser and serialiser, including the two conservatism rules that keep published text unchanged: no whitespace at the inner edges, no alphanumeric adjacent to a marker.
- ~~**Inline JSON nodes** (§13.1, right column)~~ — **moved to RIC-5, 2026-09-02.** Its own justification said "for the block model to consume", and RIC-5 is that consumer; building it here meant designing against no caller.
- ~~**One renderer** (§13.5)~~ — **moved to RIC-6, 2026-09-02.** Ship is the app that needs it, and the move surfaced the question that made it non-obvious: Ship renders with vanilla `h()` and Peek with React, so "one renderer" has to mean a node tree both map, not one component.

## `code` is the new part, and it is the point

Measured 2026-09-02: **200 of 548 published messages carry a backtick span** — more common than bold (179) — and **no renderer has ever handled one.** Peek's editor has code spans disabled and its parser has no backtick rule. This is Miky's 2026-08-21 request, and it is one mark, not a project.

## Two things to be careful about

- **`textParsing.ts` is not all mark code.** It also holds mention and bracket-reference regexes bound to Peek's mock fixtures (`PEOPLE`, `TOPICS`, `APP_FILES`). **Only the mark layer moves.** The mention layer is RIC-2's.
- **A `nostr:` reference is the token, not the product behaviour.** This ticket makes the token parse and render; RIC-2 decides what a mention *does*.

## Done when

*Amended 2026-09-02 when two build items moved out — the original text asked for "both serialisations", and the second one went to RIC-5 with its consumer.*

The package exports a parser and serialiser for **marker text**; **Peek's marker code is replaced by it rather than duplicated**; a body containing a backtick span renders as code in Peek; and the round-trip is checked against a sample of the **real published corpus**, not hand-written fixtures — 548 message bodies exist to test against and a fixture that agrees with the parser proves nothing.

## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.6.0` — `content.ts`, with `code` and fenced code added to the dialect. estiva-foundation#25.
- Peek deletes its copy and reads the package; `code` re-enabled in the editor, so backticks can be typed and not only read. peek#112.
- SPEC §13.2 amended: rule 2 does not fence a backtick. estiva-docs#56.
- `test/corpus-bodies.json` — 152 real published bodies. It found two defects the unit tests could not see: `stripInlineFormatting` was never idempotent, and rule 2 was wrong about backticks.
