issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Delete is hidden from an agent's owner, who the relay would permit
issues.description:
**`ProjectPage.tsx` gates the Delete control on `canDelete: project.author === me`.** The relay is more permissive than that, so the one person who most needs the control never sees it.

## What the relay actually allows

`validate_standard_deletion_event` (`buzz-relay/src/handlers/side_effects.rs:179`) accepts an `a`-tag deletion when the actor is the target's author **or** `is_agent_owner(target_author, actor)`. So the owner of an agent may delete objects that agent authored. Ship never offers it.

## How it was found

An empty `Read-state sandbox` project, authored by the agent, could not be removed by anybody:

- **Archive was refused** — `restricted: not a channel member`. Archive publishes `KIND_LL_CHANGE`, which is in the relay's `requires_h_channel_scope` list, so it is scoped to the project's record Folder. That Folder was a channel with no members, which makes archive, rename, status and re-pairing all impossible. The relay's own comment on that list anticipates this: *"one of them forgetting the `h` would put an unreachable object in the shared space that nobody can unpublish."*
- **Delete would have worked**, because a deletion derives its channel from an `e` tag only. An addressable target leaves `channel_id` as `None`, so no membership check runs at all. But Ship hid the button from the owner, and there is no `delete-project` command in the agent CLI either — `store.deleteProject` exists and nothing exposes it. It took a one-off script.

## Why Ship cannot just widen the check

Ownership lives in `users.agent_owner_pubkey`, set from the NIP-OA attestation and read only server-side. **No event carries it and no HTTP route returns it**, so Ship has no way to compute the real predicate. Ship's directory is `kind:0` profiles and nothing else.

## Proposed fix

Offer the control and let the relay adjudicate, which is exactly what **Archive** already does. The confirm dialog is already honest — it says this is a NIP-09 request relays may decline, warns that issues are not deleted, and points at archiving as the reversible option — and a refusal already surfaces as `Delete rejected — <reason>`.

The alternative, exposing agent ownership so a client can compute it, is a relay change and a bigger question than this ticket.

## Done when

A person who owns the authoring agent can delete that agent's project from Ship, and someone with no claim to it gets a legible refusal rather than a hidden control.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The launcher's project picker shows pre-rename names for every project but one
issues.description:
Seen creating an issue from the launcher: the picker offered 'Peek's Intelligence' for a project Ship calls 'Intelligence in Peek'. The project was renamed by a change event; the picker showed the name still on the root.

My optimisation, and the trade was deliberate but wrong at the edge. creatableUnderAsViewer (src/nostr/foreign.ts, PRO-4) resolves ONE project properly — to learn the manifest, which is per kind rather than per object — and takes every other project's label straight off the root event's name/title tag. Fifty resolves to fill a dropdown seemed the expensive way to ask a cheap question.

But a title is a folded field in Ship, exactly so a rename by somebody who does not own the record has somewhere to live. Reading the root tag reads the name before any rename. So the picker is right for whichever project happens to sort newest and stale for the rest.

Not fixable by resolving everything: that is 50 objects at ~940ms each, which is the cost the shortcut exists to avoid.

Options: fetch the projects' change events in one extra query filtered by #a over all the addresses, and fold just the title field — one round trip for the whole list rather than one per project. That is the same shape as the batching in interop 0.6.0 and reuses foldChanges.

Done when: a renamed project shows its current name in the picker, and filling the picker still costs a bounded number of requests rather than one per project.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: estiva-agent's vendored copy of Ship's fold is stale, so the CLI answers wrong
issues.description:
The CLI shows no display key for an issue whose key lives in the change stream.

estiva-agent vendors Ship's src/ at identical paths — the seam comment in ship/web/src/api/index.ts says so and calls them 'never edited from the UI'. The copy has drifted:

  ship    src/fold.ts:593  ref: fields.ref?.value ?? tag(event, 'ref')
  agent   src/fold.ts:578  ref: tag(event, 'ref')

So 'ship issues' prints a blank for the issue created from Peek, while Ship's UI correctly shows INT-1. The change event is on the relay; only the agent's fold cannot see it.

This is the second drift found in two days. The first was cosmetic — kinds.ts lacks PRO-2's stage field, same values and labels, nothing misbehaves. This one produces a wrong answer, which is the difference that makes it worth a ticket rather than a note.

Why it matters more than one field: the agent's own header argues that it reads through Store and foldFolder rather than querying directly, precisely so 'this CLI and ship.estiva.app agree'. A silently divergent copy defeats the stated reason for the design.

The vendoring has no mechanism behind it. Nothing copies, nothing compares, nothing fails when the two differ — it is a convention held up by whoever remembers.

Options: a check in CI that diffs the vendored files against Ship's and fails on drift; or publishing the fold as a package the way protocol and interop were extracted, which is the direction SHA-3 and SHA-5 already went.

Done when: 'ship issues' shows INT-1 for the Peek-created issue, and something fails when the two copies diverge again.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: A manifest cannot say which fields the owner fills in, so a consumer shows a blank and an agent invents one
issues.description:
Found by PRO-4, and the half that RFC 0.4 §13.9 deliberately left open.

An issue created from Peek arrives with no display key. That is correct: a ref is the project title plus a count of its siblings, so only Ship can compute one, and Ship's manifest rightly declares add-issue with just a title. §13.9 records the rule that follows — a property the owner derives must live in the change stream, because a NIP-33 address is (kind, pubkey, d) and the owner cannot rewrite a root it did not sign.

What is missing is a way for the manifest to SAY so. A consumer holding the object cannot tell 'you may not set this, the owner will' from 'this is simply absent'. Both render as a blank.

Today that is cosmetic. It stops being cosmetic when an agent fills these forms from context, which is §13.4's second caller and the reason object-creating actions were made renderable at all. Nothing tells it not to invent an issue number, and a made-up PRO-15 is indistinguishable from a real one. That is the driver: a label saying 'this field is mine to fill in' is the difference between an assistant leaving it alone and confidently making one up.

Three shapes, researched:

1. INFER. A field is settable iff some action's input.properties names it. Ship's status and assignee have actions; ref has none, so the inference picks out exactly the right field today. Free, no manifest change. But it cannot tell 'the owner will assign this' from 'nobody can set this and nobody will', and those want opposite renderings — pending versus absent.

2. ON THE SLOT — {tag: 'ref', derived: true}. Sits where a consumer is standing when it needs the answer: a blank slot is the moment you choose between drawing a dash and drawing 'not yet assigned'.

3. ON RECORDS — records.derived: ['ref']. Coherent, since the rule is 'derived fields live in the change stream' and records describes the change stream. But it is a different part of the document from the one a renderer reads.

Prior art, all solving this: JSON Schema / OpenAPI readOnly ('may appear in a response, must not be sent in a request'); GraphQL, where the field is simply absent from CreateIssueInput, which is option 1 formalised by a type system; Linear and Jira, where issue keys are server-assigned and the API refuses to set one.

Recommendation: option 2. It is where the consumer reads, it is one optional key, and unlike option 1 it distinguishes pending from absent.

Note on what it is NOT: authority here is an honour system — anyone can publish anything, as §13.4 already says about vocabulary validation. So this declares intent, not enforcement, which argues for the cheapest honest expression rather than the most rigorous.

Done when: a manifest can mark a field owner-derived, the runtime carries it through to the resolved object, a consumer can render 'not yet assigned' distinctly from a blank, and Ship declares it for ref.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Peek needs window.__readState(), because four things were built, wired and never ran
issues.description:
Ship got this in ship#72 and it changed how quickly its read-state bugs were found. Peek has the more complicated read path and none of the visibility.

## The evidence, all from one day

Four separate times, Peek's read-state code was correct and something one layer out meant it never ran. None of it was visible to a unit suite, and all of it surfaced only by somebody using the thing and noticing an absence:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `useMergedReadState` was written by CRO-5, given a cache to fill by CRO-6 and a diff by CRO-7, and **mounted by none of them** (peek#97) | the merge never ran; the cache stayed empty; the dual-run had no data |
| the horizon cache was never written | consequence of the above, invisible |
| the dual-run comparison was never computed | consequence of the above, invisible |
| the debug menu holding the readout **has no button on the real app** (peek#105) | it computed all day with nothing able to open it |

Each ticket was green. Each PR was correct. The failure was always in the seam between the code and the thing that runs it.

## What to build

`window.__readState()`, mirroring Ship's, plus the parts Peek has and Ship does not.

```
__readState()                    the queue, the cache, the diff, and whether the read path has run at all
__readState.flush()              publish now instead of waiting on the debounce
__readState.refresh()            re-read and re-merge from the relay
__readState.marker('<context>')  one context's value, as a date
```

Report at least:

- **the queue** — `known`, `pending`, `published`, `hydrated`, the retry backoff. `pending` non-empty with a reason is the smell.
- **`lastAttempt`** with a named outcome, as Ship has: `nothing-pending`, `no-session`, `not-hydrated`, `unchanged`, `published`, `rejected`, `failed`. This is the difference between *"Peek did not publish"* and *"Peek could not publish, and here is the gate"*.
- **the merged frontier**, and when it was last fetched.
- **the horizon cache** — how many contexts Convex holds, and how many of them the relay is missing. That number is the cache earning or not earning its place.
- **the dual-run diff**, so it can be read without the debug menu at all.
- **`hasRun`** — whether the read path has executed even once this session.

That last one is the point. A diagnostic that answers *"the merge has never run"* would have caught peek#97 the moment anybody looked, instead of three tickets later.

## Notes

- Ship's version is not gated on a build flag, for the reason that a diagnostic absent from production is one that is never there when it is needed. Same argument applies, and Peek is equally internal.
- Read-only apart from `flush()` and `refresh()`, both of which do only what the app already does on a timer.
- Peek's state is spread across `useReadStateSync.ts` (queue), `readStateQueue.ts` (pending) and Convex (cache), so this needs a little assembly rather than one snapshot.
- Worth checking whether the same shape belongs in `@estiva-app/protocol` once two apps have it, rather than a third copy.

## Done when

`__readState()` answers, on production, why a read marker did or did not reach the relay — without a devtools snippet that re-implements the bridge. Three such snippets were written today and each got the wire format wrong in a different way (bare-array `/query`, the NIP-98 nonce, camelCase `/token`), and every one of those bugs looked like a bug in the app.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The roadmap's counts are hand-maintained, so they drift silently
issues.description:
**The header and the table disagreed with each other, and both disagreed with Ship.**

`ROADMAP.md` read **"48 open of 129, across nine active projects"** while the ten rows directly beneath it summed to **53 of 84**. Neither matched what Ship reports. Eight of the ten project rows were wrong; the widest gaps were `Peek: Feedback & Bugs` (5 / 15 → 1 / 16) and `Agent / Steer` (1 / 7 → 1 / 16).

Refreshed against `ship issues` in https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/46 — the header is now **52 open of 116, across ten active projects**, and every total was checked against the `issues` field `ship projects` reports for the same project (zero mismatches).

## Two things the refresh surfaced

- **"Five _completed_ projects are archived"** was wrong on the adjective. Three are Completed; **Other** — this project — and **Estiva ID: Feedback & Bugs** are Planned. Other holding an open OTH-3 is precisely why OTH-3 needs its own line beneath the table.
- **The bugs list named tickets that are not bugs.** `PEE-1`–`PEE-6` are *Intelligence in Peek* tickets, not `Peek: Feedback & Bugs`. One `PEE` prefix serves both projects — SHI-4 in miniature, inside the same paragraph that argues for fixing SHI-4.

## The underlying problem, which the PR does not fix

The counts are maintained by hand, so they drift silently and in both directions. The header and its own table had drifted apart *from each other*, which means nobody was reconciling even within the one file. A refresh stays true only until the next issue is filed: CON-8 was created minutes before this count and is one of the 52.

Three ways to close it properly, and they are genuinely different:

1. **Drop the counts** and link to Ship, which the document already names as the source of truth for ticket detail one line above the table.
2. **Generate them** — a small script reading `ship issues`, run when the roadmap is edited. `open` is `Todo` + `In Progress`; `total` should use the `issues` field from `ship projects`, which is what this PR's numbers were reconciled against.
3. **Leave it manual** and accept the drift, on the grounds that the document calls itself a working reference and a living document.

## Done when

Either the counts are no longer hand-maintained, or the roadmap stops asserting numbers it has no way to keep true. Verify by adding an issue in Ship and checking whether the roadmap's total is still correct without anyone editing it.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Peek publishes edits as kind:40003 instead of patching Convex
issues.description:
**Peek's edits never leave Convex, so every other reader shows stale text.**

`convex/messages.ts:543` `editBody` is a `ctx.db.patch(m._id, { body })` on Peek's own row and publishes nothing. The action beside it, `deleteMessage`, does publish — `publishDeletions` → `buildDeletion` → one `kind:5` per target (`src/api/actions.ts:226`). Peek publishes messages, replies, reactions, resolutions and deletions outward; **edits are the one thing it keeps local.** `40003` appears nowhere in the repo, and Peek's `KIND` table (`convex/nostr/events.ts:41`) has no edit kind.

The consequence is live today and is not agent-specific: a human edits in Peek, the relay keeps the original `kind:9` body, and Ship's conversation view — and every other reader — shows the old text indefinitely, with nothing announcing the divergence.

By ADR 0001's own rule this is a conformance defect rather than a missing feature:

> Convex may never be the source of truth for something the relay owns

Convex's `messages.body` is currently exactly that for the body of a `kind:9`.

## Scope — the publish half only

**CON-4 owns the model**: the wire shape, the ordering rule, what a reader sees, who may edit. This is Peek's implementation of whatever CON-4 decides and should not land ahead of it. Filed separately only so the Peek-side defect is visible and assignable; CON-4's warning stands — Peek building its own answer is the drift SHA-3 removed.

The mechanism already exists in Buzz and needs no relay change:

- `build_edit` (`crates/buzz-sdk/src/builders.rs:377`) — kind 40003, content = the full new body, tags `h` = channel and `e` = target event id, 64KB cap. The original `kind:9` is never mutated, so its event id is stable and replies pointing at it survive.
- `validate_edit_ownership` (`crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:810`) — signer must be the target's effective author *or* the owning human of the agent that authored it; target must be in the same channel; a self-edit is re-gated on current membership so a removed member cannot mutate old messages.
- The relay does **not** fold. `/query` returns edits in the aux closure alongside rows (`crates/buzz-relay/src/api/bridge.rs:383`); the client folds latest-wins by `created_at` (`desktop/src/features/messages/lib/formatTimelineMessages.ts:222`).

## The gate to clear first

**`40003` is in no `allowedKinds` list** — not Peek's `[9, 7, 5, 9007, 27235, 1851, 9101, 9002, 9008]`, not Ship's, not the agent's. Adding it is an Estiva ID seed change plus a re-seed per app. Gate 1's lesson applies directly: a grant has two halves, and `allowed_kinds` can read as correct while every use is refused because the deployment half lives in `.env`.

Also unmeasured: whether the Estiva relay deploy accepts a 40003 at ingest. It is native Buzz code rather than a new kind, so it should — but that is inference, not a probe, and it is cheap to settle before building (the DMS-2 principle).

## Done when

Editing a message in Peek publishes a `kind:40003` the relay accepts, and the edited text is what a **different reader** sees — verified from Ship's conversation view or the agent, not from a second Peek window (Track A's lesson: two windows share one Convex deployment and prove nothing). Convex's patch is no longer the only record of the edit.

Related: **AGE-3** (agent edits its own message) is unblocked by this — 40003's ownership rule already covers the agent case.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: @estiva-app/ui's Field never associates its label with the control
issues.description: Found writing PRO-4's form test. Field renders: {children} No htmlFor, and the control is a SIBLING of the label rather than nested inside it — so there is neither an explicit nor an implicit association. A screen reader announces an unlabelled edit box; clicking the label focuses nothing. How it surfaced: getByLabelText(/title/i) in a Testing Library test fails with 'Found a label with the text of: /title/i, however no form control was found associated to that label'. That message is the defect stated precisely, and it is why ActionFormPanel.live.test.tsx queries by role instead — with a comment pointing here rather than working around it silently. Not every control is affected. Select takes an ariaLabel and ActionFormPanel passes field.label, so pickers are reachable by name; TextInput and Textarea are not, and they are the ones inside Field. The fix is available: TextInput spreads InputHTMLAttributes and Textarea will be the same, so both already accept an id. Field does not generate one. Suggested shape — Field calls useId(), renders htmlFor, and provides the id through context so TextInput/Textarea adopt it when the caller passed none. Making callers pass a matching id by hand is the worse option: it is silently breakable and there is nothing to catch a drift. Six call sites across the suite today, so the change is small now and gets no smaller. Done when: a Field-wrapped TextInput is reachable by getByLabelText, clicking the label focuses the control, and a test in @estiva-app/ui pins it so the next primitive added under Field inherits the association rather than the bug.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Peek's cachedPeople should move into interop — Ship pays a request a tick without it
issues.description:
Found finishing SHI-13. Measured against production, per reference per tick, warm:

  Ship project (13 children)  1 request
  Ship issue                  1 request
  Peek topic (50 messages)    2 requests

The extra one is the profile lookup. resolveForeignObject takes an optional PeopleFn; Peek passes cachedPeople(query), Ship passes nothing and so re-reads kind:0 for every author of every child on every tick. A referenced Peek topic is the cross-app case PRO-7 exists for, so it is the one that should be cheapest, not dearest.

Peek's implementation is already the right one and is not trivial: one batched query for the whole set rather than one per pubkey, separate TTLs for a hit and a miss (a missing profile must not be re-asked as often as a stale one), and a cacheAround seam so the batching and the TTLs can be tested without a relay. It lives in peek-app/src/nostr/foreign.ts.

Copy it into Ship and there are two, drifting. It belongs beside createProjectionCache in @estiva-app/interop, for the same reason that one is there: a consumer supplies its environment, the runtime owns the policy.

Watch for: PeopleFn is already a public type, so this is additive. Peek's tests for cacheAround should travel with it — see PRO-13, which is about the interop suite living in the wrong repo for the same reason.

Done when: interop exports a people cache, Peek uses it instead of its local copy with no behaviour change, Ship passes it, and a referenced Peek topic costs one request per tick measured against production.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: ForeignReferences re-resolves every reference from scratch on every tick — 4 requests each, no cache
issues.description:
Found while measuring SHI-12. After the workspace read, this is the largest per-tick cost, and the only one that scales with what is on screen.

ForeignReferences.tsx bumps a nonce on useRefresh, and the effect re-runs resolveForeign for every naddr in the open issue's description. Measured against production: 4 requests per reference, ~600ms, identical on a second resolve — nothing is cached, and no request is conditional on anything having changed.

Per tick, on an issue with N references, on the 10s cadence: 4N requests, 24N a minute. The whole tab has 300 a minute (human_api_calls_per_min, api/bridge.rs). The workspace read is 34 and read state is 1, so ~210/min is spent before references; N=3 is 72 more and the headroom is gone. Confirmed at 244 req/min with N=2.

PRO-10 made this re-resolve for a good reason and the reason still holds: resolving once made the widget a screenshot with a timestamp nobody can see, and the demo claimed liveness. So the fix is not to stop refreshing.

What is missing is a reason to skip. Candidates, cheapest first:
1. Hold the resolved object and re-resolve only when the reference set changes — wrong on its own, that is the screenshot again.
2. Cheap liveness check: one query for the referenced address's latest created_at, refetch the rest only if it moved. 4 requests becomes 1 in the common case.
3. Share one cache across widgets, keyed by address, so the same project referenced from three issues resolves once.

2 and 3 compose. 2 is the one that changes the arithmetic.

Done when: an issue showing three references costs no more than one request per reference per tick while nothing changes, the widget still updates within one tick when the referenced object does, and both are measured against production rather than reasoned about.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Ship's 5s poll does not fit the relay's read quota, even after the protocol work
issues.description:
The package half is done (protocol 0.4.0 concurrency, 0.5.0 request count). What is left is Ship's cadence, and it is arithmetic.

Buzz meters POST /query at human_api_calls_per_min — fixed 60s window, default 300, applied to every bridge call whatever tier the caller is (enforce_http_admission, api/bridge.rs).

Measured against production with protocol 0.5.0: a warm loadAll is 34 requests and 0.9s (was 66 and 8.8s).

  5s poll  -> ~12 reads/min -> 408 req/min  OVER 300
  10s poll -> ~6 reads/min  -> 204 req/min  fits

Ship polls at 5s (REFRESH_MS in web/src/lib/useRefresh.ts). Faster reads made this worse, not better: at 9s a read the poll only managed ~6/min by accident, because useWorkspace coalesced onto the in-flight one. Now that reads are fast, the 5s interval is real.

This is live. I hit 'rate-limited: quota exceeded; retry in 10s' while measuring, on the published serial client.

Options, cheapest first:
1. Raise REFRESH_MS to 10s. One constant. Costs freshness.
2. Back off on 429 and honour the relay's 'retry in Ns' hint, so the ceiling degrades instead of erroring. Should probably happen regardless.
3. Read incrementally — only events since the last read — so a poll costs a fraction of 34. The real fix, and much bigger.

Note 1 and 3 interact: with incremental reads a 5s poll is affordable, so do not raise the interval and then treat it as settled.

Done when: a signed-in Ship tab left open for five minutes issues no query that comes back rate-limited, measured against production rather than reasoned about.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: A workspace read is 66 requests against a 300/min budget — Ship is already over it
issues.description:
Found while measuring SHA-14. Concurrency fixed latency; this is the volume, and it is the one that bites.

Buzz meters every POST /query against human_api_calls_per_min — a fixed 60s window, default 300, and enforce_http_admission (api/bridge.rs) reads the HUMAN limit unconditionally whatever tier the caller is. Ship's loadAll is 66 requests, so 22% of a minute's whole allowance per read, and no client gets more than ~4.5 workspace reads a minute.

Ship polls every 5s. At a 9s read that is ~6 reads/min = ~396 req/min. Already over 300. I hit 'rate-limited: quota exceeded; retry in 10s' on the published serial client while measuring, so this is live now.

With SHA-14 merged a read is 1.6s, so the poll gets ~12 reads/min = ~792 req/min — 2.6x over. Faster reads must not be taken as headroom to poll harder.

Why 66 and not 33: queryAll spends one extra confirmation round trip per filter. A filter whose whole result fits in one page still asks twice, because a short page is not trusted to mean 'complete' — the relay's real ceiling may be lower than the requested pageSize, and NIP-01 has no truncation signal. That distrust is correct and has a test.

The way out is to stop guessing: the relay advertises limitation.max_limit in NIP-11. Read it once per Relay, cache it, and a page shorter than the ACTUAL ceiling is conclusively the end — 66 requests becomes 33, plus one NIP-11 fetch. Ship then fits inside the budget at a 5s poll.

Not the only option; slowing the poll or scoping the read would also work, and are Ship-side. This one is in the package and helps every consumer.

Done when: a Ship loadAll costs one request per filter, the paging tests still pass unchanged (including 'paging does not trust RELAY_PAGE_CEILING'), and a measured read against production stays under the quota at a 5s poll.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Relay.queryAll runs independent filters sequentially — Ship's read is 66 round trips
issues.description:
In @estiva-app/protocol, bridge.ts: 'for (const filter of filters)'. Every filter is paged to completion before the next one starts, though they are independent.

Measured against production (estiva.estiva.app) through Ship's store.loadAll:

  33 filters -> 66 HTTP requests, strictly serial
  median request 206ms
  100% of wall clock spent inside query(), one at a time
  total 9.0s (a second run measured 14.0s)

With a concurrency of 8 over the same filters, same relay, same session:

  sequential 8991ms
  concurrent 1860ms   -> 4.8x, byte-identical answer
                         (15 projects, 159 issues, 429 changes, 327 conversations)

Why it matters beyond speed: Ship polls every 5s and its read takes ~9s, so a read is in flight ~90% of the time. That is what made ship#63 (a status change appearing to do nothing) reachable at all rather than a rare race — and with the fix merged, a status change still takes ~9s to show. Peek and estiva-agent read through the same client.

Not simply 'delete the loop': paging is per filter on the until cursor, and queryAll throws rather than truncating when a cursor cannot advance. Concurrency must preserve that, keep the de-duplication by event id, and stay bounded so a workspace with many Folders does not open an unbounded fan-out at the relay.

Done when: loadAll against production completes in under 2s, returning the same fold as today, with a test that pins the bound and the throw-rather-than-truncate behaviour.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Changing a status did nothing: the re-read after a write joined a read that predated it
issues.description:
Reported: changing a project from Planned to In Progress does not work.

The write was never broken. The relay holds SIX identical 'status -> in_progress' changes for the Projection layer project between 11:53:54 and 11:54:16 — one person clicking a control that kept snapping back. The folded status has read in_progress throughout.

Cause: useWorkspace.refresh coalesced ('if (inFlight.current) return inFlight.current'), and act() awaits it after every write and renders what it resolves with. A read that started BEFORE the write cannot contain it. loadAll against production takes ~9s and the poll runs every 5s, so a read is in flight ~90% of the wall clock — a click almost always lands inside one.

Fix: the poll keeps coalescing; the refresh handed to act always starts a new read, with a 'latest' ticket so an older read landing second cannot overwrite newer state.

PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/ship/pull/63

Done when: picking a status shows the new value without a reload, and a test fails if the re-read is coalesced again.

Residual (filed separately against Shared foundation packages): the status still takes ~9s to appear, because Relay.queryAll runs independent filters sequentially.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Ship has no unread surface, so half of cross-app read state is unobservable
issues.description:
**Blocks CRO-9 check 2 (Peek → Ship), which cannot be run at all today.**

CRO-8 gave Ship the whole machine: it publishes NIP-RS blobs under its own slot, fetches every slot, and merges with the max rule. Verified against production — reading an issue advanced three `thread:` contexts and no container, and all 53 of Ship's contexts appear in Peek's merged frontier.

**And none of it is visible in Ship.** There is no dot, no bold row, no count, nothing. CRO-8 said "before any UI work" and that was the right scope for it, but the consequence is that the project's headline claim is only half observable: *read it in Ship, it clears in Peek* can be checked; *read it in Peek, it clears in Ship* cannot, because Ship never showed unread in the first place.

This is not a regression. Ship has never had unread state — it polls and re-renders, and a person reads the activity feed to see what moved.

## Why Ship is the easy side

No database to reconcile. `web/src/api/readState.ts` already computes the merged frontier, so **the merged state can simply be the read state** — none of the cache-versus-source-of-truth question Peek needed CRO-6 for, and no dual-run needed either, because there is no incumbent to compare against.

The context mapping is already built and tested:

| Ship object | context |
| --- | --- |
| project | its Folder's channel uuid, bare |
| an issue's discussion | `thread:<root event id>` |

## What to decide, because it is not obvious

Peek is conversations-first and a dot on a topic row is self-explanatory. Ship is issues-first, and an issue is not a container — its unread-ness is a property of its **discussions**, which most issues do not have. So:

- **Where does it go?** `IssueRow` / `IssuesTable` / `Board` are the candidates for an issue; `ProjectsView` for a project. An issue with no conversation has nothing to be unread about, and marking every issue with activity unread would make the whole list bold on day one.
- **Does a project's dot roll up its issues' discussions?** A project's own container context covers its channel; an issue's thread is a separate context. Rolling up is a product decision, not a protocol one.
- **What about `activity`?** Ship's changes feed is the thing people actually scan. It may be a better home for "new since you looked" than a per-row dot, and it is not a NIP-RS context at all.

## Traps

- **§11.3 is applied at read time, never by writing extra keys.** `effective(thread:<root>)` is the later of the thread's own marker and its container's. Writing the container's value onto each child gives the same answer today and is permanent, because blobs are grow-only.
- **Ship has no cache behind the protocol.** Peek keeps one (CRO-6) so a container read before the horizon still reads as read. Ship's 90-day horizon is all there is, so a project untouched for longer reads as never-read. Decide whether that is acceptable or whether Ship needs its own cache.
- **Absence means unread** (SPEC §11.6). Ship has years of history and no read state for any of it, so on the first run everything is unread. That is correct and it is also a terrible first impression — needs a deliberate answer, not a default.
- Do not put any of this in `src/` or `lib/nostr/`: vendored into `estiva-agent` by copy, held by `scripts/conformance.test.ts`.

## Done when

Ship shows unread state derived from the merged NIP-RS frontier, reading in Peek clears it in Ship without a reload, and CRO-9 check 2 is runnable.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The interop suite stayed in Peek, so the package travels with 9 tests instead of 76
issues.description:
**`@estiva-app/interop` is published and its exhaustive suite is not in it.** The 67-case `projection.test.ts` lives in `peek-app/interop/`, where the code used to be. The package carries 9 tests of its own — the public surface, README accuracy, and core resolution against the built artifact.

That is backwards. ADR 0002 §10 constraint 3: *its tests run with no app; untested code does not travel.* These tests need no app — they run against an array standing in for the relay — so nothing excuses them staying behind. The consumer that happens to have been first is not their home.

## What makes it more than a move

The suite is **vitest** (`describe/it/expect`); the foundation packages are **node:test** (`assert`). Adding vitest to one package would make it the only one, so the cases have to be converted.

**Do not do this with a regex.** I tried, and it produced assertions that had silently lost their assert:

```
expect(found?.openCount, 2)        // was expect(...).toBe(2)
expect(found?.tickets).length, 10) // syntactically mangled
```

11 of them, and the dangerous ones are the ones that still parse. A suite that looks converted and asserts nothing is worse than no suite, because it reports success. Convert by hand, or with a codemod that is itself tested against the before/after of a few known cases.

## The one wrinkle

`resolveFolderProjectSlotsForTest` is used twice and is deliberately **not** exported from the package's public entry point — a test helper in a public API is a promise nobody meant to make. Import it from `../dist/projection.js` rather than `../dist/index.js`; that keeps the public surface honest while giving the suite what it needs. Protocol's `.ts` tests already run against `dist`, so the pattern exists.

## Done when

The 67 cases run in `packages/interop/test` under `node --test`, Peek's copy is deleted rather than left beside it, and the count is checked: 76 tests in the package, not 9. **Spot-check that a few converted assertions still fail when the behaviour they cover is broken** — that is the only thing that distinguishes a real conversion from the one above.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Peek has no URL for any object — you cannot link to a topic
issues.description:
**Selecting a topic does not change the address bar.** Peek has no routing at all: no hash routes, no per-object paths. Copying the URL of anything in Peek gives you `https://peek.estiva.app/`, which names nothing.

## Why this is filed now, and separately

It is the prerequisite for RFC 0.5 §7 (addressing) and **it does not depend on that decision.** Whatever grammar is accepted, Peek needs per-object URLs first — and it needs them anyway, because "send me a link to that conversation" is a thing people ask for in a chat app and there is currently no answer.

Filed apart from the grammar deliberately, per roadmap rule 2: §7 is in a draft RFC gated on SHA-13, so its implementation tickets are not filed yet. This one is not gated on anything.

## The asymmetry that surfaced it

Ship's URLs already carry the address — `#/issue/<addr>` and `#/project/<addr>` — so copying Ship's address bar already yields something resolvable, wrapped in an app URL. Peek's yields nothing. So the common case (a person copies the URL they are looking at) works in one direction of the suite and is impossible in the other.

## What to build

Per-object routes for Topic at minimum. If §7 is accepted by the time this is picked up, use its grammar:

```
peek.estiva.app/topics
peek.estiva.app/topic/<slug>-<d>
```

where `<d>` is the channel uuid — a Topic's `d` **is** its channel uuid, measured across all 50 production channels (RFC 0.4 §5.2), so no new identifier is needed.

If §7 is not decided yet, a hash route carrying the uuid is still strictly better than nothing and is forward-compatible: the identity is in the URL either way, and only the shape around it changes.

## The infrastructure half

Path routing needs an index.html fallback in Peek's nginx config, or a real path 404s on reload. Ship's `router.ts` documents this trap from the other side — it uses hashes *because* `deploy/nginx.conf` has `try_files … =404` with no rewrite. Peek is served differently (port 8082, its own deploy), so check rather than assume the same applies.

## Done when

A person can copy the URL of a Peek topic, paste it somewhere, and land back on that topic — including on a cold load in a new tab, which is the case a hash-free path breaks first.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Degrade honestly where the on-device model is unavailable
issues.description:
**A meaningful share of people will never see prefill, and nothing should look broken for them.**

## Why it is a real ticket rather than a caveat

Chrome's Prompt API is **stable in Chrome 138+ and desktop only** — Windows 10/11, macOS 13+, Linux, ChromeOS Plus. **Not Android. Not iOS.** It also needs **22 GB** of free storage and either **>4 GB VRAM** or **16 GB RAM with 4+ cores**, and the model downloads on first use per origin.

So the population that gets prefill is: recent Chrome, on a desktop, with room and hardware, after a download has completed. Everyone else — including anyone on a phone, and anyone in Safari or Firefox — gets the form.

## What to build

- **Check before offering.** `LanguageModel.availability()` decides whether prefill is mentioned at all. Do not show a feature that will not run.
- **Never block on the download.** The form opens immediately, always. Prefill arrives if and when it can, and the person can start typing over it.
- **Say nothing rather than apologise.** A form that opens empty is the normal case, not a degraded one. An error, a greyed-out sparkle, or "AI unavailable on your device" makes a working product feel broken.

## The state that needs a decision

**Prefill arriving after the person has started typing.** The model is not instant and the form is usable immediately, so the two will race. Overwriting what somebody typed is unacceptable; discarding a useful suggestion silently is a waste. This needs a designed answer rather than whichever the implementation makes easy.

## Done when

The form is fully usable on a device that will never run the model, prefill is never offered where it cannot run, no download blocks anything, and the typing-race has a designed behaviour rather than an accidental one.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Prefill the form from the thread, using the action's own schema as the constraint
issues.description:
**The cheap version of intelligence, and the reason it is cheap is that the contract already exists.**

> **Miky (2026-08-31)** — *"Explore Prompt API as it could allow us cheaply prefill the form based on the context from the thread."*

## The insight this rests on

**A manifest action's `input` is already a JSON Schema.** Ship declares `add-issue` with `type: object`, `properties`, `required`. Chrome's Prompt API takes a JSON Schema as `responseConstraint` on `prompt()`.

So the same declaration that draws the form constrains the model. **No mapping layer, no per-app prompt engineering, and it works for an app nobody here wrote** — an HR tool declaring `add-candidate` gets prefill on the day it publishes its manifest.

## Why on-device is the point, not a detail

The Prompt API runs Gemini Nano locally — *"No data is sent to Google or any third party."* A work thread is confidential, and sending one to a cloud model to save typing would be a disclosure. **This is the only shape of this feature consistent with how the rest of the suite treats privacy.**

## The API, concretely

- `LanguageModel.availability()` before offering anything
- `LanguageModel.create()` to get a session; first use per origin downloads the model, with a `downloadprogress` event
- `session.prompt(input, { responseConstraint: <the action's input schema> })`
- `session.contextWindow` / `session.contextUsage`, and a `contextoverflow` event

## The open design question

**How much thread to send.** A long topic will not fit the context window. Current conversation, last N messages, or the whole thread each produce different output, and the choice is worth testing rather than deciding on paper. `contextUsage` is how you find the ceiling honestly.

## Never auto-submit

Prefill and confirm. A wrong issue filed silently is worse than no issue, and the person is right there. Miky's own framing: *"we just confirm it or edit it before submission."*

## Done when

Opening create-issue from a real conversation arrives with the title and description already filled from that conversation, every field is editable, nothing submits without a person, and the values conform to the manifest's declared schema because the schema was the constraint.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Topic and people search in the launcher, over NIP-50
issues.description:
**The relay already has search, and nothing uses it.**

> **Miky (2026-08-31)** — *"Try to make searching in Peek's topic work. Check if Buzz has some search feature."*

**It does.** The relay's NIP-11 advertises `supported_nips: [1, 2, 10, 11, 16, 17, 23, 25, 29, 33, 38, 42, 50, 56, 43]` — **NIP-50 is live** and read from production on 2026-08-31.

## What it does

The launcher finds things as well as creating them: topics by name, people by name, and — the useful one — messages by content.

> **Miky (2026-08-19)** — *"We could also add basic Topic search and People / Team search to make it little bit more useful."*

## Why it belongs in this project rather than in Peek's navigation

The launcher is the one surface where "do a thing" and "find a thing" are the same gesture. Splitting them means Cmd+K does half the job and something else does the other half.

## Watch

- **A search returns only what the reader may read.** A result set is access-filtered, so an empty result and a refused one look identical — the same rule as everywhere else in the suite.
- **There is no relevance ranking to lean on.** Order is the client's decision, and a result count is "of what I fetched" rather than a total.
- **NIP-50 is advertised, not measured.** Confirm what the relay actually returns for a `search` filter before designing around it — advertised support and working support are different claims, and this workspace has been caught by that distinction before.

## Done when

Cmd+K finds a topic, a person and a message from production by typing part of them, and the empty state distinguishes "nothing matched" from "nothing you can read".

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Assign and update an existing issue, not only create
issues.description:
**Not every capture is a new object.**

> **Katerina, 2026-08-19** — *"it would also be useful to assign existing issue, not just create new one"*

Deciding in conversation that somebody will pick something up, or that a thing is now done, is the same moment as creating — with a different verb and an existing target.

## What it does

The launcher offers the manifest's **field-setting** actions as well as its object-creating ones. Ship already declares `set-issue-status`, `assign-issue`, `set-project-status` and `assign-project`, and the runtime already resolves them into controls: a select where the manifest names a vocabulary, a people picker where it asks for a pubkey.

**Nothing new has to be declared.** These actions have been in Ship's manifest since it was written and no consumer has offered them from a launcher.

## The part that needs designing

**Choosing the target.** Creating needs a container; updating needs a specific object. Candidates worth trying rather than assuming: objects already referenced in this conversation, objects in this Folder, and search (see the search ticket).

Objects referenced in the thread is the strongest default — it is the same context the person is already looking at.

## Done when

Changing an issue's status or assignee from a Peek conversation publishes a real change event, Ship reflects it, and the target was chosen without leaving the thread.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Put the created object back in the thread as a reference widget
issues.description:
**Without this the capture leaves no trace, which is the actual complaint.**

> **Katerina, 2026-08-19** — *"Now I have no clue this whole conversation has an issue assigned, as I have to open the thread first."*

Creating the issue elsewhere solves the typing and not the knowing. The thread has to end up carrying the thing that was created.

## What it does

After a successful publish, post a message into the conversation carrying a reference to the new object. It renders through the object's own projection — so a Ship issue looks like a Ship issue, drawn in Peek's design language, live rather than a screenshot.

The end state is already designed: Katerina's Storybook covers *"a reply carrying the new issue as a reference widget."*

## Why it is its own ticket

The publish and the trace are separable, and the trace is the half that changes behaviour. A version that creates the issue and says nothing in the thread is worse than useless — it is the current context switch with an extra step.

## Watch

The widget has to survive everything a foreign object can do: the person reading it may not have access, it may be deleted later, it may be a kind this build of Peek does not know. Those states are already specified — see the design guide's *Something from another app, inside yours*.

## Done when

Creating an issue from a thread leaves a message in that thread which renders the issue live, and a person who cannot read the issue sees the absence honestly rather than a blank card.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Wire the launcher's forms to the projection runtime, so a submit publishes
issues.description:
**The forms exist and do nothing.** Katerina's prototype draws every object-creating action from a manifest-shaped declaration — Ship create issue and project, Peek start a conversation and create a topic — and *"submits publish nothing yet; the projection runtime plugs into one function."*

This is that function.

## What it does

Take the action the person chose, the values they filled in, and the container they are in, and publish the event the manifest names. That is `buildActionEvent` in the projection runtime — it already exists and already validates against the manifest's own vocabulary before publishing.

## Depends on

**PRO-4** (render object-creating actions as forms) and **PRO-1**'s publish path. PRO-4 owns *rendering a declared action*; this owns *what Peek does when somebody submits one*. They must not build the same thing twice.

## Two things not to get wrong

**Never silently pick the destination.** The person is in a conversation, not a project. Something has to choose which container the new object lands in, and the honest default is the one this conversation already belongs to — but it must be shown before it happens. Creating an object in another app somewhere the person did not look is the fastest way to make a shared workspace feel untrustworthy.

**Confirm against what the relay accepted, not against what was sent.** A publish can be refused after it looks accepted — the relay answers a rejected write with `200` and `accepted: false`. A form that closes optimistically will show a success for something that never landed, until a reload.

## Done when

Choosing "create issue" in Peek publishes a real Ship issue to production, Ship's own fold shows it as an ordinary issue, and a refusal surfaces with its reason instead of a closed dialog.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] SPEC mandates `records`; the runtime correctly stopped requiring it
issues.description:
**The runtime is already fixed. The specification is not, and the specification is what a stranger implements from.**

## What happened

Both resolvers required `records`, so an app declaring none returned null for the *whole* projection and rendered as **nothing** — which RFC 0.4 §13.3 spends several paragraphs establishing is the worst available outcome, because a blank card reads as *"that app is broken."*

It was never caught because **Ship was the only app that had ever published a manifest, and Ship folds.** Peek is the first publisher that does not: a topic's name is a tag the relay wrote, and a message is immutable. Nothing of Peek's has change events at all.

Fixed in `interop/projection.ts` during PRO-6 — `foldRuleOf()` supplies a substitute rule used **only to fold, never to query**, and callers branch on `manifest.records` to skip the filter.

## The live divergence

**SPEC §7 still mandates it:**

> *An app that publishes objects other apps should render MUST publish a `kind:31990` handler information event whose `content` is a JSON document with `records` and `projections`.*

So a third-party implementer reading the specification either declares a `records` they do not need, or concludes they cannot publish a manifest at all without inventing change events. **The reference implementation and the document disagree, and the document is the one we tell people is the standard.**

**The runtime's own note cites the wrong document.** It reasons *"Nothing in RFC 0.4 §13.1 makes `records` mandatory"* — correct about the RFC, which only describes `records` in a table, and false about SPEC §7, which is ratified and says MUST. Worth correcting in place so the next reader does not re-derive it.

## What to change

1. **SPEC §7** — `projections` is required; `records` is OPTIONAL, and an app with no change events declares none.
2. **SPEC §7.1** — say what a consumer does without it: **skip the change query entirely.**
3. Fix the code comment's citation.

## The trap to write down with it

The first fix used `changeKind: -1` as an unmatchable sentinel and let the queries run. **53 tests passed; production refused the entire filter** — `invalid type: integer -1, expected a 16-bit unsigned number`.

A kind is a `u16` on the wire, so **there is no out-of-band value to reach for.** The query has to be *skipped*, not made unmatchable. A consumer that reaches for a sentinel breaks every query in the batch, not just its own — and the fake relay in the tests will not tell it.

## Done when

SPEC says `records` is optional and says what a consumer does without it, the code comment cites the right document, and a manifest declaring no `records` renders correctly — verified against production rather than against the test relay, since the test relay is what accepted `-1`.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Accept or amend RFC 0.5
issues.description:
**A reading session and a decision, like SHA-10 — and a cheaper one.**

[RFC 0.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/RFC-0.5-ASSOCIATION.md) specifies how files in different apps relate. It exists because RFC 0.4 lets a Folder hold several files of one kind, so **the container can no longer be the relationship** — a project's conversation used to *be* a topic because they shared one channel.

## What accepting settles

- **Three tiers** — none, basic (one file names another, shown in a panel, shared not personal), facet (files are perspectives on one thing and their conversations merge).
- **Facets merge, and never copy.** One comment, two views, ordered by time, origin unlabelled.
- **Declaration is one-sided, effect two-sided** — forced, because a `kind:39000` topic is relay-signed and Peek can never tag it.
- **The access-compatibility invariant** — a facet may not merge conversations that are not equally readable.
- **The two change cases**: removing a facet splits the thread *list* and never a thread; deleting an object never deletes its comments.

## Why it is cheaper than 0.4's acceptance

**No new kind and no Buzz change.** A facet is a tag on a file record, signed by that file's author — so authorization falls out of who holds the key rather than needing a permission model. The expensive relay-maintained version stays available for when the trigger fires.

## What it does not settle

Deliberately deferred with triggers in §8: who may create a facet beyond "you can sign the file", relay enforcement of the invariant (a read rule does it today), and whether a merged view labels which facet a comment was written against.

## The one thing worth arguing about

**§4, the invariant.** It is the only clause that forbids something people will want — faceting a private discussion onto a public object. The argument for it is that the failure is not disclosure (the relay still gates content) but **context collapse for the one person who can see both sides**, who then answers privately in what looks like a public place. If that argument does not hold, the invariant should go rather than be quietly ignored.

## Done when

Accepted or amended, and if amended, what changed and why is on this issue. Association and facet tickets get filed only after that — per rule 2, nothing is filed against the undecided parts.

---

## §7 Addressing was added 2026-08-31, and it is part of this decision

RFC 0.5 gained a section on **what a link looks like**, because the question
turned out to be protocol rather than per-app taste: *people copy the address
bar*, so the URL an app puts there has to be resolvable by a different app. That
is wire-visible under SPEC §10's test — two apps can disagree and a user sees it.

**The grammar:**

```
https://<app>.estiva.app/<type>s                  a directory of that kind
https://<app>.estiva.app/<type>/<slug>-<d>        one object
```

- the **`d` is the whole identity, untruncated** — a consumer resolves
  `{kinds:[<type>], "#d":["<uuid>"]}`, one query, no index and no service that
  can go down and take every link with it
- the **kind comes from the path segment**, so `/project/` means 30850
- the **slug is decorative** — renaming changes it and the link still resolves

**Two findings behind it, both measured rather than assumed.**

*An naddr cannot be the suffix.* It is bech32 over `(kind, pubkey, d, relay
hints)` **plus a checksum over the whole string**, so a slice of it is checksum
bytes rather than the `d` and resolves to nothing without an index. It is also
not stable for one object — relay hints are part of the encoding, and both forms
are live today: Ship's `referenceFor` passes a hint, the runtime's `buildObject`
passes none.

*The pubkey does not need to be in the URL.* `d` is a v4 uuid (0.4 §4.3), so
`(kind, d)` is unique. Measured on production: 235 records across 30850/30851/
39000, **zero** non-uuid `d`, **zero** `(kind, d)` shared by more than one
author. This gives §4.3's existing MUST a second and quieter reason — an app
using a readable `d` would not fail loudly, it would collide and resolve to the
wrong object.

**A consumer resolves an app it has never met** by matching a pasted URL against
the patterns every app publishes in its manifest (`urls`, alongside `web`).
`kind:31990` is global, so this needs no per-app integration and no registry.

## What §7 additionally requires

- **Paths, not hashes.** Ship uses hash routing because it is static files with
  `try_files … =404`. Path URLs need an index.html fallback per app.
- **Peek has no object URLs at all** — no routing, no per-topic path. That is
  the prerequisite, and it is filed separately because it does not depend on
  this decision.
- **Messages still have no URL.** A `kind:9` has no `d`, so it has no place in
  the grammar — the same gap §13.6 records for projections, and PRO-11's.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Comments and Mentions are two sections, not one list
issues.description:
**SPEC §6.4 now requires this, and neither app does it.**

## The rule

SPEC §6.4 has always said a thread attaches to whatever anyone in it referenced, *at any point*, and that the **whole** thread attaches — not just the message carrying the reference. That rule is correct and reads as surprising, and the amendment of 2026-08-31 says why it is safe: **attachment has two strengths and an app MUST present them separately.**

| | in the data | presented as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **a comment** | uppercase `A` at the thread root — the thread *is* about this object | the object's own discussion |
| **a mention** | the address referenced inside a message | *Mentioned in*, secondary and collapsed |

## Why it matters more than it looks

Ship's `conversationsAbout()` currently merges both into one list. So a twenty-message conversation that name-drops an issue on message twenty-one lands **inside that issue's comments**, indistinguishable from a comment somebody wrote about it.

That is also what makes the §6.4 rule defensible at all. Message content is immutable, so an accidental mention attaches **permanently** and cannot be withdrawn — acceptable for a secondary section, indefensible for the primary one.

## Three things to get right

1. **A mention may suggest, never write.** An app MAY offer "add this to the panel"; it MUST NOT create an association on its own. Mentions arrive retroactively and by accident, and a shared record must not reorganise itself because somebody typed a reference.
2. **Counts are approximate.** There is no server to compute "the 5 most recent mentions", so any number is really "of what I fetched". Do not present it as authoritative.
3. **Unreadable means invisible** — see the privacy rule below.

## The privacy rule, and its cost

If a mentioning conversation is one the reader cannot access, **they do not see that it exists** — no count, no locked row, no placeholder.

The consequence has to be accepted deliberately rather than discovered: **two people open the same object and honestly see different numbers, and neither is told.** Do not "fix" that later by showing a global count; the inconsistency is the privacy working.

## Done when

Both apps show two sections, a mention never lands in the comments, a mentioning conversation the reader cannot read is absent rather than redacted, and the count is not presented as authoritative.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Projections are address-only, so a message can never be rendered
issues.description:
**A message cannot be declared in a manifest, and that is measured rather than inferred.**

Confirmed on production while building PRO-6: *"A Message carries no `d` and is not addressable."* Every resolver in the consumer runtime starts from an `AddressPointer`.

## The gap

| object | identified by |
| --- | --- |
| project, issue, document, folder | address — `naddr` |
| Peek topic | address — `naddr` (the relay's `39000`) |
| **a conversation** | **the root event's id — `nevent`** |
| **a message** | **its own event id — `nevent`** |

`projections` is keyed by kind and resolved from an `naddr`; Ship's manifest declares its `web` template as `naddr` outright. So a manifest cannot say how a message renders, and a consumer holding a `nevent` has nothing to look up.

**Why it stayed hidden:** every Ship object is addressable, so the layer works in the one direction it has ever run. It only appears when you ask what a *message* widget would resolve through.

## This is one of six, and the other five are on PRO-6

PRO-6's comment records six things the manifest could not express, all measured against production. **Read them before starting here** — they are siblings of this one, not background:

- `list` matched the parent's *address* while Peek's `h` holds a bare uuid
- `title` is required and a message has none
- **`records` was required by both resolvers**, so an app that folds nothing rendered as *nothing* — §13.3's worst outcome, never caught because Ship was the only publisher and Ship folds
- a `changeKind: -1` sentinel passed 53 tests and was refused by production, because a kind is a `u16`
- a Topic carries no `h` — it is not *in* a container, it *is* one

The third is the most severe and the least specific to messages: **any app that does not fold got an empty render.** Worth deciding whether it belongs here or against the runtime extraction in PRO-1.

## What to change

- a projection may be declared for an event-identified object, not only an addressable one
- the consumer resolves `nevent` alongside `naddr`
- the `web` template learns a second form, so "open this in the app that owns it" works for a message

**A message is not replaceable and has no folded state**, so most of what `records` describes does not apply to it. A projection for an event-identified object is a thinner thing, and the manifest should say so rather than leaving a consumer to infer which halves are meaningful.

**Not declaring actions was the right call in PRO-6** and stays true until this lands: a reply names an *event id*, and the action vocabulary only names a parent *address*, so declaring one would tell a consumer to publish a malformed reply.

## Done when

The consumer resolves `nevent`, Peek's manifest declares a Message projection, a second app renders a real production message through it, and its `web` link opens that message in Peek. **RFC 0.4 §13.6 records the gap** — update it to record the resolution.
