issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Quickstart: build an Estiva app from the scaffold, end to end
issues.description:
**The claim this whole project rests on is that app number four is cheap. Nobody has tested it.**

Depends on SHA-6, which produces the scaffold. This is the walk-through that proves the scaffold is sufficient — and it is GTM material, because the business goals recorded 2026-08-18 are *"recruit engineers in the team"* and *"get a grant"*. An engineer evaluating this suite will judge it by how fast they get something running.

## What it covers

From nothing to a working app: install the four packages, sign in through `@estiva-app/identity`, read and write through `@estiva-app/protocol`, render with `@estiva-app/ui`, and get the app-shell behaviour from `@estiva-app/platform`. Ending at something that reads a real Folder from production and renders it.

**Install auth on a new machine must be nothing** — `npm install`, no token, no `.npmrc`. That was a stated goal of ADR 0002 and this is where it gets checked on a machine that has never seen this workspace.

## The traps it has to name

These each cost a failed release to learn, and a newcomer will hit them in the same order:

- a package's **first** publish is manual; trusted publishing can only be configured on a package that already exists
- `registry-url` in `actions/setup-node` breaks OIDC and reports the failure as `404 Not Found`, which reads as "the package does not exist"
- a **new package name** is invisible on the read path for minutes after a successful publish — 204 seconds measured, while `npm access` already lists it

## Done when

The quickstart exists and **somebody follows it on a machine that has never built this suite, without asking a question that is not answered in it.** Every question they do have to ask is a gap — record it on this issue and fix the doc rather than answering it privately.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Say what changes when unread moves
issues.description:
**Unread is the most-noticed thing in the product, and this is the ticket that stops the cutover being a surprise.**

CRO-7 dual-runs and cuts over. This owns everything around it: what people are told, what "correct" looks like on the day, and what to watch.

## Why it is not boilerplate

The ordering constraint on CRO-6 exists precisely because of this: NIP-RS's fetch horizon defaults to 7 days and **absence of a context means unread**, so cutting over before the horizon cache exists makes every quiet container read as unread. A person seeing every old topic light up does not think "the read-state migration has a horizon problem" — they think the app is broken.

And the failure mode is asymmetric. Unread that *stays* unread is annoying and visible. Unread that is wrongly marked **read** is invisible, and it loses somebody a message.

## What this ticket owns

- **what people are told, and when** — one short note before the cutover saying unread now follows you across apps and devices, and what to do if something looks wrong
- **the day-one check**: a quiet container that should stay read, a busy one that should show correctly, and a second device agreeing with the first
- **the rollback position** — Convex still holds the horizon cache during the dual-run, so what exactly is the way back, and how long does it stay available
- **what proves it worked** — read in Ship, unread clears in Peek, on a second device, verified against the relay rather than the UI

## Done when

The note is written and sent, the day-one checks are run and their results are on this issue, and the rollback window is stated as a date rather than as "for a while".

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Publish the package and write the "add comments to your app in an hour" guide
issues.description:
**GA for the conversation standard, and the guide is the deliverable that tests the claim.**

The goal from 2026-08-28: Leaf, *"and in future other apps"*, get full comment functionality — reactions, formatting, edit, delete, read/unread — by reusing rather than rebuilding. Until somebody does that in an hour, the claim is untested.

## The guide

Written for the HR-tool builder of RFC 0.4 §15: someone who wants people commenting on candidates and has no interest in Nostr. It has to answer, without them reading our source:

- what container a comment needs, and how their app gets one
- how to render a thread, and what they own versus what the package owns
- what they get for free later — unread when *Cross-app read state* lands
- **what to do if they want to diverge**, because some will, and the spec is what they fall back to

## The honest caveat it must carry

Comments are membership-scoped, not end-to-end encrypted. The relay operator is the organisation and can read them. That is the right trade for business software — it is what makes search, retention and offboarding possible — but a builder must not discover it later. Same discipline DMS-11 applies to DMs.

## Done when

The package is on npm, Peek and Ship consume it from the registry, and **a third app — Leaf, or a scratch app — has comments working end to end using only the guide.** Time it honestly and put the real number on this issue, including if it is not an hour.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Extract @estiva-app/conversation, with Peek and Ship as the two consumers
issues.description:
**The extraction, and it comes after CON-2 rather than before it.**

Right now the conversation model has exactly one implementation. Extracting from a single consumer produces a package shaped like that consumer — SHA-7 is the outstanding bill for doing this with the live socket, and the note on that issue says it plainly: *"a single implementation with a single caller, and no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API."*

CON-2 (Ship gets reactions) is what makes Ship a real second consumer. **Do that first, then extract what the two agree on.**

## What goes in

The fold, the components, and the affordances: threading, reactions, edit, delete. This package is allowed to contain a fold — it sits **above** `@estiva-app/protocol`, which deliberately contains none. It is a convenience an app adopts, never a requirement.

## What stays out

- **unread** — it joins when *Cross-app read state* lands
- **the composer's editor** — that is *Rich text and blocks*; this package takes formatted content, it does not decide the format
- **anything only one app needs.** If Ship wants it and Peek does not, it is not shared yet

## The rule this package lives under

SPEC's conformance list must stay sufficient to implement conversations **without** this package. If the package becomes the only place that knows how commenting works, a defect in its fold is a defect in every app at once and invisible from all of them.

## Extraction constraints, checked while writing

No imports from either app's data layer. Every environment touch an injected parameter. Tests that run with no app. The file placed where it is going. See SHA-11.

## Done when

Peek and Ship both render conversations from the package with their local copies deleted, and **whatever the second consumer forced to change is written on this issue — including "nothing"**, which is the answer that retires the worry.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Edit a comment: one model, both apps
issues.description:
**Neither app can edit a comment, and the reason it is not trivial is that the content is immutable.**

A `kind:9` and a `kind:1111` are both non-replaceable, so an edit cannot overwrite what it edits. Whatever an app shows as "edited" is a **fold over two events** — and per SPEC §10 the fold is exactly where apps are allowed to differ, so two apps folding the same pair may legitimately show it differently.

That makes this a specification question before it is a UI one.

## What to decide and write down

- **the wire shape** — how an edit names the event it replaces, and how a reader orders two edits landing in the same second (the `ts` rule from SPEC §6.2 applies)
- **what a reader sees** — current text with an "edited" marker is the obvious answer; whether history is reachable is a product call, and it is a different one for a comment on an issue than for a message in a chat
- **who may edit** — the author, and nobody else. Same shape as delete, and the same trap: an app that offers the control to a non-author is offering something the relay will refuse

## Why it belongs here rather than in either app

It is going into the conversation package, so getting two apps to agree *before* extraction is the whole point. Peek building it alone would produce Peek's answer, and Ship would inherit it — which is the drift SHA-3 spent 5,400 lines removing.

## Done when

The edit model is in SPEC, both apps implement it, an edit made in one is rendered correctly by the other, and a non-author is not offered the control.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Roll the format out against the existing 487 events, with the alsoRead-shaped compatibility story
issues.description:
**The migration is the steady state, not a window that closes.** Depends on RIC-1.

## What cannot move

Measured on production 2026-08-28:

| corpus | events | carrying structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| messages (`kind:9`, `kind:1111`) | 398 | 165 |
| descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 89 with a body | 76 |

A `kind:9` is **not replaceable at all**. A `30850`/`30851` is replaceable only by its author, and REW-11 established that rewriting stamps a `created_at` the relay will not backdate. So whichever format RIC-1 picks, **every one of these events keeps its current shape permanently.**

## What this ticket owns

- the declaration: how a reader knows which form it is holding, in the shape `emits.alsoRead` already uses one level down — the owner is the only party that knows what it used to write
- **one safe renderer**, imported by both apps. Ship's plain-text stance is a security position and the renderer has to honour it rather than route around it
- the read path in both apps handling both forms, permanently, with no flag day

## The failure to avoid

A reader that handles only the new form shows a thread that begins in the middle — newest content present, everything older silently gone. Nothing reports it. That is exactly why `alsoRead` exists, and it is written up in SPEC §7.3.

## Done when

Both apps render both forms, a message written before the cutover and one written after appear identically to a reader, and the compatibility declaration is in SPEC rather than only in code.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Record the cross-app widget demo — a Peek conversation live inside a Ship issue
issues.description:
**Demo material, and the business goals are what make it a ticket rather than a nicety.** From 2026-08-18: *"Recruit engineers in the team"* and *"Get a grant"* — plus *"Finish the short video demos as it's great material for quick pitching."*

## Why this specific demo

Miky, 2026-08-18: *"instead of cooperation of 2 apps (which is pretty common in SAAS todays via integration with each other), we have now 3 apps integrating all together and that's where I think people will actually get it, because that's unusual."*

Two apps integrating is a screenshot anybody can produce. **The thing that is hard to fake is liveness plus reciprocity** — an object from app A rendered inside app B, updating without a reload, while B's object renders inside A. That is what PRO-6 and PRO-7 make true for the first time.

## What to capture

- a Peek conversation rendered inside a Ship issue description, in Ship's own design language
- somebody posting into that conversation *from Peek*, and the Ship view updating with no reload
- the reverse direction, so it reads as a suite rather than a one-way integration

**Publish from a second identity, not a second window.** Track A learned this the expensive way: two windows on one account prove nothing, because both are served by the same Convex deployment and the reply arrives by reactivity alone.

## Done when

The recording exists, it is linked from this issue, and the thing on screen was verified against the relay rather than against the UI's report.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Publish @estiva-app/interop, and write the page a third-party builder starts from
issues.description:
**GA for the projection layer.** Ships only after PRO-7 — a package with one consumer that has never pushed back on its API is SHA-7's mistake, and this surface is larger than the socket's.

## What ships

The manifest consumer runtime as a published package: resolve a manifest, resolve an object, resolve its actions, build the event an action emits. Depends on `@estiva-app/protocol`. Contains **no fold** — manifest semantics are normative, an app's interpretation is not.

## The page that matters more than the package

A builder who has never seen this suite needs to answer two questions without reading our source:

1. **"How do I render an object from an app I know nothing about?"** — install, resolve the manifest, render the slots you implement, ignore the ones you do not.
2. **"How do I make my objects renderable by other apps?"** — publish a `kind:31990`, declare projections and actions, and here is a worked example.

Write it against the HR-tool scenario from RFC 0.4 §15, because that is the test: a hiring app declares a Candidate, and Peek renders it without knowing what hiring is.

## Done when

The package is on npm, both Peek and Ship consume it from the registry rather than from source, and **somebody who has not worked on this suite renders a Ship issue in a scratch app using only the published page.** If that person is not available, say so on this issue rather than marking it done on our own reading — the claim is about a stranger, and we are not one.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: assign can set an assignee and never clear one
issues.description:
`assign <ref> <pubkey|me>` takes a 64-character key or `me`, and has no way to express "nobody". Once an issue is assigned, the assignment cannot be cleared from the CLI or from MCP at all.

The asymmetry is with the command written next to it: `edit-project --lead none` clears a project's lead perfectly well, writing an empty value rather than removing anything, because an append-only stream has no undo and "set to nobody" is a fact like any other. The fold reads issue `assignee` from the same kind of change field, so the mechanism is identical and only the surface is missing.

Found while verifying AGE-15 (#23). The end-to-end check there wanted to take a key from `ship people` and assign it to a throwaway issue — and could not, because that assignment would have been permanent. The check was run against an already-assigned issue instead, which is a weaker test chosen only to avoid an irreversible write.

That is the real cost: a write nobody can undo makes the safe way to test it unavailable, so the command is exercised less than the ones that are reversible.

Shape: accept `none` (and an empty value) in `assign`, exactly as `--lead` does, writing an empty assignee. The note should read "Unassign" — which is already what the Ship UI writes for a cleared assignee (`web/src/pages/IssuePage.tsx`), so the activity feed stays one vocabulary.

Worth checking while there: whether any other write in the CLI can set a value it cannot clear.

Done when: a person can clear an issue's assignee from the CLI and from MCP, and the change reads as an unassignment on ship.estiva.app.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: assign refuses names and nothing exposes pubkeys, so the agent can only ever assign to itself
issues.description:
`assign` takes a 64-character hex pubkey or `me`, and refuses a display name. The new `edit-project --lead` refuses one for the same reason, and the reason is right: display names are self-set, so assigning by name would let a person redirect who work lands on by renaming themselves.

The gap is that nothing in the CLI or MCP ever *tells* you a pubkey. So in practice the only assignment the agent can make is to itself — assigning to a colleague requires having their key already pasted in from somewhere else. A correct refusal has made a whole verb unusable.

The directory is already being fetched. `Store.profiles()` reads kind:0 for a set of pubkeys and `resolvePubkeys` in ship.ts already turns them into names for `show` and the activity lines. This is the same data read in the other direction.

Shape: a read-only `ship people`, listing the pubkeys the workspace has profiles for with their display names, and the same over MCP. No write, so no new signing.

Two things to get right:
- **Names are not unique and are not evidence.** The listing is a lookup aid, not a resolver. `assign` must keep taking a pubkey; this command must not become a way to assign by name through the back door, and its output should make the pubkey the identity and the name the decoration.
- Which pubkeys to list is a decision — everyone who has authored or been assigned anything visible is the honest set, and it should say so rather than implying it is the whole team.

Done when: a person can find a colleague's pubkey from the CLI and use it with `assign`, without leaving the tool.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: create-topic is the one write verb the CLI has and MCP does not
issues.description:
Every other write exists on both front-ends: comment, set-status, assign, create-issue, create-project, reply, say. `peek create-topic` exists in the CLI and has no MCP tool, so Claude Desktop and Claude Code plugin users cannot create a topic while a terminal user can.

The repo states the two front-ends dispatch the same `AgentCommand` objects and that a disagreement between them means one has grown its own copy of something. This is a disagreement, and it should be resolved deliberately rather than left as an accident.

It may be deliberate. `create-topic` is the only command signing kind:9007, and the signing-ceiling refusal is exercised in agent-cli.test.ts using exactly that command and that kind — so it is possible the credential cannot sign 9007 at all and the tool was left out to avoid offering something that always fails. That should be *checked* rather than assumed: the refusal path exists precisely so an unpermitted command fails up front with a readable reason, which is a better answer than a missing tool.

Either outcome is fine, but one of them should be written down:
- if the ceiling permits 9007, add `peek_create_topic` alongside the others
- if it does not, say so where somebody looking for the tool will find it, and let the CLI command keep failing loudly

Done when: the CLI and MCP offer the same write verbs, or the reason they do not is recorded.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: peek reply can only reply to a conversation, never to a message inside one
issues.description:
`peek reply <topic> <conversation>` resolves a conversation *root* and publishes with `replyTo: { rootId: thread.id, parentId: thread.id }` — the two are hardcoded equal. `Store.postMessage` already takes a distinct `parentId`, and the wire format already carries a root/reply pair for a reply to a reply, so nothing new is needed on the protocol side.

The effect is that the agent can join a conversation but cannot answer a particular person in it. In a thread with several participants its reply attaches to the opening message, which reads as answering whoever started the thread rather than whoever it is actually responding to.

This is almost certainly the second half of AGE-3. The request there was "give claude the ability to reply to its own message", and the answer to whether the agent can do that is: it *can* reply to a conversation it started — `peek reply` has no author check — but it cannot reply to a specific message within one, whoever wrote it. The limitation is threading depth, not authorship.

Shape: let `reply` take a message id as well as a conversation id, resolving to `{ rootId: <conversation>, parentId: <message> }`. `peek topic` already prints the messages, so the ids are available to whoever is calling.

Done when: the agent can reply to a named message inside a conversation and Peek renders it nested under that message rather than under the thread root.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The activity feed is already folded on every read and nothing exposes it
issues.description:
`foldFolder` returns `activity: Change[]` — every change in the workspace, oldest first, in exactly the order the fold replayed them. Every `loadAll` computes it. The only command that surfaces any of it is `show`, as one issue's `history`.

So an agent asked "what happened since yesterday" has to list issues and infer from statuses, which cannot see a rename, a reassignment, a move, or anything that was changed and changed back.

The data is free — no new query, no new fold, it is the stream the state was folded from.

Shape: `ship activity [--since <when>] [--project <ref>] [--limit <n>]`, and the same over MCP. Values that are pubkeys should render as names the way `show` already does via `resolvePubkeys` — an activity line reading "Claude set assignee to b38fd268…" was a real defect once and this is the surface that would reproduce it.

Worth deciding: `--since` wants a timestamp, and changes carry both `created_at` (one-second resolution) and a `ts` tag in milliseconds. Use the same ordering the fold uses rather than a second rule, or the feed and the state can disagree.

Done when: the agent can answer "what changed in this workspace recently", including changes no status column would show.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: There is no way to read one project: show is issue-only and the listing omits the description
issues.description:
`ship show` resolves issues only, and `ship projects` returns ref, title, status, folder, issue count and lead — **not the description**. So there is no way to read a project's description at all, from the CLI or from MCP.

AGE-8 made this awkward on its own terms: the agent can now set a project description it cannot read back, which means it cannot check its own work or amend a description without overwriting it blind.

Shape: let `show` take a project as well as an issue, and return what the project surface in the app shows — description, status, lead, its issues, its conversation, and its change history. Resolution should go through `findProject`/`resolveOne` rather than a fourth lookup rule; note that `show` currently resolves by shape, so a reference matching both an issue and a project needs a decided answer rather than a guess.

Cheap, and it is all data `loadAll` already folds — no new query.

Done when: `ship show` on a project name or address returns its description, status and lead, and the same is available over MCP.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Archiving is the agent's only cleanup path and it is not reachable from the CLI or MCP
issues.description:
`Store.archiveProject`, `linkProjectFolder` and `deleteProject` have **no caller anywhere outside src/store.ts**. They are implemented, tested by nothing, and reachable from neither the CLI nor MCP.

Archiving is the one that matters, because it is the agent's *only* cleanup path: Estiva ID refuses kind:5 for claude-agent, so the agent cannot delete, and NIP-09 is author-scoped so nobody else can tidy up after it either. Today a project the agent creates by mistake is permanent and stays in everyone's project list.

That risk is not theoretical — `ship projects` already hides 5 archived projects, and creates are rate-limited in a way that makes a careless retry produce duplicates the agent cannot remove.

Shape: `ship archive-project <ref>` and `--unarchive`, over the existing `archiveProject`. Note the fold's rule — unarchiving writes an empty value rather than deleting the change, because an append-only stream has no undo. Same pairing over MCP.

`deleteProject` should probably stay out of reach: it only removes the project *record*, leaving its issues orphaned and unreachable from any app, and it is author-scoped so it would only ever work on the agent's own projects.

Open question for `linkProjectFolder`: 3 of 14 production projects are already re-linked, so somebody is doing this somewhere. Worth finding out whether that was the UI or a script before deciding the agent needs the verb.

Done when: the agent can archive and unarchive a project from the CLI and MCP, and an archived one stops appearing in the default `ship projects` listing.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The agent cannot amend an issue it filed: title, description and project are unreachable
issues.description:
`create-issue` files an issue and that is the last say the agent has over it. Afterwards the CLI and MCP can change only `status` and `assignee`, so a typo in a title the agent wrote can only be answered with a comment, and a mis-filed issue cannot be moved at all.

Nothing new is needed underneath — this is AGE-8 again, for the other object. Both folds read `fields.title`, `fields.description` and `fields.project` for issues, and the Ship web UI edits all three: apps/ship/views/issue.ts:73 (Rename), :81 (Description), :167 (`set('project', …, 'Move to …')`).

**An issue's parent can change.** The standing guidance in our notes is that it cannot, and that refiling a mis-filed issue means archiving and republishing. That is wrong: `projectAddr: fields.project?.value ?? parent` in both folds, and Ship ships a Move control today. The guidance should be corrected whether or not this command gets built.

Shape: mirror `edit-project` — `ship edit-issue <ref> [--title] [--description] [--project <ref>]` plus `ship_edit_issue`, planned by a pure exported function so the decisions are testable without a relay.

One difference from AGE-8 worth getting right: an issue change carries the *issue's own* folder (the app uses `ctx.folderOf(issue)`), not the record folder a project change needs. Do not copy edit-project's folder rule across.

Worth checking while building it: after a move, the issue event's `h` is immutable, so the issue's conversation stays in the old Folder while the issue renders under a project in a new one. Confirm what that looks like in Peek before calling it done.

Done when: a person can fix an issue's title and description and move an issue between projects, from the CLI and from MCP, and the result is visible on ship.estiva.app.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The agent can create a project but never change one: title, description, status and lead are unreachable
issues.description:
`ship create-project` is the only project write the agent has. After creation the project is frozen from the CLI and from MCP: there is no way to set its description, status, lead, or to rename it.

The three mutating ship commands (`comment`, `set-status`, `assign`) all resolve through `resolveIssueFor` -> `findIssue(state.issues, ...)`, so they are issue-scoped by construction. Passing a project address to `set-status` fails cleanly with a no-match error rather than doing something wrong. MCP exposes a strict subset of the same commands, so it has the identical gap.

Nothing new is needed underneath. `Store.setField` already takes any target address, and both folds — the agent's `src/fold.ts` and estiva-ship's — already read project `title`, `description`, `status` and `lead` from change fields. The Ship web UI writes exactly those four through the same `setField` (apps/ship/views/project.ts), so this is a missing CLI surface over machinery that is already live and already rendered.

Two things a fix must get right:
- A project change carries the folder the *record* is in (`project.originFolder`), not its content folder. The Ship UI comments that getting this wrong is rejected at ingest, and a project re-linked to a Peek topic is exactly where the two differ.
- Project status is its own vocabulary — planned / in_progress / completed / cancelled — not the issue one. Reusing ISSUE_STATUSES would validate the wrong words.

Also missing and library-only, reachable from neither CLI nor MCP: `Store.archiveProject`, `linkProjectFolder` and `deleteProject` have no caller anywhere outside `src/store.ts`. Archiving matters most, since it is the agent's only cleanup path for a mis-filed project.

Related to AGE-3 (edit own message) as the same family — the agent can create but not amend — but a different object and a different mechanism.

Done when: a person can change a project's description, status, lead and title from the CLI and from MCP, and the result is visible on ship.estiva.app.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: npm run check invokes site/check.mjs, which is not in the repo
issues.description:
**A documented guardrail that has never run.** Found while adding RFC 0.4 to the docs site; incidental to SHA-9 rather than caused by it.

`estiva-docs/package.json` declares:

```json
"check": "node site/check.mjs"
```

**`site/check.mjs` does not exist.** `git ls-tree origin/main site/` returns `build.mjs`, `nav.mjs`, `search.js`, `serve.mjs`, `styles.css` — and nothing else. Running `npm run check` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, so the script has never worked in this repo's history.

## Why it matters more than a missing file usually would

`site/nav.mjs` documents the guarantee this script was supposed to provide, in a comment above the unpublished-pages set:

> A link to a file that is NOT published must not silently 404. `build.mjs` turns those into plain text with a marker, and **`check.mjs` fails the build if a published page links to an unpublished one** — otherwise the split above leaks as a trail of dead links pointing at documents nobody outside can read.

So the repo **states** that a published page linking to an internal document is a build failure. It is not. `build.mjs` still does its half — degrading the link to marked plain text — but nothing enforces the rule, and nothing reports when it is broken.

This is the shape `operations/SILENT-FAILURES.md` collects: a safety mechanism that is described where people will read it, believed to be running, and absent.

The unpublished set is not small — both ADRs, `FILES_ARCHITECTURE.md`, `NIP-FC.md`, and now RFC 0.3 and RFC 0.4 — so there is real surface for a published page to link into.

## Two possible resolutions, and they are genuinely different

1. **Write `check.mjs`.** Walk the published pages, resolve every internal link against `BY_FILE`, fail on any that resolves to a member of the unpublished set. This is what the comment promises.
2. **Delete the `check` script and the sentence in `nav.mjs`**, and rely on `build.mjs`'s marker alone.

Either is defensible. What is not defensible is the current state, where the comment describes a check that does not exist — a reader has no way to tell which of the two is true.

## Done when

Either the check exists and fails a deliberately-introduced bad link, or the claim is removed from `nav.mjs` so the repo stops describing a mechanism it does not have. **Verify by introducing a link from a published page to an unpublished one and confirming the build's actual behaviour** — not by reading the script.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] ADR 0002: record what makes an in-app implementation extractable
issues.description:
**A short amendment to the decision record that owns package decisions.**

The rule agreed for the projection layer, rich text and the conversation standard: **functionality lands in a real app first and is packaged afterwards.** Extraction with no consumer produces a package shaped like nothing — SHA-7's lesson, where the live socket went into `@estiva-app/protocol` as a single implementation with a single caller that no second consumer ever pushed back on.

But *"we will extract it later"* is exactly how `liveTopics.ts` became a ticket. So the intention has to be **checkable while the code is being written**, not asserted afterwards:

1. **No imports from the app's data layer, store or config.** The dependency runs one way.
2. **Every environment touch is an injected parameter** — query function, signer, clock. Never a module-level global.
3. **Its tests run with no app.** If a test needs a deployment or a browser, the package cannot carry that test, and untested code does not travel.
4. **Put it where it is going.** A path that lies about what a file is, is how a thing quietly grows app-shaped.

## Both outcomes are already in the tree, which is why this is worth writing down

- **`projection.ts` passes all four** and is extractable today. Its own header: *"takes a query function and knows nothing about Convex."* It fails only (4) — it lives under `convex/`.
- **`textParsing.ts` fails (1)** — it imports Peek's own `PEOPLE` and `TOPICS` fixtures, so the parser needs Peek's directory to run and cannot leave the building.
- **`liveTopics.ts` failed (2)** — module singleton, credential provider, `navigator.onLine`, all of which SHA-7 now has to relocate.

## Why ADR 0002 rather than the roadmap

ADR 0002 owns where packages live, how they publish, and who owns a breaking change. This is the same class: a decision about packages that is not an implementer's to make case by case.

## Done when

ADR 0002 carries the four constraints and the three worked examples, and the projection layer's extraction ticket cites it.

title.value: [MS2] ADR 0002: record what makes an in-app implementation extractable

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Accept or amend RFC 0.4
issues.description:
**A reading session and a decision, not an investigation.** Nothing is waiting on more evidence.

RFC 0.4 supersedes 0.3 — same document, next version, §1–§12 renumbered nowhere so every existing cross-reference keeps resolving. PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/28

## What is in hand

- Both questions that could have invalidated the containment model are answered against production (§5.2, §5.3)
- REW-11 rehearsed §4.2 at one-tenth scale and produced two failure shapes nobody predicted
- §10.1's trigger has **fired** — upstream shipped `kind:30621`, parameterized-replaceable, global-only, single-writer
- The projection layer (§13) is described from running code rather than proposed
- §14's two content models are measured, not argued

## What accepting does and does not settle

**Does:** the containment model, the projection vocabulary including the slots-closed / widgets-open-with-a-chain decision, the two content models, and that §6 is unfrozen with Ship's description field as its test bed.

**Does not:** which content format (open question 7), who may register a widget type (8), the reaction horizon (10), or the folder command/state kind numbers (1) — which §12.1 says should be allocated upstream if this goes upstream, making them the tail of §10.1 rather than a separate decision.

## The adjacent decision, and it is the same moment

**§10.1 — upstream proposal or private fork implementation.** Its own stated trigger is the first line of folder command or state code. On today's merits proposing looks right: relay-maintained state needs a Buzz change either way, and private kinds are the same work with none of the review plus a permanent merge burden.

## Done when

The RFC is accepted or amended, and if amended, what changed and why is on this issue. Folder implementation gets tickets only after that.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Hide the delete control from a non-author instead of offering one that fails
issues.description:
**Normative already, and worth a ticket because getting it wrong is silent.**

SPEC §6.5 says a NIP-09 `kind:5` is **author-scoped**: a relay honours a deletion only from the pubkey that signed the original, and *"an app MUST therefore hide the control from non-authors rather than offer one that silently fails."*

Archive and delete also have genuinely different reach and MUST NOT be offered as two styles of the same control — archive is a change event on a field, reversible and available to anyone in the Folder; delete is a request that relays MAY decline and that leaves children untouched.

## Why now

The *Conversation standard* project is aiming at a package other apps adopt. **Whatever that package does about deletion is what every adopting app will do**, so the semantics need to be right before it exists rather than discovered by an app that shipped a button doing nothing.

## The consequence this workspace keeps paying

**An identity that cannot sign `kind:5` publishes permanently, and no other identity can clean up on its behalf** — NIP-09 is author-scoped, so the author is that identity. That is AGE-2, still open, and it is why several probe records and verification comments are on production for good.

Any app or agent adopting this model needs to know its own signing ceiling *before* it publishes something it may want to remove, not after.

## Done when

Both apps hide delete from non-authors, archive and delete are visibly different affordances rather than two labels on one, and an identity without `kind:5` is told **before** it publishes rather than at the failed deletion.

title.value: [MS2] Hide the delete control from a non-author instead of offering one that fails

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Ship gets reactions
issues.description:
**Ship has none.** A grep for reaction handling across `estiva-ship` returns nothing — no `kind:7` read path, no write path, no UI. So "reactions are everywhere" describes an intention rather than the ecosystem.

Peek has the full stack: `ReactionPicker`, `Reaction`, the emoji set, optimistic updates and the target-addressed sync.

## Why this is the right next step rather than building the package first

The package is supposed to be the thing a third app adopts. **Right now the model has exactly one implementation**, which is SHA-7's shape — a single implementation with a single caller, never pushed back on. Ship implementing reactions is the second consumer that shows which parts of Peek's approach are the model and which are Peek's.

Build it in Ship, under the extraction constraints (no app-data-layer imports, injected environment, tests that run with no app, placed where it is going), so the eventual package is an extraction rather than a rewrite.

## Watch for

- **`kind:7` has no `h` tag** — reactions are fetched by target, not by channel. See the sibling horizon ticket; Ship must choose a horizon deliberately and say what it is.
- **Reactions attach to messages, not to blocks** (RFC 0.4 §7.2). Whether they attach to *objects* — an issue, a project — is not settled and should not be quietly decided here.
- Ship must read reactions on both `kind:9` and `kind:1111`, since its conversations span both permanently.

## Done when

A reaction added in Ship appears in Peek and vice versa, against production, verified by reading the event back from the relay rather than by trusting either UI — and the two apps agree on the count.

title.value: [MS2] Ship gets reactions

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Decide the reaction horizon, and say it where a reader can see it
issues.description:
**A decision, and a small one, but it is currently made by an undocumented constant.**

SPEC §6.6 now records the mechanism: a reaction is a `kind:7`, and **it carries no `h` tag**, so reactions cannot be found the way messages are. They must be fetched addressed by target — collect the event ids on screen, query for reactions pointing at them.

That forces a choice of N, and the choice is invisible: reactions on older messages simply do not appear, and **nothing reports that they were not asked for.** The reference client's N is `REACTION_TARGET_LIMIT = 100`.

**An undocumented cap is indistinguishable from "nobody reacted"** — which is the failure shape PEE-10 fixed elsewhere in Peek, where an empty container and an unreadable one had to become different things on screen.

## What to decide

- what the horizon **should** be — a fixed target count, a time window, or "everything currently rendered"
- whether it is a guarantee an app states, or a per-app choice the spec only requires be documented
- what a reader sees at the boundary, if anything

## Done when

SPEC §6.6 carries the answer, the constant is named after it rather than the other way round, and this issue records the reasoning — this is RFC 0.4 open question 10.

title.value: [MS2] Decide the reaction horizon, and say it where a reader can see it

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Mentions become resolvable: NIP-27 references inline, not display names
issues.description:
**Half of this is already right.** `buildMessage` takes `mentions: string[]` and emits `p` tags, so **who** was mentioned is on the wire and resolvable by anyone.

**The inline token is the problem.** It is the person's display name — `@Ada Lovelace` — and the parser that turns it into a chip resolves it against a local directory: `textParsing.ts` imports Peek's own `PEOPLE` and `TOPICS`. Two consequences, and the second is permanent:

- another app cannot render the chip without holding the same directory, so a mention degrades to plain text across the ecosystem
- **message content is immutable, so a rename desynchronises the text from the `p` tags forever**

## The fix

NIP-27's inline `nostr:npub…` (and `nostr:naddr…` for objects), which is the specified answer and is not currently used inside message bodies. A mention becomes self-describing: resolvable by any app, stable across renames.

**It is additive.** The `p` tags stay. Existing messages keep working because the old display-name form is still parseable — this is `alsoRead`'s shape applied to inline content: publish the new form, read both.

## Why this is filed while the format decision is not

The mention encoding is separable from the bold/italic question. It is about *reference resolution* rather than *presentation*, its defect is diagnosed, and its fix is a ratified NIP. If the format decision later subsumes it, this ticket folds into that work rather than being wasted.

## Also note

`textParsing.ts` importing app fixtures is what makes it un-extractable today, so this ticket moves the parser toward being packageable as a side effect. See the projection layer's extraction constraints.

## Done when

Peek publishes mentions as inline `nostr:` references, both forms render, a mention resolves in a second app with no shared directory, and a renamed person's old messages still resolve to the right identity.

title.value: [MS2] Mentions become resolvable: NIP-27 references inline, not display names

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Decide the content format, knowing 487 published events cannot move
issues.description:
**A decision, not an implementation.** Per roadmap rule 2, the tickets that depend on this are deliberately not filed until it is made — filing them now would be a backlog that looks like progress.

## What is true today, measured on production

| corpus | events | carrying structure | dialect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| messages (`kind:9`, `kind:1111`) | 398 | **165 (41%)** | `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `__underline__`, `#`, `>`, `-`, `1.` |
| descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 89 with a body | **76 (85%)** | the above **plus tables, fenced code, links** |

**Two undocumented dialects, three producers, two renderers that disagree.** Peek's composer serialises TipTap to an ad-hoc marker syntax; Ship's composer is a plain textarea; the agent CLI writes freehand markdown and is the heaviest producer of structure on the relay. Peek parses the markers back; Ship renders them literally. So 41% of messages read formatted in one app and raw in the other, right now.

They do not even agree among themselves: the agent uses backticks constantly, Peek's editor has code spans **disabled** and its parser has no backtick rule.

## Ship's position is correct and must survive

Ship renders bodies as text on purpose — *"untrusted text from other people and other apps: rendered as text, never as markup."* **The fix is not to make Ship render markdown.** It is to specify a format and ship one renderer that is safe by construction.

## The three candidates (RFC 0.4 §14.5)

1. **Specify the existing marker dialect** — cheapest, matches the message corpus, caps expressiveness near what Peek's editor emits.
2. **A CommonMark subset** — standard parsers, matches what descriptions already contain, but it is a *superset* of the message dialect so the two models diverge further.
3. **Structured blocks as JSON** — what block editing and §6 anchoring actually need; costs the most and makes `content` opaque to anything that does not parse it.

RFC 0.4 §14.5 **recommends a split** — (1) for messages, (3) for rich text, sharing an inline layer — but recommending is not deciding.

## Whichever is chosen

**The 487 existing events do not move.** They are non-replaceable or replaceable-only-by-author, and REW-11 established that rewriting stamps a `created_at` the relay will not backdate. Every candidate needs an `alsoRead`-shaped answer: a declaration of the old form, and a reader that handles both permanently. **The migration is the steady state, not a window that closes.**

## Done when

The format is written into SPEC as a numbered section, the compatibility story for the existing corpus is stated, and this issue records which candidate was chosen **and what it costs** — not only which one won.

title.value: [MS2] Decide the content format, knowing 487 published events cannot move

issues.author: f3a38fa646debd4162125e0aed87b6d2393fb1ed9702b6875dcbc0c6529d64d1
issues.title: Rendering the initial issue list takes a long time
issues.description: We have more than 120 issues and it takes time to render it. We should render only small portion.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] truncate must not be applied to a structured field
issues.description:
**Small, real, and visible in production right now.**

Ship's manifest declares `subtitle: { field: "content", truncate: 120 }`. Against the descriptions production actually holds — **76 of 89 carrying markdown structure, the longest 5,706 characters** — that renders the first 120 characters of raw markup as an object's subtitle.

This issue's own description would render as `# Goal` followed by a sentence fragment.

## The rule

`truncate` is a plain-text operation and MUST NOT be applied to a structured field. RFC 0.4 §13.3:

- `subtitle` carries a **plain-text summary**
- `body` carries **structure**

An app whose description is structured owes the consumer a plain-text summary rather than expecting the consumer to flatten markup it does not know the grammar of.

## Depends on

The `body` slot, and the content-format decision — a summary can only be derived automatically once the format is specified. **In the meantime the honest fix is not to declare a `truncate` on a field that carries structure**, which is a one-line manifest change and strictly better than what is rendered today.

## Done when

Ship's manifest no longer truncates a structured `content` into `subtitle`, and no consumer renders raw markup as a summary.

title.value: [MS2] truncate must not be applied to a structured field

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Ship renders a Peek object — the second consumer that stops this coming out Peek-shaped
issues.description:
**This is the ticket that makes the extraction trustworthy**, and it should be treated as a requirement of the extraction rather than a follow-up to it.

SHA-7 exists because `createLiveRelay` went into `@estiva-app/protocol` as a single implementation with a single caller: *"no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API."* Every line of the projection consumer runtime is in that same position today, and it is a larger surface.

## What to build

Ship resolves a `nostr:naddr…` reference to a Peek Topic or Message inside a project or issue description and renders it through the manifest — its own tokens, its own design language, zero lines that know what Peek is.

## What this specifically tests

- **The fallback chain**, because a Message is not one of the four closed widget types
- **The `list` slot**, because a Topic carries one
- **Ship's plain-text discipline** meeting a body that may carry structure — see the *Rich text and blocks* project, and do not quietly start rendering markup here
- **A relay-signed author**, which Ship has never had to attribute

## Done when

Ship renders a real Peek Topic and a real Message from production, and **whatever the second consumer forced to change in the runtime is written on this issue — including "nothing"**, which is the answer that retires SHA-7's worry rather than deferring it.

Only after this should the runtime be published as a package.

---

## What PRO-6 established, 2026-08-31

Peek's manifest is written and merged, so the shape of this ticket is no longer
guesswork. Three things below were **not** knowable when it was filed, and two
of them are larger than anything in "What to build".

### 1. A Message is not addressable, and every resolver here starts from an address

Confirmed against production: a `kind:9` carries **no `d` tag**. It is a regular
event, referenced by event id, never by `kind:pubkey:d`.

`resolveForeignObject` takes an `naddr`, `referenceToPointer` returns an
`AddressPointer`, and the root is fetched with `{kinds, authors, '#d'}`. None of
that reaches a message. **Resolving a Message needs a second entry point keyed
on event id** — `nevent`/`e` rather than `naddr`/`a` — and that is the larger
half of this ticket. Note the knock-on: comments and changes are fetched by
`#a`, which a non-addressable root cannot be the target of either.

### 2. The `list` slot does not resolve for an object reached by address

`list` was implemented in PRO-2 down the *folder* path, where containment is
discovered from the Folder's contents. `resolveForeignObject` never resolves
it: `rawSlotValue` returns undefined for a `children` spec, so the slot is
dropped.

Measured: 5 of 5 real production Topics resolve by address through Peek's
manifest and render **title and subtitle and no messages**. So "a Peek
conversation inside a Ship issue" does not fall out of the manifest as filed —
wiring `list` into the by-address path is work this ticket owns.

### 3. A Topic carries no `h` tag — it *is* the container

So `resolveFolderProject` cannot find one, and a Topic is reached by address:
`39000:<relay pubkey>:<channel uuid>`.

### Still true, and now with detail

- **The fallback chain** — Peek declares `widget: ["message", "card"]`. Nothing
  consumes a chain yet; a consumer reading `widget` as a string sees an array.
  That is PRO-3's, and this ticket is its first caller.
- **The relay-signed author** — a `39000` is signed by the relay, so "who wrote
  this" resolves to the relay's pubkey. Any attribution slot must not render it
  as a person.
- **Ship has no consumer runtime at all.** It is a producer only: `src/manifest.ts`
  and `scripts/publish-manifest.ts`, no `ForeignObjectWidget`, no resolver. The
  second consumer is being built from nothing, not adapted.

### Blocked on

**Peek's manifest is written but unpublished.** Publishing `kind:31990` is
refused at two of SPEC §8's three gates — a fresh key gets
`relay_membership_required`, and Estiva ID refuses to sign for `claude-agent`
(`App claude-agent may not sign kind 31990`). Neither `estiva-peek` nor
`estiva-ship` carries 31990 in `allowed_kinds`; Ship publishes from a raw key
registered as a relay member. Until an identity is settled, Ship can only
resolve Peek's manifest from a local copy, which tests the runtime and not the
discovery. See PRO-6.

### What actually changed in the runtime, for the "including nothing" answer

PRO-6 already forced four changes, so that answer will not be "nothing":
`match: 'address' | 'identifier'` on `children`, `field: 'pubkey'` as a slot
source, `records` made optional in both resolvers, and the discovery that a
kind is `u16` so an unmatchable-filter trick is refused by the relay. Those came
from the *producer* side. This ticket collects what the consumer side forces.

title.value: [MS2] Ship renders a Peek object — the second consumer that stops this coming out Peek-shaped

description.value:
**This is the ticket that makes the extraction trustworthy**, and it should be treated as a requirement of the extraction rather than a follow-up to it.

SHA-7 exists because `createLiveRelay` went into `@estiva-app/protocol` as a single implementation with a single caller: *"no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API."* Every line of the projection consumer runtime is in that same position today, and it is a larger surface.

## What to build

Ship resolves a `nostr:naddr…` reference to a Peek Topic or Message inside a project or issue description and renders it through the manifest — its own tokens, its own design language, zero lines that know what Peek is.

## What this specifically tests

- **The fallback chain**, because a Message is not one of the four closed widget types
- **The `list` slot**, because a Topic carries one
- **Ship's plain-text discipline** meeting a body that may carry structure — see the *Rich text and blocks* project, and do not quietly start rendering markup here
- **A relay-signed author**, which Ship has never had to attribute

## Done when

Ship renders a real Peek Topic and a real Message from production, and **whatever the second consumer forced to change in the runtime is written on this issue — including "nothing"**, which is the answer that retires SHA-7's worry rather than deferring it.

Only after this should the runtime be published as a package.

---

## What PRO-6 established, 2026-08-31

Peek's manifest is written and merged, so the shape of this ticket is no longer
guesswork. Three things below were **not** knowable when it was filed, and two
of them are larger than anything in "What to build".

### 1. A Message is not addressable, and every resolver here starts from an address

Confirmed against production: a `kind:9` carries **no `d` tag**. It is a regular
event, referenced by event id, never by `kind:pubkey:d`.

`resolveForeignObject` takes an `naddr`, `referenceToPointer` returns an
`AddressPointer`, and the root is fetched with `{kinds, authors, '#d'}`. None of
that reaches a message. **Resolving a Message needs a second entry point keyed
on event id** — `nevent`/`e` rather than `naddr`/`a` — and that is the larger
half of this ticket. Note the knock-on: comments and changes are fetched by
`#a`, which a non-addressable root cannot be the target of either.

### 2. The `list` slot does not resolve for an object reached by address

`list` was implemented in PRO-2 down the *folder* path, where containment is
discovered from the Folder's contents. `resolveForeignObject` never resolves
it: `rawSlotValue` returns undefined for a `children` spec, so the slot is
dropped.

Measured: 5 of 5 real production Topics resolve by address through Peek's
manifest and render **title and subtitle and no messages**. So "a Peek
conversation inside a Ship issue" does not fall out of the manifest as filed —
wiring `list` into the by-address path is work this ticket owns.

### 3. A Topic carries no `h` tag — it *is* the container

So `resolveFolderProject` cannot find one, and a Topic is reached by address:
`39000:<relay pubkey>:<channel uuid>`.

### Still true, and now with detail

- **The fallback chain** — Peek declares `widget: ["message", "card"]`. Nothing
  consumes a chain yet; a consumer reading `widget` as a string sees an array.
  That is PRO-3's, and this ticket is its first caller.
- **The relay-signed author** — a `39000` is signed by the relay, so "who wrote
  this" resolves to the relay's pubkey. Any attribution slot must not render it
  as a person.
- **Ship has no consumer runtime at all.** It is a producer only: `src/manifest.ts`
  and `scripts/publish-manifest.ts`, no `ForeignObjectWidget`, no resolver. The
  second consumer is being built from nothing, not adapted.

### Blocked on

**Peek's manifest is written but unpublished.** Publishing `kind:31990` is
refused at two of SPEC §8's three gates — a fresh key gets
`relay_membership_required`, and Estiva ID refuses to sign for `claude-agent`
(`App claude-agent may not sign kind 31990`). Neither `estiva-peek` nor
`estiva-ship` carries 31990 in `allowed_kinds`; Ship publishes from a raw key
registered as a relay member. Until an identity is settled, Ship can only
resolve Peek's manifest from a local copy, which tests the runtime and not the
discovery. See PRO-6.

### What actually changed in the runtime, for the "including nothing" answer

PRO-6 already forced four changes, so that answer will not be "nothing":
`match: 'address' | 'identifier'` on `children`, `field: 'pubkey'` as a slot
source, `records` made optional in both resolvers, and the discovery that a
kind is `u16` so an unmatchable-filter trick is refused by the relay. Those came
from the *producer* side. This ticket collects what the consumer side forces.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Peek publishes a manifest for Topic
issues.description:
**Scope narrowed to Topic, 2026-08-31.** A Message cannot be declared in a manifest at all — measured on production, and now **PRO-11**. Topic is the half that can exist.

## Where this actually stands

**The manifest is written and merged** — [peek#80](https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/80), *"Peek declares its own objects, and six things that could not be expressed"*. **Read the comment on this issue before picking it up**; it carries six findings measured against production, none of them visible from the Ship direction, and they are worth more than this description.

**It is blocked on an identity, and the blocker is not in this project.** Publishing a `kind:31990` fails two of SPEC §8's three gates: a fresh key is refused at ingest with `relay_membership_required`, and the agent identity is refused *before* ingest — `App claude-agent may not sign kind 31990`. Ship publishes from a registered relay member; Peek has none. Granting one is a seed change in Estiva ID plus a hand re-seed on the box.

The publish script is **complete and unrun**, and takes a signer rather than a key file, so whichever identity is granted drops in.

## Why the ticket exists

Peek has only ever been a *consumer* — it reads Ship's manifest and renders Ship's objects, and has never published one. This is the producer half of the second consumer that stops the projection layer coming out Peek-shaped; PRO-7 is the reader half.

## What remains

1. Decide which identity publishes Peek's manifest, and grant it `31990` — an Estiva ID change, the two-halves shape from Gate 1
2. Run the completed script
3. Confirm a second app resolves it from the relay by `#k` query

**Verified so far without publishing:** all 5 real production Topics resolve by address through the unpublished manifest.

## Done when

Peek's `kind:31990` is live on production, the verifier passes it, and a second app renders a real production Topic through it.

**One caveat carried into PRO-7:** the `list` slot resolves through the folder path but **not** for an object resolved by address — so a consumer holding a Topic `naddr` currently gets a title and no messages.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Two machine-facing fields on an action, added now because retrofitting one is a migration
issues.description:
**Small, and the reason to do it now is timing rather than value.**

An action declares `{ id, label, appliesTo, emits, input }`. That is enough to draw a control and not enough for anything else to decide to use one — `label: "Change status"` is a button caption.

Add two optional fields (RFC 0.4 §13.4):

| field | for |
| --- | --- |
| `description` | prose describing what the action does and when it applies, distinct from `label` |
| `effect` | `safe` \| `writes` \| `destructive` — whether invoking without confirmation is acceptable |

## These are fields, not a design

The layer that would consume them is **deliberately parked** — no app has a harness yet, and designing against zero implementations is worse than SHA-7's single-consumer problem. See the roadmap's "not filed, and why".

**The argument for adding them anyway is `alsoRead`'s argument one level up:** adding a field now costs a line each; adding one after several apps have published manifests is a migration across every one of them, and a manifest is republished by its owner alone.

`effect` also has an immediate non-agent use: a consumer can require confirmation for a `destructive` action without knowing what the action does.

## Done when

Both fields are in the manifest schema and Ship populates them for its six actions. Consumers may ignore them; nothing yet reads `description`, and that is expected.

title.value: [MS2] Two machine-facing fields on an action, added now because retrofitting one is a migration

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Render object-creating actions as forms — the declared schema nobody draws
issues.description:
**Ship already declares this and the consumer already refuses it.** `add-issue` carries a real input schema — `type: object`, `properties`, `required` — and `resolveActions` skips it, saying why:

> *"An action that creates a whole new object (`add-issue`) needs a form and a parent, so it is skipped rather than drawn as a control that cannot work."*

That was the right call at the time. Field-setting and commenting render; object creation does not. So the manifest can describe the single most useful cross-app action and no app can offer it.

## What to build

A consumer draws a form from `input.properties` and `input.required`, publishes the declared kind, and sets the parent from `emits.setTag` / `toAddressOf`.

**Validate against the manifest's own vocabulary before publishing.** The owning app cannot enforce anything — anyone can publish anything — so a consumer that skips the check is the one putting junk in a shared record. Keeping that side of the honour system is the consumer's job.

## The same mechanism serves a second caller

*"Take this Peek conversation and create a job description in the HR tool"* is this action shape with the form filled from context rather than by hand. Nothing extra is needed for that — which is why this ticket is worth more than its size suggests — but the intelligence layer itself is deliberately parked. See the roadmap.

## Done when

Peek renders `add-issue` as a form and creates a real Ship issue through it, the relay accepts the event, Ship's own fold shows it as an ordinary issue, and a value outside a declared vocabulary is refused **before** publishing with a message naming what was allowed.

title.value: [MS2] Render object-creating actions as forms — the declared schema nobody draws

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Widget vocabulary: open, with a fallback chain that terminates in a closed type
issues.description:
**`card | row | table | stat` is a union type in one consumer's source.** An app declaring anything else renders nothing, and no document says what the legal values are or who may add one. A third app is blocked on a spec change plus an upgrade in every consumer — the two-sided deployment that stands between a builder and shipping.

## The decision (RFC 0.4 §13.3)

A manifest MAY declare any widget name, and MUST declare it as an ordered chain:

```jsonc
"widget": ["profile", "card"]   // a profile if you know it, otherwise a card
```

**A chain MUST terminate in a type this spec closes** — `card`, `row`, `table`, `stat`. `["profile","card"]` is legal; `["profile"]` alone is not. A consumer walks the chain and renders the first type it implements.

## This is the third use of a pattern already in the tree

Not a new invention. `slots` already accept `tag: ["name","title"]` meaning *first that resolves* — added by REW-11 because a renamed tag cannot be rewritten on published events. `emits.alsoRead` is the same idea for kinds. Both exist because **published events are immutable and consumers upgrade at different times**, which is exactly the condition a widget vocabulary lives under.

## Why not either pure option

- **Closed**: provably too small on day one — "card with list" does not fit — and every addition is a lockstep deployment.
- **Bare open**: the fallback *is* the risk. An unrenderable widget is the PEE-10 failure mode, where present-but-blank reads as *"that app is broken"*. The terminal type is what makes that impossible.

## Done when

A manifest declaring an unknown widget renders correctly through its fallback in the consumer, a chain that does not terminate in a closed type is rejected with a readable reason, and the conformance check covers both directions — producers terminate, consumers walk.

title.value: [MS2] Widget vocabulary: open, with a fallback chain that terminates in a closed type

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Add the image, list and body slots, so the flagship layout stops being bespoke code
issues.description:
**Slots are scalar today** — `title`, `subtitle`, `status`, `meta` — and that is why the pattern's own showcase bypasses the pattern.

"A project card with its issues underneath" is what Peek actually shows, and it is **not a manifest projection at all**. It is `TopicProjectPanel.tsx`, bespoke consumer code that knows about Ship. The one layout most cited as proof the mechanism works is the one the mechanism cannot express.

## Add three, and keep the set closed

RFC 0.4 §13.3 — slots stay a **closed** vocabulary, because a slot is *semantic*: a consumer must know what it **means** to render it at all, so an unknown slot name is unrenderable by definition and openness buys nothing.

| slot | holds |
| --- | --- |
| `image` | avatar, thumbnail or cover, as a URL |
| `list` | child objects **by address**, so the consumer resolves each and renders it with its own projection |
| `body` | structured content per RFC 0.4 §14 |

**`list` is the interesting one.** It holds addresses, not rendered content — so a consumer resolves each child and applies that child's own projection, which is what makes "project card with its issues" compose rather than being a special case. It is also recursive, so it needs a declared depth limit before somebody nests two folders into a render loop.

## Done when

Ship declares a `list` slot for a project's issues, Peek renders it through the manifest, and `TopicProjectPanel.tsx`'s bespoke path is deleted rather than left beside it.

title.value: [MS2] Add the image, list and body slots, so the flagship layout stops being bespoke code

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Extract the manifest consumer runtime, with the seam designed in from the first line
issues.description:
**The code already works and lives in one app.** `peek-app/convex/nostr/projection.ts` does `resolveManifest → resolveForeignObject → resolveActions → buildActionEvent` — roughly 1,300 lines, and none of it is Peek-specific in its logic. It is the single highest-value extraction available.

**It is already most of the way there, and its own header says so:** *"takes a query function and knows nothing about Convex."* That is why this is tractable; contrast `textParsing.ts`, which imports Peek's own `PEOPLE` and `TOPICS` fixtures and cannot leave the building.

**But the path lies.** It lives under `convex/` while having nothing to do with Convex, and that is how a thing quietly grows app-shaped.

## The four constraints, checked while writing rather than after

1. No imports from the app's data layer, store or config — the dependency runs one way.
2. Every environment touch is an injected parameter: query function, signer, clock. Never a module-level global.
3. Its tests run with no app. A test needing a deployment or a browser cannot travel with the package, and untested code does not travel.
4. Put it where it is going.

## Do not publish it as a package yet

SHA-7 is the warning: `@estiva-app/protocol` took the live socket as a single implementation with a single caller, and no second consumer ever pushed back on its API. **The second consumer here is Ship rendering a Peek object**, and it should exist before this is a published package. Land the seam first, publish after the second consumer has bent it.

## Done when

The runtime is a standalone module with no app imports, its tests run with neither Convex nor a browser, Peek consumes it with no behaviour change, and whatever the second consumer forces to change is written on this issue — **including "nothing", which is the answer that retires the worry.**

title.value: [MS2] Extract the manifest consumer runtime, with the seam designed in from the first line

issues.author: f3a38fa646debd4162125e0aed87b6d2393fb1ed9702b6875dcbc0c6529d64d1
issues.title: Research: Shared Conversation, rich text fields, widget layout library, intelligence actions register
issues.description:
# Goal
Further strengthen the RFC 0.3 and include it in the roadmap based on research of 4 topics for whole ecosystem. One of the goal is as following: Imagine that your fresh builder of new SAAS application that doesn't exist in the ecosystem. You e.g. want to build software for hiring, but you want to be plugged in into the rest of Estiva apps. All the foundational packages should make it super easy to plug in. Currently we have those foundational packages that makes it easier for new saas builder
* identity package to authenticate users
* protocol to access buzz/nostr backend
* ui so you can reuse our design building blocks

I'm thinking extend those or add more based on 4 following topics:

1: How to make sure that conversation across all apps works consistently
* Message are read / unread (we have project for that)
* Reactions are everywhere
* You can edit / delete
* Huddle: how you can start a huddle either you and your AI or with just specific person to brainstorm about that thing regardless in which app you current are

Research question: Should we somehow include or create new package that focus on unifing the conversation experience across apps?

2: How to make sure the rich text fields like project description are consistent across all apps
* having blocked editing ala notion
* being able to embed widget from other apps like project or issue widget similarly you can paste in peek

Research question: SHould this again be somehow standalone or extended current package so the new saas builder can easily use this?

3: Widget library
* Basic idea objects (files) has properties and the widget library has list of different templates/layouts that all the apps can use to display that object in their app. Example you have Ship project. The library describe bunch of different templates. Ship in the manifest says that for project you can have "inline template" - just project name, "card template" - project name, description, assignee, status, "card with list" - similar as previous + list of issues (e.g. such we use in Peek now). Then the 3rd app like Peek see a reference of object from Peek and reads the manifest and see what tempaltes are available. Peek decide what template will use and then apply the design tokens from UI foundational library to render it
* In other words to display file/object with properties and actions from other app, the app needs: 1. manifest from the other app 2. the widget template library 3: the ui library. If SAAS builder use those foundational libraries they can build thing like HR tool easily, because let's say there is new object like "Candidate profile". The HR tool defines in the manifest and says what templates should others apps use to show the candidate profile and then e.g. Peek can renders it, even though it has no clue how the HR tool works.

4: Available actions
Kind a same thing as #3 but for actions/intelligence + AI to know what can be done from other apps in their apps. E.g using the HR tool example. HR tool can say that on Candidate object you can "vote up or down" to send the candidate to next round or not. Then AI, or simply some kind of command feature can list that this action is available.

The action has some payloads and can e.g. ask use in the 3rd app to provide that payload or automatically based on context give it. Create new issue in SHip will show the form or it can create new issue based on AI automatically filling those form fields based on Peek conversation.
TBD
