issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: ship projects listed 11 projects, then 9, with no project archived in between
issues.description:
Observed 2026-08-28 while closing out track F. **Not diagnosed** — filed so it is not lost, with what was ruled out.

## What happened

`npx tsx scripts/agent.ts ship projects` returned **11 projects** earlier in the session, including *"Catch up the Buzz fork"*. Roughly an hour later, the same command in the same checkout returned **9**, and *"Catch up the Buzz fork"* was absent from the list.

Between the two runs I published about fifteen events — issue comments (`kind:9`, `kind:1111`) and status changes (`kind:1851`) — plus filed two new issues. Nothing that should touch a `kind:30850` project record.

## What is ruled out

- **The project still exists and still resolves.** `ship issues --project "Catch up the Buzz fork"` returns its 11 issues, so the record is readable and `resolveOne` finds it by name. Only the *list* omits it.
- **It is not archived.** The record `30850:…:5b2701f3-da02-47f1-9ff5-14bdfb1dd822` is on the relay, `created_at 2026-08-24 10:38:56`, with no `archived` tag.
- **It is not the page ceiling.** This was my first hypothesis — the relay's `max_limit` halved to 1000 with the Buzz catch-up, and this checkout predates SHA-8. But running the same command from a worktree at `origin/main`, which has `queryAll` and `@estiva-app/protocol` 0.2.0 installed, **also returns 9**. So paging is not the difference.
- **It is not a shortage of records.** The relay holds **43** `kind:30850` events with **43 distinct `d` tags**. The command lists 9 of them.

## Why it matters

43 records to 9 listed is a large filter, and whatever it is moved between two runs an hour apart. `ship projects` is the first command anyone runs, and `--project` accepts a name — so a project that silently drops out of the list while remaining addressable is the kind of gap that makes a summary confidently wrong. It is adjacent to the `coverage` block's purpose, but coverage counts *issues*; nothing reports a project the listing cannot see.

Two candidate directions I did not pursue: whether the fold filters projects on something recency-dependent (which would explain the change over time), and whether 43 records include duplicates or test records that a dedupe rule is collapsing inconsistently.

## Done when

The listing is either stable, or it reports what it filtered — the same argument the `coverage` block already makes for issues. If the 43-to-9 filter is intentional, one sentence in `ship projects`' output saying so is enough.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Client queries ask for limit 2000; the relay now clamps at 1000, silently
issues.description:
Found during CAT-8, after the Buzz catch-up deployed on 2026-08-28.

## What changed under us

Upstream #3635 aligned the relay's REQ ceiling with its advertised NIP-11 `max_limit`. Measured on production before and after the deploy:

    before   max_limit 10000 advertised, effective REQ ceiling 2000
    after    max_limit  1000 advertised, effective REQ ceiling 1000

## What the clients ask for

`limit: 2000` at **four call sites, as a duplicated literal with no shared constant**:

    lib/agent/apps/ship.ts:120       kinds:[ISSUE]    limit: 2000   <- loadAll
    lib/agent/apps/peek.ts:207       kinds:[MESSAGE]  limit: 2000
    scripts/manifest-reader.ts:113   kinds:[kind]     limit: 2000
    scripts/manifest-reader.ts:125   kinds:[change]   limit: 2000

`estiva-ship` carries its own copy of the same code, so the real count is higher. There is also a `limit: 500` at three more sites — fine today, but the same class of literal.

## Why this is a foundation ticket rather than an app bug

The number is a **property of the relay**, duplicated into callers that cannot know when it changes. `@estiva-app/protocol` already owns the wire format after SHA-3; it is the only place that can hold a page ceiling and keep every consumer honest. Two apps plus the agent plus the manifest reader currently each hard-code an assumption about a server they all talk to.

## The failure mode, and why it is worth fixing before it happens

**NIP-01 has no truncation signal.** A caller asking for 2000 and getting 1000 receives a short list and no indication why. So the symptom is not an error — it is Peek quietly missing older history, or Ship quietly missing issues, with every local signal green.

**Nothing is truncated today.** Headroom measured on production 2026-08-28:

    kind 9     messages   314 / 1000   (31%)
    kind 1851  changes    280 / 1000   (28%)
    kind 30851 issues     119 / 1000   (12%)
    total events         1367          (an unfiltered limit-2000 query would clamp)

So this is filed while it is cheap. The margin halved and the code does not know it; `kind:9` is the one to watch, and Peek's message load is the query that would lose data first.

## Suggested shape

1. `@estiva-app/protocol` exports the page ceiling and a paging helper, so a caller asks for "all of them" rather than a number it invented.
2. Read the ceiling from the relay's own NIP-11 `limitation.max_limit` rather than hard-coding it — the relay already advertises it, and CAT-1 caught this change *only* by reading upstream's source. Reading NIP-11 would have made it self-correcting.
3. Failing that, one shared constant with a comment naming the relay-side source.

## Done when

No call site names a page size as a literal; a query that would exceed the relay's advertised ceiling either pages or fails loudly rather than returning a short list; and one test asserts that a result at exactly the ceiling is treated as "possibly truncated" rather than "complete".

Relevant to PEE-6/7/8 (Peek's per-channel subscriptions and paging) and to Ship's `loadAll`.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The MCP server runs whatever branch the shared checkout is parked on, and its coverage field reports that as a workspace limit
issues.description:
**Through MCP, every Ship listing is 13 issues short — and the field whose job is to warn about that reports the wrong reason for it.**

Measured this morning, same identity, same relay, minutes apart:

| read path | coverage |
| --- | --- |
| `mcp__estiva__ship_list_issues` | `reachable 95, unreachable 13, total 108`, plus the note *"Do not describe this list as complete"* |
| `ship issues` from a worktree at `origin/main` | `reachable 108, unreachable 0, total 108` |

`estiva_ping` rules out the boring explanations: the server signs as `b38fd268…` from `/home/miky/.estiva-agent.env` and reads `https://estiva.estiva.app` — the same credential, identity and relay the CLI used.

## The cause is which code is running

`scripts/mcp-server.sh` does `cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."` and then `exec node node_modules/tsx/dist/cli.mjs scripts/mcp-server.ts`, so a session gets whatever is checked out in `~/estiva-agent` at the moment its server starts. That checkout has been parked on `peek-161-claude-code-plugin` (`3f8cbbb`) since 2026-08-24 22:47. The three server processes alive right now started 2026-08-28 at 01:34, 07:20 and 10:02 — all three from that revision, six commits behind `origin/main`.

`loadAll` lives in `src/store.ts`, one of the six files that differ. On `3f8cbbb` discovery is `relay.query([{ kinds: [KIND.PROJECT], limit }])` and widens into project Folders only; on `origin/main` it asks for `{ kinds: [KIND.ISSUE] }` in the same round trip and widens into each issue's own Folder. That is SHI-7, and it is not in the running server.

**It is not a stale data cache**, which is worth stating because it is the first guess: the same server returned SHA-7 within seconds of it being filed. Only the code is old.

## Why this is worse than a stale CLI

`CLAUDE.md` can tell a person to read from a worktree at `origin/main`. Nothing can tell an agent, because the answer carries no revision — `estiva_ping.runtime` reports platform, WSL, node, entry path and client, and no commit.

And the failure is silent and authoritative at once: a list that is 13 short, plus a note asserting the shortfall is a known limit of the *workspace* rather than of the binary. An agent following the tool description exactly will report the wrong thing confidently, which is the failure mode `coverage` exists to prevent.

## Two changes, independently worth having

1. **Report the revision in the answer.** `estiva_ping.runtime` gains the git revision and a dirty flag for the tree it is running from. This is the one that turns any future instance of this into a one-call diagnosis instead of an afternoon.
2. **Stop launching from a mutable working tree.** AGE-1 covers the committed `plugin/server/index.js` bundle going stale through a merge; this is the other half — the `mcp-server.sh` entry runs whatever branch a peer left checked out, and the shared checkout is routinely on somebody's branch. A pinned worktree, a built artifact, or the plugin path AGE-1 is fixing would each do it. **Not an implementer's choice to make silently:** it decides whether a local edit to the agent is testable by restarting a session, which is the reason the current shape exists.

## Done when

A freshly started session's `ship_list_issues` reports `unreachable: 0` for the workspace as it stands, and the revision that produced that answer is readable from the answer itself.

**Keep the negative control.** The number must still rise above zero for an issue genuinely sitting in a Folder this reader cannot see — the field is not being removed, it is being made trustworthy. Verify by reading a listing, not by reading the diff.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Give the live relay socket a second consumer, and extract the plumbing it needs
issues.description:
**SHA-3 put the socket in the right package on the wrong footing, and this is the ticket that pays for it.**

`createLiveRelay` and `createChannelSubscriptions` are in `@estiva-app/protocol` as of 0.1.0. Everything else in that package arrived as a **byte-identical duplicate** pinned by 21 wire vectors, so the extraction could not change behaviour and needed no second consumer to find the seam — SHA-3 says so in its own first paragraph. The socket was never duplicated. It is a single implementation with a single caller, and no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API. That is exactly the failure SHA-4 and SHA-5 avoid by extracting *during* REW-2 and REW-3, and the socket skipped it.

## What is Peek-shaped and unproven

Not `live.ts` itself — the plumbing that stayed behind in `peek-app/src/nostr/liveTopics.ts`, which the second app will otherwise write again from scratch:

- **One instance per tab, as a module singleton.** `max_subscriptions` is per connection and the relay authenticates a connection once, so a connection per component mount is wrong rather than merely wasteful. React StrictMode makes it concrete: anything owned by an effect is built twice.
- **A credential provider read on every connect, never captured.** A token captured at module load survives a silent renewal as a dead credential, and a reconnect then signs `22242` with it.
- **`navigator.onLine` → `relay.reconnect()`.** A socket whose peer became unreachable stays OPEN until TCP gives up, reporting `live` and delivering nothing. Reconnection is driven by `onclose`, which never fires.

None of that interprets events, so "share the wire format, never the fold" does not send it back to an app. It is browser lifecycle, which makes it **`@estiva-app/platform`'s (SHA-2), not `protocol`'s**. `freshness.ts` is the opposite case: its four states and their copy are product voice and stay in the app.

## Sequence it after the cutover, not inside it

REW-6 keeps Ship's 5s poll deliberately (`apps/ship/app.ts:85`), and the roadmap already calls "adopting Peek's conventions naively" a release blocker. Do not swap Ship's transport during the rewrite. Land this after REW-8.

## A cheaper second consumer, if the API wants stressing before then

`estiva-agent` already imports `@estiva-app/protocol`, and `live.ts` declares its own `WebSocket` types and reads the global *inside function bodies* precisely so a non-browser runtime can use it — Node 22 has a global `WebSocket`. A live tail in the agent would exercise the API from a second runtime for very little code.

**It is not free, and the cost is in Estiva ID, not here.** `claude-agent` has no `22242` in `allowed_kinds` and an empty `relay_auth_urls`. PEE-4 is the shape to copy — a grant has two halves, and `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` is the deployment half.

## Done when

A second consumer holds a live authenticated socket against `wss://estiva.estiva.app` and receives an event **it did not publish** (a two-window test of one identity proves nothing — PEE-8 learned that), the per-tab / credential / online plumbing lives in a package rather than in two apps, and whatever the second consumer forced to change in `live.ts` or `subscriptions.ts` is written on this issue — including "nothing", which is the answer that retires the worry.

title.value: [MS2] Give the live relay socket a second consumer, and extract the plumbing it needs

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Widening the timestamp window accepts a historical event, then aborts it at COMMIT
issues.description:
Found while surveying CAT-1/2/3 on 2026-08-27. **This is not a merge risk.** Both halves are already on `nfb-demo-kinds` at the upstream merge-base, so the defect is live on the branch today and the catch-up neither causes nor fixes it.

## The contradiction

`6e5db342a` (#6) replaced the hard-coded `MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS = 900` in `crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs` with a configurable `BUZZ_MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS`, so an operator can widen the ingest window for a history import. Its own commit message gives the reason: Peek is migrating four months of real messages off an old Convex deployment, and restamping them to `now` would corrupt the shared record for every other app reading the relay.

Migration `0021_created_at_fence_floor.sql` enforces a **commit-time** floor instead, `CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS = 960` in `crates/buzz-db/src/replica_fence.rs`, armed by the writer pool on **every** connection via the `after_connect` hook in `crates/buzz-db/src/lib.rs`. It is a `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` constraint trigger, so it fires during COMMIT and re-evaluates `clock_timestamp()` rather than `now()`.

The two do not agree, and nothing reconciles them. `CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS` even documents the assumption it is built on — that the ingest envelope is 900 — which stopped being true when #6 landed.

## What happens

For any event carrying an `h` tag, which is every Issue, Change, comment and message, `channel_id` is NOT NULL and the guard applies. So with the window widened:

1. Ingest accepts the event. The client is told `accepted: true`.
2. The insert succeeds.
3. The transaction **aborts at COMMIT** with `check_violation`, because `created_at` is more than 960 s before commit time.

The usable range for channel-scoped events is therefore `900 < x <= 960`, not whatever is configured. The knob still works for global kinds — `channel_id IS NULL` is the one structural exemption, which covers profile and discovery snapshots — so it is not inert, just unusable for the case it was written for.

Migration 0021 states the intent plainly: there is *deliberately NO in-band bypass* for channel-bearing rows, and any operational backfill of them must run on a connection outside the relay writer pool, with the replica breaker held closed from before the transaction begins until its WAL is replayed. That is a real procedure, and it is not what #6 built.

## Verified against production, 2026-08-27

Read-only, nothing written:

- The guard is fully installed and enabled: `events_created_at_floor` exists on **9 relations** — the `events` parent plus all 8 partitions. The enforcement half is live.
- `BUZZ_MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS` is **not set** on the box and not in the relay container env, so the window is the default 900 and sits inside the 960 floor. **There is no live impact right now.** The defect bites the next time somebody sets the knob for an import and believes the `accepted: true` they get back.

**Not verified:** the accept-then-abort sequence itself. Proving it needs a real signed event with an old `created_at` published through the writer pool, and that is a write to production. It belongs on a throwaway — see CAT-6, which is already standing up a production-shaped database.

## Why this is worth an issue rather than a comment

It is the exact failure shape this ecosystem keeps producing: every local signal agrees, the client is told the write succeeded, and the row never lands. A future operator reaching for this knob during a migration has no reason to suspect the relay will take the event and then drop the transaction, and the 200-with-`accepted` idiom means nothing obvious surfaces.

## Done when

Either the floor is derived from the configured ingest window rather than a hard-coded 960 — which is the change that makes the knob mean what it says, and needs the replica-fence proof re-examined because the fence subtracts the same constant — **or** the knob is documented as global-kinds-only and the channel-scoped history import gets the outside-the-pool, breaker-closed procedure written down where an operator will find it. Whichever is chosen, one test must publish a channel-scoped event older than the floor and assert the outcome, so the accept-then-abort path can never be silently reintroduced.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: A deleted message stays visible in another tab until reload
issues.description:
**Reported by Miky, 2026-08-25**, while testing M3's live delivery in two browser windows.

## What happens

Delete a message or a reply in one window. In another window on the same topic, signed in as the same person, the message **sometimes stays on screen**. Reloading that window clears it.

Replies and new messages propagate correctly. Only deletion was observed sticking.

## What the reload tells us

**Convex had already deleted the row.** If it had not, a reload would have brought the message back — instead the reload is what removes it. So this is a *rendered state* problem, not a data one: the stale window is holding a view that no longer matches the query it was built from.

That also rules out the obvious suspect. Peek deletes the Convex rows **first** and publishes the `kind:5` afterwards — `src/api/actions.ts` says "the rows are gone by the time this runs" — so the other window should lose the message by Convex reactivity, before the relay is involved at all. The relay path is not in the loop for a same-account delete.

## Where to look

`src/api/messages.ts`, the merge that produces a topic's groups. Two layers there could hold a message past its row:

- `o.deletedIds` — a **per-tab** override set. The deleting tab adds to it; the other tab's copy is empty, so it is not filtering anything, and it is only the Convex row's disappearance that should remove the message there.
- `sentLocal` / `o.sentMessages[topicId]` — the optimistic copy, filtered by `remoteIds`. A locally-sent message whose row later vanishes is a shape worth checking: `sent = sentLocal.filter((c) => !remoteIds.has(c.id))` keeps the local copy precisely *when the remote row is absent*, which is also exactly what a deletion produces.

That last one is a plausible mechanism for "the author's own tab keeps it" and is cheap to test, though it does not obviously explain a *second* tab keeping someone else's.

## What is not established

**Whether this predates M3.** It was found on the day PEE-8 shipped live delivery, and PEE-8 touches `useTopicView` — but only by adding an effect and a returned value, and it does not touch the merge path above. It is very likely older and simply unnoticed until somebody watched two windows at once, which is not a normal way to use Peek. Worth confirming rather than assuming: the same repro with the socket disabled would settle it in a minute.

## Done when

A message or reply deleted in one tab disappears from every other open tab without a reload, and the mechanism is understood rather than papered over with a refetch.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Projects created since REW-11 render untitled in Peek
issues.description:
**Every project created since REW-11 renders with no title in Peek.** Live now, measured, and caused by REW-11 — this is fallout from my own change, not a pre-existing gap.

## What is wrong

Ship's manifest declares the project card's title slot as:

    title: { tag: 'title' }

REW-11 changed the record to emit `name` instead of `title` (upstream's NIP-MP vocabulary). The projection was not changed with it, so Peek asks for a tag that new records do not carry and gets nothing.

Measured against production, 15 project records:

| shape | count | renders in Peek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| carries `title` (pre-REW-11) | 11 | fine |
| carries `name` (REW-11) | **4** | **untitled** |

One of the four is the real `Agent / Steer` project; the rest are archived probes. Every project created from now on joins that column.

Ship itself is unaffected — `fold.ts` reads `name ?? title`. This is only the cross-app projection, which is exactly the surface REW-11 was supposed to improve.

## Why an array does not fix it

`title: [{ tag: 'name' }, { tag: 'title' }]` looks like a fallback and is not. Peek's `resolveSlots` sends **array slots to `meta`** and only single specs to the named slot, so that spelling would drop the title out of `slots.title` entirely and render both as meta chips. The array form means "render all of these", not "first that resolves".

## The fix, and it is the same shape as `alsoRead`

Let `tag` take a list, meaning *first that resolves*:

    title: { tag: ['name', 'title'] }

Backwards compatible — a string behaves exactly as today. It belongs in the manifest rather than in Peek for the same reason `alsoRead` did: the owning app is the only party that knows which tag it used to write, and hardcoding "also try title" in Peek would fix Ship and nothing else.

Three small changes: `SlotSource` in `estiva-ship/src/manifest.ts`, `resolveSlot` in `peek-app/convex/nostr/projection.ts`, and `protocol/SPEC.md` §7.2 where slot sources are specified.

## The lesson, which is the general one

REW-11 verified the record shape, the fold, and the relay's acceptance. It did not verify **the other app's rendering**, which is the thing the change existed to serve. `publish-manifest.ts` would have caught it on the first run — it checks exactly this — but it was itself broken by REW-11 in a way that masked the failure behind an earlier one (SHI-8).

Two changes to the same record, one hiding the other's damage.

## Done when

`npm run manifest` resolves the `kind:30850` title slot, and a project created after REW-11 renders with its name in Peek's card alongside one created before it.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: publish-manifest can no longer see the project record it creates
issues.description:
**`npm run manifest` fails one of its own checks on every run, and the script is wrong rather than the manifest.**

    ❌ kind:30850 has a real object to project

## Why

`publish-manifest.ts` verifies the manifest by creating a real project and issue and resolving every declared slot against them. It reads them back with:

    const raw = await store.rawFolders([folder])

`rawFolders` filters by `#h`. Since REW-11 the project record is **global** — it carries `buzz-channel` and no `h` — so the record it just created is not in the result, `state.projects[0]` is undefined, and the `kind:30850` projection check fails.

The `kind:30851` checks still pass, because issues are still channel-scoped. That asymmetry is the whole of REW-11 working as designed; this script simply predates it.

## Why it matters more than a red line

The script is the only thing that checks a published manifest can actually project a real object. Half of it is now permanently red, which is the state in which people stop reading output — and the `kind:30850` half is the one covering the record type that just changed shape.

## Fix

Use `store.loadAll()` instead of `rawFolders([folder])`, or add an unscoped `{kinds:[30850], authors:[…], '#d':[…]}` fetch for the record alongside the `#h` read for its contents. `loadAll` is the method that sees both shapes and is what the app and the agent use; `rawFolders` is documented as the read-one-container path and is correct to miss a global record.

## Also worth fixing while there

`RELAY_URL` defaults to `http://localhost:3000`, so a bare `npm run manifest` silently publishes nothing useful and every check passes against a relay nobody meant. Publishing to production is `RELAY_URL=https://estiva.estiva.app npm run manifest`, which is written down nowhere.

## Found by

Republishing the manifest for REW-10. Noticed alongside a second thing worth recording separately: the script reads `src/manifest.ts` off the **working tree**, so running it in a checkout behind `origin/main` republishes the old declaration and reports every check green. The only thing that catches that is reading the published `kind:31990` back off the relay and comparing the field you changed.

## Done when

`npm run manifest` passes every check against production, and the command for publishing to production is discoverable from the script rather than from someone's shell history.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: A manifest cannot declare a kind it used to emit, so migrating one loses its history
issues.description:
**A manifest can say which kind an app emits, but not which kinds it has *ever* emitted — and because old events are unmigratable, that difference is permanent rather than transitional.**

Surfaced by REW-10, which moves Ship's comments from `kind:9` to NIP-22 `kind:1111`. Not urgent: nothing writes `1111` yet.

## The mechanism

`ManifestAction.emits.kind` is a single `number` (`convex/nostr/projection.ts`), and Peek reads it in two places:

- **line 113**, `commentKindOf(manifest)` — which kind to *query* for an object's comments
- **line 1238** — which kind to *publish* when a Peek user comments

So the moment Ship's manifest declares `1111`, Peek asks for `{kinds: [1111], "#a": [address]}` and every comment written before the flip — all of them `kind:9` — stops appearing under the issue widget. Nothing errors. The comments are intact on the relay and Ship still shows them; only Peek's projection loses them.

**And they can never be migrated.** A `kind:9` message is not replaceable at all — unlike a project record, which at least its own author could rewrite. Every `kind:9` comment in existence stays `kind:9` permanently, so this is not a window that closes. It is the steady state.

## Two fixes, and they are different in scope

**1. Peek reads a legacy kind too.** Smallest change, lands today, needs nothing from Ship. But it is Peek hardcoding a fact about one app's history, which is exactly what `commentKindOf` was written to avoid — its own comment says hardcoding "would quietly stop finding comments the moment an app said something different." It also does nothing for the next app that migrates a kind.

**2. The manifest schema learns to express it.** Something like `emits: { kind: 1111, alsoRead: [9] }` — the owning app declaring its own history, which is the only place that knowledge actually lives. Consumers query the union and publish the current one.

This is the general fix and it is a **cross-repo change**: the schema is defined in `estiva-docs/protocol/SPEC.md` §7 and implemented by Ship as producer (`src/manifest.ts`) and Peek as consumer. Filed here because Peek is where the comments disappear and where either fix has to land, but option 2 needs SPEC.md and Ship too.

## Worth noting the asymmetry

Peek's *publish* path is already correct for either fix — `projection.ts:1208` builds proper NIP-22 tags (uppercase `A`/`K`/`P` for the root, lowercase for the parent) regardless of which kind it stamps on them. It is only the *read* that is single-kinded.

## Ordering

Nothing breaks until Ship's REW-10 writer half lands, which is itself blocked on the Estiva ID grant (AGE-2) and on PEE-9. But whichever fix is chosen should land **before** that writer, because the failure is silent: comments stop appearing in one app and no log anywhere says why.

## Done when

After Ship's comment kind changes, a Ship issue rendered in Peek still lists the comments written before the change, alongside the ones written after.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The agent's signing ceiling is narrower than its job, and refuses at the last step
issues.description:
**The `claude-agent` credential cannot sign several kinds its own job requires.** Each refusal arrives late — after the work is done, at the last publish — and one of them leaves litter that nobody can clean up.

## Measured

    kind:5     App claude-agent may not sign kind 5      (NIP-09 deletion)
    kind:1111  App claude-agent may not sign kind 1111   (NIP-22 comment)
    kind:31990 App claude-agent may not sign kind 31990  (NIP-89 handler information)
    kind:31989 App claude-agent may not sign kind 31989  (NIP-89 handler recommendation)

Probed against production by attempting a signature, which is the only route available — the authoritative `allowed_kinds` query needs psql on the box.

## Why each one bites

**`kind:5` is the worst, because it is not recoverable.** `Store.deleteProject` dies at the signer *after* the thing being cleaned up has already been published. NIP-09 is author-scoped, so no human can delete on the agent's behalf either: the author is the agent key. The only fallback is a `kind:1851` archive plus a rename admitting what the record is. Verification runs this session left three such records on production, permanently.

**`kind:1111` blocks REW-10's writer half** for the agent, and the app's credential (`estiva-ship`) needs checking for the same grant. This should ride Gate 1's batch rather than earn its own trip to the box.

**`31990`/`31989`** mean the agent cannot publish or refresh Ship's NIP-89 manifest. In practice `publish-manifest.ts` sidesteps this with a local `.manifest-key` rather than Estiva ID, which works and is worth knowing is a *separate identity* from everything else the agent does.

## The shape, not just the list

The ceiling is enforced server-side and refuses at the last step, so the cost is always paid twice: once doing the work and once discovering it was never publishable. **Probe the kind before building anything that publishes it** — signing one throwaway event is seconds and is the only check that does not need the box.

## Done when

The agent's `allowedKinds` covers what it is asked to do — at minimum `1111` so it can comment under REW-10, and a decision recorded on `kind:5` either way. If deletion stays refused, say so where somebody reaches for `deleteProject`, because the current failure mode is "publish, then discover you cannot undo it".

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: The committed plugin bundle can go stale through a merge, and ships without an install step
issues.description:
**Anyone installing the Claude Code plugin today gets an agent that silently misses 13 issues.** `origin/main`'s committed bundle does not match `origin/main`'s source.

## The state

Rebuilding a pristine `origin/main` leaves `plugin/server/index.js` dirty by 198 insertions and 187 deletions. The committed bundle is missing SHI-7's issue-Folder widening, so a plugin install folds discovered issues without their `kind:1851` changes — the exact failure SHI-7 was careful to avoid, shipped by a different route.

A plugin runs **no install step**. There is no `npm ci`, no build, nothing that would notice. What is in the repo is what runs.

## Why CI did not catch it, which is the part worth fixing

`.github/workflows/check.yml` has the right check:

    - name: The committed plugin bundle is current
      run: git diff --exit-code -- plugin/

But it validates **the branch, not the merge result**. The sequence:

1. `plugin/` was added in #8.
2. SHI-7's mirror (#7) was cut from a `main` where `plugin/` did not exist yet, so `git diff -- plugin/` had nothing to diff and the step passed **vacuously**.
3. #8 merged, then #7 merged. Neither PR was ever red, and `main` ended up behind its own source.

This is a property of any generated file kept in the tree, not a one-off: whenever two PRs are open at once and only one of them regenerates, green-when-you-opened is not green-when-you-merge.

## Options

- **Require branches to be up to date with `main` before merge** (a GitHub branch-protection setting). Cheapest, and catches every instance of this shape, not just this file.
- **Run the check on `main` after merge** as well as on PRs, so a stale bundle is at least loud rather than silent.
- **Stop committing the artefact** and build it at package time — biggest change, removes the class entirely, and loses the property that the plugin needs no install.

The first is probably enough and costs a checkbox.

## Immediate

ship#36's companion, estiva-agent#9, rebuilds the bundle and so fixes the current staleness as a side effect. That does not fix the mechanism.

## Done when

`git diff --exit-code -- plugin/` passes when run against `origin/main` itself, and something prevents a stale bundle reaching `main` again rather than relying on whoever opens the next PR to notice.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Topic sync reads only kind:9, so Ship's NIP-22 comments will vanish
issues.description:
**Peek's topic sync is hardcoded to `kinds: [9]`. When Ship's REW-10 lands, every Ship comment disappears from the Peek topic conversation.** Not "loses its widget" — disappears.

## Why

`peek-app/src/nostr/sync.ts:66`:

    const filter: Record<string, unknown> = {
      kinds: [9],
      '#h': [plan.channelUuid],
      limit: PAGE_LIMIT,
    }

Ship posts a comment as a `kind:9` into the project's Folder, which *is* the Peek topic's channel. That is the whole "one container, many projections" claim — the Ship comment and the Peek topic message are one event, not two records nobody reconciles.

REW-10 moves Ship's comments to NIP-22 `kind:1111`. A `1111` carrying the same `h` is still in the same channel and still a message in that conversation, but this filter will not ask for it.

## What this is not

**The widget/projection path is fine and needs nothing.** `convex/nostr/projection.ts` already defines `KIND_COMMENT = 1111`, and `commentKindOf(manifest)` reads the comment kind off the app's own NIP-89 manifest rather than hardcoding it — the comment there says hardcoding "would quietly stop finding comments the moment an app said something different." It queries `{ kinds: [commentKind], '#a': [address] }`, which is exactly what a `1111` presents. That path adapts by itself once Ship republishes its manifest.

So the two Peek surfaces disagree: one was designed for this change and the other was not.

## What to change

Read `1111` alongside `9` in the topic sync, and thread it the same way. Two things to get right:

- **NIP-22's case is the whole spec.** Uppercase `A`/`E`/`K`/`P` name the thread *root* — the object under discussion. Lowercase name the *immediate parent*. A reply three deep has nothing but the uppercase pair saying what it is about.
- **A `1111` rooted at an address has no root event id.** Ship's issues are addressable, so a top-level comment on one is its own conversation root — the same shape as a `kind:9` with no `e` tag. `estiva-ship/src/fold.ts`'s `parseNip22Comment` is the reference implementation; it maps both shapes into one thread and is already merged-pending in ship#36.

## Ordering

**This should land before Ship's REW-10 writer half.** The writer is currently blocked anyway — Estiva ID refuses to sign `1111` (`App claude-agent may not sign kind 1111`), which is a Gate 1 item — so there is time. But the failure if the order slips is silent: no error anywhere, comments simply stop appearing in Peek, and the first person to notice will be a human wondering where a conversation went.

## Done when

A `kind:1111` comment published into a topic's channel appears in that topic's conversation in Peek, threaded under the right parent, and existing `kind:9` messages still appear exactly as they do now.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Buzz drops a verified NIP-OA owner when the agent is already a relay member
issues.description:
Measured against ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb — the exact image production runs — on a scratch Postgres configured like production (BUZZ_REQUIRE_RELAY_MEMBERSHIP=true, BUZZ_ALLOW_NIP_OA_AUTH=true). Throwaway keys throughout; production was never touched.

THE GAP

A cryptographically valid NIP-OA attestation is silently discarded when the agent presenting it is already a direct relay member. The request succeeds with 200 and users.agent_owner_pubkey stays null.

Same throwaway agent key, three runs:

  not a relay member, valid attestation      -> 200, agent_owner_pubkey SET
  direct relay member, valid attestation     -> 200, agent_owner_pubkey NULL
  membership row deleted, same request       -> 200, agent_owner_pubkey SET

WHY

Both call sites that materialise the owner guard the fallback behind !require_relay_membership:

  crates/buzz-relay/src/api/bridge.rs:808  (HTTP bridge, POST /events)
  crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/auth.rs:244  (WebSocket NIP-42)

enforce_relay_membership returns Ok(None) for a direct member — it only returns Some(owner) on the ViaOwner branch, which is reached only when the agent is NOT a member. On a closed relay a member's attestation therefore never reaches materialize_nip_oa_owner. The comment at auth.rs:242 says "on closed relays, enforce_relay_membership already handles NIP-OA delegation", which is true for non-members and does not cover a member that presents a tag.

WHY IT MATTERS

claude-agent (b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46) is a direct relay member on production. This is the last open piece of PEEK-164 and the prerequisite for PEEK-173.

The failure is the shape CLAUDE.md warns about: every hop reports success. The header is sent, the signature verifies, the relay answers 200, and the column stays null forever. Nothing short of reading the relay database shows it.

Also worth recording: materialisation runs BEFORE ingest, so the owner is written even when the event itself is rejected. The proof run had its kind:9 refused for a missing h tag and agent_owner_pubkey was set regardless.

CHOSEN WORKAROUND

Remove claude-agent from relay_members so it is admitted through its owner. No relay change, reversible by re-inserting the row. The cost is that every agent surface must then send the x-auth-tag header, so the estiva-id and estiva-agent changes must be deployed and the Desktop extension repacked and reinstalled first.

A relay-side fix — extracting the owner for direct members too at both call sites — would remove that coupling entirely and is the better long-term answer.

RELATED

estiva-app/estiva-id#51, estiva-app/ship#32, estiva-app/estiva-agent#5.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Let a project record be global: drop KIND_LL_PROJECT from requires_h_channel_scope
issues.description:
**One line in the relay, plus a deploy. It is the only thing standing between REW-11's merged reader and its writer.** Measured against production 2026-08-24.

## Why

Ship's project record is meant to go global so it can be discovered without channel access — `["h", uuid]` becomes `["buzz-channel", uuid]`. The relay refuses:

```
200 {"accepted": false, "message": "invalid: channel-scoped events must include an h tag"}
```

Probed in three shapes against `estiva.estiva.app`: with `buzz-channel`, without it, and a control still carrying `h`. The first two get that message; the control gets past this gate. So the refusal is the `h` requirement specifically, not the tag vocabulary and not the kind.

This is a **third gate**, separate from the two that were known. The kind is fully registered and Estiva ID signs it happily; `requires_h_channel_scope` is a different list and nobody had read it.

## What to change

`crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:494`, `requires_h_channel_scope` — remove **one** line:

```rust
    | KIND_LL_PROJECT      // ← delete this
    | KIND_LL_ISSUE        // ← keep
    | KIND_LL_CHANGE       // ← keep
```

**Issues and changes must keep the requirement.** The comment above those lines is right about them: the Folder is both how objects are grouped and how access is enforced, and an issue without one has no owner and no reader. Only the *record* goes global. Removing all three would be a different and much larger change, and is not wanted.

### This shrinks the fork rather than growing it

Worth knowing before anyone prices it as new divergence: those three lines are **ours**, added by `d207a1148` (the commit that registered 30850/30851/1851) — `git blame` confirms it. The function itself is upstream's, untouched. So this removes one line from one of our own commits and leaves the fork *closer* to upstream, not further.

That also means it is not new conflict surface for [CAT-2] or [CAT-4]. Related observation while checking: the fork is now **8 commits** past the upstream merge-base, not the four CAT-2's title names — four `feat(kind):` commits plus #1, #3, #5 and #6. CAT-2 was accurate when written; the fork has grown since.

## Where it goes, and how it deploys

- **Branch `nfb-demo-kinds`, never `main`.** Our `main` carries **zero** `KIND_LL` entries in that function — it does not have the Linear-lite kinds at all — so a PR against `main` would be meaningless or actively wrong. `relay-image.yml` builds `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb` from `nfb-demo-kinds`.
- `nfb-demo-kinds` is not rustfmt-clean. Do not run `cargo fmt` — it reflows unrelated comments.
- **The relay has no update timer.** estiva-id, peek and ship each have one; buzz does not. Deploy by hand on the box: `cd /opt/buzz && docker compose pull relay && ./run.sh restart` — pull `relay` only, since `run.sh pull` also pulls postgres/redis/minio.

## Traps

- **HTTP 200 does not mean accepted.** This gate returns `200` with `accepted: false`. Any verification that checks the status code will report success against a relay that still refuses. Read the `accepted` field.
- **Verify by image id, not by health.** A healthy relay serving the old image is the exact shape that has cost hours here before.
- **Sequencing against the catch-up.** Doing it *before* the 625-commit merge means CAT-4 has to carry it through; doing it *after* means REW-11 waits for the entire catch-up. Before is better — it is a one-line deletion inside a commit CAT-4 is already preserving, and it unblocks work that is otherwise finished.
- **This does not finish REW-11.** After the deploy, `buildProject` in `estiva-ship/src/events.ts` still has to emit the new tag array, mirrored into `estiva-agent`. The comment there carries the exact shape. The reader side is already merged and needs nothing.
- **A global project record is world-readable** — its name becomes public to anyone on the relay. That trade is argued in RFC 0.3 §4.2 and stated on REW-11; this ticket is the mechanism, not the decision.

## Done when

A `kind:30850` carrying `buzz-channel` and no `h` is accepted by production — confirmed by reading `accepted: true` off the response, not the status code — while a `kind:30851` and a `kind:1851` without `h` are both still rejected. The running relay's image id matches `:nfb`.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Discovery runs through project records, so 13 issues are invisible
issues.description:
**13 of 93 issues on production are invisible to `ship.estiva.app` and to the agent. They are intact, readable and correctly written — discovery just never reaches them.** Measured 2026-08-24.

This was assumed to be an access-control problem, and [REW-11] was justified partly on fixing it. It is not, and REW-11 does not fix it — measured 13 before and 13 after.

## Why they are invisible

`Store.loadAll` discovers **from projects**:

1. query `kind:30850` unscoped → every project record the reader can see
2. widen into those projects' Folders (`projectFolders`) and pull `FOLDER_KINDS` by `#h`
3. fold everything

An issue is only ever reached in step 2, through its parent. So an issue whose parent does not resolve is never in scope — not because of permissions, but because nothing asked for it.

Root cause of all 13, checked one at a time:

| cause | count |
| --- | --- |
| parent project record was **deleted** — resolves by `#d`, by bulk query, by nothing | 12 |
| no `a` tag naming a project at all | 1 |
| **access-gated project record** | **0** |

And the part that rules access out entirely: **all 13 sit in Folders the reader can already see.** Every one of their `h` values resolves to a `kind:39000` the reader gets back. On this relay all 50 channels are `open`, so channel gating is not currently biting Ship anywhere.

Worth naming the interaction with [SHI-3]: deleting a project is exactly what strands its issues, and 12 of these are that. Whatever SHI-3 builds should not make more of them.

## What to change

`loadAll` should discover issues directly as well as through parents — the same unscoped `{kinds: [30851]}` query that `coverage()` in `estiva-agent`'s `lib/agent/apps/ship.ts` **already runs to count them**. The count is honest; the read is not. Close the gap.

Sketch, in `src/store.ts`:

- pass 1 queries `kind:30850` **and** `kind:30851`, unscoped
- the widening set is the union of `projectFolders(...)` and every discovered issue's own `h`
- the existing 4-pass bound and the rest of the loop are unchanged

## Traps

- **Discovering the issue event is not enough — you must widen into its Folder too.** Measured: 14 `kind:1851` changes target these 13 issues (6 `status`, 7 `assignee`, 1 `project`). An issue pulled in by the direct query but never widened into folds with the *default* status, so six of them would render as `todo` when they are not. That is the silent-wrong outcome, worse than being missing, because nothing looks broken.
- **The app needs somewhere to put a parentless issue.** Twelve have a dangling `a` tag and one has none. `Issue.projectAddr` is already optional so the fold copes, but the UI groups by project and currently has no bucket for these. That design decision is the real work in this ticket; the query change is small.
- **Keep the `coverage` block even when it reads zero.** It is the honest-limit mechanism, not a bug counter. After this it would measure something real — issues in Folders the reader genuinely cannot read — which is the case that will appear with the first private Folder.
- **`src/store.ts` is vendored into `estiva-agent` at an identical path.** The change lands in both, `diff -r src` must stay clean, and `conformance.test.ts` must pass without regenerating the fixture.
- **Cost.** `loadAll` already pulls up to 2000 events with no cache. This adds one unscoped query to pass 1 and widens the Folder set; on today's data that is 13 extra `#h` filters in a call that is already one round trip. Worth a number before assuming it is free.

## Done when

`coverage` reports **0 unreachable** against production; each of the 13 renders with the status and assignee its change stream actually sets, not a default; a parentless issue has a defined place in the app rather than appearing and being unclickable; and `diff -r` against `estiva-agent` is clean with conformance passing.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Exercise Peek, Ship and the agent against the new relay
issues.description:
**M5 · the last ticket, and the one that says whether this worked.** Blocked by the deploy.

## Why a separate ticket

The deploy ticket verifies the *relay*. This one verifies the **ecosystem**, because that is what a person actually experiences and it is the thing 625 commits of change could break in ways no relay-side check would notice.

Verify the user-facing action, not the mechanism. A green build, a matching image id and a healthy endpoint are all compatible with Peek being broken.

## What to exercise, by hand, against production

**Peek**
1. Sign in with Estiva ID — exercises NIP-98 and the token path.
2. Open a topic with history — exercises the channel read path and membership gating.
3. Post a message — exercises `kind:9` publish and the `accepted` field.
4. React to something — `kind:7`, whose channel is *derived* from its target rather than carried, so it exercises a path that is easy to break.
5. Confirm a Ship project widget still renders in the sidebar — exercises `naddr` resolution and the NIP-89 manifest path across apps.

**Ship**
6. List projects and open one — exercises `30850`/`30851` reads and the fold.
7. Comment on an issue — `kind:9` with an `about` tag, or `kind:1111` if REW-10 has landed.
8. Change a status and an assignee — `kind:1851` change events.

**The agent**
9. `npx tsx scripts/agent.ts ship projects` from `estiva-agent` — exercises the client-credentials grant, `/sign`, NIP-98 and `/query` in one command. It is the cheapest end-to-end check in the ecosystem and it fails loudly.

**Cross-app**
10. Create an issue in Ship, confirm it becomes visible in Peek. This is the interop claim the whole suite rests on.

## Traps

- **Use a real identity, not a fresh one.** History, membership and profile resolution only exist for an account with a past.
- If something is broken, the useful question is *which layer* — the probe (M3) already proved kinds, so a failure here is projection, auth, or an app-side assumption, not the registry.
- Watch the relay logs during this, not after. `docker logs`, not journalctl — history stops at container start and a journalctl grep returning nothing proves nothing.
- A partial pass is a fail. Ten checks, ten results recorded.

## Done when

All ten pass and are recorded on this issue. If any fail, this issue carries what broke and what was measured — and the rollback decision belongs here, not in a separate conversation.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Deploy :nfb to the box and verify by image id
issues.description:
**M5 · deploy.** Blocked by the throwaway rehearsal. Do not start until every migration is accounted for.

## The relay is the exception in this ecosystem

Every other service has an update timer. **Buzz does not.** Deploy is manual, by design, and `operations/PRODUCTION.md` says so:

```bash
cd /opt/buzz && docker compose pull relay && ./run.sh restart
```

**Pull `relay` only.** `run.sh pull` also pulls postgres, redis and minio — which on a catch-up deploy means changing the database engine and the relay in one step, with two candidate causes if it goes wrong.

## Order, and the verify step is not optional

**merge → confirm the image built → confirm the box pulled it → restart → verify by image id → exercise the apps.**

`relay-image.yml` builds `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb` from `nfb-demo-kinds`. A merged change sits in the registry until someone pulls it, so a "deployed" relay can be running last month's code indefinitely.

**Verify by comparing the running image id to `:nfb`, never by health.** A healthy relay serving a stale image is precisely the state this project can produce, and it is invisible from the health endpoint. This ecosystem has shipped that failure before — a production re-seed that ran before the new image had been pulled, wrote the old values back, and exited 0.

## Before the restart

- **Take a fresh production backup and confirm it restores.** M4 established the procedure; this is the moment it matters.
- Announce the window. The estimated outage comes from M4's measured migration timings against production row counts.
- Have the rollback ready: the previous image id, written down, before the pull.

## Traps

- Migrations run on startup, so the restart *is* the migration. There is no separate step to abort at.
- The relay's CORS list in `/opt/buzz/.env` names each app's origin, and **omitting an origin turns that app off**. A merge should not touch it, but confirm it survived — it is environment, not code, and an upstream change to how origins are read would be silent.
- If the relay does not come up, the fastest correct move is rolling back the image, not debugging in place. Both apps are down while you think.

## Done when

The running image id matches `:nfb`, the relay serves reads and writes, and the actual outage duration is recorded on this issue against M4's estimate — the gap between them is the useful number for next time.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Rehearse the migrations on a throwaway with a production-shaped database
issues.description:
**M4 · the milestone that exists because there is no staging.** Blocked by the merge and the migration audit.

## Why this cannot be skipped

Upstream migrations run against Postgres on relay startup, and the relay's database is the only shared dependency in the ecosystem — Peek and Ship both read and write it, Estiva ID signs for it, the agent CLI and MCP server read through it. A failed or destructive migration takes everything down at once.

There is **no staging workspace**. So this ticket builds the rehearsal that would otherwise not exist.

## What to build

A relay instance running the merged image against a **production-shaped database** — same schema version, and data whose *shape* matches: the same kinds present, the same tag cardinalities, comparable row counts on anything a conditional migration touches.

Shape matters more than volume. The known refuser triggers on `kind:30078` rows with ambiguous `d`/`t` tag cardinality — a copy with no `30078` rows at all would pass and prove nothing.

**Options, in order of fidelity:** a restore from a production backup into an isolated instance; a synthetic database built to match the audit's row-shape findings; or the local suite's database seeded to match. The audit (M1) says which shapes must be present.

## What to record

- every migration that ran, in order, and how long each took
- anything that refused, with its exact message and what data triggered it
- anything destructive, and whether the result is what was intended
- the schema version before and after
- whether the relay serves reads and writes afterwards — start it, publish an event, read it back

## Traps

- **Do not point this at the production database**, and do not run it on the production box where a misremembered `docker compose` could reach it. Use a separate machine or a clearly-named isolated stack.
- **Take a production backup first regardless**, and verify the backup restores. A backup nobody has restored is a hope. `~/estiva-backups` exists; confirm it covers the relay's Postgres and not only other services.
- A migration that is instant on a small copy may lock a table on production. Note timings against row counts so M5 can predict the outage window.
- If a migration refuses, that is a **finding, not a blocker to work around**. Record what data it wants repaired and file it; do not edit production data to make a rehearsal pass.

## Done when

The merged relay starts against a production-shaped database, every migration is accounted for, the relay serves a read and a write afterwards, and the expected production outage window is estimated from measured timings. If anything refused, M5 does not start until it has its own ticket.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Probe every Estiva kind against the locally built relay
issues.description:
**M3.** Blocked by the merge. This is the ticket that catches a misresolved list.

## Why a build passing is not enough

`ALL_KINDS` is a list, and a merge that drops an entry compiles cleanly. The failure appears in production as `restricted: unknown event kind` when Peek or Ship publishes — long after the merge looked fine.

So ask the relay itself, in its own words, rather than reading the source and believing it.

## What to run

`estiva-ship` has a probe built for exactly this: `npm run probe` (`scripts/probe-kinds.ts`). It asks the relay one kind at a time whether it would accept an event, and its header says why it exists:

> Run before and after patching Buzz. Before, every Estiva Ship kind should come back `restricted: unknown event kind`; after, every one should be accepted. The point is to have the relay's own words rather than an assumption about what the allowlist contains.

Point it at a **locally built relay** from the merged branch, not production:

```bash
PROBE_SECRET_KEY=<hex> RELAY_URL=http://localhost:3000 npx tsx scripts/probe-kinds.ts
```

## Traps

- **A closed relay needs the probe key admitted.** If the local relay runs with `BUZZ_REQUIRE_RELAY_MEMBERSHIP=true`, a key invented at runtime can never be a member. Admit it with `buzz-admin add-member <pubkey>` and remove it afterwards — a standing member that exists only to run tests is its own problem.
- **`/query` requires NIP-98 auth**, so a bare curl returns 401 and is indistinguishable from a refused kind. Use the probe; do not hand-roll.
- The probe publishes into a throwaway Folder it creates. Safe to repeat, but point it at localhost — running it against production writes to production.
- Extend the probe if it does not already cover all eleven of our kinds. It predates some of them.

## Done when

Every Estiva kind is accepted by the locally built relay, with the relay's own response recorded on this issue. Any refusal is a merge defect, not a probe defect — fix the merge.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Merge upstream into nfb-demo-kinds, keeping all four commits' behaviour
issues.description:
**M2 · the merge.** Blocked by all three M1 tickets — in particular the migration audit, whose answer is this ticket's gate.

## Where it goes

**Into `nfb-demo-kinds`. Never route through `main`.**

`main` carries a Revert that `nfb-demo-kinds` does not. Branching from `main` and rebasing **silently proposes deleting the members API and the relay-image workflow** — a diff that looks like a clean catch-up and is a feature deletion.

`relay-image.yml` is ours, not upstream's, and it is what builds `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb` — the image the production relay actually runs. Losing it in a merge would be invisible until the next deploy did nothing.

Merge or rebase was decided in M1. Follow that decision; do not relitigate it here.

## Keep all four commits' behaviour

Not their diffs — their behaviour. If upstream restructured `required_scope_for_kind`, our four arms need re-deriving rather than re-applying.

The check that matters is not "the merge is clean" but **"every Estiva kind is still in `ALL_KINDS` and still maps to a scope."** A dropped list entry compiles fine and fails in production as `restricted: unknown event kind`.

Kinds to confirm present after the merge:

```
30850  30851  1851  9101       (Ship: projects, issues, changes; Estiva assertions)
1111   31989  31990            (NIP-22 comments, NIP-89 handlers)
30840  30841                   (NIP-FC files and components)
9802                           (NIP-84 highlights)
9  7  5  9007  27235  9002     (already upstream — confirm unchanged)
```

## Traps

- **Do not run `cargo fmt`.** `nfb-demo-kinds` is not rustfmt-clean; formatting reflows unrelated comments and buries the real diff in noise. If CI demands it, that is a separate ticket.
- **Check the workflow settings afterwards.** Twelve upstream workflows are `DISABLED_MANUALLY` to save minutes. That is a *repo setting*, not a file, so the merge does not re-enable them — but 625 commits may have added new workflows that arrive enabled. Confirm rather than assume.
- Do not adopt anything new from upstream in this ticket. NIP-MP, git statuses and NIP-FI become *available*; using them is a decision per feature, and NIP-MP is entangled with RFC 0.3's deferred question.

## Done when

`cargo build` succeeds, the test suite passes, every kind above is present in `ALL_KINDS` with a scope mapping, `relay-image.yml` still exists, and the diff contains no reformatting. Nothing is deployed by this ticket.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Audit which upstream migrations would run, and which could refuse
issues.description:
**M1 · the one that decides whether this project is easy or hard.** Read-only.

## Why

625 commits of upstream include schema migrations, and they run against Postgres on relay startup. The relay's database is shared by everything: Peek, Ship, the agent CLI, the MCP server.

**At least one upstream migration is known to refuse rather than migrate.** `crates/buzz-db/src/migration.rs` blocks the NIP-RS pre-0007 path when existing `kind:30078` rows have ambiguous `d`/`t` tag cardinality:

> `NIP-RS migration blocked: pre-0007 database contains kind-30078 rows with ambiguous d/t tag cardinality; repair or remove those nonconforming rows before retrying`

That is a *good* migration — it fails loudly rather than corrupting. Assume there are others, and assume some of them fail less loudly.

## What to produce

**1. The list.** Every migration between our current schema version and upstream's head. Where it lives, what it does, and whether it is additive, destructive, or conditional.

**2. The refusers.** Which ones can *block*, and what data shape triggers each. For the NIP-RS one specifically: **do we currently have any `kind:30078` rows at all?** Cross-app read state (CRO-2) grants that kind, so if that project lands first the answer changes from "no" to "yes, ours" — and this ticket's answer has a shelf life.

**3. The irreversibles.** Anything that drops or rewrites a column. Those set the requirement for M4's throwaway and for whether a backup is taken first.

**4. Row counts that matter.** For any conditional migration, how much production data hits its condition. A migration that is instant on 100 rows and locks a table on 10 million is the same code.

## Traps

- **Read the production schema version, do not assume it.** The fork has been deployed by hand for months.
- Do not run anything against production. This is a reading exercise; M4 is where migrations actually execute.
- `docker compose exec -T postgres psql …` on the box reads the live schema. See `operations/PRODUCTION.md`.
- Migrations may be ordered by a mechanism that does not match commit order. Read the migration runner, not just the files.

## Done when

The four lists are on this issue, and there is a plain answer to: **would deploying upstream today break, block, or silently change production data?** If yes, say which migration and what it needs first. That answer is the gate for M2.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Check kind collisions and the conflict surface of our four commits
issues.description:
**M1.** Read-only. Can run alongside the survey.

## Why

Our four commits are all additions to the kind registry and its scope mapping:

```
d207a1148  Linear-lite Projects, Issues and Changes (30850/30851/1851)
ffeb41606  NIP-22 comments and NIP-89 handlers (1111, 31989/31990)
70f75609b  NIP-FC Files and Components (30840/30841)
e8b0dab5b  NIP-84 highlights (kind:9802)
```

They touch exactly two files — `crates/buzz-core/src/kind.rs` (constants and `ALL_KINDS`) and `crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs` (`required_scope_for_kind`). Both have been edited heavily across 625 upstream commits.

**These are conflicts in a list, which is the dangerous shape**: they resolve easily and misresolve invisibly. A dropped entry in `ALL_KINDS` means the relay answers `restricted: unknown event kind` for a kind Peek or Ship publishes — and it fails at publish time in production, not at build time.

## What to check

**1. Kind collisions.** Verified clear on 2026-08-24: none of `30850`, `30851`, `1851`, `9101`, `30840`, `30841`, `9802`, `1111`, `31989`, `31990` is claimed upstream. **Re-verify at merge time.** Upstream allocates continuously, and NIP-MP's own allocation note states both external registries are advisory rather than authoritative.

A collision is not fatal but it is a decision: either we move (breaking published events) or we diverge knowingly and record it.

**2. Conflict surface.** For each of the four commits, what upstream has done to the same regions. Specifically whether `required_scope_for_kind`'s shape changed — if upstream restructured the match, our four arms need re-deriving rather than re-applying.

**3. The `is_global_only_kind` list.** `ingest.rs` keeps a list of kinds whose `h` tag is stripped because they are user-owned global state. If upstream added to it, check nothing of ours landed there by accident — a stripped `h` on a channel-scoped kind is a silent privacy change.

## Traps

- **Read `nfb-demo-kinds`, not `main`.** `main` carries a Revert that `nfb-demo-kinds` does not, so a diff against `main` shows changes that are not real.
- Do not run `cargo fmt`. `nfb-demo-kinds` is not rustfmt-clean, and formatting reflows unrelated comments, burying the real diff.

## Done when

A per-commit conflict assessment and a re-verified collision check are recorded on this issue, with any collision called out explicitly as a decision rather than a detail.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Survey the 625-commit gap and decide merge versus rebase
issues.description:
**M1 · do this soon.** Cheap, read-only, and it is what makes the trigger for the rest of this project legible. Right now nobody can say what catching up would cost.

## Why

`estiva-app/buzz` is 625 commits behind `block/buzz` and 4 ahead (measured 2026-08-24). The number is a liability but not by itself a reason to act. The reason to act will be that something in those commits is wanted, or that a decision elsewhere needs to know what upstream's model has become — RFC 0.3 §10.1 is explicitly waiting to see what shape upstream's forge layer settles into.

This ticket produces the answer to *"what would we get, and what would it cost."* No merge, no branch, nothing pushed.

## What to produce

A written summary on this issue covering:

**What is in the gap that matters to us.** Known already, and worth confirming plus extending:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| NIP-MP projects (`kind:30621`) | a container concept close to RFC 0.3's folder |
| NIP-34 git statuses `1630`–`1633`, PRs `1618`/`1619`, issues `1621` | the forge layer; issues are marked *"📋 Designed"*, so check whether that changed |
| NIP-FI family (5 documents) | federated identity authorization — relevant to Estiva ID, separately |
| `40902` presence snapshot, `46030`/`46031` approvals, `30179` private managed agent | smaller additions |

**What has changed structurally**, not just additively — anything that would alter how Peek or Ship talk to the relay. The HTTP bridge, NIP-98 handling, channel semantics, the `h`-tag scoping rules, and the fan-out access filter are the surfaces that matter.

**Merge or rebase, decided and recorded.** With four commits either is defensible: rebase replays each conflict separately and yields cleaner history; merge is one resolution and preserves what actually happened. Pick one, say why, and note it here so M2 does not relitigate it.

## Traps

- `upstream` is configured with **push disabled**. Keep it that way; this ticket does not push anything anywhere.
- Do not create branches or start resolving conflicts. That is M2, and starting it here is how a survey becomes a two-week merge nobody scheduled.
- Read `nfb-demo-kinds`, not `main` — see the conflict ticket for why they differ.

## Done when

The summary is on this issue, the merge-versus-rebase decision is recorded with its reasoning, and there is a rough cost estimate for M2–M5. Someone should be able to read it and decide whether to schedule the rest.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Make the project record global, with buzz-channel and upstream tag names
issues.description:
**M3 · fixes a live defect and aligns with upstream at the same time.** Independent of RFC 0.3's undecided parts.

## Why — there is a real bug here, not just a divergence

Ship's project event (`kind:30850`) carries an `h` tag, so the relay files it under a channel and gates reads by membership. Consequences, both live:

- **13 of 65 issues on production are unreachable.** `loadAll` discovers from projects and widens into their Folders, so an issue whose project record does not resolve is invisible — to the CLI and to `ship.estiva.app` alike. The `coverage` block in the agent's own output reports this on every read.
- A project cannot be discovered by anyone who is not already in its channel, which makes "browse the workspace" impossible by construction.

Upstream solved the same problem differently and better: their project (`kind:30621`) is a **global** addressable event that *references* a channel via a `buzz-channel` tag. Global means discoverable by `kinds`+`authors` alone; the channel still gates the conversation.

RFC 0.3 §4.2 shows the same reasoning generalised — three of four required container properties are impossible under `h`.

## What to change

Publish `kind:30850` **without** an `h` tag, carrying the channel as a tag instead, and adopt upstream's vocabulary while touching it:

| today | change to |
| --- | --- |
| `["h", "<folder-uuid>"]` | `["buzz-channel", "<folder-uuid>"]` |
| `["title", "…"]` | `["name", "…"]` |
| description in `content` | `["description", "…"]` tag |
| `["d", "<uuid>"]` | unchanged — keep the uuid, **do not** move to a slug |
| `["lead", "<pubkey>"]` | unchanged, Estiva-specific |

Keeping `d` as a uuid is deliberate: RFC 0.3 §4.3 explains why a human slug in an address leaks a name you may later want private, and an address is immutable.

## Traps

- **Read both shapes.** Existing project records have `h` and `title`; new ones will not. The fold must accept either, indefinitely — republishing is barred by the ±15 minute drift window.
- **A global event is world-readable.** A project's *name* becomes public even to non-members. That is the intended trade for discoverability, but say it out loud before shipping — a project called "Acquisition of X" would leak. If any project needs a private name, it needs the RFC 0.3 private-folder model and does not belong in this ticket.
- Issues keep their `h` and stay channel-scoped. Only the project *record* goes global. Do not remove `h` from `30851`.
- `Store.loadAll` widens from projects into Folders. Global projects change discovery from "channels I can see" to "projects I can see" — verify the 13 unreachable issues actually become reachable rather than assuming, and record the before/after count on this issue.
- Estiva ID's ceiling is unchanged; `30850` is already granted.

## Done when

A project is discoverable by a relay query with no channel membership, its conversation is still gated, old project records still fold correctly, and the unreachable-issue count is measured before and after and recorded here.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Comments as NIP-22 kind:1111 instead of kind:9 with an about tag
issues.description:
**M3 · alignment, cheap.** Independent of RFC 0.3's undecided parts — do not wait for them.

## Why

Ship posts a comment as a `kind:9` message into the project's Folder carrying a custom `about` tag pointing at the issue address (`Store.postMessage`). The pattern is right; the tag is not standard.

**NIP-22 `kind:1111` is the standard version of exactly this idea.** From Buzz's own kind registry:

> a threaded comment scoped to any event, address or external identifier. Uppercase `A`/`E`/`I`/`K`/`P` tags name the thread root, lowercase the immediate parent. The point of NIP-22 over a bare kind:1 reply is that it can scope to an **addressable** event, which is what lets two different apps comment on the same object without either owning the comment kind.

Three reasons this is worth doing inside the rewrite:

1. **Upstream plans `1111` for issue comments too** (`VISION_PROJECTS.md`: *"Threaded comments use NIP-22 kind:1111"*). Their issue layer is designed and not built, so matching now costs nothing and buys interop later.
2. **Our relay already accepts it** — commit `ffeb41606` added `1111` to the kind registry. No gate, no re-seed, no relay deploy.
3. RFC 0.3 makes NIP-22 the conversation mechanism for *every* file type. Ship is the cheapest place to prove it, because Ship already has the one-channel-many-anchored-threads shape in production.

## What to change

- Publish comments as `kind:1111` instead of `kind:9`+`about`.
- Root tag: uppercase `A` = the issue's address (`30851:<pk>:<d>`). Parent: lowercase `a`/`e` for a reply to a reply.
- Keep the `h` tag on the project's Folder — that is what gates who can read the thread, and it is unchanged.
- Read both: fold `1111` **and** existing `kind:9`+`about` messages, so history stays visible.

## Traps

- **Do not migrate old comments.** The relay rejects `created_at` outside roughly ±15 minutes of its own clock, so republishing history would stamp every comment with today's date. Read both shapes instead, indefinitely.
- Peek renders a Ship issue widget above a conversation because the message carries `about`. If Peek reads `about` specifically, `1111` comments will lose the widget until Peek is taught the new tag — check `convex/nostr/projection.ts` before assuming, and file a Peek ticket if so.
- Estiva ID must be allowed to sign `1111`. Verify with the `allowed_kinds` query before starting; the app ceiling is separate from the relay's registry.
- `1111` is channel-scoped when it carries `h` and global otherwise. Always carry `h` — a global comment thread on a private issue would be a leak.

## Done when

A comment posted from Ship is a `kind:1111` anchored at the issue address, readable by another participant, invisible to a non-member of the Folder, and old `kind:9`+`about` comments still render in the same thread.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: fold.ts held a raw NUL byte, which made it binary to every tool that reads source
issues.description:
foldChanges keys its winners map on a composite of target and field, and the separator has to be something neither an address nor a field name can contain. NUL is the right choice. It was written as a literal 0x00 byte rather than the \0 escape, which made src/fold.ts a binary file to the tools that read source.

The consequence that bites is silent. The grep an agent gets in this environment routes through a ugrep with -I, which skips a binary file and reports no match - exit 1, nothing on stdout, nothing on stderr - for text that is plainly there. 'grep -n projectFolders src/fold.ts' came back empty with the symbol on line 361, which is how this was found. GNU grep 3.12 at least says 'binary file matches' and exits 0, so a human terminal gets a hint where an agent gets a lie.

The one that would have hurt more: git's binary heuristic scans the first 8000 bytes for a NUL, and this byte sat at 8025. A 25-byte margin, measured by shifting it 30 bytes earlier, which turns the file into 'Bin 17762 -> 17772 bytes' and every diff into 'Binary files differ'. Any edit above line 217 removing 26 bytes would have made this file unreviewable in a pull request - the one file whose behaviour the conformance fixture exists to protect.

What it did NOT break, contrary to how this was first reported: 'diff -r src ../estiva-agent/src' still detects drift on a binary file and exits 1. The drift check was never compromised.

Fixed by writing the escape instead of the byte. Proven inert at three levels:
- the recorded fold is unchanged, 5fad457070fc19c3, so fold-fixture.json and EVENTS_SHA256 are untouched;
- the shipped artifact is byte-identical - the image bundles for 71033e2 and adf86c8 are both 180647 bytes, sha fee05bfc864a4d19, with zero raw NULs, because esbuild was already emitting the escape. The bug was purely source hygiene and never reached a user;
- src/fold.ts is now UTF-8 text and grep finds things in it.

PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/ship/pull/30 - merged as adf86c8, CI green, live on ship.estiva.app.

NOT done: the vendored copy. estiva-ship main now carries the escape and estiva-agent main still carries the raw byte, so the two repos are drifted right now - the exact invariant this change touches. The mirror commit exists and is pushed, but it sits on another session's branch (janmikula/peek-172-refuse-what-cannot-be-signed, PEEK-172), because that session committed on top of it. It converges when that PR merges. Nothing to do here except not lose track of it.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Remove the old vanilla-DOM app
issues.description:
**M5 · last ticket.** Deliberately separate from the cutover, so a problem found after deploying has something to fall back to. Do not start it until the new app has served production traffic for long enough to trust it.

## What to remove

The vanilla-DOM app: `apps/ship/app.ts` (28KB), `ui.ts`, `router.ts`, `context.ts`, `views/` and whatever remains of the old `index.html`. If M1 chose a parallel directory, this is also where `apps/ship-next` takes over the `apps/ship` name.

## What must NOT be removed

This is the actual content of the ticket, because a cleanup commit is exactly where these get swept up:

- **`src/`** — `events`, `fold`, `kinds`, `manifest`, `manifest-address`, `profiles`, `store`. Vendored into `estiva-agent` at identical paths.
- **`lib/nostr/`** — same, unless SHA-3 has already replaced it with `@estiva/protocol`, which is SHA-3's decision and includes deciding what the agent does.
- **`conformance/fold-fixture.json`** and **`scripts/conformance.test.ts`**, the latter still a `tsx` script.
- **`extension/`** and its build script and test.
- **`deploy/`**.
- The remaining `scripts/*.test.ts` that cover things still present.

## Removing test coverage is the risk, not removing code

A test deleted because the code it tested moved into a package leaves the package untested and nobody notices. Before deleting any `scripts/*.test.ts`, confirm its subject is either gone or covered elsewhere — and if the subject moved into `@estiva/identity` or `@estiva/protocol`, the test should have moved with it. Say on this issue where each deleted test's coverage now lives.

## Also update the documentation that is now wrong
