issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: UI must not imply end-to-end privacy for DMs
issues.description:
**M5 · the honesty task.** Last one. It is a copy and product task, and it is the one most likely to be skipped — which is exactly why it is written down.

## Why

This project chose **DM channels** over NIP-17 gift wrap, deliberately: business software needs search, retention, offboarding and administrative recovery, and end-to-end encryption prevents all four. The relay operator *is* the organisation.

The consequence is unavoidable and must be stated: **DMs are private by membership, not private by encryption.** The relay stores them in plaintext. Anyone with relay database access can read every DM.

That is a defensible design. What is not defensible is a UI that implies otherwise. A lock icon, the word "encrypted", "private and secure", or even an unqualified "Private" next to a padlock sets an expectation the system does not meet — and in a tool for business organisations, that is the kind of misunderstanding that matters when someone decides what to type.

## What to do

1. **Audit existing copy** for anything implying end-to-end privacy — DM empty states, the composer placeholder, tooltips, settings, onboarding, marketing pages, and any lock or shield iconography.
2. **Decide what the product does say.** "Private" is accurate for membership-scoped, so it is not off-limits — but decide deliberately whether to say more, e.g. that DMs are visible to the workspace operator. This is a product and possibly a legal call, not a developer default. Bring it to whoever owns that.
3. **Write the decision down** in the repo, next to the DM code, with the reasoning. The next person to add a lock icon should find the argument before they ship it.

## Also worth deciding now, while it is cheap

The choice makes several things *possible* that are not in this project's scope, and they are easier to design for than to retrofit:

- **Export / legal hold / admin read.** Now feasible. Do not build them here, but do not accidentally preclude them.
- **Offboarding.** NIP-IA already exists (`9035` archive request, `9036` unarchive, relay-signed `8002`/`8003` deltas, `13535` list snapshot). Confirm archiving an identity does the right thing to its DMs, and record what it does.
- **Retention.** Buzz channels carry `ttl_seconds` and `ttl_deadline`. Whether DMs should ever expire is a policy question; note it and move on.

## Traps

- Do not overcorrect into alarming copy. "Your admin can read this" on every message is as wrong in the other direction — accurate, unusable, and it will just be turned off.
- Keep this out of the code-only bucket. If nobody who owns product copy has read the decision, the task is not done.

## Done when

No surface in Peek implies end-to-end encryption for DMs, the decision about what the product *does* say is recorded with its author, and the three follow-on questions above have written answers even if the answer is "not now".

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Enforce the 9-participant cap in the composer
issues.description:
**M5.** Small, and it belongs in the composer rather than in an error handler.

## Why

`handle_dm_open` caps participants (`command_executor.rs:330`):

```
"invalid: pubkeys may contain at most 8 other participants (9 total)"
```

Eight others, nine total including yourself. Note the relay counts the **deduplicated** set including the sender — `compute_participant_hash` dedupes, and `handle_dm_open` builds the full set as self plus others — so a client that also puts its own pubkey in `#p` still gets nine, but a client counting only its `#p` tags will be off by one at the boundary.

Discovering this as a relay rejection means someone has already picked ten people and written a message.

## What to change

Enforce it where people choose participants:

- stop adding recipients at 8 others, with a clear reason rather than a silently dead control
- apply the same cap to the "start a group DM" flow from the immutable-participants task, before offering it
- keep a server-side guard in the Convex `unsignedDmOpen` builder too, so a stale client gets a legible refusal rather than the relay's wire message

## Traps

- **Count the deduped set including self**, matching the relay. Off-by-one here means the UI allows exactly one case the relay refuses, which is the worst possible place for the boundary to disagree.
- Do not hardcode `8` in three files. One named constant, and cite `command_executor.rs` beside it so the next person knows where the number comes from and that it is not ours to choose.
- The cap is the relay's, not a product decision. If the product wants larger group conversations, that is a topic (a Folder with members), not a DM — worth saying in the empty state rather than leaving people stuck at nine.

## Done when

The composer refuses a tenth participant with a readable reason, no DM open request is ever sent that the relay would refuse for size, and the constant names its source.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Immutable participants: adding someone starts a new conversation
issues.description:
**M5.** A UI task driven by a protocol constraint. Worth its own issue because getting it wrong looks like data loss.

## Why

Buzz treats a DM's participant set as **immutable**. `buzz-db/src/dm.rs` states it: *"Participant sets are immutable — adding a member creates a NEW DM."* And `KIND_DM_ADD_MEMBER` (41011) implements exactly that — `command_executor.rs:521` is explicit: *"open_dm with expanded set (creates NEW DM — DM sets are immutable)"*.

This is not a limitation to work around; it is the correct behaviour. The channel id is derived from `compute_participant_hash` over the participant set, so a different set *is* a different conversation by construction. It also means nobody is ever silently added to a conversation with history they were not party to — which for business software is a feature.

But if Peek's UI offers "add someone to this DM" and the result is a new, empty conversation while the old one keeps the history, users read that as their messages disappearing.

## What to build

Present the operation as what it is: **starting a new conversation with these people, from this one.**

- Do not label it "add member" or "invite". Something like "Start a group DM with…" — the wording is the deliverable here.
- Say what happens to the current conversation: it stays, with its history, and the new one starts empty.
- Make the old conversation reachable afterwards. Consider a marker linking the two, in the spirit of Peek's existing `originDmId` / `promotedAt` pattern on huddles, which already models "this came from that".
- Show the participant set as fixed once the conversation exists.

Follow the working rule: **only offer actions that can succeed.** If the UI cannot honestly offer "add a person to this thread", it should not appear to.

## Traps

- **`41011` is not reversible and not an edit.** It creates a conversation. Confirm before publishing.
- The new DM is subject to the same 9-participant cap — check *before* offering, not after the relay refuses.
- Because opening is idempotent by participant hash, the "new" conversation may already exist with history of its own. Handle landing in an existing conversation gracefully; it is the normal case for a group you have messaged before.
- Peek's `dmConversations` will need to represent the relationship if you add the link. Do not remove fields to make room — a removed field fails the whole Convex push.

## Done when

A person who has never read this ticket uses the flow and correctly predicts what happened to the original conversation. That is the actual bar; anything less and the immutability reads as a bug.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: DM read state via the h:<channel-uuid> context convention
issues.description:
**M4.** Soft dependency on *Cross-app read state* CRO-3 (the context convention) and CRO-5 (the merge). If those have not landed, leave this until they do rather than inventing an interim scheme.

## Why it is nearly free

Once a DM is a real channel with a Folder uuid, it fits the read-context convention with no new thinking: its context id is `h:<dm-channel-uuid>`, exactly like a topic's. Threads inside it are `thread:<root-event-id>`, individual messages `msg:<event-id>`.

That is the payoff from choosing DM channels over gift wrap. An end-to-end encrypted DM would have needed its own read-state scheme, because the relay could not have told which conversation a context referred to.

## What to change

- Mark a DM read using `h:<dm-channel-uuid>` in the NIP-RS blob, through the same client CRO-4 and CRO-5 build. No DM-specific code path.
- `readState.containerId` already accepts a `dmConversations` id (§2.10, two granularities, ruling 2026-07-09), so the local cache needs no schema change — only the mapping from container to context id.
- Confirm the unread dot and Desk sections pick DMs up through the same `watermarks()` path they use for topics.

## Traps

- **Use the channel uuid, not the Convex `dmConversations` id,** as the context id. The whole point is a context another app can compute independently; a Convex id is meaningless outside this deployment. This is the single most likely mistake in this task.
- Write discipline still applies: reading one thread inside a DM advances `thread:<root>` only, never the DM's `h:` context.
- A DM with a Convex row but no channel uuid yet (see the existing-DMs task) has no valid context id. Decide what its read state means rather than emitting `h:undefined`.

## Done when

Reading a DM in Peek advances `h:<dm-channel-uuid>` in the published blob, and the unread indicator clears on a second device without a reload. Verify by reading the blob back, not by watching the dot alone.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Decide and execute what happens to existing Convex-only DMs
issues.description:
**M4 · a decision task, not only a code task.** Do not start it by writing a migration.

## Why this needs deciding rather than defaulting

Peek's existing DMs live in Convex and nowhere else, in plaintext, and they are the only copy. Once new DMs go to the relay there are two populations, and "we will sort the old ones out later" leaves the DM list showing two kinds of conversation that behave differently — some searchable server-side, some not; some visible on a second device, some not. That is worse than either clean answer.

## The three defensible options

**1. Migrate by republishing.** For each existing DM, publish `41010` for its participant set and republish each message as a `kind:9`. Result: one uniform population.

- The blocker is the **drift window**: the relay rejects `created_at` outside roughly ±15 minutes of its own clock, and the protocol spec is explicit — *"An app backfilling historical records MUST NOT expect them to be accepted."* So republished messages would carry today's timestamps, destroying the conversation's chronology. Any migration has to answer this, and "the relay will accept it" is not an available answer.
- A partial answer: carry the original timestamp in a tag and have Peek's projection prefer it for display. That keeps ordering inside Peek but means the relay's own view of the conversation is wrong, which defeats part of the point.

**2. Leave them as read-only history.** Old DMs stay in Convex, rendered as they are, marked as pre-migration and not writable. New DMs go to the relay. Honest, no data loss, no fake timestamps — but two populations forever, and the UI has to explain the difference.

**3. Discard.** Defensible only if the existing DMs are genuinely demo or internal-test data. Check before assuming: production launched with an empty database (decision 2026-07-08), so whatever is there is real usage.

## Recommendation

**Option 2**, unless the volume turns out to be trivial. The drift window makes option 1 dishonest in a way that is hard to undo — a conversation whose timestamps are all "migration day" is a worse record than one clearly labelled as older. Option 2 costs a UI affordance and keeps the record true.

## What to do

1. **Count first.** How many DM conversations and messages exist, and how old? The answer may make this trivial. Query the real deployment — `honorable-guineapig-592`, named explicitly, not `--prod`, which resolves elsewhere and has reported confidently about data nobody was using.
2. Record the decision and its reasoning on this issue.
3. Implement it, including whatever the UI must say.

## Traps

- **Do not remove any `dmConversations` field as part of this.** Removing a field from a validator fails the *entire* Convex push for every row that still carries it, at deploy time — invisible to `tsc -b` and the test suite. Sweep first, confirm zero, then remove.
- Republishing another person's messages under your own pubkey would misattribute them. Only the author can publish their own message; a migration that ignores this rewrites history under one name.

## Done when

The decision is recorded here with the counts that informed it, implemented, and the DM list behaves consistently — or visibly and deliberately explains why part of it does not.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: DM sidebar hidden set: publish kind:41012, read kind:30622
issues.description:
**M3.** Depends on DM channels existing. Self-contained and can be done in parallel with the projection task.

## Why

A DM list needs a way to say "I do not want this in my sidebar" without leaving the conversation or losing its history. Buzz models this as two halves, and both already exist:

- **`kind:41012` `KIND_DM_HIDE`** — the client's request to hide a DM. Peek publishes this.
- **`kind:30622` `KIND_DM_VISIBILITY`** — the relay's per-viewer snapshot of the hidden set. Parameterized replaceable with `d = viewer_pubkey`, carrying one `h` tag per hidden DM, republished by the relay on every hide/unhide so **the latest event is always the authoritative hidden set**.

## What to build

- **Publish `41012`** to hide a DM.
- **Read `30622`** for the viewer and treat it as authoritative for which DMs are hidden. Do not maintain a separate Convex `hidden` column as the source of truth — the relay owns this state, and a second copy is a divergence waiting to happen. Cache it if useful, the way read state is cached.
- Unhide: per `moderation_notices.rs:121`, `open_dm` *resurfaces* a hidden DM — so re-opening the same participant set clears the hidden flag. Check during the probe whether an explicit unhide command exists or whether re-open is the intended route; the comment suggests the latter.

## Traps

- **Never sign a `30622`.** It is relay-signed and result-gated: `buzz-core/src/kind.rs` lists it in `RESULT_GATED_KINDS`, and `filter.rs:reader_authorized_for_event` requires the reader to equal the event's `#p` tag. Peek reads only its own, and `ingest.rs` would reject a client-authored one anyway.
- **Hiding is not leaving and not deleting.** The DM, its participants and its history all survive; only the sidebar entry goes. Make sure the UI copy says that — "hide" that reads as "delete" is a support ticket.
- The snapshot is a full replacement, not a delta. Apply the newest event wholesale rather than merging successive ones.
- A hidden DM that receives a new message: decide deliberately whether it resurfaces. `open_dm`'s resurfacing behaviour suggests yes, but confirm against the relay rather than assuming, and record the answer here.

## Done when

Hiding a DM removes it from the sidebar, the relay's `30622` for that viewer lists its `h`, a second device reflects the same hidden set, and no other identity can read that snapshot.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Project DM channels through the existing channel projection
issues.description:
**M3.** Depends on DM messages being published. This should be a second caller, not a second projection.

## Why it should be nearly free

The relay stores each DM message with the DM channel's `channel_id`, exactly as it does a topic message. So every read-path mechanism Peek already has works on a DM channel with no new logic:

- `syncPlan` → returns `{ channelUuid, since }` for a container
- `importChannel` / `importReactions` / `importResolutions` → take events, not tokens
- the `since` cursor and `nostrSyncedAt` monotonic advance (`convex/nostr/data.ts:523`)
- reaction and deletion handling, including the `#h` fallback for kinds that carry no `h` tag
- the live WebSocket subscription from *Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates*, which subscribes per channel

If this task ends up large, that is the signal something is being reimplemented rather than reused.

## What to change

- `syncPlan` currently resolves only `topics` rows. Teach it to resolve a `dmConversations` row too, returning that channel's uuid and cursor. Keep the existing lookup shape — it scans and matches on `_id` or `seedKey` because `topics` has no `seedKey` index.
- The projection writes messages with `parentKind`/`parentId`. For a DM channel those must resolve to `'dm'` and the `dmConversations` id.
- Whatever triggers a topic sync should trigger a DM sync on the same terms — the mount-time sync, the focus/visibility refetch, and the live subscription.

## Traps

- **Do not create a parallel `dmSync.ts`.** One projection, two container types. Two projections will diverge, and the divergence will be silent because each is self-consistent.
- **`resolveExternalUser` matters more here.** A DM's other participant may have no Peek user row. The projection already mints one from a pubkey (`internal.nostr.data.resolveExternalUser`); make sure the DM path uses it rather than dropping messages from unknown authors.
- Participants come from the relay's participant set, not from an `h`-tagged member list. Do not infer membership from who has spoken.
- Do not let a DM sync mark anything read.

## Done when

A DM sent from one identity appears in the other's Peek without a reload, projected through the same code path as a topic message. Confirm by checking that the diff for this task adds callers and arguments, not a new projection.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Publish DM messages as kind:9 against the DM channel
issues.description:
**M2.** Depends on the DM channel existing. This is the smallest task in the project, and that is the point.

## Why it is small

A DM message is an ordinary `kind:9` against the DM channel's `h`. That is the same event Peek already publishes for topic messages. The existing `unsignedMessage` query in `convex/nostr/outbox.ts` refuses it only because of one guard:

```ts
// Only topic messages publish: DMs need NIP-17 gift wrap and huddles have no Buzz container.
if (m.parentKind !== 'topic') return { ok: false, reason: 'not a topic message' }
```

That comment describes NIP-17, which this project decided against. With DM channels the refusal no longer applies to DMs — only to huddles.

## What to change

Widen `unsignedMessage` (and `unsignedReply`) to accept `parentKind === 'dm'`, resolving the channel uuid from the `dmConversations` row instead of the `topics` row. Keep the huddle refusal, and **update that comment** — leaving it in place would tell the next reader that DMs need gift wrap, which is now false and is exactly the kind of stale comment that sends someone down a three-day path.

Everything else in the function already applies unchanged and should be kept: the idempotency check (`if (m.nostrEventId) return ... 'already published'`), the author check, the drift-window check, and the "channel must exist" check.

## Traps

- **Keep the drift-window check.** The relay rejects `created_at` outside roughly ±15 minutes of its own clock. The existing code checks this *before* signing so an old row costs nothing and the reason is legible rather than arriving as a generic relay rejection.
- **Keep first-publish-wins idempotency.** A row with a `nostrEventId` must never publish twice.
- `unsignedReply` refuses when the parent is unpublished, because Buzz rejects a reply to an event it does not know. That rule is unchanged for DMs.
- Reactions and deletions need no work at all: `buzz-core/src/filter.rs` derives a kind:7 or kind:5's channel from its target at ingest, so they follow the DM channel automatically.

## Done when

A DM sent in Peek appears on the relay as a `kind:9` with the DM channel's `h`, and is readable back by the other participant but not by a third identity. Verify the last part — it is the privacy boundary this whole design rests on.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Open a DM channel with kind:41010 and record its uuid
issues.description:
**M2.** Depends on the grant and the probe. This is the "start a conversation" half.

## Why

Peek's `dmConversations` table exists but has no relay counterpart — DMs are Convex-only today. This gives each one a real channel on the relay, using the same pattern `topics.channelUuid` already establishes.

## What to build

**Publish `kind:41010`** when a DM is first needed, with one `#p` tag per other participant. The relay builds the full participant set as self + others, deduplicated, so **do not include your own pubkey** in `#p` — it is added server-side and duplicates are collapsed by the participant hash either way.

**Record the returned channel uuid** on the `dmConversations` row, mirroring `topics.channelUuid`. Follow the existing shape in `convex/nostr/data.ts`: `storeChannelUuid` is an `internalMutation` with **first-write-wins** semantics (`if (t.channelUuid) return { minted: false }`). Use the same rule — two tabs opening the same DM simultaneously must converge on one channel, not race.

**Lean on idempotence rather than bookkeeping.** Because the channel id is derived from `compute_participant_hash`, re-opening a DM with the same people returns the same channel. So "message this person" never needs to ask whether a DM already exists — publish `41010` and use what comes back. `find_dm_by_participants` is the relay's own lookup and it is keyed the same way.

## Where it belongs

The unsigned event should be built in Convex, signed and published in the browser, and the resulting id recorded back — the three-step division in `src/nostr/bridge.ts`. Convex has the data and needs no credential to shape the event; the browser has the token and is the only place it belongs; the channel uuid is a fact, not a secret.

Add an `unsignedDmOpen` query alongside `unsignedMessage` in `convex/nostr/outbox.ts` rather than inventing a second pattern.

## Traps

- **`HTTP 200` does not mean accepted.** A duplicate returns `200 {"accepted":false,...}`. For this command a duplicate is success — the DM already exists. Read the field; do not treat the status code as the answer, and do not treat a duplicate as an error.
- **Do not publish a `kind:9007`.** `41010` creates the channel itself.
- The relay caps participants at **8 others, 9 total** (`command_executor.rs:330`). Enforcement in the UI is a separate task, but this code should fail legibly rather than passing 12 pubkeys and reporting the relay's rejection verbatim.
- `41010` is a *command*, persisted for idempotency. Republishing an identical one is safe.

## Done when

Opening a DM in Peek produces a channel on the relay, the uuid is on the `dmConversations` row, and opening the same DM again from a second tab yields the same uuid with no duplicate row.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Probe DM open and send against the live relay
issues.description:
**M1.** Do this immediately after the grant and before writing any UI. It is a throwaway probe whose only job is to convert four assumptions into four observations.

## Why

Four things about DM channels are believed but not yet verified against the live relay, and each one fails in a way that looks like something else:

1. `41010` is accepted over the **HTTP bridge**. `ingest.rs:1498` restricts only `KIND_GIFT_WRAP` and `KIND_PRESENCE_UPDATE` to WebSocket, so DM commands should be fine on the path Peek already uses — but this is the assumption the whole project's independence rests on. If it is wrong, this project needs the WebSocket publish path from *Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates* and the plan changes shape.
2. The response identifies the created DM channel. `handle_dm_open` returns `(channel, was_created)` internally; what reaches the client over the bridge needs checking, because Peek must record the channel uuid somewhere.
3. **Opening is idempotent.** `open_dm` derives the channel from `compute_participant_hash` over the deduped participant set, so a second `41010` with the same people should return the same channel with `was_created: false`. Remember `HTTP 200` does not mean accepted — the `accepted` field is authoritative, and a duplicate is not a failure.
4. A `kind:9` with the DM channel's `h` is accepted and readable back by a participant.

## What to build

A script under `scripts/` in the style of `probe-kinds.ts` / `probe-agent.ts` — it reports which hop broke, which a single rejection at the end does not tell you. Steps: mint a token, publish `41010` with one `#p`, read the response, publish it again and compare, publish a `kind:9` to the returned channel, then `/query` it back.

Use two real Estiva ID identities. A key invented at runtime cannot be a relay member and would fail at admission for reasons unrelated to DMs.

## Traps

- Publishing writes to **production**; there is no staging workspace. A test DM between two real identities is visible to those identities. Use your own and a second identity you control, and say in the ticket which ones.
- NIP-98 auth is required on every bridge route, so a bare curl returns 401 and is indistinguishable from a refused kind. Go through the existing signer.
- The relay rejects `created_at` outside roughly ±15 minutes of its own clock.

## Done when

All four observations are recorded on this issue with the relay's own words. If (1) fails, say so loudly and add the WebSocket dependency to the project description before anyone starts M2.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Grant Peek kinds 41010/41011/41012, re-seed, verify the row
issues.description:
**M1 · blocking gate for everything else.** One gate only — the kinds are already accepted by the relay.

## Why

All four DM kinds are already in Buzz's `ALL_KINDS`, so the relay accepts them today: no Buzz change, no relay deploy, none of the `nfb-demo-kinds` branch work. The only gate is Estiva ID's per-app ceiling in `estiva-id/src/db/seed.ts`, where `peek` currently has `[9, 7, 5, 9007, 27235, 1851, 9101, 9002]`.

## What to change

Add to the `peek` entry's `allowedKinds`:

| kind | const | what |
|---|---|---|
| `41010` | `KIND_DM_OPEN` | open (or idempotently re-open) a DM with `#p` participants |
| `41011` | `KIND_DM_ADD_MEMBER` | creates a **new** DM with the expanded set |
| `41012` | `KIND_DM_HIDE` | hide a DM from the sidebar |

`kind:9` is already granted and is what DM messages are.

## Do NOT grant 30622

`KIND_DM_VISIBILITY` (30622) is **relay-signed**. The relay republishes it on every hide/unhide, and it is result-gated — `buzz-core/src/kind.rs` lists it in `RESULT_GATED_KINDS`, and `filter.rs:reader_authorized_for_event` enforces that the reader must equal the event's `#p` tag. Peek only ever *reads* its own. Granting it would let Peek forge a visibility snapshot, and `ingest.rs` would reject it anyway as relay-signed-only.

## Do NOT publish kind:9007 for a DM

`handle_dm_open` (`command_executor.rs:310`) calls `open_dm`, which writes the channel row directly. The `41010` command creates the channel. Publishing a `9007` as well would create a second, unrelated container — the exact fork the pairing rules exist to prevent.

## Deploying it — the part that silently does nothing

**`update.sh` on the box runs `migrate`, never `seed`.** A seed-only change deploys into the image and then has no effect. A manual re-seed is required.

**Verify the row, never the `seeded N app credential(s)` log line:**

```bash
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U estiva_id -d estiva_id -tAc "select client_id, allowed_kinds from app_credentials"
```

## Done when

The psql output lists `41010`, `41011` and `41012` for `peek`, and `/sign` accepts a `kind:41010` without a `kind_not_allowed` refusal.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Prove cross-app read state end to end
issues.description:
**M5 · the proof.** Last task. Everything before this is machinery; this is the thing the project promised.

## Why a dedicated task

Every prior task verifies its own layer, and all of them can pass while the feature does not work. The relay can hold correct blobs, both clients can merge correctly, and the sidebar can still show a stale dot — because the UI reads a cache, or a context id differs by one character between two apps, or a publish is debounced past the point anyone waits.

So this task checks the thing a person actually experiences, in the shape the project was asked for: **read it in one app, it is read in the other.**

## What to verify

Do these as a person, in real browsers, against production. Not as a test suite.

1. **Ship → Peek.** Open a Ship issue whose Folder maps to a Peek topic showing unread. Read it. Without reloading Peek, the topic's unread indicator clears.
2. **Peek → Ship.** The reverse.
3. **Second device.** Same identity, a different browser profile or machine. Read in one, confirm the other follows. This is the plain cross-device case NIP-RS was designed for and it must not have regressed.
4. **Thread granularity.** Read one thread in a topic with several unread threads. Only that thread clears — the topic stays unread, and no later top-level message is marked read. This is the write-discipline rule, and it is the one most likely to be quietly wrong.
5. **Container marks children read.** Mark the whole container read; threads whose events predate the frontier clear, and a reply newer than the frontier stays unread.
6. **The horizon.** A container read well over the horizon ago still reads as read (the cache is doing its job), while a genuinely never-read container still reads as unread. These two must stay distinguishable.
7. **Monotonicity under concurrency.** Both apps open, read in both within a few seconds, then reload both. No context goes backwards.

## Traps

- **Do not verify from logs or the dual-run diff.** Those were the previous task's job. Check the visible state — the dot, the Desk section, the bold row.
- Give the debounced publish and the fetch interval time to settle before declaring a failure, but write down how long it took. "It works within 30 seconds" and "it works" are different products, and the answer belongs on this ticket.
- Test with an identity that has real history, not a fresh one. The horizon and cache behaviour only exist for accounts with a past.

## Done when

All seven pass and the observed propagation delay is recorded on this issue. If any fail, the finding belongs here as a comment with what was measured — a half-working cross-app read state is worse than none, because people stop trusting the dot and then stop reading it.

title.value: [MS2] Prove cross-app read state end to end

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Ship publishes and merges the same read contexts
issues.description:
**M4.** Depends on the convention and on Ship's 30078 grant. This is the task that turns a Peek feature into a suite property.

## Why

Ship is where the other half of the cross-app scenario happens: you read a comment on an issue in Ship, and the corresponding Peek conversation should stop being unread. Until Ship publishes to the same contexts, Peek is only syncing with itself across devices — useful, but not the point.

Ship is well placed for this. It reads the relay directly and folds events client-side (`src/fold.ts`), it already polls every 5 seconds with a `visibilitychange` refresh (`apps/ship/app.ts:85`, `:721`), and it has no Convex layer to reconcile — so the merged NIP-RS state can simply *be* its read state, with no cache-versus-source-of-truth question at all.

Note Ship is mid-rewrite onto React conventions. Coordinate: this is small enough to do in the current vanilla-DOM app, but if the rewrite is already underway it belongs there instead of being written twice.

## What to build

The same client as Peek's, against the same contexts:

- its own `slot-id` and `client_id`, persisted locally — **distinct from Peek's**, since these are per installation
- publish `kind:30078` blobs via Estiva ID `/sign` plus the NIP-44 endpoints (Ship signs through `estivaIdSigner`, so this is the same path it already uses)
- fetch all the viewer's slots and merge with the max rule
- mark read using the convention: `h:<folder-uuid>` for a project's Folder, `thread:<root-event-id>` for an issue's comment thread, `msg:<event-id>` for a single comment

## The mapping decision worth getting right

Ship's natural containers are a **project** and an **issue**, and they do not map one-to-one onto the convention. A project has a Folder, so `h:<folder-uuid>` is exact. An issue is an *object inside* a Folder, not a container of its own — so an issue's comment thread is a `thread:<root-event-id>`, not an `h:`.

Getting this wrong in the direction of using `h:` for an issue would make reading one issue mark the whole project read. Follow the write discipline from the convention: advancing a thread must never advance its container.

## Traps

- **Duplication is the house pattern here, deliberately.** `lib/nostr/` and `src/` are vendored by copy into `estiva-agent` at identical paths, kept honest by `conformance/fold-fixture.json` and `scripts/conformance.test.ts` (commit b990b57). If this read-state client ends up in `lib/` or `src/`, it must be copied to the agent and covered by the conformance check, or the two will drift — which is the exact failure PEEK-165 found.
- Ship's `renewAccessToken` is the same operation as Peek's `refreshAccessToken` under a different name. Do not assume shared code; there is none.
- Ship's 5-second poll makes it easy to accidentally publish a blob on every tick. Debounce on actual read events, not on refresh.

## Done when

Ship publishes a blob under its own slot, and Peek's merge picks it up — verified by reading a Ship issue and watching the corresponding context advance in Peek's merged state, before any UI work.

title.value: [MS2] Ship publishes and merges the same read contexts

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS3] Dual-run merged read state against Convex, then cut over
issues.description:
**M3 · the cutover.** Last task in M3. Depends on publish, merge and the cache.

## Why do it in two steps

Read state is unusually forgiving to verify, and it would be a waste not to exploit that. The merge is a grow-only CvRDT: a wrong implementation **converges** rather than corrupts, and the worst outcome of a disagreement is a container that reads as unread when it should not. So the change can be run in parallel with the existing behaviour and compared on live data before anything is switched.

## Step 1 — dual-run

Compute both, use the existing one, log the difference:

- **A:** today's Convex-native read state (`readState.ts` written directly by `useMarkRead`)
- **B:** the merged NIP-RS state from the previous tasks

Render from **A**. Record where A and B disagree, with the context id, both timestamps and which is ahead. Leave it running long enough to cover a weekend — the horizon interacts with idle time, which is precisely when a bug would appear.

Expect and ignore two benign classes of disagreement:

- **B ahead of A** for anything read in another app or on another device. That is the feature working.
- **A ahead of B** immediately after a local read, until the debounced publish lands.

What to actually investigate: **A ahead of B persistently** (a publish is being lost, or a context id is being written under the wrong scheme), and any case where **B moves backwards** (a monotonicity violation, which is a bug in the merge and must be fixed before cutover).

## Step 2 — cut over

When the diff is quiet apart from the benign classes:

1. Render from the merged state (via the cache, per the previous task).
2. `useMarkRead` publishes a NIP-RS blob and updates the cache; it no longer treats Convex as authoritative.
3. Keep `readState` as the cache. **Do not drop the table or its fields.**

## Traps

- **Do not remove fields from the `readState` validator as part of this.** Removing a field from a table's validator fails the *entire* Convex push for every row that still carries it, and it fails at deploy time — not at `tsc -b`, not in the test suite. If anything must go, ship a sweep first, run it, confirm zero, then remove.
- Do not delete `useMarkRead`'s local write. The cache update is what keeps the UI instant; the publish is asynchronous and debounced.
- Keep the dual-run logging behind the existing debug surface rather than `console.log`, so it can be left on.

## Done when

The sidebar and Desk render from merged state, marking read still feels instant, and the dual-run diff shows nothing outside the two benign classes over a multi-day window. Confirm against the actual UI, not just the logs.

title.value: [MS3] Dual-run merged read state against Convex, then cut over

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] Repurpose Convex readState as the horizon cache
issues.description:
**M3.** Do this before the cutover task, or the cutover regresses unread for every quiet container.

## Why — a real regression risk, not a theoretical one

NIP-RS fetches with `since: now - horizon`, default **7 days**, and the spec is explicit about the consequence:

> Absence of a context in all fetched blobs means the read state for that context is **unknown** — clients SHOULD treat unknown contexts as unread (conservative default). [...] *Contexts that were read but have aged out of the time horizon are indistinguishable from never-read contexts.*

For Peek this bites hard. A topic read three weeks ago and untouched since has no blob inside the horizon, so it reads as **unread** and lights up the sidebar. Peek has long-lived topics; this would look exactly like the freshness bugs this whole programme is trying to fix.

The spec names the mitigation: *"Clients MAY extend the horizon or maintain a local cache."*

## What to build

**Keep `convex/readState.ts` — change its job.** It stops being the source of truth and becomes the durable local cache that outlives the horizon. Concretely:

- merged NIP-RS state is written into `readState` as it arrives, taking the max per context (never lowering — same monotonic rule)
- the UI reads from `readState`, as it does today, so nothing downstream changes
- a context absent from the relay fetch but present in `readState` keeps its cached value rather than reverting to unread

This is a happy fit: `watermarks()` in `readState.ts` is already a per-container watermark map, which is the same shape as a NIP-RS `contexts` map. The table is not being retired — it is being repurposed, and it earns its place.

Consider also extending the fetch horizon beyond 7 days for Peek, since the relay stores the events anyway. Cheap, and it narrows the window the cache has to cover. Do both rather than choosing.

## Traps

- **Max, never overwrite,** in both directions. Relay-into-cache and cache-into-relay must both take the later timestamp. An overwrite in either direction can lower a read position, which the protocol forbids and users experience as messages un-reading themselves.
- Do not let the cache become a second source of truth that diverges. It holds exactly what the merge produced, plus history the horizon has forgotten — never a value the merge did not produce.
- Convex is per-deployment, so the cache is per-app. That is fine and expected: the relay is the shared layer, the cache is local.

## Done when

Set a container's read timestamp older than the horizon, clear the relay's recent blobs, and confirm the container still reads as read. Then confirm a genuinely never-read container still reads as unread — the two must stay distinguishable, which is exactly what the horizon alone cannot do.

title.value: [MS2] Repurpose Convex readState as the horizon cache

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] NIP-RS client: fetch all slots and merge with the max rule
issues.description:
**M3.** Depends on the publish task. This is the half that makes cross-app work, and the merge rule is where a subtle bug would be invisible.

## What to build

The read side of `src/nostr/readState.ts`.

**Fetch all slots** — the exact filter from the spec:

```json
{"kinds":[30078],"authors":["<own-pubkey>"],"#t":["read-state"],"since":<now - horizon>}
```

Note `authors` is the viewer themselves: these are your own blobs from all your own installations. Default horizon 7 days (see the horizon task for why that matters and what to do about it).

**Then, per the spec:**

1. Decrypt each blob via `/nip44/decrypt`.
2. Discard blobs failing validation — content not valid JSON, missing/non-integer `v`, unknown `v`, missing `client_id`, `client_id` not a 1–64 char string, missing `contexts`, `contexts` not an object. Individual bad entries are dropped without discarding the whole blob (non-integer or out-of-range timestamp, context id over 256 bytes).
3. Identify your own blob by matching the decrypted `client_id`.
4. **Merge all valid blobs, including your own.**

**The merge rule:**

```
effective[context] = max(timestamp) across all blobs
```

A grow-only max-register CvRDT — associative, commutative, idempotent. **Clients MUST NOT lower a read timestamp, only advance it.**

**Hierarchy at read time:** a container's frontier propagates to its children, so `effective(thread:<root>)` is the max of its own merged value and the containing `h:` context's value. If the root or message event cannot be resolved to its container, degrade to the context's own merged value alone.

## The conflict case, which will happen

If **multiple blobs decrypt to your own `client_id`** — from a rotation that orphaned a blob, or a backup/restore that duplicated identifiers — the spec is explicit: treat the one with the **highest `created_at`** as yours, merge the others in as if they belonged to other instances, and SHOULD delete the stale duplicates via NIP-09.

Also: if you fetch your own `d` coordinate and the decrypted `client_id` does not match yours, the coordinate is **conflicted**. Do not publish to it — generate a new random slot-id first.

## Traps

- **Merge is over *your own* slots, not other people's.** This is not a read-receipt protocol and must never fetch another pubkey's read state. NIP-RS is explicit that anything exposing what a user has read to others requires explicit consent.
- Do not "optimise" by trusting only your own blob. Reading Ship's slot is the entire point.
- Idempotence means re-running the merge must be free of side effects. Do not advance local state as a side effect of merging.
- A blob that fails to decrypt is not an error worth surfacing — it may belong to a rotated key. Skip it quietly.

## Done when

Two installations for the same identity (two browsers is enough) converge: mark a topic read in one, and the other reflects it after a fetch. Then verify the monotonic property directly — a stale blob arriving late must not lower an already-advanced context.

title.value: [MS2] NIP-RS client: fetch all slots and merge with the max rule

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: [MS2] NIP-RS client: slot identity and publishing the read-state blob
issues.description:
**M3.** Depends on the NIP-44 endpoints and the 30078 grant. This is the write half; the read half is the next task.

## What to build

`peek-app/src/nostr/readState.ts` — publishing a NIP-RS blob.

**Slot identity.** On first run, generate and persist locally (localStorage, not sessionStorage — it must survive a browser restart):

- `slot-id`: 32 random hex chars. The `d` tag is `read-state:<slot-id>`.
- `client_id`: a stable string, 1–64 chars, identifying this installation.

These are per **installation**, not per app-version and not per session. Peek-in-Chrome and Ship-in-Chrome own different slots by design; that is what makes the merge meaningful.

**The event:**

```json
{
  "kind": 30078,
  "tags": [["d", "read-state:<slot-id>"], ["t", "read-state"]],
  "content": "<nip44 ciphertext of the blob below>"
}
```

Exactly one `d` tag and exactly one `["t","read-state"]` tag — the spec says events with zero or more than one of either MUST be ignored, so getting this wrong produces silence, not an error.

**The plaintext blob:**

```json
{ "v": 1, "client_id": "<client-id>", "contexts": { "<context-id>": <unix-seconds> } }
```

Context ids come from the convention task — `h:<folder-uuid>`, `thread:<root>`, `msg:<id>`. Do not invent Peek-private ids.

Encrypt via the Estiva ID `/nip44/encrypt` endpoint; sign via `/sign`. Peek never holds a key.

## Write discipline — the rule that is easy to break

Marking a **thread** read advances only its `thread:<root>` context. Marking a **message** read advances only `msg:<id>`. Neither may advance the parent `h:` context. Advancing the container from a thread read silently marks later top-level messages as read, which users experience as lost messages.

Peek's `readState` table already models two granularities (container id, or a message id for one thread's replies — ruling 2026-07-09), so the distinction already exists locally. Map it faithfully rather than flattening it.

## Traps

- **Debounce publishing.** Opening five topics must not publish five events. 30078 is parameterized-replaceable so a rapid series just overwrites, but it is wasteful and each publish costs a `/sign` and a `/nip44/encrypt` round trip. Batch on a few seconds' idle, and flush on `visibilitychange` to hidden.
- **Publish the whole blob, always.** It is a replaceable snapshot, not a delta. A partial blob silently *loses* contexts — and because the merge is grow-only across *other* slots, the loss is invisible until it is the only slot left.
- Respect the caps: ≤10,000 context entries, context id ≤256 bytes, timestamps 0–4294967295, total event under the relay's size limit.
- Timestamps are **unix seconds**, matching `created_at` semantics — not milliseconds. Peek stores milliseconds internally; convert at the boundary.

## Done when

A blob appears on the relay for the viewer, decrypts to valid JSON with the expected contexts, and marking a thread read leaves the container context untouched — verify by reading the blob back, not by reasoning about the call.

title.value: [MS2] NIP-RS client: slot identity and publishing the read-state blob

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Write the Estiva read-context convention into the protocol spec
issues.description:
**M2 · the actual protocol work.** Small, and every later task in this project references it. Do it before writing client code, so the client is written against a decision rather than becoming one.

## Why

NIP-RS deliberately declines to prescribe context identifiers. §Context Identifiers: *"Interoperability between different client implementations on context ID conventions is outside the scope of this NIP."*

That single omission is the whole reason "read it in Ship, it's read in Peek" does not already work. The merge rule, the encryption, the slot model and the fetch filter are all specified and already implemented in the relay. The convention is the missing piece — and it is the piece that decides whether app three gets cross-app read state on arrival or becomes a third disagreeing opinion.

The spec does define two optional well-known schemes explicitly *for* cross-client interop, and we should adopt them rather than invent alternatives.

## What to write

A section in `estiva-docs/protocol/SPEC.md` fixing the Estiva suite's context identifiers:

| grain | context id | notes |
|---|---|---|
| container | `h:<folder-uuid>` | the Folder — a Peek topic, a Ship project's Folder, a DM channel, a document's Folder. Lowercase UUID v4, matching the relay's `h_grammar` advertised in NIP-11 |
| thread | `thread:<root-event-id>` | NIP-RS well-known scheme. 64-char lowercase hex |
| message | `msg:<event-id>` | NIP-RS well-known scheme. 64-char lowercase hex |

`h:<folder-uuid>` is the load-bearing choice: because every Estiva app puts its objects in Folders, one convention covers a Peek topic, a Ship project and a DM channel without any app knowing about the others.

## Also record these rules, because they are easy to get wrong

- **Write discipline** (from NIP-RS): marking a thread read MUST advance only `thread:<root>`; marking a message read MUST advance only `msg:<id>`. Neither may advance the parent `h:` context — otherwise reading one reply silently marks later top-level messages read.
- **Hierarchy at read time:** a container's frontier propagates down, so `effective(thread:<root>)` inherits the container term. Marking a container read clears threads whose events predate the frontier; replies newer than it stay unread until their own marker advances.
- **Monotonic:** clients MUST NOT lower a timestamp. There is no mark-as-unread in this protocol. If Peek ever wants that feature it needs a separate mechanism — say so here so nobody promises it.
- **No huddle context is being standardised.** Huddles are still an experiment; if they land as channels they get `h:<folder-uuid>` for free. Do not reserve a scheme for them now.

## Done when

The section is merged in `estiva-docs`, and the remaining tasks in this project cite it rather than restating it. Per the estiva-docs rule — *if changing code in repo X makes a doc wrong, it lives in X* — this belongs in estiva-docs precisely because it constrains three repos at once.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: Grant Peek and Ship kind:30078, re-seed, verify the row
issues.description:
**M1 · blocking prerequisite.** One gate only — the kind is already accepted by the relay.

## Why

`kind:30078` is already in Buzz's `ALL_KINDS`, so the relay accepts it today: no Buzz change, no relay deploy, none of the `nfb-demo-kinds` branch work. The only gate is Estiva ID's per-app ceiling.

Current state in `estiva-id/src/db/seed.ts`:

- `peek` (line ~79): `[9, 7, 5, 9007, 27235, 1851, 9101, 9002]`
- `estiva-ship` (line ~99): `[30850, 30851, 1851, 9, 5, 9007, 31989, 27235]`

Neither has `30078`. `src/domain/policy.ts:80` refuses anything unlisted with `kind_not_allowed`, so without this every publish fails with a 422 that never reaches the relay.

## What to change

Add `30078` to **both** the `peek` and `estiva-ship` entries' `allowedKinds`.

Also add it to the `claude-agent` service credential if the agent should be able to mark things read — decide deliberately rather than by omission. (A read-state write from an agent acting for a person is defensible; from a bot is meaningless.)

## Deploying it — the part that silently does nothing

**`update.sh` on the box runs `migrate`, never `seed`.** A seed-only change deploys into the image and then has no effect whatsoever. A manual re-seed is required after deploy.

**Verify the row, never the `seeded N app credential(s)` log line:**

```bash
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U estiva_id -d estiva_id -tAc "select client_id, allowed_kinds from app_credentials"
```

## Traps

- No `t`-tag or URL-prefix constraint applies to 30078 — the `nip98_url_prefixes` machinery is specific to kind:27235. Nothing extra to configure.
- Re-issuing a credential **replaces** its secret. If you touch `claude-agent`, its existing secret stops working and `~/.estiva-agent.env` needs updating.

## Done when

The psql output above lists `30078` for `peek` and `estiva-ship`, and a browser session can sign a `kind:30078` event through `/sign` without a `kind_not_allowed` refusal.

issues.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
issues.title: NIP-44 encrypt/decrypt in Estiva ID, scoped to self-encryption
issues.description:
**M1 · blocking prerequisite for M3.** Nothing in the NIP-RS client can be written until this exists.

## Why

NIP-RS requires the read-state blob's `content` to be NIP-44 ciphertext, with the conversation key computed as `nip44_conversation_key(user_privkey, user_pubkey)` — the user encrypting to themselves. That needs the user's **private** key.

Peek holds no keys by design (PEEK-40/41), and Estiva ID exposes `/sign` and nothing else. Enumerating `estiva-id/src/http/routes/` gives: auth, authorize, tokens, refresh, invites, recovery, roles, directory, profile, logout, admin, sign. There is no encryption endpoint of any kind.

## What to build

Two endpoints in `estiva-id/src/http/routes/`, mirroring `sign.ts` in shape — bearer token in, operation performed as the token's subject, no key ever leaving the service:

- `POST /nip44/encrypt` → `{ plaintext }` ⇒ `{ ciphertext }`
- `POST /nip44/decrypt` → `{ ciphertext }` ⇒ `{ plaintext }`

## Scope it to SELF-encryption only — this is the important part

**Do not accept a peer pubkey.** Both endpoints operate on `nip44_conversation_key(own_priv, own_pub)` and nothing else.

The reason is the difference between two very different security postures. A *general* `/decrypt` is a decryption oracle: any app holding a token could read anything ever encrypted to that user. A **self-only** `/decrypt` can read only what the user encrypted to themselves — today, read-state blobs. That is still sensitive (it reveals what you have read and when, which is behavioural data) but it is bounded.

Build the narrow version. Widening later is a deliberate decision with its own review; starting general and narrowing later does not happen in practice.

## Also required

- **Rate limit both endpoints** and emit **audit entries**, from the start. Read positions are behavioural data about a person.
- Follow the existing policy seam: `src/domain/policy.ts` is where `/sign` decides what is permitted. Encryption has no kind to check, but the `app.status !== 'active'` gate and the same refusal vocabulary should apply — a disabled app must not be able to decrypt.
- NIP-44 v2 specifically (ChaCha20 + HMAC-SHA256, padded). Use an audited implementation rather than hand-rolling the padding scheme; `@noble/*` is already in the dependency tree.

## Traps

- `/sign` deliberately ignores any pubkey it is handed and signs as the token's subject. Keep that principle: these endpoints must not accept an identity argument at all, so there is nothing to get wrong.
- Do not log plaintext or ciphertext. Estiva ID's own audit table records *that* an operation happened, not its content.
- NIP-44 is not interchangeable with NIP-04. Do not fall back to NIP-04 for any reason.

## Done when

A Peek browser session can round-trip a string through `/nip44/encrypt` then `/nip44/decrypt` and get it back, an attempt to pass a peer pubkey is refused, a disabled app is refused, and both calls appear in the audit log without their contents.
