activity.value:
**This is the ticket that makes the extraction trustworthy**, and it should be treated as a requirement of the extraction rather than a follow-up to it.

SHA-7 exists because `createLiveRelay` went into `@estiva-app/protocol` as a single implementation with a single caller: *"no second consumer has ever pushed back on its API."* Every line of the projection consumer runtime is in that same position today, and it is a larger surface.

## What to build

Ship resolves a `nostr:naddr…` reference to a Peek Topic or Message inside a project or issue description and renders it through the manifest — its own tokens, its own design language, zero lines that know what Peek is.

## What this specifically tests

- **The fallback chain**, because a Message is not one of the four closed widget types
- **The `list` slot**, because a Topic carries one
- **Ship's plain-text discipline** meeting a body that may carry structure — see the *Rich text and blocks* project, and do not quietly start rendering markup here
- **A relay-signed author**, which Ship has never had to attribute

## Done when

Ship renders a real Peek Topic and a real Message from production, and **whatever the second consumer forced to change in the runtime is written on this issue — including "nothing"**, which is the answer that retires SHA-7's worry rather than deferring it.

Only after this should the runtime be published as a package.

---

## What PRO-6 established, 2026-08-31

Peek's manifest is written and merged, so the shape of this ticket is no longer
guesswork. Three things below were **not** knowable when it was filed, and two
of them are larger than anything in "What to build".

### 1. A Message is not addressable, and every resolver here starts from an address

Confirmed against production: a `kind:9` carries **no `d` tag**. It is a regular
event, referenced by event id, never by `kind:pubkey:d`.

`resolveForeignObject` takes an `naddr`, `referenceToPointer` returns an
`AddressPointer`, and the root is fetched with `{kinds, authors, '#d'}`. None of
that reaches a message. **Resolving a Message needs a second entry point keyed
on event id** — `nevent`/`e` rather than `naddr`/`a` — and that is the larger
half of this ticket. Note the knock-on: comments and changes are fetched by
`#a`, which a non-addressable root cannot be the target of either.

### 2. The `list` slot does not resolve for an object reached by address

`list` was implemented in PRO-2 down the *folder* path, where containment is
discovered from the Folder's contents. `resolveForeignObject` never resolves
it: `rawSlotValue` returns undefined for a `children` spec, so the slot is
dropped.

Measured: 5 of 5 real production Topics resolve by address through Peek's
manifest and render **title and subtitle and no messages**. So "a Peek
conversation inside a Ship issue" does not fall out of the manifest as filed —
wiring `list` into the by-address path is work this ticket owns.

### 3. A Topic carries no `h` tag — it *is* the container

So `resolveFolderProject` cannot find one, and a Topic is reached by address:
`39000:<relay pubkey>:<channel uuid>`.

### Still true, and now with detail

- **The fallback chain** — Peek declares `widget: ["message", "card"]`. Nothing
  consumes a chain yet; a consumer reading `widget` as a string sees an array.
  That is PRO-3's, and this ticket is its first caller.
- **The relay-signed author** — a `39000` is signed by the relay, so "who wrote
  this" resolves to the relay's pubkey. Any attribution slot must not render it
  as a person.
- **Ship has no consumer runtime at all.** It is a producer only: `src/manifest.ts`
  and `scripts/publish-manifest.ts`, no `ForeignObjectWidget`, no resolver. The
  second consumer is being built from nothing, not adapted.

### Blocked on

**Peek's manifest is written but unpublished.** Publishing `kind:31990` is
refused at two of SPEC §8's three gates — a fresh key gets
`relay_membership_required`, and Estiva ID refuses to sign for `claude-agent`
(`App claude-agent may not sign kind 31990`). Neither `estiva-peek` nor
`estiva-ship` carries 31990 in `allowed_kinds`; Ship publishes from a raw key
registered as a relay member. Until an identity is settled, Ship can only
resolve Peek's manifest from a local copy, which tests the runtime and not the
discovery. See PRO-6.

### What actually changed in the runtime, for the "including nothing" answer

PRO-6 already forced four changes, so that answer will not be "nothing":
`match: 'address' | 'identifier'` on `children`, `field: 'pubkey'` as a slot
source, `records` made optional in both resolvers, and the discovery that a
kind is `u16` so an unmatchable-filter trick is refused by the relay. Those came
from the *producer* side. This ticket collects what the consumer side forces.

activity.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
activity.value:
**A message cannot be declared in a manifest, and that is measured rather than inferred.**

Confirmed on production while building PRO-6: *"A Message carries no `d` and is not addressable."* Every resolver in the consumer runtime starts from an `AddressPointer`.

## The gap

| object | identified by |
| --- | --- |
| project, issue, document, folder | address — `naddr` |
| Peek topic | address — `naddr` (the relay's `39000`) |
| **a conversation** | **the root event's id — `nevent`** |
| **a message** | **its own event id — `nevent`** |

`projections` is keyed by kind and resolved from an `naddr`; Ship's manifest declares its `web` template as `naddr` outright. So a manifest cannot say how a message renders, and a consumer holding a `nevent` has nothing to look up.

**Why it stayed hidden:** every Ship object is addressable, so the layer works in the one direction it has ever run. It only appears when you ask what a *message* widget would resolve through.

## This is one of six, and the other five are on PRO-6

PRO-6's comment records six things the manifest could not express, all measured against production. **Read them before starting here** — they are siblings of this one, not background:

- `list` matched the parent's *address* while Peek's `h` holds a bare uuid
- `title` is required and a message has none
- **`records` was required by both resolvers**, so an app that folds nothing rendered as *nothing* — §13.3's worst outcome, never caught because Ship was the only publisher and Ship folds
- a `changeKind: -1` sentinel passed 53 tests and was refused by production, because a kind is a `u16`
- a Topic carries no `h` — it is not *in* a container, it *is* one

The third is the most severe and the least specific to messages: **any app that does not fold got an empty render.** Worth deciding whether it belongs here or against the runtime extraction in PRO-1.

## What to change

- a projection may be declared for an event-identified object, not only an addressable one
- the consumer resolves `nevent` alongside `naddr`
- the `web` template learns a second form, so "open this in the app that owns it" works for a message

**A message is not replaceable and has no folded state**, so most of what `records` describes does not apply to it. A projection for an event-identified object is a thinner thing, and the manifest should say so rather than leaving a consumer to infer which halves are meaningful.

**Not declaring actions was the right call in PRO-6** and stays true until this lands: a reply names an *event id*, and the action vocabulary only names a parent *address*, so declaring one would tell a consumer to publish a malformed reply.

## Done when

The consumer resolves `nevent`, Peek's manifest declares a Message projection, a second app renders a real production message through it, and its `web` link opens that message in Peek. **RFC 0.4 §13.6 records the gap** — update it to record the resolution.

activity.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
activity.value:
**A reading session and a decision, like SHA-10 — and a cheaper one.**

[RFC 0.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/RFC-0.5-ASSOCIATION.md) specifies how files in different apps relate. It exists because RFC 0.4 lets a Folder hold several files of one kind, so **the container can no longer be the relationship** — a project's conversation used to *be* a topic because they shared one channel.

## What accepting settles

- **Three tiers** — none, basic (one file names another, shown in a panel, shared not personal), facet (files are perspectives on one thing and their conversations merge).
- **Facets merge, and never copy.** One comment, two views, ordered by time, origin unlabelled.
- **Declaration is one-sided, effect two-sided** — forced, because a `kind:39000` topic is relay-signed and Peek can never tag it.
- **The access-compatibility invariant** — a facet may not merge conversations that are not equally readable.
- **The two change cases**: removing a facet splits the thread *list* and never a thread; deleting an object never deletes its comments.

## Why it is cheaper than 0.4's acceptance

**No new kind and no Buzz change.** A facet is a tag on a file record, signed by that file's author — so authorization falls out of who holds the key rather than needing a permission model. The expensive relay-maintained version stays available for when the trigger fires.

## What it does not settle

Deliberately deferred with triggers in §8: who may create a facet beyond "you can sign the file", relay enforcement of the invariant (a read rule does it today), and whether a merged view labels which facet a comment was written against.

## The one thing worth arguing about

**§4, the invariant.** It is the only clause that forbids something people will want — faceting a private discussion onto a public object. The argument for it is that the failure is not disclosure (the relay still gates content) but **context collapse for the one person who can see both sides**, who then answers privately in what looks like a public place. If that argument does not hold, the invariant should go rather than be quietly ignored.

## Done when

Accepted or amended, and if amended, what changed and why is on this issue. Association and facet tickets get filed only after that — per rule 2, nothing is filed against the undecided parts.

---

## §7 Addressing was added 2026-08-31, and it is part of this decision

RFC 0.5 gained a section on **what a link looks like**, because the question
turned out to be protocol rather than per-app taste: *people copy the address
bar*, so the URL an app puts there has to be resolvable by a different app. That
is wire-visible under SPEC §10's test — two apps can disagree and a user sees it.

**The grammar:**

```
https://<app>.estiva.app/<type>s                  a directory of that kind
https://<app>.estiva.app/<type>/<slug>-<d>        one object
```

- the **`d` is the whole identity, untruncated** — a consumer resolves
  `{kinds:[<type>], "#d":["<uuid>"]}`, one query, no index and no service that
  can go down and take every link with it
- the **kind comes from the path segment**, so `/project/` means 30850
- the **slug is decorative** — renaming changes it and the link still resolves

**Two findings behind it, both measured rather than assumed.**

*An naddr cannot be the suffix.* It is bech32 over `(kind, pubkey, d, relay
hints)` **plus a checksum over the whole string**, so a slice of it is checksum
bytes rather than the `d` and resolves to nothing without an index. It is also
not stable for one object — relay hints are part of the encoding, and both forms
are live today: Ship's `referenceFor` passes a hint, the runtime's `buildObject`
passes none.

*The pubkey does not need to be in the URL.* `d` is a v4 uuid (0.4 §4.3), so
`(kind, d)` is unique. Measured on production: 235 records across 30850/30851/
39000, **zero** non-uuid `d`, **zero** `(kind, d)` shared by more than one
author. This gives §4.3's existing MUST a second and quieter reason — an app
using a readable `d` would not fail loudly, it would collide and resolve to the
wrong object.

**A consumer resolves an app it has never met** by matching a pasted URL against
the patterns every app publishes in its manifest (`urls`, alongside `web`).
`kind:31990` is global, so this needs no per-app integration and no registry.

## What §7 additionally requires

- **Paths, not hashes.** Ship uses hash routing because it is static files with
  `try_files … =404`. Path URLs need an index.html fallback per app.
- **Peek has no object URLs at all** — no routing, no per-topic path. That is
  the prerequisite, and it is filed separately because it does not depend on
  this decision.
- **Messages still have no URL.** A `kind:9` has no `d`, so it has no place in
  the grammar — the same gap §13.6 records for projections, and PRO-11's.

activity.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
activity.value:
**Write documents and descriptions in blocks** — drop in a table, a code snippet, or a live widget from another app, and comment on any single block rather than the whole page.

---

# Context

## Source

> **Miky (2026-08-21)** — "Support code snippets in rich formatting"

> **Miky (2026-08-24)** — "You will be able to comment on specific blocks in Leaf." … "You will be able to reference in Peek or Ship conversation not just whole Leaf document, but just specific block like a table or paragraph."

> **Miky (2026-08-28)** — "Build rich text field based on block where you can embed widgets from other apps. Before building Leaf, I will make it work in Ship."

## Problem

Every app has description fields and none of them agree what text is. Measured on production 2026-08-28: **76 of 89 issue descriptions carry markdown structure** — tables, fenced code, links — and Ship renders all of it as literal characters. Deliberately, because the body is untrusted text from other apps. So the person who wrote a table sees a table nowhere.

The deeper job is addressability: **let me point at one paragraph, not the whole document.** That is also the thing Leaf needs in order to exist.

## Usage scenarios

> **Miky, 2026-08-21, writing feedback in Peek**
> Asked for code snippets in rich formatting. Today a code fence he types is stored, rendered raw in Ship, and rendered raw in Peek too — Peek's editor has code spans disabled while the agent writes backticks constantly.

> **Miky, 2026-08-24, describing Leaf to Katerina**
> Wants to reference "just specific block like a table or paragraph" from a Peek or Ship conversation. Nothing addressable exists below the document today.

## Less about / More about

- **Less about** — a better editor in one app.
- **More about** — one content model that survives being read by an app that did not write it.

---

# Solution

Two content models, kept apart, sharing only their inline layer.

A **message** carries inline marks on immutable content. A **rich text field** is a tree of blocks, and **a block is addressable** — which is what answers RFC 0.4 §6. Attachments sit below a message and inline in a field; messages carry reactions and blocks do not.

Build it in **Ship's description field**, not in Leaf.

## Options considered and rejected

- **Build it in Leaf first.** This is the deadlock RFC 0.3 wrote down and could not escape: Leaf should not start before §6 is answered, and §6 should not be frozen before Leaf can test it. Ship's description field is a block-structured field that exists today with a second app already reading it.
- **Make Ship render markdown.** Ship's plain-text rendering is a security position — *"untrusted text from other people and other apps: rendered as text, never as markup"* — not an oversight. The fix is a specified format and one safe renderer.
- **One content model for both messages and fields.** Rejected on Miky's correction, 2026-08-28, and the production corpora agree: two dialects are already in use.
- **Which format** — three candidates, decided in RIC-1, not pre-empted here.

## Prior art

Notion's block model is the target experience. ProseMirror / TipTap is already in Peek and stays the *editor* — what is shared is the format, never the editor.

---

# Milestones

**MS1 — Framing & Shaping · complete.** RFC 0.4 §14 accepted; §6 unfrozen; Ship's description named as the test bed rather than Leaf.

**MS2 — Internal Beta.** RIC-1 (decide the format) and RIC-2 (NIP-27 mentions).

**Filed 2026-09-02, the day RIC-1 landed**, per roadmap rule 2 — held back until then because implementation tickets against an undecided design are a backlog that looks like progress:

- **RIC-4** — inline mark vocabulary in `@estiva-app/protocol`, with one safe renderer
- **RIC-5** — the block model for a rich text field
- **RIC-6** — Ship's issue description becomes blocks
- **RIC-7** — anchor a comment to a single block — the §6 answer, and the thing Leaf is waiting on. Depends on RIC-5 persisting block ids

**MS3 — GA + GTM.** Roll the format out against the existing published corpus, **re-measured at 731 bodies on 2026-09-02** — the 487 in RIC-3's title is five days stale, and the growth is itself the argument for a permanent reader. They cannot move whichever candidate wins, so the compatibility story is `alsoRead`-shaped and permanent rather than a window that closes.

activity.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
activity.value:
**Unblocked by RIC-1.** [SPEC §13.3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) specifies a rich text field as a JSON block document. Nothing writes one today — this is the first implementation, and §13.3 was written ahead of it deliberately.

## What a block document is

```jsonc
{ "type": "doc", "content": [
  { "type": "paragraph", "id": "b1", "content": [ … ] }
] }
```

Block types: `paragraph`, `heading` (level 1–3), `bulletList`, `orderedList`, `listItem`, `blockquote`, `codeBlock`, `table`, `horizontalRule`, `attachment`, and `widget` — which names a §7.5 widget and inherits that section's fallback chain.

## The `id` is the whole reason this is JSON

**Every block carries an `id` unique within the document, stable across every edit that does not replace the block.** That is what a comment anchors to, and it is the only thing JSON buys over text. An implementation that generates ids at render time has built a tree and not an addressable one — the anchor ticket then has nothing to bind to.

## What to build

- parse, serialise and **validate** a block document in `@estiva-app/protocol`
- id generation and preservation across edits
- write `["content-format", "estiva-blocks-1"]` on publish; **honour its absence on read** (§13.4)
- an unknown block type renders its inline text and is never dropped silently

**Moved here from RIC-4 (2026-09-02):** the **inline JSON node parser and serialiser** — §13.1's right column, `{"type":"bold"}` and friends. RIC-4 shipped the marker-text serialisation and stopped there deliberately: its own words for this item were *"for the block model to consume"*, and until this ticket exists there is no consumer to design it against. It is a small symmetrical addition to `content.ts`, and it is needed here on day one, because a block's inline content is exactly these nodes.

So this ticket owns the block layer **and the inline layer's second serialisation**. What stays shared with messages is the *vocabulary* — the same six marks, the same meanings — not the encoding.

## Done when

The package round-trips §13.1's inline JSON nodes against the marker text of the same content, so the two serialisations provably carry the same marks; the package can round-trip a block document; ids survive an edit that does not replace the block; a document containing an unknown block type still renders its text; the `content-format` tag is written on publish and its absence is treated as marker text on read; and **a legacy description that begins with `{` is still read as marker text** — §13.4 forbids deciding by sniffing, and that is the case which proves it.

activity.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
activity.value:
**Unblocked by RIC-1.** This is the project's premise: the block model is proved in a field that exists today, with a second app already reading it, rather than in Leaf. It is also the escape from RFC 0.3's deadlock — Leaf should not start before §6 is answered, and §6 should not freeze before something can test it.

## What Ship does today

Every body goes through `textContent` in `apps/ship/ui.ts`'s `h()`, deliberately: *"no template strings holding user data — a project title goes through `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, because on a shared relay the titles are written by other people."*

**That position does not change.** [SPEC §13.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) makes it explicit that rendering a body as plain text stays conformant; what is forbidden is *interpreting* one as markup. Ship gains structure by rendering a parsed model through the same node construction, not by relaxing anything.

## What must keep working

Measured 2026-09-02, and none of it moves:

| corpus | bodies | carrying structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| root descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 157 | 135 (86%) |
| description changes (`kind:1851`) | 26 | 21 (81%) |

The change events are the easy ones to miss: **a description edited after creation lives in the `value` tag of a `kind:1851`, not in anyone's `content`.** RFC 0.4 §14.2 missed them and so did the first RIC-1 probe. §13.4's rule is per event, not per object — a description created as text and later edited into blocks is an untagged root plus a tagged change, and the fold must read the tag from the event it took the value from.

## Moved here from RIC-4: the one safe renderer

**Moved 2026-09-02.** SPEC §13.5's *"one renderer that is safe by construction"* was RIC-4's third build item and shipped as neither — Peek got a React renderer of its own, and Ship still has nothing. It belongs here because **Ship is the app that needs it**, and building it in RIC-4 meant designing it against no caller.

One open question comes with it, and it is why this was not obvious: **Ship renders with vanilla `h()` and Peek with React.** "One renderer" therefore cannot mean one component. It has to mean the package emits a node tree — marks and blocks already resolved, nothing to interpolate — and each app maps that to its own DOM. That is what makes §13.5's guarantee structural rather than a convention every app has to remember.

Peek's `MessageBody` is the working reference for the mapping; it should not be the second implementation of the parsing.

## Before starting

The shared `~/estiva-ship` checkout was **123 commits behind `origin/main`** on 2026-09-02, and the layouts differ: `CLAUDE.md` names `web/src/pages/IssuePage.tsx` while that checkout has `apps/ship/views/issue.ts`. Read `origin/main` from a worktree.

## Done when

The package emits a renderer-agnostic node tree and Ship maps it through the same `textContent` node construction it uses today; Ship writes a block document with the `content-format` tag; an untagged legacy description still renders exactly as it does now; **Peek reading the same description does not regress**; and the check is run against a production description of each kind — a root, and one whose current value came from a `kind:1851` — rather than against a locally created issue.

activity.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
activity.value:
**Unblocked by RIC-1.** [SPEC §13.1](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) names six marks — bold, italic, underline, code, link, reference — and two serialisations of them: markers in a message, JSON nodes in a block document. This ticket is the one implementation.

## Why it belongs in the package

Wire-visible content, so SPEC §10's test applies: *would the relay notice if two apps disagreed?* It already does. Today there are **three producers and two renderers and no shared code** — Peek's `src/lib/textParsing.ts` is the only implementation of the marker dialect anywhere, and Ship has none on purpose.

## What to build

- **Marker text** (§13.2) — parser and serialiser, including the two conservatism rules that keep published text unchanged: no whitespace at the inner edges, no alphanumeric adjacent to a marker.
- ~~**Inline JSON nodes** (§13.1, right column)~~ — **moved to RIC-5, 2026-09-02.** Its own justification said "for the block model to consume", and RIC-5 is that consumer; building it here meant designing against no caller.
- ~~**One renderer** (§13.5)~~ — **moved to RIC-6, 2026-09-02.** Ship is the app that needs it, and the move surfaced the question that made it non-obvious: Ship renders with vanilla `h()` and Peek with React, so "one renderer" has to mean a node tree both map, not one component.

## `code` is the new part, and it is the point

Measured 2026-09-02: **200 of 548 published messages carry a backtick span** — more common than bold (179) — and **no renderer has ever handled one.** Peek's editor has code spans disabled and its parser has no backtick rule. This is Miky's 2026-08-21 request, and it is one mark, not a project.

## Two things to be careful about

- **`textParsing.ts` is not all mark code.** It also holds mention and bracket-reference regexes bound to Peek's mock fixtures (`PEOPLE`, `TOPICS`, `APP_FILES`). **Only the mark layer moves.** The mention layer is RIC-2's.
- **A `nostr:` reference is the token, not the product behaviour.** This ticket makes the token parse and render; RIC-2 decides what a mention *does*.

## Done when

*Amended 2026-09-02 when two build items moved out — the original text asked for "both serialisations", and the second one went to RIC-5 with its consumer.*

The package exports a parser and serialiser for **marker text**; **Peek's marker code is replaced by it rather than duplicated**; a body containing a backtick span renders as code in Peek; and the round-trip is checked against a sample of the **real published corpus**, not hand-written fixtures — 548 message bodies exist to test against and a fixture that agrees with the parser proves nothing.

## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.6.0` — `content.ts`, with `code` and fenced code added to the dialect. estiva-foundation#25.
- Peek deletes its copy and reads the package; `code` re-enabled in the editor, so backticks can be typed and not only read. peek#112.
- SPEC §13.2 amended: rule 2 does not fence a backtick. estiva-docs#56.
- `test/corpus-bodies.json` — 152 real published bodies. It found two defects the unit tests could not see: `stripInlineFormatting` was never idempotent, and rule 2 was wrong about backticks.

*Amended on closing, 2026-09-02.* The original clause also said the tag is **written on publish**, which nothing in this ticket's scope can do — the package has no publisher, and RIC-6 is the first writer of a block document. That half was already stated verbatim in RIC-6's done-when, so it is dropped here rather than duplicated into a clause this ticket could never satisfy.

## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.7.0` — `blocks.ts` and the inline layer's JSON serialisation. estiva-foundation#27.
- The read half of §13.4 is met by `contentFormatOf` in `@estiva-app/interop` (#26, another session, landed mid-ticket), not by this package. `behaviour.test.ts:1502` is the no-sniff control; the protocol side adds the matching case — a `{`-leading legacy body parses as marker text and `parseBlockDocument` refuses it.
- 227 tests, with controls: dropping `code` from the JSON encoding fails 4, re-minting ids unconditionally fails 2.

**Note for RIC-6: 0.7.0 is merged but not yet published.** The registry serves 0.6.0 until somebody pushes the `protocol@0.7.0` tag.

activity.value:
**Unblocked by RIC-1.** This is the project's premise: the block model is proved in a field that exists today, with a second app already reading it, rather than in Leaf. It is also the escape from RFC 0.3's deadlock — Leaf should not start before §6 is answered, and §6 should not freeze before something can test it.

## What Ship does today

Every body goes through `textContent` in `apps/ship/ui.ts`'s `h()`, deliberately: *"no template strings holding user data — a project title goes through `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, because on a shared relay the titles are written by other people."*

**That position does not change.** [SPEC §13.5](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/blob/main/protocol/SPEC.md) makes it explicit that rendering a body as plain text stays conformant; what is forbidden is *interpreting* one as markup. Ship gains structure by rendering a parsed model through the same node construction, not by relaxing anything.

## What must keep working

Measured 2026-09-02, and none of it moves:

| corpus | bodies | carrying structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| root descriptions (`kind:30850`, `kind:30851`) | 157 | 135 (86%) |
| description changes (`kind:1851`) | 26 | 21 (81%) |

The change events are the easy ones to miss: **a description edited after creation lives in the `value` tag of a `kind:1851`, not in anyone's `content`.** RFC 0.4 §14.2 missed them and so did the first RIC-1 probe. §13.4's rule is per event, not per object — a description created as text and later edited into blocks is an untagged root plus a tagged change, and the fold must read the tag from the event it took the value from.

## Moved here from RIC-4: the one safe renderer

**Moved 2026-09-02.** SPEC §13.5's *"one renderer that is safe by construction"* was RIC-4's third build item and shipped as neither — Peek got a React renderer of its own, and Ship still has nothing. It belongs here because **Ship is the app that needs it**, and building it in RIC-4 meant designing it against no caller.

One open question comes with it, and it is why this was not obvious: **Ship renders with vanilla `h()` and Peek with React.** "One renderer" therefore cannot mean one component. It has to mean the package emits a node tree — marks and blocks already resolved, nothing to interpolate — and each app maps that to its own DOM. That is what makes §13.5's guarantee structural rather than a convention every app has to remember.

Peek's `MessageBody` is the working reference for the mapping; it should not be the second implementation of the parsing.

## Before starting

The shared `~/estiva-ship` checkout was **123 commits behind `origin/main`** on 2026-09-02, and the layouts differ: `CLAUDE.md` names `web/src/pages/IssuePage.tsx` while that checkout has `apps/ship/views/issue.ts`. Read `origin/main` from a worktree.

## Done when

The package emits a renderer-agnostic node tree and Ship maps it through node construction that cannot interpolate markup; an untagged legacy description still renders exactly as it does now; **Peek reading the same description does not regress**; and the check is run against a production description of each kind — a root, and one whose current value came from a `kind:1851` — rather than against a locally created issue.

*Amended on closing, 2026-09-02.* Two changes, both stated rather than quietly absorbed:

- **"Ship writes a block document with the `content-format` tag" moved to RIC-8.** Nothing in this ticket wrote one, and holding the write back was deliberate: a published event cannot be unpublished, so the read path should be seen working on production first. It now has been.
- **"the same `textContent` node construction it uses today"** was written when Ship rendered with a vanilla `h()`. Ship's UI is React + Vite and has been since before this ticket started; the guarantee is unchanged — every string reaches the DOM as a React child, no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, nothing to interpolate — but the mechanism named was already wrong.

## Delivered

- `@estiva-app/protocol@0.9.0` — `toRenderTree`, one resolved tree for either content model, plus `contentFormatOf` moved down from interop so two folds could read a tag without depending on the projection layer. estiva-foundation#29, #30.
- `@estiva-app/ui@0.3.0` — `EditableText.displayNode`, because the component moved into the shared library mid-ticket. estiva-ui#4.
- Ship renders both descriptions: ship#80 (issue), ship#82 (project).
- The fold carries the format, identically in two repositories: ship#80 and estiva-agent#32, with the conformance fixture's `expected` re-recorded and its `events` and pinned checksum untouched.

## What the verification was worth

The browser check found what four green suites and three green CI runs did not: after ship#80, the **project** description — the longest real body in the workspace at 6,446 characters — still rendered 49 literal `**` and `#` markers. ship#82 fixed it, and `scripts/ric6-live-check.ts` is kept as the check that catches it next time.

**Peek cannot have regressed**, and it is worth saying why rather than asserting it: nothing Ship publishes changed shape. Every description is still the marker text it was. That stops being true the day RIC-8 lands, which is why a Peek check is in *that* ticket's done-when.

root.body:
**Unread follows you around now.**

Read a conversation in Peek and it stops being unread in Ship, and on your other devices. Same the other way. It used to be per-app, which is why the same thing could look unread in one place and read in another.

Two things worth knowing:

- **There is no "mark as unread."** The protocol cannot express it — a read marker only ever moves forward. If you want to come back to something, star it or leave yourself a note.
- **Reading a thread is not reading the conversation.** Opening one reply thread clears that thread. The conversation stays unread until you have been in it. That is deliberate.

In Ship it shows as a **"new since you last read this"** divider inside a conversation, rather than dots in the lists.

If something looks wrong — particularly anything showing as **read when you have not read it** — say so, and say which app and roughly when. That direction is the one we cannot see from here.

root.body:
**Note from RFC 0.3 — reserve a namespace, do not change the plan.**

[RFC 0.3](../protocol/RFC-0.3-FOLDERS.md) splits what "Folder" means today. A folder becomes an addressable container that *references* a channel; the channel keeps doing access and conversation. A Peek topic becomes a file listed in a folder rather than being a channel itself.

**What survives unchanged:** conversation read state stays keyed on the channel, so `h:<channel-uuid>` is still the right container context and this ticket's convention holds as written. Do not redesign it.

**What to add:** one sentence reserving a *folder*-level context — reading "everything in this folder" is a different frontier from reading one conversation, and it will want a scheme. Something like `folder:<folder-address>`, noted as reserved and unspecified.

Reserving it costs a line now. Discovering it later means either colliding with an app-private id somebody chose in the meantime, or a migration of published blobs — and NIP-RS blobs are grow-only, so a bad context id is effectively permanent.

RFC 0.3 is a draft and its undecided parts are not this ticket's problem. This is the one interaction worth carrying.

root.body:
Docs: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/44 — §13.6 now records the resolution, and SPEC gains §7.6.

**The old §13.6 asked for something that turned out to be unnecessary.** It wanted the manifest to "say which halves are meaningful" for an event-identified object. It does not need to: a regular event is immutable and cannot be the target of an `a` tag, so it has no folded fields, no comments addressed to it and no actions — a consumer discovers all of that from the object. **No manifest field was added because none was needed**, and the note is corrected in place rather than dropped.

**And it could not have predicted the thing that actually bites.** NIP-89 types a `web` template per NIP-19 entity, so an app owning both shapes needs one of each. Publishing only the naddr form is invisible from an app whose objects are all addressable — a consumer holding a message substitutes nothing and renders it while silently offering no way to open it.

SPEC §7.6 exists for the reason §7.5 and §7.1 did this week: the spec said nothing about addressability, so a stranger building from the published text would have written an address-only consumer and found out when a message arrived.

**Done-when, complete except one clause I do not control:**

1. consumer resolves nevent ✅
2. Peek declares a Message projection ✅
3. a second app renders a real production message ✅
4. its web link opens that message — **manifest ✅, app ❌.** Peek has no routing; the template points at a route nothing serves. Filed as the object-URL ticket.
5. §13.6 records the resolution ✅

Leaving this open rather than closing on four of five. The one gap is a real thing a person would hit, and it is filed where it belongs rather than hidden in a done ticket.

**This ticket starts one layer lower than it assumes.** There was no `nevent` support anywhere in the suite — not in the runtime, not in the protocol package. So before a consumer can resolve one, the format has to exist.

`EventPointer` is deliberately *not* interchangeable with `AddressPointer`: an address names whatever is currently at (kind, pubkey, d) and survives replacement; an id names one immutable event. Confusing them resolves to the wrong thing rather than erroring.

Two of my own test bugs surfaced: asserting byte-equality (wrong claim), and a "refuses an naddr" case that passed on a bech32 checksum error without reaching the hrp check it was written for. Both fixed.

**Remaining chain, and it is three releases:** protocol 0.3.0 → `resolveForeignEvent` in interop → apps. Plus Peek's `web` template gaining an nevent form, and RFC 0.4 §13.6 updated to record the resolution rather than the gap.

Worth noting the *rendering* half is already done: PRO-7's `buildChildObject` renders non-addressable children, so a message inside a Topic's list draws correctly today. What is missing is the **entry point** — a consumer holding a bare nevent.

root.body:
**Renaming a project does not fix its refs, and that is deliberate. Recording it so nobody tries it twice.**

Hit today: a new project *Peek's Intelligence* produced `PEE-1`…`PEE-6`, colliding with *Peek: Feedback & Bugs*, which produces the same prefix. Renaming it to **Intelligence in Peek** changed the project title and **left all six issues on `PEE-`**.

**Why.** The ref is computed once at `create-issue` — `nextRef(refPrefix(project.title), siblings)` — and written onto the issue event as a `['ref', …]` tag. `edit-project --title` cannot reach into six already-published events, and `edit-issue` has no `--ref`.

**That is the right design, not the bug.** `store.ts` says so: refs are *"display-only, per the spec: never used for addressing, never authoritative"* and the collision is *"cosmetic… the address is the identity."* Re-stamping on rename would break every prior citation of a ref in a PR or a comment.

**One consequence worth knowing before the fix is designed:** after a rename, `nextRef` counts only siblings already carrying the new prefix, so the next issue in that project is `INT-1`, not `INT-7`. A renamed project therefore ends up holding `PEE-1…6` followed by `INT-1…`, which is worse than either consistent option. Whatever this ticket does, it should decide what happens to a project that has already been renamed.

Left as-is deliberately: re-filing six issues would mean six permanently cancelled ones, since `kind:5` is refused to this identity (AGE-2).

**This cannot be built as written — it needs PRO-11 first.**

Found while writing RFC 0.5, not while working on this ticket. A **Message** is identified by its event id, not by an address, and `projections` is keyed by kind and resolved from an `naddr` — Ship's manifest declares its `web` template as `naddr` outright. So a manifest cannot declare how a message should be rendered, and a consumer holding a `nevent` has nothing to look up.

Not a mistake in this ticket: the gap is invisible from the direction currently in production, because every Ship object is addressable. It only appears when you ask what a *message* widget would resolve through.

One thing to carry into the work when it starts: a `39000` is signed by the **relay**, so resolving "who wrote this" on a Topic returns the relay's pubkey rather than a person. Any attribution slot has to handle that rather than rendering the relay as an author.

root.body:
PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/80

**Blocked on an identity, and the blocker is measured.** Publishing kind:31990 fails at two of SPEC §8's three gates: a fresh key gets `relay_membership_required` at ingest, and the agent identity is refused *before* ingest by Estiva ID — `App claude-agent may not sign kind 31990`. Ship publishes from a registered relay member; Peek has none. Granting one is a seed change in Estiva ID plus a hand re-seed on the box. **The script is complete and unrun**, and takes a signer rather than a key file so whichever identity is granted drops in.

Writing the manifest was most of the value — **six things could not be expressed**, none visible from the Ship direction:

1. `list` matched the parent's *address*; Peek's `h` holds the bare uuid → added `match: 'address'|'identifier'`.
2. `title` is required and **a message has none**. Body can't be it (structured, PRO-8). Added `field: 'pubkey'` — no slot source could name an event's author.
3. **`records` was required by both resolvers.** Nothing of Peek's folds, so its manifest declares none, and both returned null for the whole projection — the object rendering as *nothing*, §13.3's worst outcome. Never caught because Ship is the only app that had published a manifest, and Ship folds.
4. My first fix for (3) used `changeKind: -1` as an unmatchable sentinel. **53 green tests; production refused the entire filter** — `invalid type: integer -1, expected a 16-bit unsigned number`. A kind is u16, so the query must be *skipped*, not made unmatchable.
5. A Topic carries **no `h`** — it is not in a container, it *is* one. `resolveFolderProject` cannot find it; it resolves by address.
6. A Message carries no `d` and is **not addressable** (confirmed on production). Every resolver starts from an AddressPointer.

**For PRO-7:** (6) is its larger half — rendering a Message needs resolution by event id, which does not exist. And the `list` slot resolves in the folder path but **not** for an object resolved by address, so a consumer holding a Topic naddr gets a title and no messages.

No actions declared, deliberately: a reply names an *event id* and the action vocabulary only names a parent *address*, so declaring it would tell a consumer to publish a malformed reply.

Verified what could be: **5 of 5 real production Topics resolve by address through the unpublished manifest.**

https://github.com/estiva-app/ship/pull/53 — a status now declares what it *means*, not only what it is called.

Review feedback corrected my scope call, and the existing code argued for it better than I did. Peek decided open-vs-done with a hardcoded English word set matched on lowercased labels, and **its own comment admitted** *"an app whose statuses are spelled differently shows an empty section until its values are added here — the failure worth having"*. For a layer whose purpose is making the third app cheap, that is PEE-10: blank reads as "that app is broken".

So the owning app declares it: `stage: open | started | done | dropped`.

**`dropped` is the one that earns its place.** A cancelled ticket is neither open nor done — counted as open a finished project sits at 3/4 for ever; counted as done it claims abandoned work. Only the owner knows which statuses have that shape.

**The boundary:** stage says what a status means, never what to draw. "1/3" vs a progress bar vs nothing stays the consumer's call — an owner that could set that would be designing another app's UI, which is §13.1's iframe objection. Declaring meaning is the inversion working; declaring layout would be it breaking.

Optional on the type, because a manifest published before this cannot be given one — the alsoRead reason a level up.

root.body:
The nostr mechanism for this already exists in Buzz: kind:40003, KIND_STREAM_MESSAGE_EDIT.

Shape (crates/buzz-sdk/src/builders.rs, build_edit): kind 40003, tags h=channel and e=target event id, content = the new body. 64KB cap. The relay validates it in ingest.rs via validate_edit_ownership — the signer must be the target's effective author, OR the owning human of the agent that authored it, and the target must be in the same channel. There is an e2e test for exactly that second case: an owner editing a message their agent wrote.

The relay stores the 40003 rather than rewriting the original, so readers fold it over the kind:9 the same way Ship folds 1851 changes over a root event. That is the model this project already uses, which makes it a good fit rather than a new concept.

Peek does not use any of this. convex/messages.ts editBody is a ctx.db.patch on Peek's own row and publishes nothing, while the action beside it (deleteMessage) does publish kind:5. So today a human edit in Peek never reaches the relay: Peek shows the new text and every other reader — Ship's conversation view, the agent, any future app — keeps showing the old one, with nothing announcing the divergence. That is a live correctness gap, not only a missing feature, and it is squarely on the road to dropping Convex.

Two things to confirm before building: whether 40003 is accepted against a kind:9 target specifically (the constant is documented around the 40002 stream-message line), and what a reader should do with several edits — last-write-wins by created_at is the obvious rule and matches the existing fold.

Related: AGE-3 asks for the agent to edit its own message and cannot be satisfied while edits are Peek-local. 40003's ownership rule already covers the agent case.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
Checked how Peek does it when a human edits, since that should be the model. It is not a Nostr mechanism at all.

convex/messages.ts editBody is a ctx.db.patch on Peek's own row. Nothing is published. The action beside it, deleteMessage, does publish — publishDeletions sends one kind:5 per target. Peek publishes messages, replies, reactions, resolutions and deletions outward; edits are the one thing it keeps local.

Two consequences. The agent cannot copy Peek's approach: it has no Convex, only the relay, so there is no convention to follow because none exists on the wire. And more importantly this is not only an agent problem — when a human edits in Peek, the relay keeps the original body, so Ship's conversation view and every other reader show the old text indefinitely with nothing announcing the divergence.

So this ticket cannot be satisfied in a way anybody else would see. The decision is upstream of the agent: either Peek publishes edits as a convention that keeps the event id and readers honour it, or edits stay Peek-local and the agent's version is honestly out of reach. Worth deciding there first.

Note Peek's buildDeletion takes targetEventId and emits an e tag — the same shape measured working here yesterday.

root.body:
**Correcting this issue: its central claim is wrong.** I filed it, and I found out while adding a page to the site.

I wrote that the guardrail `nav.mjs` describes "is not running and has not been". **It runs on every build.** It lives in `site/build.mjs` (~line 267), not in the missing `check.mjs`: it resolves each internal link through `BY_FILE`, treats the `INTERNAL` set as a deliberate downgrade, collects anything else into `problems`, and calls `process.exit(1)`.

It is not theoretical either — **it caught a real bad link in the design guide while I was writing it.** I had linked `/spec/` as a URL; the checker only resolves markdown paths, so it correctly refused the build until I wrote `../protocol/SPEC.md`.

**What is actually true** is narrower and much less interesting: `package.json` declares `"check": "node site/check.mjs"` and that file does not exist, so `npm run check` fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. A broken script reference, not a missing safety net.

So the two resolutions I proposed were both wrong, because both assumed the check needed writing. The real options are:

1. **Delete the `check` script from `package.json`** — the work it names is already done in `build.mjs`, which is the right place for it since it needs the render pass anyway.
2. **Keep the script and point it at the existing logic**, if a check separate from a build is wanted.

Either is minutes. **Do not write a new `check.mjs`** — it would duplicate a guardrail that already works, and two implementations of one rule is the drift this workspace keeps paying for.

One thing worth fixing regardless: `nav.mjs`'s comment names `check.mjs` as the enforcer, which is what sent me down this path. The comment should name `build.mjs`.

**Accepted 2026-08-28.** https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/30

**Settles:** the containment model (§4–§8), the projection vocabulary (§13), messages and rich text as two models sharing an inline layer (§14), and §6 unfrozen.

**Settles none of §12.** All ten open questions survive acceptance — worth stating, because "accepted" reads as "finished". Four have tickets: RIC-1 (content format), CON-1 (reaction horizon), §10.1, and the folder kind numbers §10.1 governs. **Component anchoring is unfrozen, not chosen** — its three mechanisms are all still live.

**§10.1 left open on purpose.** Its trigger fired (upstream shipped `kind:30621`), but the *latest* responsible moment it names — the first line of folder command or state code — has not arrived. Firing makes it easier, not forced. It is now the only thing between the accepted design and folder tickets, since §12.1 makes the kind numbers its tail rather than a separate decision.

**One amendment, and it was worth the reading pass.** §13.3 said an unknown slot is "unrenderable by definition", which reads as though the case cannot arise. It arises on every rollout: the slot set is closed but it *grows*, and producers and consumers upgrade at different times — so every manifest declaring `list` will be read by something that has never heard of one. Same staggered-upgrade condition the widget chain exists for, and slots have no chain.

A consumer MUST now ignore a slot it does not implement and still render the rest — safe because `title` is required. Two obligations make it real: a producer must not put information *only* in a newer slot, and a consumer must not treat an unknown slot as an error. **This is PRO-2's problem specifically** — it adds three slots to a consumer that predates them.

**A rule that was implicit and is now written down:** SPEC absorbs an accepted part when it is *implemented*, not when it is accepted. Otherwise SPEC documents a protocol no app speaks.

root.body:
**Fixed. Two PRs, and they want to land together — `src/store.ts` is vendored at identical paths and `conformance.test.ts` enforces it.**

    estiva-app/ship#49
    estiva-app/estiva-agent#14

The four default parameters are gone rather than renamed — no caller outside `store.ts` passed a limit — and `loadAll` and `rawFolders` now use `queryAll`. Both copies verified **byte-identical** after the change.

## The open question is answered, from the relay source

**The clamp is per filter, not per response.** `buzz-db/src/event.rs` does `q.limit.unwrap_or(100).min(clamp)` and the bridge calls `query_events` **once per filter** (bounded-concurrent, order-preserving, `bridge.rs:1269`).

So `rawFolders`, which maps one filter per Folder, gets the ceiling **for each Folder** rather than sharing one across all 61. The pessimistic reading — ~298 events of headroom — does not apply; the real margin is far larger. That question could not be settled from production, which has never produced a response over 1000, but the source settles it without waiting.

## And a trap worth more than the fix

**A filter carrying no `limit` at all gets 100, not the ceiling.** `q.limit.unwrap_or(100)`. So "just delete the limit" is **worse than the bug** — it would have cut these reads from 2000 to 100 while looking like a cleanup. `queryAll` is correct precisely because it always sends an explicit `limit: pageSize`.

Both facts are now in the doc comment so nobody has to re-derive them from Rust.

## Verification

    ship    typecheck clean · npm test passes · conformance 56 changes / 7 conversations
    agent   typecheck clean · npm test passes (CLI, MCP, extension) · conformance agrees
            committed plugin/server/index.js bundle rebuilt — 13 queryAll references,
            no limit parameter on loadAll or rawFolders

## On the miss itself

The earlier pass grepped `limit: [0-9]+` against default parameters written `limit = 2000`. One character. Two lessons worth keeping: **the headroom figure was in the wrong unit** — I measured per kind (321/1000) where the multi-kind `FOLDER_KINDS` filter makes ~702 per response the right number — and **"0 literals left" was an artefact of the pattern, not a property of the code**. A check that cannot see what it checks reads exactly like a passing check.

Holding `in_progress` until both merge.

root.body:
**Reopening. I marked this done and it was not — my own check could not see the sites it was checking.**

`src/store.ts` still names 2000 at four places and still calls `query`, not `queryAll`:

    463  loadFolder(folder, limit = 2000)
    474  loadFolders(folders, limit = 2000)
    506  loadAll(limit = 2000)              <- Ship's main read path
    593  rawFolders(folders, limit = 2000)

feeding real filters at 522, 523 and 597.

**Why I missed them.** I grepped `limit: [0-9]+` — the object-literal form. These are **default parameters**, `limit = 2000`. One character, `:` versus `=`, hid all four, and I then reported "0 page-size literals left" twice on the strength of it. A check that cannot see the thing it checks is worse than no check, which is the failure mode I flagged twice today in other tooling and then committed myself.

**My headroom figure was also measured in the wrong unit.** I reported per-kind (largest 321 of 1000) and called it comfortable. But `rawFolders` uses `FOLDER_KINDS = [PROJECT, ISSUE, CHANGE, MESSAGE, COMMENT]` — a **multi-kind** filter, so the response is the sum across five kinds. Per *response* the real figure is ~702, which is a much tighter margin than I described.

**And an open question I had not even asked.** `rawFolders` maps one filter per folder into a single `/query` call. Whether the relay clamps **per filter or per response** decides whether the ceiling is ~1000 total or ~1000 each — with 61 folders that is the difference between ample and nearly exhausted. Production cannot answer it, having never produced a response above 1000.

Credit where due: all three of these came from the other session's review, not from me.

**Constraint on the fix:** `src/store.ts` is **byte-identical in both `estiva-ship` and `estiva-agent`** (verified), and `conformance.test.ts` exists to enforce that. So it is one edit applied twice, and the two PRs want to land together.

Taking it now.

**All three parts done. Package published; two consumer PRs open.**

    estiva-foundation#10   MERGED, and @estiva-app/protocol@0.2.0 is on the registry
    estiva-agent#13        open — 9 call sites
    estiva-app/ship#47     open — 1 call site

`npm view @estiva-app/protocol version` → **0.2.0**, so the publish is verified against the registry rather than against the release workflow's green tick. Tag format is `<dir>@<version>` (`protocol@0.2.0`) — **not** the scoped package name, which is what the workflow's `DIR="packages/${name}"` expects; I had that wrong before checking.

## The distinction that shaped the change

Not every `limit` literal was the bug. Two categories, and conflating them would have broken things:

**Page sizes standing in for "everything"** — 9 in the agent, 1 in Ship. All moved to `queryAll`: channels, messages in a folder, all messages for per-folder counts, **issues (the `loadAll`)**, folders, manifest records, changes, profiles, and Ship's discovery check.

**Deliberate bounds** — left alone. `limit: 1` existence and newest-addressable lookups; the small reads in `probe-agent.ts` (20), `agent-renewal-soak.ts` (5), `manifest-reader.ts` (10), `publish-manifest.ts` (20). And `cli.ts`'s connectivity probe reads whatever one request gives, which is the point of a probe.

**`src/store.ts` needed no change** — its limits are all `limit: 1`. That is fortunate: it is the copy vendored at identical paths in both repos, so not touching it keeps them byte-identical and avoids the cross-repo drift `conformance.test.ts` exists to catch.

## One site that was neither

`peek read --limit` is **user-supplied**, default 200. Above the relay's ceiling it was silently clamped, so someone asking `--limit 5000` got 1000 and was told nothing — the same failure reaching a person directly. It now pages and trims above the ceiling and stays a single request below it.

## Verification

    foundation   145 tests pass, typecheck clean, CI green on PR and main
    agent        npm test passes (CLI, MCP, extension), tsc clean,
                 conformance agrees: 56 changes, 7 conversations
    ship         npm test passes, typecheck clean,
                 conformance agrees: 18 issues, 56 changes, 7 conversations

Both conformance runs report the **same** fold numbers, which is what that fixture is for — and it matters here specifically because this changed *how events are fetched* in both repos.

## Done when — against the ticket

- *No call site names a page size as a literal* — met, with the bounds distinction above recorded rather than glossed.
- *A query exceeding the ceiling pages or fails loudly* — pages, and throws where no correct answer exists (more than one page sharing a `created_at`).
- *One test asserts a result at exactly the ceiling is treated as possibly truncated* — met, plus the stronger case: the fake relay clamps to 40 while the caller asks for 500 and all 200 events still return, so correctness does not depend on the constant being right.

root.body:
**Part 1 of 2 open: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-foundation/pull/10** — `@estiva-app/protocol` 0.2.0. The package half; the consumer half follows once it publishes.

## What it adds

- **`RELAY_PAGE_CEILING`** — the number, in the one place that talks to the relay for a living, instead of copied into four call sites that cannot know when the relay changes it.
- **`Relay.queryAll(filters, { pageSize, maxPages })`** — every matching event, paged on the `until` cursor, rather than the first page.

## The decision worth recording, because the obvious version is wrong

Paging until a page comes back smaller than the page size **reintroduces this bug**. It trusts `RELAY_PAGE_CEILING` to equal the relay's real limit; if the relay's were ever *lower*, every page would look short and the first would be mistaken for the whole set.

So the termination rule is **whether the `until` cursor still advances**, which holds whatever the true ceiling is, at the cost of one extra round trip at the end. Pinned by a test where the fake relay clamps to **40** while the caller asks for **500** — all 200 events still return.

Two more, both learned by getting them wrong first:

- **Dedup by id is not the termination signal.** Under two filters matching the same events, a page of already-seen ids means "these filters overlap", not "stop". The first draft conflated them and **its own test caught it** — the shared `seen` set was doing double duty for the returned union and for deciding when to stop.
- **It throws where no correct answer exists.** If the cursor cannot advance and the page is full, more than `pageSize` events share one `created_at`; no value of `until` reaches past them without skipping some. Better to say so than return a plausible subset.

## Verification

145 tests pass, typecheck clean, and **this repo actually has working CI** — unlike buzz, the PR gets an independent check rather than "no checks reported".

## Versioning, deliberately

**Minor, not patch.** Consumers pin `^0.1.0`, which excludes 0.2.0, so nothing picks this up silently. That is the intent: they have to change anyway to stop naming a page size, and an accidental upgrade would be worse than an explicit one. `PROTOCOL_VERSION` and `package.json` moved together — the drift test in `runtime.test.mjs` covers it.

## Still to do

1. Merge #10, then publish by pushing the tag `@estiva-app/protocol@0.2.0` (release fires on `*@*`).
2. Consumer PRs: replace the four `limit: 2000` literals in `estiva-agent` (`apps/ship.ts`, `apps/peek.ts`, `manifest-reader.ts` ×2) with `queryAll`, bump the range to `^0.2.0`, and do the same for `estiva-ship`'s copies. The three `limit: 500` sites are the same class and should go the same way.

Unrelated observation from the worktree: `package-lock.json` on `estiva-foundation` `main` is **stale for identity 0.1.1** — `npm install` corrects it to `0.1.1`. Kept out of this PR to avoid mixing changes; worth a one-line commit.

root.body:
**The backup trap is now closed. `~/estiva-backups` restores — verified 2026-08-28, not inferred.**

My earlier comment left this as the one open "hope rather than fact": the backup covers the relay's Postgres, but nobody had restored one, and the age private key lives in a password manager. Done now, end to end.

**Method.** A fresh archive was taken with `KEEP=15` so the 14-day retention pruned nothing (it prunes at `KEEP=14`, and there were exactly 14 — worth knowing before anyone runs it by hand). Decrypted with the age identity, **`./buzz.sql` extracted alone** — `buzz.env`, `estiva-id.env` and `estiva-id.sql` were left inside the archive deliberately, since they carry `BUZZ_RELAY_PRIVATE_KEY`, `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEK`, users and passkeys. Restored into a throwaway Postgres 17.

**Restore: 0 errors.** 61 tables, schema version **34**, 1399 events, 61 channels, 171 channel members.

**Fidelity against live production, per kind — 23 kinds compared:**

    21 kinds     identical
    kind 1111    76 backup / 77 prod   (+1 written after the dump)
    kind 1851   292 backup / 293 prod  (+1 written after the dump)
    totals     1399 backup / 1401 prod

Both deltas are events written in the ~20 minutes after the dump, which is what a live relay should look like. **No kind holds more rows in the backup than in production**, which is the direction that would have meant loss.

**So a restore is now a fact:** the archive decrypts, `buzz.sql` is complete and consistent, and it replays into an empty Postgres cleanly at schema 34 — the version the catch-up moved production to.

**Two follow-ups this surfaced, neither blocking.** The age key was rotated during this exercise (`recipient.pub` on the box now `age17r8r3306…`, was unchanged since 2026-08-07 until today) — so **the 14 pre-existing archives are encrypted to the retired key**. They are SSH-gated and low risk, but cannot be re-encrypted without decrypting first; the clean move is to let 14-day retention refill with new-key archives and delete the old ones once you are comfortable. Separately, the three 37 KB archives in `~/estiva-backups` are from 2026-08-07, old-key, and far too small to be a useful restore point.

**Only `buzz.sql` was proven.** `estiva-id.sql` — users, passkeys, encrypted Nostr keys — was not restored or inspected, by choice. That is the more sensitive half and deserves its own rehearsal by someone who can hold the KEK.

**Exercised 2026-08-28 against the caught-up relay (`sha256:67b436a9f9ef…`, schema 34). Nothing broke. 3 of 10 items pass; 6 need a browser and a real signed-in identity; 1 is now moot. No rollback needed.**

## Passing

**Item 9 — the agent, the cheapest end-to-end check.** `ship projects` → 11 projects. That is the client-credentials grant, `/sign`, NIP-98 and `/query` in one command, all working post-merge.

**Item 6 (read half) — Ship's `30850`/`30851` reads and the fold.** `ship issues --project "Catch up the Buzz fork"` → 11 issues, coverage 96 reachable.

**Item 10 — cross-app interop, the claim the suite rests on.** The Ship project's Folder `8eb734fa…` is visible through Peek's read path as *"Project: Catch up the Buzz fork"*. `peek topics` → 40 topics.

**Writes, on the new image.** Since the 14:02 deploy the relay accepted **3 × `kind:9`** and **2 × `kind:1851`** from the agent — the comments and status changes on CAT-4 and CAT-11 are themselves the evidence. **Zero `ERROR` lines in the relay log since restart.**

**CORS, which is the gate that breaks both browser apps with no server-side symptom** — and it has a working negative control:

    https://peek.estiva.app   200  access-control-allow-origin: https://peek.estiva.app
    https://ship.estiva.app   200  access-control-allow-origin: https://ship.estiva.app
    https://evil.test         200  (no allow-origin header)   <- correct

Both apps serve `200`.

## The finding: the client asks for more than the relay will now give

The merge halved `max_limit` to 1000 (`10000` advertised before). The **shared client code still asks for `limit: 2000`** in at least four places:

    lib/agent/apps/ship.ts:120      kinds:[ISSUE],   limit: 2000    <- loadAll
    lib/agent/apps/peek.ts:207      kinds:[MESSAGE], limit: 2000
    scripts/manifest-reader.ts:113  kinds:[kind],    limit: 2000
    scripts/manifest-reader.ts:125  kinds:[change],  limit: 2000

The relay **clamps silently** — NIP-01 has no "truncated" signal, so a caller gets fewer events and no indication why. Current headroom, per kind:

    kind 9    messages   314 / 1000   (31%)
    kind 1851 changes    280 / 1000   (28%)
    kind 30851 issues    119 / 1000   (12%)
    total events        1367          (an unfiltered limit-2000 query WOULD clamp)

**So nothing is truncated today** — every kind the apps query is well under 1000, which is why items 6, 9 and 10 pass. But the margin halved while the code believes it has 2000, and the failure when it arrives is silent history loss in Peek and silent missing issues in Ship. **This wants its own ticket; I have not filed it because the code lives in `estiva-agent` *and* `estiva-ship`, and per the house rule an issue cannot change parent afterwards — asking where it belongs rather than guessing.**

## Needs a browser and a real identity — not done

Items **1** (Estiva ID sign-in), **2** (open a topic with history), **3** (post a message), **5** (Ship project widget in the Peek sidebar / `naddr` + NIP-89 resolution), **7** (comment on an issue in Ship's UI) and **8** (change status and assignee in Ship's UI).

Ship and Peek talk to the relay **from browser code**, so nothing I can run server-side exercises their real path. CORS passing is necessary but not sufficient.

## Item 4 — reactions, and why it is now moot

The ticket calls `kind:7` "a path that is easy to break" because the channel is derived from the target rather than carried. It was worse than that: **pre-merge, a reaction to an h-less event panicked the ingest worker** after inserting the row (`expect("reaction path has channel")`, `ingest.rs:2434/2440`). CAT-9 made that reachable by allowing global project records, and production holds **11** of them with **0** reactions — so it was live and untaken.

**The merge carries `16b7ae7ce`, which removes it**, verified absent from the deployed source. The agent has no reaction verb, so a live `kind:7` publish still needs Peek — but the hazard is gone rather than untested.

## Rollback decision

**None.** No failures, no ingest errors, all boot gates verified on production data, and the one client-visible change (`max_limit` 10000 → 1000) has 3× headroom on the largest kind.

**Not marking done** — 6 of 10 items are browser work that only a signed-in person can do.

The PR head was a real merge commit with `upstream/main` as a second parent. **Squash collapsed it into a single-parent commit, so upstream's 702 commits are not in the ancestry.** Consequences, measured:

    git merge-base upstream/main origin/nfb-demo-kinds   b78a684cf   <- UNCHANGED
    is 69096c9a8 an ancestor of nfb-demo-kinds?          NO
    git rev-list --count nfb-demo-kinds..upstream/main   710

So git reports **710 behind** while the tree is level with `69096c9a8`. **CAT-1 chose merge over rebase precisely because "a merge commit preserves the merge-base, so the next catch-up is measurable" — squash removed that property.** The decision was right; the merge button undid half of it.

**Two ways this bites whoever does the next catch-up:**

1. A survey run the way CAT-1/CAT-2 were run reports ~710 behind and concludes nothing has been caught up.
2. **`git merge upstream/main` would try to re-apply all 702 commits' diffs to a tree that already contains them**, producing enormous spurious conflicts that look like a catastrophic divergence.

## Mitigation in place, and the better fix

Pushed a marker tag — safe, `relay-image.yml` triggers on branches only, so no rebuild:

    upstream-merged/69096c9a8 -> c8a4d521c

**So the real gap is `69096c9a8..upstream/main`, not `nfb-demo-kinds..upstream/main`.** Measure the next catch-up from the tag:

    git rev-list --count upstream-merged/69096c9a8..upstream/main
    git merge-tree --write-tree origin/nfb-demo-kinds upstream/main   # still correct for conflicts

**A stronger fix exists and was not done unilaterally:** an ancestry-only merge, `git merge -s ours upstream/main` pinned at `69096c9a8`, which changes no file but repairs the merge-base so every ordinary git command is right again. It needs a push to `nfb-demo-kinds`, which rebuilds the image for no content change. Worth doing before the next catch-up rather than during it.

**For next time: use a real merge commit, not squash, for an upstream catch-up.** Squash is right for a feature PR and wrong for this one — CAT-1's reasoning should say so explicitly.

Renewal (PEEK-108) measured against production, not reasoned about.

Broke the stored accessToken to \"broken-on-purpose\", left expiresAt in the future and refreshToken intact, reloaded, did a write. Result: accessToken …XijAnhsptwqg → …QJ2W0EMZIh5Q, refreshToken …xZVhym_hg6E8 → …ExrEHV0XEmTg. So /sign returned 401 on the bad bearer, the refresh grant succeeded, and Estiva ID rotated the refresh token. renewAccessToken has exactly one call site (apps/ship/app.ts:106, the signer's renew), so nothing else could have produced that rotation.

Two earlier tests of the same thing were wrong and are worth not repeating: deleting the token, and setting expiresAt to the past. Both make validToken return null, so boot decides probe_silently and the live estiva_id_session cookie re-enters you silently — it tests the probe, not renewal. validToken checks presence and expiry only and never validates the token string, which is why the string is the thing to break.

Caveat: this exercised the OLD vanilla app's use of @estiva-app/identity, which is what production serves. web/ is not in the Dockerfile, so REW-2's own done-when is still unmet pending REW-8.

root.body:
**Deployed 2026-08-28 09:39 UTC. Running image matches `:nfb`, reads and writes verified, outage measured.**

**What was deployed is CAT-11 only, not the catch-up.** `:nfb` was one commit ahead of the running image; the 702-commit CAT-4 merge is still unpushed. Migrations on the branch: 24. Production schema: 24. **No schema change ran** — `Database migrations complete` fired 26 ms after start with nothing to apply. So this was a clean rehearsal of the procedure with a trivial payload.

## Image id — and a correction to my own predicted value

    registry index digest   sha256:e6aed9aae3e0621c33b…
    local :nfb after pull   sha256:e6aed9aae3e0621c33b…
    container .Image        sha256:e6aed9aae3e0621c33b…
    (previously running)    sha256:eba55f4636c4…

All three agree, so the container runs what the tag resolves to — not merely "the tag was pulled".

**I predicted `3d069db2bf7d` and that was wrong.** That value came from `docker manifest inspect --verbose`, which reports the **per-platform manifest** digest *inside* the index. The tag resolves to the **index** digest, `e6aed9aae3e0`, which is what `RepoDigests` and `buildx imagetools inspect` report. Two different fields, both called "digest". Anyone verifying by digest should compare `docker image inspect --format "{{index .RepoDigests 0}}"` against `docker buildx imagetools inspect <tag>` — never against `manifest inspect --verbose`.

## The check that cannot be misread

Digests are metadata. The deployed **binary** was inspected directly:

    docker exec buzz-prod-relay-1 grep -c \
      "wider than the commit-time created_at" /usr/local/bin/buzz-relay
    -> 1

CAT-11's warning string is in the running artifact. That is the difference between "the registry moved" and "the box is running the new code".

## Reads and writes

- NIP-11 answers; `max_limit` is still **10000**, which is correct and a useful negative control — the drop to 1000 arrives with CAT-4, so this confirms the merge is *not* deployed.
- A REQ through the HTTP bridge + NIP-98 returned 11 issues.
- **This comment is the write test.** It is a real signed `kind:1111` published through the freshly deployed relay; if you are reading it, the write path works.

## Outage: measured against M4's estimate

    container created      09:39:37.745
    container started      09:39:44.234
    relay first log        09:39:44.376
    TCP listening          09:39:51.164

    process start -> listening      6.79 s
    container created -> listening 13.42 s   <- the real outage window

**M4 estimated 8.8 s and that was measuring the wrong span.** The process boot is actually *faster* than the rehearsal — 6.79 s versus 8.8 s — but the rehearsal ignored **~6.5 s of container teardown and recreation** that `--force-recreate` costs. So the useful correction for next time: **budget ~13–15 s, not ~9 s**, and the gap is compose overhead rather than anything the relay does.

**Boot is dominated by one thing, and it is not migrations.** The A3 git object-store conformance probe ran 09:39:44.465 → 09:39:51.142 — **6.68 s of the 6.79 s boot**. Migrations were ~26 ms with nothing to apply. When CAT-4 deploys with ten migrations (~235 ms measured on production shape in M4), boot should be ~7 s plus a quarter second — still the S3 probe that sets the floor. Which also means: **if MinIO is slow or unreachable, that is where a deploy hangs.**

root.body:
web/ can sign in. ship#44, CI green on both jobs. identity 0.1.1 published through OIDC; ship#43 (old app adopts the package) also green.

THE SEAM PAID OUT. web/src/api/store.ts has said since REW-1: "Sign-in through Estiva ID replaces this signer in REW-2; Store cannot tell the difference." It does and it cannot — nothing below the signer changed.

BOOT ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING, and it is the one thing a reviewer should look at. api/store.ts builds its signer at module scope, so the session must be settled before that module first evaluates. main.tsx therefore awaits bootAuth() and imports App DYNAMICALLY. A static import would evaluate the store while the callback was still being redeemed and the app would come up ANONYMOUS immediately after a successful sign-in — everything renders, the relay answers what an anonymous reader may see, and the only symptom is that you are not who you just signed in as. A test asserts the token is in storage before boot returns, which is as close as a unit test gets to asserting an import order.

Shared: decideBoot, SHELL_COPY, the labels, isRecoverable. Ship-only: the rendering, using Ship own primitives. ADR 0002 section 2 is why the package ships no components — identity depending on @estiva-app/ui is the stated trigger for folding ui back into the foundation repo, and a package shipping sign-in screens is how that happens by accident.

Two things I changed in my own work rather than shipping: main.tsx top-level await became an async IIFE (it works, but it ties the file to the build target for nothing), and setNavigate is a documented test seam because jsdom implements no navigation and will not let location.assign be spied — without it "we left for Estiva ID" and "we did nothing" are the same observation.

10 new tests, all on silent failures. web/ 105 to 115.

STILL NOT DONE. The four by-hand flows this done-when requires need a DEPLOYED build with ID_BASE set. A local build is anonymous-only by design, so a local run cannot exercise them at all — which is a feature (a local build cannot reach production identity by accident) and a constraint here.

The checklist, once #43 and #44 are merged and deployed, in this order:

1. COLD SIGN-IN. Open ship.estiva.app in a fresh tab. Expect a silent probe to land you in without a prompt if you have an Estiva ID session, or one "Continue with passkey" button if not. Then check the identity menu shows your name rather than Anonymous.
2. DEEP LINK. Open ship.estiva.app/#/p/<some-project> signed out. After entry you should be on that project, not the default screen. This is the fragment surviving a redirect that cannot carry one.
3. SILENT RENEWAL ACROSS AN EXPIRY. Stay on a page for longer than the access-token TTL and act — comment or change a status. It should just work, with no navigation. If you get bounced to Estiva ID, renewal is not being reached.
4. FAILED RENEWAL DROPS TO THE SHELL. In devtools, delete ship.estiva-id.token from localStorage, then reload. Expect the shell with an honest reason, not a blank page and not a silent anonymous session.
5. SIGN-OUT THAT ACTUALLY SIGNS OUT. Sign out, then RELOAD. You must NOT be let straight back in. This is the one that regressed before (PEEK-122): clearing the local token leaves the estiva_id_session cookie alone, so a silent probe walks you back in and it looks like sign-out did nothing.

I can verify 1, 2 and 5 from the relay afterwards by reading which pubkey authored events. 3 and 4 need eyes on the screen.

    image:            ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb
    running image id: sha256:eba55f4636c4…
    status:           Up 2 days (healthy)

1. **MinIO must be reachable before the relay restarts.** The git object-store conformance probe is a fail-closed startup gate — a missing S3 backend presents as a relay that never comes up, not a degraded one. Two other boot gates fail the same way: the community-deletion serving fence, and the roster fence.
2. **`BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=true` is what makes migrations run at startup.** Production has it set. Without it the relay logs `Skipping database migrations…` and starts anyway — so if it is ever unset, a deploy silently skips the schema change.
3. **Expected downtime is seconds.** Measured on a production-shaped restore (CAT-6): ~235 ms for all ten migrations, and 8.8 s from container start to `TCP listening` including migrations. Add image-pull time, which could not be measured off-box.
