root.body:
**Reproduced, fixed, two PRs open. And one correction to this issue's own description.**

- relay: https://github.com/estiva-app/buzz/pull/11
- docs: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/23

## Correction: it is not silent data loss

This issue says the event is *"accepted at ingest"* and the caller *"sees `accepted: true`"*. **That is wrong.** Measured against a relay with the window at `63072000` — the value the knob's own doc comment gives as the import example:

| published | result |
| --- | --- |
| channel-scoped (`h` tag), 120 days old | **REFUSED — HTTP 500 `internal server error`**, not stored |
| global (no `h`), 120 days old | accepted and readable |
| channel-scoped, dated now | accepted and readable |

So the caller **does** learn it failed. What it gets is a bare `500`, with the real reason only in the relay log:

    events.created_at 2026-04-29 … is more than 960 s before commit time …;
    below the replica-fence floor

The defect is therefore narrower than filed, and worth restating precisely: the knob **accepts a value it cannot honour** for the one case it exists for; the failure reaches the operator as a generic server error; and nothing warned at startup. The global-kind exemption works exactly as 0021 documents — that half of my analysis held.

## Which done-when route, and why

The second: **document and warn**, not derive-the-floor-from-the-window. Widening `CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS` is the tempting fix and the wrong one — the replica fence subtracts the same constant, so the two uses must not diverge, and moving it means re-examining that proof. That reasoning is now written into the docs so nobody later takes it as the easy option.

## What the PRs do

Relay (97 insertions, **no existing line changed**): the doc comment now says widening helps *global* kinds only and names the real route; a startup warning fires when the window is past the floor; and `Config::drift_window_exceeds_commit_floor()` is a named predicate reading `buzz_db::replica_fence::CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS` rather than a literal 960, so the warning cannot drift away from the trigger.

Docs: `SILENT-FAILURES.md` already had a row for this and it was **actively misleading** — it implied widening the window is the fix. Corrected, plus an *Importing history* section with both real routes.

## Verified

CI is `disabled_manually` on this fork, so PR #11 will show no checks. Compiled locally in the pinned toolchain instead: clippy `-D warnings` clean; the new test plus all eleven existing config tests pass; and end to end a relay at `63072000` emits **exactly one** warning (`configured=63072000 floor=960`) while the same relay at the 900 default emits **none** — so it is conditional, not noise.

## Not done, precisely

**Both PRs are unmerged**, so this is not done.

And one clause is only partly met. The done-when asks that *"one test must publish a channel-scoped event older than the floor and assert the outcome"*. My publish-and-observe was **manual**; the automated test I added covers the config predicate, not the publish path. The publish-path assertion does exist — `created_at_floor_guard_aborts_old_channel_rows_at_commit` in `buzz-db` — but it is **upstream-only** and arrives with CAT-4's merge, not on `nfb-demo-kinds` today. So after CAT-4 lands, that clause is covered by upstream's own test; before it, it is not.

## Follow-up worth its own ticket

The client still gets a bare `500` rather than a refusal naming the floor. Mapping that specific `check_violation` to a clear rejection would be a genuine improvement, but it touches ingest's error mapping and risks reclassifying unrelated database errors. Deliberately not bundled.

root.body:
**Rehearsed 2026-08-27 against a production-shaped database. Nothing refused. Production was read, never written. Estimated outage window: seconds.**

Relay built from CAT-4s merge commit `b09aeba7f` (702 commits of upstream), run in an isolated docker stack — throwaway Postgres 17.10 + Redis + MinIO on their own network, ports 3100/deliberately not 3000.

## The database, and that it really is production-shaped

Read-only `pg_dump` of **buzz only** — no `.env`, no MinIO, no secrets — restored with **zero errors**. Verified against the numbers I measured directly on production earlier the same day:

| | restore | production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| schema version | 24 | 24 |
| channels | 61 | 61 |
| `events` partitions | 8 | 8 |
| `kind:39002` rosters | 64 | 64 |
| global `kind:30850` | 11 | 11 |
| `workflow_runs` | 0 | 0 |
| events | 1324 | 1275 (hours earlier) |

**`kind:30078` went 0 → 3 between the two reads.** This ticket warned that "a copy with no `30078` rows at all would pass and prove nothing" — so the copy is now *better* shaped than it would have been this morning. The three rows are `estiva-peek:stars:v1`, Peeks app-private storage (CRO-11s convention), **not** read-state: none matches the `read-state:` d-tag pattern, none carries the `t: read-state` tag, and **0 have the ambiguous `d` cardinality** the known refuser looks for. So CAT-3s conclusion stands, now on evidence rather than absence — and note its premise expired within a day.

## Every migration, in order, with timings

Ten, not eight — `0033` and `0034` arrived with upstreams next 77 commits. Applied to the production-shaped copy, each in its own transaction as sqlx does. Against a measured **~127 ms** `docker exec`+psql baseline (3 samples: 131/122/130), net SQL time:

    0025 relay_invites                 ~9 ms
    0026 replica_heartbeat             ~0 ms
    0027 channels_id_lookup_index      ~0 ms
    0028 long_reaction_payloads       ~10 ms
    0029 community_deletion           ~67 ms   <- heaviest
    0030 community_deletion_recovery  ~26 ms
    0031 workflow_run_error_codes      ~0 ms
    0032 channel_roster_snapshot_fence ~7 ms   <- the one I had flagged
    0033 private_managed_agent_fts   ~116 ms
    0034 replica_heartbeat_vacuum      ~0 ms
    ------------------------------------------
    total                            ~235 ms

**Nothing refused. Nothing destructive.** 1324 events and 61 channels preserved; floor guard and roster fence both on 9 relations (parent + 8 partitions).

**0032s missing `lock_timeout` is confirmed as a tail risk, not a cost.** ~7 ms of work at this scale. It remains worth adding one line, because the exposure is an unbounded *wait* behind a conflicting lock, not duration.

## The real startup path, not just the SQL

A second fresh restore, migrated by **the relay itself** with `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=true`. `_sqlx_migrations` went **24 → 34|34**, and every gate reported in its own words:

    Database migrations complete
    partition range already covered by an existing partition   (x8)
    Community deletion serving fences verified
    git object-store backend admitted: A3 conformance probe passed
    Channel roster fence verified

**Relay reached "TCP listening" in 8.8 s** from container start, migrations included. So the restart dominates the migration by ~40x, and the outage window is **seconds** — CAT-7 should add image-pull time, which cannot be measured from here.

## Schema version before and after

**24 → 34**, by sqlx, recorded in `_sqlx_migrations`.

## The relay serves a read and a write afterwards — PASS

Published a real signed `kind:30851` into a fresh Folder and read it back by `#h` filter through `@estiva-app/protocol`; id matched byte-for-byte. With a **negative control** — the same query against an unknown folder returned 0 events — so "returned something" is distinguishable from "returns everything regardless of filter".

## 0032s runtime constraint, which my CAT-3 comment said this ticket must test

Tested directly against a real channel with 3 active members:

- a roster whose `p` tags **match** canonical membership → **accepted**
- a roster with **one bogus extra member** → `ERROR: kind 39002 roster does not match canonical channel membership`

So the trigger enforces what it claims and is not a blanket block on `39002` writes.

Then the tool itself, which is what I was actually worried about. `buzz-admin reconcile-channels --channel <id>` on a 4-member production channel: **"Reconciled 1 channels"** — the emitted roster passes the trigger. Full reconcile across the community: **"Reconciled 0 channels (60 already had events, 60 total)"** — no channel is missing discovery metadata, and nothing violated the fence. **That risk is retired.**

## The backup trap — answered, and it needs a human

`~/estiva-backups` **does** cover the relays Postgres: `/opt/backup/backup.sh` dumps `buzz.sql` (events, channels, memberships) alongside `estiva-id.sql`, both `.env` files and a MinIO tar.

**But I could not verify that it restores.** Everything is encrypted to an age public key whose private half is deliberately **not on the box** — it lives in a password manager. The archive also bundles `BUZZ_RELAY_PRIVATE_KEY` and `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEK`, which is material I should not be decrypting regardless. So "a backup nobody has restored is a hope" is still true, and **retiring it is a human task**: decrypt one archive with the password-manager key and restore `buzz.sql` into a throwaway.

Two things worth knowing meanwhile: the boxs backups are **current and healthy** — daily timer, todays at 03:34, 3.2 MB and growing week over week. The copies in `~/estiva-backups` are **three weeks stale** (37 KB, 2026-08-07) and are not what a restore should be tested against.

## Also found here — a correction to my own CAT-3 comment

I wrote that migrations "run automatically at relay startup". They run **only when `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE` is set**. Production has it `true`, so the claim holds there, but it is conditional: without it the relay logs `Skipping database migrations because BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE is not enabled` **and starts anyway**. A rehearsal that forgot it would have looked clean and tested nothing.

And two startup gates that were not in my list of three, both found by the relay refusing to boot: the **community-deletion serving-fence** check, and a **git object-store conformance probe** that requires a reachable S3 backend. Both fail closed before the relay listens, so a deploy missing MinIO presents as a relay that never comes up rather than a degraded one. **CAT-7 needs MinIO reachable before the relay restarts.**

## Nothing filed against M5

No migration refused, so per the done-when there is no blocking ticket to open before CAT-7. The residual items are one-liners, not blockers: add `lock_timeout` to 0032, and have a human verify the backup restores.

Four things SHA-3 already put in place for this one:

1. The Signer seam is in @estiva-app/protocol 0.1.2 — the interface, its reasoning (why pubkey is synchronous and sign is not, and why a signer cannot sign as somebody else), and secretKeySigner. estivaIdSigner is what stayed behind in both apps precisely so this ticket can take it, and it is still byte-identical between estiva-ship and estiva-agent.
2. authorizationHeader(signer, args) is exported, so an identity signer plugs into the relay clients with nothing else to write. 3. The globals pattern: declare each inside the module that uses it, read it inside a function body. That is what let protocol keep types:[] and no lib:dom while being imported by a Convex backend, a browser bundle and tsx from one artifact. I expect identity NOT to manage this as cleanly — it is browser-shaped throughout and no Convex tree will import it — and I will record which rather than assert it. If the answer is "identity needs lib:dom", that is an ADR 0002 4a amendment, not a shrug.
4. The release path works and is routine now: 0.1.1 and 0.1.2 both went out on a tag through OIDC with no credential in GitHub. So this package costs one manual first publish (browser 2FA, once ever) and then tags.

One thing to decide deliberately rather than discover, from ADR 0002 section 2: identity depending on @estiva-app/ui is the stated trigger for folding ui back into the foundation repo. Sign-in screens shipping real components would do it. The ticket already says keep the shell RENDERING per-app and share only the state machine and the reason vocabulary, which avoids the trigger — worth holding that line on purpose.

root.body:
**All eleven kinds accepted by a relay built from the merge. 2026-08-27, nothing deployed, nothing pushed.**

Relay built from CAT-4s merge commit `b09aeba7f` (702 commits of upstream), run locally against a throwaway Postgres 17 + Redis + MinIO. The relay applied its own 34 migrations at startup through `run_migrations`, so this exercised the real startup path and its fail-closed gates — including **"Channel roster fence verified"**, which is migration 0032s new gate passing on a running relay rather than inferred.

**The relays own words:**

    ✅ kind:9007  Folder (precondition)   accepted
    ✅ kind:1111  NIP-22 comment          accepted
    ✅ kind:31990 NIP-89 handler info     accepted
    ✅ kind:31989 NIP-89 recommendation   accepted
    ✅ kind:30850 Project                 accepted
    ✅ kind:30851 Issue                   accepted
    ✅ kind:1851  Change                  accepted
    ✅ kind:9101  Estiva assertion        accepted
    ✅ kind:9802  NIP-84 highlight        accepted
    ✅ kind:30840 NIP-FC File             accepted
    ✅ kind:30841 NIP-FC Component        accepted

**No refusals, so no merge defect.** Combined with CAT-4s set-difference check (no kind lost a scope arm), the `restricted: unknown event kind` failure this ticket exists to catch does not occur.

**The probe covered 7 of 11 and has been extended.** It predated `9101`, `9802`, `30840` and `30841` — exactly as this ticket warned. So a merge that dropped any of those four would have passed the old probe silently. Patch is 38 lines on `scripts/probe-kinds.ts`, held locally and **not pushed**; it is worth landing in `estiva-ship` on its own merit, because the gap it closes is permanent, not merge-specific.

**Also added, and it is the more valuable half: a positive control for CAT-9.** The probe only ever tested that h-less objects are *rejected*. It never tested that a project record without an `h` is *accepted* — which is the asymmetry CAT-9 created, REW-11 depends on, and an upstream merge is most likely to "tidy up". Asked directly:

    CAT-9 asymmetry — a global project record SHOULD be accepted:
    ✅ kind:30850 Project, no h tag       accepted

    Folder enforcement — these SHOULD be rejected:
    ❌ kind:30851 Issue, no h tag         REJECTED — invalid: channel-scoped events must include an h tag
    ❌ kind:1851  Change, no h tag        REJECTED — invalid: channel-scoped events must include an h tag

Both halves of the asymmetry, from the relay, on a build of the merge. The unit test `a_project_record_may_be_global_but_its_contents_may_not()` also passes, but it lives in the relay and cannot tell you the deployed behaviour — this can.

**One correction to my CAT-3 comment, found here.** I wrote that migrations "run automatically at relay startup". They run **only when `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE` is set** — production has `BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=true` in both `.env` and the running container, so the claim holds *there*, but it is conditional rather than unconditional. Without it the relay logs `Skipping database migrations because BUZZ_AUTO_MIGRATE is not enabled` and starts anyway. **CAT-6 must set it**, or the rehearsal will look clean while testing nothing — which is this projects signature failure shape.

**Two more startup gates worth knowing for CAT-6/CAT-7**, neither in my earlier list of three: a **community-deletion serving-fence** check (`Community deletion serving fence is unsafe` → refuses to boot) and a **git object-store conformance probe** that requires a reachable S3 backend and aborts startup without one. Both fail closed *before* the relay listens, so a deploy missing MinIO or a fence precondition presents as a relay that never comes up, not as a degraded one.

Local NIP-11 from the merged build also confirms CAT-1s prediction by measurement: **`max_limit` is 1000** here versus **10000** on production.

root.body:
Done-when met. Document merged (estiva-docs#19), migration merged (peek#76) and PROVED against the live relay.

Miky starred a topic in the deployed app at 20:21:14, after the 20:17:49 deploy. One kind:30078 on the relay, and every part of SPEC 12 it should obey:

  1c9ee87f04  by=f3a38fa6  d=estiva-peek:stars:v1  t=estiva-peek-appdata  h=(none)  idOK=true  len=516

d uses the registered client_id as the prefix, not a friendly name, so two apps cannot collide by construction (12.2). One t tag so a reader filters by #t instead of fetching every 30078 the person owns. No h tag — the MUST NOT, because the relay classifies the kind global-only on write while its read path treats an explicit h as authoritative.

THE PROOF THAT MATTERS IS A FAILURE. 12.4 claims encryption is what makes "app-private" true rather than aspirational. I hold a workspace credential the relay just served that event to, and:

  POST /nip44/decrypt -> 400 {"error":{"code":"bad_request","message":"Could not decrypt that ciphertext","detail":{"reason":"undecryptable"}}}

Negative control, so "undecryptable" is not just a broken endpoint: encrypting and decrypting my OWN blob round-trips — "agent-owned probe" comes back verbatim. So the endpoint works and the refusal is specific to somebody else data. Self-only /nip44/decrypt is doing exactly what CRO-1 built it to do, and Miky stars are private from the agent while both are members of the same workspace.

That is a better demonstration than reading the contents would have been.

CHOSEN AND WHY, since the done-when asks: layer 2, kind:30078, NOT the NIP-51 set this ticket preferred. Full reasoning in the comment above — the deciding fact is that Peek cannot sign 30000 or 30003 (ceiling has 30078 from CRO-2 and neither of those), so layer 1 needed a seed line, a production re-seed and a deploy, and it still could not cover starred people with no nostrPubkey or topics with no channel.

ONE SPEC FOLLOW-UP, not blocking: 12.5 lists four size numbers and calls the relay 256 KiB ingest cap operative. Building this found a fifth that binds tighter for every app in the suite — /nip44/encrypt refuses a plaintext over 65535 bytes, and ciphertext exceeds plaintext, so the relay cap is never what you hit first. 12.5 exists to stop somebody finding the wrong number and right now it names one.

Also open, deliberately: restoreFromRelay is never called on load. missingLocally is exposed for an affordance somebody asks for. Auto-restoring would resurrect stars a person cleared whenever the blob went stale, and a blob goes stale exactly when a publish failed.

root.body:
**Merged 2026-08-27. Local commit `b09aeba7f`, parents `0bd67427b` + `69096c9a8`. Nothing pushed — see the last section, the push is a separate decision.**

Done in a `git worktree` (shared `~/buzz` is on a peer branch and was never touched), on a branch with **no upstream tracking**, so an accidental `git push` cannot reach `nfb-demo-kinds` and cannot rebuild `:nfb`.

**Upstream moved mid-task**, `0720f5380` → `69096c9a8`: **702 behind, not 625**. Re-measured with `git merge-tree` before resolving. Same four files conflict, so CAT-2s analysis held structurally — but two of its five hunks were mischaracterised.

**CAT-2 said all five hunks were keep-both. Two were not.**

- **`ingest.rs` is one sorted `use` list both sides edited.** Keep-both would have duplicated ~50 identifiers and not compiled. Correct resolution is a **set union**: 58 ours + 55 theirs = **61** (52 common, our 6 Estiva kinds, upstreams 3 new ones). Re-wrapped by hand — `cargo fmt` is forbidden here.
- **Both `buzz-db` hunks share the closing brace that sits AFTER the `>>>>>>>` marker.** Deleting markers alone would have let `is_owner_channel_member` swallow the next functions signature. Each ours-side needed its own brace. This one would have compiled into something wrong rather than failing loudly.

**The real find: a semantic conflict that produced no marker at all, and broke the build.**

The fork widened `enforce_relay_membership` from `(state, community: CommunityId, …)` to `(state, tenant: &TenantContext, …)` — that is #10, *"Record a proven owner on every gated path"*. Upstream kept the narrow signature and added **two new endpoints**, `api/gifs.rs` and `api/workflows.rs`, calling it the old way. **Neither file exists on the fork**, so both auto-merged with no conflict and the tree did not compile: two `E0308`s.

Resolved by passing `&tenant` at both sites — which is what the fork already did to `media.rs`, `audio/handler.rs` and `git/transport.rs`, and what the adjacent `enforce_http_admission` / `check_nip98_replay` calls in those same functions pass. All ten call sites now agree.

**Worth recording why the other resolution was the trap:** narrowing the signature back to `CommunityId` also compiles, and silently reverts #8/#9/#10 across every gated path. The tests for that behaviour live in `buzz-db`, not in the crate that fails.

**This is what "CI is disabled_manually" costs.** A PR carrying this merge would have shown nothing pending and read as green. The only reason it was caught is that it was compiled locally.

**Done-when, clause by clause**

| clause | result |
| --- | --- |
| builds | `cargo clippy -p buzz-relay --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean in `rust:1.95` |
| test suite passes | **926 passed / 0 failed / 54 ignored** |
| every kind in `ALL_KINDS` + a scope mapping | 10/10 Estiva, plus the six already-upstream confirmed |
| `relay-image.yml` still exists | yes, 78 lines, still `push: branches: [nfb-demo-kinds]` |
| no reformatting | no formatter run; the only hand-formatting is the import list that had to be re-wrapped to resolve it |

**Stronger than "the merge is clean":** the set difference of scope-arm identifiers before → after the merge is **empty**. Nothing was dropped. That is the `restricted: unknown event kind` failure this ticket was filed about, and it does not occur. `KIND_HTTP_AUTH` (27235) has no arm, but it had none before either — correct for an auth header rather than a published event.

**CAT-9 verified at runtime, not just in the source:** `a_project_record_may_be_global_but_its_contents_may_not ... ok`. `KIND_LL_PROJECT` is absent from both `requires_h_channel_scope` and `is_global_only_kind`; the only two mentions are the comment explaining the absence, which is exactly what made it auditable.

**Two things about the green suite that matter.** First, 8 of 980 failed until I gave them a migrated database — 6 as `PoolTimedOut`, 2 as `assert 500 != 404` where a DB error maps to 500. All 8 pass against Postgres. Second, the briefs **745/2 baseline is not usable** post-merge: `buzz-relay --lib` alone is now 980 tests. Do not compare to it.

**Workflow trap checked, not assumed.** Eight new workflow files arrive (13 → 21) and new files default to **active** — but none fires on a push to `nfb-demo-kinds`: `staging-dev-relay-image` is `workflow_dispatch` only, and `sprig-image`, `codex-security-review` and `mesh-lifecycle` are `main`/tag/PR-scoped. GitHub honours `issue_comment` and `pull_request_target` only from the default branch, so `codex-security-review`s repo-wide comment trigger stays dormant on this branch. I also checked for **renames**, since a renamed workflow loses its `disabled_manually` setting — there are none; `sprig.yml` and `sprig-image.yml` both exist. `gh` confirms 12 disabled, `relay image` the only active one.

**Not done, and deliberately.** The push. `relay-image.yml` fires on `push: branches: [nfb-demo-kinds]`, so pushing rebuilds `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb`. There is **no `buzz-update.timer`** on the box (the other four services have one; buzz does not — and `relay-image.yml`s own comment claiming "the box pulls it on a timer" is **stale and should be deleted**). So a push arms the tag rather than deploying it, and the next manual `docker compose pull relay` for any unrelated reason ships 702 commits. That belongs to CAT-7 with its eyes open, not to this ticket.

**Amendment 2026-08-27, later the same day: the count is 10, not 8 — and the chain has now been rehearsed on a fresh database.**

**Upstream moved while CAT-4 was being done**, `0720f5380` → `69096c9a8`, taking the gap from 625 to **702 behind**. Two more migrations arrived with it:

    0033_private_managed_agent_fts.sql
    0034_replica_heartbeat_vacuum_truncate.sql

So it is **`0025`–`0034`, ten new migrations**, not the eight above. Nothing else in the audit changes — both additions are additive, and the existing 24 are still byte-identical, so the checksum refusal is still ruled out. Treat the count in my earlier comment as pinned to `0720f5380` and re-derive it at merge time; it moved twice in one day.

**Rehearsed against a throwaway Postgres 17.10, all 34 in order: every one applies cleanly.** 60 tables. That is not CAT-6 — a fresh database is not production-shaped, and none of the row-count or lock-contention questions are answered by it — but it does retire "do they apply at all".

**0032s roster trigger landed on 9 relations** — the `events` parent plus all 8 partitions. That is the prediction in my earlier comment confirmed by measurement rather than inferred from the floor guard: `verify_channel_roster_fence_catalog`, the one genuinely new fail-closed gate, will pass. A fresh database shows the same 8-partition topology production has.

**A method warning worth more than the result.** My first pass applied each file with `psql` in autocommit and reported **four failures** — `0007`, `0008`, `0029` with *"LOCK TABLE / SET LOCAL can only be used in transaction blocks"*, and `0011` cascading because its table was never created. **All four were my harness, not the migrations.** sqlx wraps every migration in its own transaction; `psql` without `-1` does not. Reported as-is it would have read as "four upstream migrations are broken" and could have stalled this track on nothing. If anyone rehearses these, use `psql -1` per file, or drive them through `run_migrations` — and note that going through `psql` skips the three fail-closed gates entirely, so it tests the SQL and not the startup path.

root.body:
Migration built. peek#76, blocked on estiva-foundation#7 (protocol 0.1.2, adds KIND.APP_DATA).

CHOSEN: layer 2, kind:30078 per SPEC 12 — NOT the NIP-51 set this ticket preferred and I recommended. Recording why, since the done-when asks for the choice and the reasoning.

Three findings reversed it, and the first would have failed at the last step:

1. Peek cannot sign a NIP-51 set. Its ceiling is [9,7,5,9007,27235,1851,9101,9002,9008,1111,30078,41010,41011,41012,22242]. 30078 is granted by CRO-2; 30000 and 30003 are not. Adding them is a seed line, a production re-seed and a deploy — and the estiva-id seed comments record THREE features that shipped, worked everywhere they were checked, and failed at /sign because a ceiling arrived after the code.
2. It needs two kinds, not one. NIP-51 bookmark sets carry e/a/t/r. Starred PEOPLE are a follow set, 30000, with p tags.
3. Neither half has a portable identifier. personKey is seedKey ?? _id, users.nostrPubkey is v.optional, topics.channelUuid is v.optional. A standard kind full of Convex ids is a standard kind nobody else can read.

Applying 12.1 two-question test honestly gives layer 2 anyway: nothing else has asked to see Peek stars, and the person should own them. The portability problem DISSOLVES at layer 2 — only Peek reads the blob, so app-local ids are legitimate rather than a compromise. The portable identity travels where it exists (channel uuid, pubkey) so a later promotion to NIP-51 is a re-publish, not a second migration.

Convex is not removed and should not be. The SET is the person and lives on the relay. The RENDERING — titles, resolved state, names, avatars — is derived from workspace data. That is 12.1 layer 3 used legitimately for an index.

A FIFTH SIZE LIMIT, and it binds tighter than the one 12.5 calls operative. For an app holding no keys — every Estiva app — /nip44/encrypt refuses a plaintext over 65535 bytes, and ciphertext exceeds plaintext, so the relay 256 KiB ingest cap is never what you hit first. Worth adding to the 12.5 table.

Concurrency declared as 12.3 requires: ACCEPT THE LOSS. Last write wins at one-second resolution. Cost is one star, recoverable by clicking again — unlike a read marker whose loss is invisible, which is why NIP-RS pays for slots and this does not.

Not automatic, deliberately: restoreFromRelay exists and is never called on load. A stale blob would resurrect stars somebody cleared, and a blob goes stale exactly when a publish failed. missingLocally is exposed for an affordance somebody asks for.

Verified: tsc -b, 498 tests (was 481), npm run build, and 30078/65535/appdata/estiva-peek in the built bundle.

STILL UNPROVEN and it needs a human: the agent credential cannot sign 30078 (ceiling [27235,1851,9,30851,30850,9007,1111]), so the blob must come from a Peek session. Star one thing after the deploy. The check is then unusually clean — I can confirm the event at the right coordinate with the right tags, and I CANNOT decrypt it despite holding a valid workspace credential, because /nip44/decrypt is self-only. That is 12.4 being true rather than aspirational, demonstrated by failing to read it.

root.body:
Document written: SPEC 12 plus the reasoning in RATIONALE. estiva-docs#19. The three-layer model, the two-question test, the address/tag/content shape, the limits and the encryption requirement are all as filed.

Two corrections, both measured.

SIZE. The ticket says max_content_len is 65536 on the live relay. That number is in NIP-11 `push` object — it bounds the NIP-PL push executor, not stored events. push.limitation.max_plaintext_len (32768) is also the push executor. limitation.max_message_length (524288) is the whole websocket message. The cap that actually applies is MAX_EVENT_CONTENT_BYTES = 256*1024 at crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:1540, and it is not advertised in NIP-11 at all — so an implementer reading the relay own document finds three wrong answers and not the right one. 12.5 is a table saying so. Second reader caught by that same push object: the ROADMAP already records push.keys[].id being mistaken for relay identity.

THE `h` TAG IS WORSE THAN THE TICKET SAYS. The ticket says the relay refuses to channel-scope a 30078 so a stray `h` merely signals confusion. ingest.rs classifies the kind global-only on WRITE, but its own comment records the read path treating explicit `h` tags as authoritative — so a stray `h` does not scope the event AND does make it answer #h queries. That asymmetry is why 12.2 is a MUST NOT rather than a style note.

Also verified, in favour of the ticket: ingest performs no other d_tag validation on 30078; the NIP-RS predicate is narrow (kind + exactly one d + read-state:<32 lowercase hex> + exactly one ["t","read-state"], lib.rs:3675); 30078 requires users:write; and the is_buzz_mesh_status precedent is real, though it needs BOTH the buzz-mesh-member-status: d-tag prefix AND a ["k","buzz-mesh-status"] tag, so it cannot fire by accident. Avoiding that prefix on 30003 is still the right advice.

THE MIGRATION IS BLOCKED, and not for a reason this ticket anticipated. Chosen home is NIP-51 30003 per the done-when. But a star target is not relay-addressable: convex/desk.ts toggleStar takes a topic seedKey/_id or, for a DM, the partner person key — and topics.channelUuid is v.optional (schema.ts:91), so some topics have nothing relay-addressable to point at at all.

That splits the migration:
- DM stars are portable TODAY and are really "starred person". A pubkey is the most portable identifier there is, so this half is a clean 30003 with p tags.
- Topic stars wait on topics having a stable relay identity. RFC 0.3 5.2 verified that they do have one — the relay 39000 per channel — but only for topics that have a channel.

So "stars" was one candidate and is two problems. Not bolting it onto a docs PR because it moves production per-user state and wants its own review. Say the word and I will do the DM half plus a Convex-to-relay read merge, or pick a different first case.

Not done: document unmerged, migration not started.

root.body:
Written: SPEC 11 plus the reasoning in RATIONALE. estiva-docs#19.

One correction to the ticket, measured not reasoned. The container context is the BARE channel uuid, not `h:<folder-uuid>`.

NIP-RS declines to prescribe context ids but grandfathers one — "a bare channel identifier remains the channel context" — and Buzz own clients write exactly that: contexts.set(channelId, …) at desktop/src/features/channels/readState/readStateStorage.ts:34, same in mobile, with msg: and thread: for the finer grains and no h: anywhere.

So a prefix does not namespace an empty space, it creates a SECOND convention for an object the ecosystem already agrees about. The failure is not an error message: one app marks a container read, the other still shows it unread, and both are behaving correctly. Blobs are grow-only, so reconciling later means tolerating both keys forever or migrating published blobs — the permanence this ticket comment warned about.

The folder model was the strongest argument for namespacing and does not survive it. RFC 0.3 7.1 is "one channel per folder, not one per file", so the container context still identifies the same object upstream identifies. What the folder model adds is that the finer grain matters more — thread: already covers that, same spelling — and that "everything in this folder" becomes a distinct frontier, which is why 11.5 reserves folder:<address> as the ticket comment asked.

Adopted verbatim as filed: thread:/msg:, the write discipline, read-time hierarchy, monotonic-with-no-mark-as-unread, and no huddle scheme.

Promoted from tidy to load-bearing: marking a thread read advances only thread:<root>, never the parent. Today a container holds one topic so getting it wrong is invisible. A container holding five topics marks four of them read — so this rule starts mattering exactly when RFC 0.3 lands.

Two things for whoever writes CRO-4/5. The relay does NOT advertise NIP-RS and supported_nips does not include 78, so a client cannot discover the support and must not gate on it. And the horizon has no protocol default — NIP-RS only says blobs are "best-effort recent activity hints bounded by a time horizon", so the 7 days CRO-6 assumes is a client choice, which is what makes CRO-6 a real prerequisite rather than an optimisation.

Not done until #19 merges.

root.body:
**There is now a concrete reason to do this merge, and it is not the commit count.** Found 2026-08-27 while answering "does the catch-up make sense yet". My CAT-1 comment said the gap contains nothing we want; **that was wrong** — it was true of *kinds*, and I generalised it further than the evidence supported.

**`16b7ae7ce fix(relay): stop panicking the ingest worker on reactions to project events (#5294)`** — upstream, not on the fork.

A `kind:7` reaction whose target carries no `h` tag leaves `channel_id` as `None` on the reaction write path, and the trace action is built with `channel_id.expect("reaction path has channel")`. The fork still has both calls, at `ingest.rs:2434` and `:2440`, under a comment asserting the thing that is no longer true:

    // This branch is the reaction path; channel_id is always Some here,
    // so WriteInsertGlobal does not apply.

**CAT-9 is what falsified that.** Dropping `KIND_LL_PROJECT` from `requires_h_channel_scope` created a class of h-less reactable event that upstream did not have when the `expect` was written, and REW-11 shipped it to production. `KIND_REACTION` is **not** in `requires_h_channel_scope`, so nothing obliges a client to attach an `h` to the reaction either.

Note the ordering, which is the bad part: the reaction row is **inserted before** the panic. So the write persists, the caller sees a failed request, and the ingest worker dies on a path that ran to completion.

**Measured against production today:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| global `kind:30850` project records | **11** |
| `kind:7` reactions total | 6 |
| `kind:7` with `channel_id IS NULL` | **0** |

So the path is **reachable and has never been taken**. Eleven live triggers; nobody has reacted to a project record yet. It is latent, not firing — but it is reachable by a conforming client doing an ordinary thing, and the fix is already written upstream.

Two more in the gap worth reading rather than assuming benign, both touching code we do run:

- `e2e007910 fix(security): enforce durable community ban on NIP-43 relay-admin kinds 9030-9033` — Estiva ID writes `9030`/`9031`.
- `22be8bb35 fix(relay): avoid subscription lock inversion` — track A is building per-channel subscriptions on PEE-5/6.

**Sequencing this does not change.** The merge itself is local and safe; `relay-image.yml` triggers on `push: branches: [nfb-demo-kinds]`, so **pushing** is what rebuilds `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb`. There is no `buzz-update.timer` on the box — confirmed, the other four services have one and buzz does not — so a push arms the tag rather than deploying it, and the next manual pull for any unrelated reason ships 625 commits. Do the merge and CAT-5 in a worktree unpushed; hold the push for the CAT-7 window.

Conflict surface is pinned to `upstream/main` at `0720f5380` (see CAT-2). Re-measure with `git merge-tree` before resolving if upstream has moved.

root.body:
**List 4 closed — read from production 2026-08-27, read-only SELECTs, nothing written. Two of my earlier verdicts change.**

**Schema version 24**, read not assumed. 24 migrations applied, none failed. So the eight new ones are `0025`–`0032` exactly as the checkout predicted.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `channels` | **61** |
| `workflow_runs` | **0** |
| `events` | **1,275** |
| `events` partitions | **8** |
| `kind:30078` rows | **0** |
| `kind:39002` rows | **64** |

**Downgrade: 0032 is no longer "the one to plan around".** At 1,275 events across 8 partitions the trigger creation is milliseconds of work. The missing `lock_timeout` is still a real defect but it is a **tail risk, not an expected cost**: the danger is an unbounded *wait* if another transaction happens to hold a conflicting lock on `events`, and because migrations run at startup that would present as a relay which never becomes ready. Add `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 5s` locally and it is gone. I overstated this before I had the row counts.

**The partition-cloning assumption is now proven, not inferred.** Every parent trigger on `events` sits on exactly **9 relations** — the parent plus all 8 partitions:

    events_created_at_floor                     9
    events_enqueue_push_match                   9
    events_refresh_channel_ttl                  9
    trg_events_guard_nip_rs_hard_delete         9
    trg_events_nip_rs_watermark                 9
    trg_events_purge_soft_deleted_nip_rs        9

So 0032s trigger will reach all 9 the same way, and `verify_channel_roster_fence_catalog` — the one genuinely new fail-closed gate — will pass. `trg_events_guard_channel_roster_snapshot` is correctly absent today, which is the negative control for that reading.

**The NIP-RS refuser is doubly inert.** Version 24 is above the gates `>= 7` early return, **and** there are zero `kind:30078` rows for it to find. Note for CRO-2: even once read-state rows exist, this gate still cannot fire at version 24.

**Upgrade: the part of 0032 that actually matters is the runtime rejection, not the lock.** Production already holds **64 `kind:39002` rosters across 61 channels**, so the relay is actively emitting them. The trigger is `BEFORE INSERT`, so it does not validate the 64 existing rows — but every future roster snapshot must match `channel_members` exactly or raise `23514`. That is live traffic meeting a new constraint, and `buzz-admin`s "emit 39000/39002 for channels missing them" command is the most likely thing to trip it. **CAT-6 should exercise that command specifically**, not just run the migrations.

**Revised plain answer:** deploying upstream today would not break, block or silently change production data. 0025–0031 are all effectively instant at this scale. The residual risks are one missing `lock_timeout` and one new runtime constraint on a kind we already write — both cheap to handle, neither a reason to delay.

root.body:
One measured warning from SHA-3, because this package will hit it harder than protocol did.

tsconfig.base.json sets types: [] and lib: ["es2022"], and that is not style — it is what makes one published .d.ts compile in Peek (types: ["vite/client"]) and in Ship (types: ["node"]). es2022 contains none of: URL, btoa, fetch, WebSocket, TextDecoder, setTimeout. A service worker and an install prompt cannot avoid far more than that.

What worked in protocol: declare each global INSIDE the module that uses it and read it INSIDE a function body. The first keeps it out of every consumer global scope; the second means importing the package touches no global, which matters because an eager read at module scope throws on import in a runtime that lacks it. Transport-shaped things (fetch, WebSocket) are also parameters with the global as the default.

That will not stretch to a service worker, whose whole body is ServiceWorkerGlobalScope. Expect to need a separate entry point with its own tsconfig and lib: ["webworker"], emitted separately and never imported by the app-side entry — and to say so in the ADR, because it is the first package that genuinely cannot obey section 4a as written.

Also: the ticket says SHA-2 exists to force the release process into existence. That process now exists and has shipped three packages, so this is just a feature. There is no reason to do it before somebody wants a PWA.

1. The Signer seam is already in @estiva-app/protocol — the interface, its reasoning (why pubkey is sync and sign is not, and why a signer cannot sign as somebody else), and secretKeySigner. estivaIdSigner is what stayed behind, deliberately: it knows about Estiva ID, which is this ticket. It is the one thing left duplicated between ship and estiva-agent lib/nostr/, byte-identical, and it is yours to remove.

2. authorizationHeader(signer, args) is exported, so an identity signer plugs into the relay clients with nothing else to write. The rule it encodes — the auth event is signed by the same signer as the content, or the app holds a perfectly signed event it cannot publish (PEEK-44) — has one definition now.

3. lib.es2022 has none of the globals this code needs: not URL, btoa, fetch, WebSocket, TextDecoder, or the timers. Declaring each inside the module that uses it, and reading it inside a function body, is what keeps the published .d.ts clean AND lets a Convex backend import the package without touching a global its runtime lacks. 4. Worth knowing before identity ships any component: @estiva-app/ui already publishes .d.ts files naming HTMLButtonElement and Element. root.body:
**Audit done 2026-08-27, read-only. Three of the four lists are complete; list 4 needs production and I could not reach the box from this session — see the end. Not marking this done.**

**Plain answer: deploying upstream today would not break or silently change production data. The one thing it could do is BLOCK, and the blocker is migration 0032, on a lock rather than on data.**

**1. The list.** Fork ships 24 migrations (`0001`–`0024`), upstream 32. **Eight new: `0025`–`0032`.** Purely additive — 841 insertions, **zero deletions, and all 24 existing files byte-identical**. That last point matters more than the eight: sqlx keys `_sqlx_migrations` on a checksum, so a *modified* old migration would refuse the whole run with `VersionMismatch` before applying anything. **That failure mode is ruled out.** The fork adds no migrations of its own, so there is no numbering collision and nothing of ours to preserve — the direction is one-way.

| | what | risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0025 | `relay_invites` table | new table, none |
| 0026 | `replica_heartbeat`, single row | none |
| 0027 | index on `channels`, no `CONCURRENTLY` | ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on `channels`; duration ∝ channel count |
| 0028 | `reactions.emoji` → `VARCHAR(66)` | varchar *widening* is catalog-only, no rewrite |
| 0029 | community deletion: +3 cols on `communities`, many new tables/triggers | `NOT NULL DEFAULT` with a constant → no rewrite on PG11+; touches nothing on `events` |
| 0030 | drop/add constraints on `community_deletion_requests` | table created empty in 0029, so CHECK validation passes trivially |
| 0031 | `+workflow_runs.error_code` (nullable) **+ a backfill UPDATE** | duration ∝ `workflow_runs` rows |
| 0032 | **`BEFORE INSERT ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger on the partitioned `events` table** | **the real one — see below** |

**2. The refusers.** The important finding: **the refusal risk is not mainly in the migrations.** `run_migrations` wraps `MIGRATOR.run` in an exclusive advisory lock and three fail-closed gates, and migrations run **automatically at relay startup** — so a refusal is a relay that never becomes ready, not a crash-loop.

- `reject_legacy_nip_rs_cardinality_ambiguity` — the one this ticket quotes. **Inert for us.** It early-returns when `max(version) >= 7`; we are at 24. It cannot fire regardless of what `kind:30078` rows exist, so CRO-2 landing does *not* give this ticket's answer a shelf life. That premise in the description is wrong.
- `verify_floor_guard_catalog` — requires migration 0021's trigger on `events` **and every partition**. **Already on the fork and already passing in production**, since the running relay calls it at startup (`buzz-db/src/lib.rs:453`). So production's partition topology already satisfies a parent-created trigger cloned across all partitions — a useful positive.
- `verify_channel_roster_fence_catalog` — **new with the merge.** Same shape, for 0032's trigger, across `public.events` and every partition, requiring it enabled and exact-shaped. Materially de-risked by the line above, because the same topology assumption is already proven for the floor guard.

**3. The irreversibles: none.** Nothing drops or rewrites a column. 0028 widens a varchar (no rewrite); 0030 drops *constraints* on a table that 0029 created empty. A backup before CAT-6 is still worth taking, but no migration here forces it.

**Why 0032 is the one to plan around.** It installs a row-level `BEFORE INSERT` trigger on `events` — the monthly range-partitioned table holding everything — and it is the **only one of the four DDL migrations with no `lock_timeout`** (0029, 0030 and 0031 each `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 5s`). So it waits indefinitely for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on `events` and, while waiting, queues every insert behind it. On a live relay that is the classic Postgres migration stall. Mitigation is operational, not a code change: quiesce writes, or add a local `lock_timeout` and retry.

It also adds a **new runtime rejection path**: a `kind:39002` roster whose `p` tags do not exactly match `channel_members` now raises `23514`. Note our `buzz-admin` has a command that emits `39000`/`39002` "for channels missing them" (`buzz-admin/src/main.rs:568`) — post-merge those snapshots must match canonical membership exactly or the insert is refused.

**4. Row counts that matter — OUTSTANDING.** SSH to the box is blocked from this session, so I did not read production and am not guessing. Three reads decide the remaining risk, all read-only:

```
select max(version) from _sqlx_migrations where success;
select count(*) from channels;                 -- 0027 index build
select count(*) from workflow_runs;            -- 0031 backfill UPDATE
select count(*) from pg_inherits where inhparent = public.events::regclass;  -- 0032 trigger fan-out
```

Expectation, to be falsified rather than assumed: version 24, channels in the low hundreds, `workflow_runs` **empty** (Estiva ships no workflows), and one partition per month of operation. If that holds, 0025–0031 are all sub-second and the entire decision reduces to scheduling 0032's lock.

**Separate finding, not a migration risk — a live defect on `nfb-demo-kinds` today.** `BUZZ_MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS` (#6) widens the *ingest* window, but migration 0021 enforces a **commit-time** floor of `CREATED_AT_FLOOR_SECS = 960`, armed by the writer pool on every connection. Both are already on the branch at the merge-base, so the merge does not cause this. For any event carrying an `h` tag (→ `channel_id NOT NULL`), widening past 960s means **accepted at ingest, then the transaction aborts at COMMIT**. Usable range is effectively `900 < x <= 960`; Peek's four-month Convex import — the stated reason the knob exists — cannot work through the relay. 0021's own comment says there is "deliberately NO in-band bypass" and that such backfills must run outside the writer pool with the replica breaker closed. Code read across four files, **not live-verified.** Filing separately if you agree.

root.body:
**Decision: merge, not rebase.** Survey done 2026-08-27, read-only, nothing pushed.

**Measured today:** `origin/nfb-demo-kinds` is **12 ahead / 625 behind** `upstream/main` (this ticket says 4 ahead — stale). Gap is 2801 files, +497k/-65k, but the churn is overwhelmingly mobile/desktop/agent/acp/voice. Relay surfaces: `ingest.rs` 13 commits, `bridge.rs` 10, `req.rs` 6, `migrations` 9.

**Why merge:**
1. `nfb-demo-kinds` is the build source for `ghcr.io/estiva-app/buzz:nfb`. A rebase needs a force-push, and 8 `origin/*` feature branches plus a shared working checkout are based on it.
2. Rebase replays 12 commits over 625 and re-resolves the same import-list conflict up to 12 times. **CI on this fork is `disabled_manually`**, so a mis-resolution at an intermediate commit is caught by nothing.
3. A merge commit preserves the merge-base, so the *next* catch-up is measurable. Track F is deliberately two-speed; there will be a next time. Rebase destroys that record.

**Never branch from `origin/main`:** it is **byte-identical to the merge-base** (`b78a684cf`, zero diff). Its only two commits are `63e566ff3` (members API, #2) and `5a45bd734` reverting it (#4) — net zero. That Revert deletes **654 lines across 6 files**: `relay-image.yml` (78), `kind.rs` (75), `members.rs` (449), `ingest.rs` (47), `router.rs` (6), `api/mod.rs` (1). `nfb-demo-kinds` has those same features via *different* commits (#1, #3), so the Revert would apply against them rather than conflict.

**This ticket's "what is in the gap" table is 10/13 wrong.** Already on the fork at the merge-base: NIP-34 git `1618`/`1619`/`1621`/`1630`–`1633`, `40902` presence snapshot, `46030`/`46031` approvals. Only **three** kinds genuinely arrive: `30621` NIP-MP project, `30179` private managed agent, `30178` team catalog. 625 commits, 3 new kinds — the gap is not protocol surface, it is hardening (multi-community, replica fencing, community deletion, roster fencing, instrumentation).

**Structural change that affects Peek and Ship (#3635):** upstream deleted the fork's `MAX_HISTORICAL_LIMIT = 2_000` and clamps REQ to the advertised NIP-11 value, now `DEFAULT_MAX_PAGE_LIMIT = 1_000`. So the effective historical ceiling **halves, 2000 → 1000**, and advertised `max_limit` goes **10_000 → 1_000**. The roadmap lists NIP-11 capabilities as verified against production; that verified fact changes. A truncated page reads as missing data, not an error — relevant to PEE-6/7/8 and Ship's `loadAll`.

New read gates in the gap are kind-specific (`30175` author-only-unless-shared, `30178` behind a shared tag) and touch no Estiva kind. `requires_h_channel_scope` is **untouched upstream**.

**Rough cost, M2–M5:** CAT-4 merge ~half a day (4 files, 5 hunks, all additive — see CAT-2) plus a local clippy run in the pinned toolchain since CI gives nothing. CAT-5 probe ~1–2h. CAT-6 rehearsal is the real cost, ~1 day, and it is where the risk lives (CAT-3: migration 0032). CAT-7/8 ~half a day. **Call it 2.5–3 days, gated on CAT-3's outstanding production reads, not on merge difficulty.**

Done. The done-when asks which registry and what install auth looks like on a new machine, so: public npm, scope @estiva-app, and the install auth is nothing. npm install, no token, no .npmrc, no registry config — on a laptop, in three CI workflows, and in whatever builds the scaffold. That was the point of choosing public.

The loop, on the public registry: hello 0.0.1 published by hand, installed into fresh clones of Peek, Ship and the agent, each toolchain's own CI commands green. Then 0.0.2 published by CI through OIDC with no credential in GitHub, all three upgraded, 0.0.2 present in Peek's and Ship's built bundles, and an export existing only in 0.0.2 compiling in the agent. @estiva-app/ui@0.1.0 shipped under the same rules the same day and both apps consume it, so the throwaway was overtaken by the real thing.

Three findings, each cost a failed release. Provenance is skipped, not refused — publishing from a private repo records no attestations and does not fail, which was the last unmeasured claim in the ADR. registry-url in actions/setup-node breaks OIDC and reports it as 404 'package not found' about a package that plainly exists, because setup-node writes a placeholder token npm then authenticates with. And a new package NAME is invisible on the read path for minutes after a successful publish — 204s for hello, while npm access already listed it; a new version of an existing package took 1s.

ADR: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/14 and https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/15, both merged. §7 is now the recipe for the next package rather than a to-do list.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
Public npm is live. @estiva-app/hello@0.0.1 published, then installed into clean clones of Peek, Ship and the agent and checked with each toolchain's own CI commands. The pipeline then carried a real package the same day: @estiva-app/ui@0.1.0, consumed by both apps and merged.

Two things this ticket assumed that turned out false, both recorded in ADR 0002:
- A granular token in CI does not work. The tagged release built and then got EOTP — the account requires 2FA for writes and the token may not bypass it. npm removes direct publish from 2FA-bypass tokens entirely in January 2027, so the answer is trusted publishing (OIDC) and no npm credential in GitHub at all.
- A new package's first publish cannot use OIDC, because a trusted publisher is configured on a package that already exists. Creating a package is a once-ever manual act with an interactive 2FA challenge; every release after it is CI.

Also: a first publish is invisible on the read path for minutes while npm access already lists it — hello took 204s to become installable. A 404 straight after publishing is not a failed publish.

Vercel is obsolete (confirmed), so the done-when's Vercel clause is Peek's GitHub Actions gate, which passes.

Still open: the 0.0.1 → 0.0.2 upgrade leg on the public registry, and trusted publishing configured for both packages. Layout decision landed differently than first written — protocol/platform/identity in estiva-foundation, ui in its own repo, reasoning in the ADR.

**The writes are ported** — on branch `rew-ship-rewrite` (not pushed), 4 commits. `src/`, `lib/nostr/`, `conformance/` untouched; conformance passes unchanged; `diff -r` against estiva-agent clean.

**What works (driven through the new app on the local relay, each result read back through the old app, never through the new UI's own report):**
- New issue (ref derived as today: `nextRef(refPrefix(title), visible refs)`; the address is the identity), status, assignee, project move, title and description edits, a thread about an issue (with the `nostr:naddr` reference Peek needs) and a reply, a thread on a project, archive / unarchive. Delete is offered to the author only and asks first.
- Each write is one change to one object. There is no bulk action, multi-select or "apply to all" anywhere.
- `accepted` is authoritative: only the relay's `ok` is read; a 200 rejection is a failure with its reason, a thrown request is a failure. Tested.
- The clock is checked before signing: the relay's `date` header (CORS exposes it), once per five minutes; more than ten minutes off refuses every write with a sentence; an unreachable check does not block. Tested.
- Nothing says "saved": after an `ok` the workspace is re-read and the page shows what the relay holds; a refusal shows the reason in the banner and changes nothing on screen.
- Folders: an issue's events go to the issue's own Folder, a project's record changes to the record's Folder, threads and new issues to the content Folder. Tested.
- Forms are dialogs from the shared parts: New project (with the optional Folder link, checked before publishing), New issue (asks for the project from the Issues page; says "create a project first" when there is none), Pair with another Folder, and a confirmation for Delete with today's warning.

- **Creating a project** is refused by the local relay — "channel-scoped events must include an h tag". The record is REW-11's global shape and needs CAT-9; the local `buzz:nfb` image predates it, and the old app is refused identically. Production has CAT-9; the local image needs updating to test it here.

replies.body:
@Katerina Kelepouri Miky asked me to write this up for you. Two things — the Desktop one is already fixed, and the VS Code one now exists.

## First: you do *not* need to delete your bot

The error you got was my bug, not anything you did — new bots were being created without permission to reach the relay, so they could sign in and then read nothing.

I repaired your existing bot directly, so **the credential you already typed into Claude Desktop is still the right one**. No deleting, no re-entering. Just ask it something again and it should answer.

(Miky's message above about creating a new one was written before the repair — it would work, but it's extra work you don't need.)

## Now: using it in VS Code

You'll need VS Code with the **Claude Code** extension installed.

### 1. Make a second bot

Not because the first one is broken — because **the secret is only shown once**, and yours is already in Desktop. There's no way to look it up again, and asking for a new secret would stop Desktop working. Two bots is the normal way to do this: you can have five, roughly one per app or machine.

- Go to **id.estiva.app** → your account → **Your bots**
- Under *What is it for?* type something like `VS Code`
- Click **Make a bot**
- **Copy the secret straight away** — it disappears when you close that panel. Copy the client id too (there's a button).

### 2. Install the plugin

In Claude Code — either the panel in VS Code or the terminal — type these two, one after the other:

`/plugin marketplace add estiva-app/estiva-agent`

`/plugin install estiva@estiva`

If it tells you to reload, run `/reload-plugins`.

### 3. Give it your credential

Unlike the Desktop extension there's no settings dialog, so it reads a small file in your home folder. **The easiest way is to let Claude write it for you** — paste this into Claude Code, with your two values swapped in:

> Create a file at ~/.estiva-agent.env containing ESTIVA_ID_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id and ESTIVA_ID_CLIENT_SECRET=your-secret, and make it readable only by me.

Then reload with `/reload-plugins`, or just restart VS Code.

### 4. Check it

Ask it:

> Is the Estiva connection working?

That runs a four-step check and tells you which step failed, if any. Then try something real — *what Ship issues are open?*

You get the same twelve things Desktop has: read and comment on Ship issues, set status, assign, create issues and projects, and read and reply in Peek topics.

## If it misbehaves

- **The plugin installed but there are no Estiva tools** — type `/plugin`, open the **Errors** tab, and send me what it says.
- **An error mentioning `node`** — the plugin is a small Node program and yours may not have it. Tell me and I'll sort it.
- **`invalid_client`** — usually the Desktop bot's secret used by mistake, or a character lost in copying. The new bot's secret is the one you want.
- **Anything else** — paste the exact message here. That's genuinely more useful than a description.

One honest caveat: I couldn't run those two install commands myself to check them — there's no Claude Code where I run. Everything after them is tested, but if step 2 does something unexpected, you're the first person to see it, and I'd like to know exactly what.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Done.** Confirmed on production: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/72

A `kind:9` signed by the agent and POSTed straight to the relay into **Estiva Suits Updates** — a topic on the viewer's Desk — while they were looking at **Feedback on Peek**. It went unread without being opened and without a reload. The topic actually on screen stayed quiet, which is the per-channel scoping holding.

That is the done-when: a change originating outside Peek's Convex reaching a topic nobody is looking at, through a subscription held by the *working set* rather than by the open topic.

## The gap was larger than the ticket's framing

"Takes time to appear" was generous. Only the open topic had a relay read path — **nothing else had one at all** — so a Ship-side change to any other topic had no route in whatsoever. Not slow: absent.

## The set, and the bound

`watchableChannels` returns the inbox, then Desk open work, then stars, in that order — which is also the order to drop from when the bound bites. A topic in two lists is one subscription.

**The bound is 32, not 1024.** `max_subscriptions` is a ceiling rather than a licence: each subscription is a relay-side index entry and a fan-out check on every event in the community. The useful set is what a person is looking at, and a workspace can grow topics indefinitely while a Desk cannot grow attention.

A topic that is both open and on the Desk costs **one** REQ — PEE-6's refcount collapses the two holders. That is exactly why the manager was built refcounted rather than keyed on the current screen, and this is the first ticket that actually exercises it.

## DMs cannot be done, and the trap was right to ask

The ticket says to verify rather than assume that the channel subscription covers DMs. It does not: **`dmConversations` carries no `channelUuid` at all.** DMs live entirely in Convex with no relay representation until track C gives them one (DMS-3).

So two of the three surfaces in the title are delivered and the third is not buildable yet. There is a test asserting a DM in the inbox contributes nothing, so that stays true rather than quietly changing the day `dmConversations` grows a field.

## Two details that would have bitten

**The effect keys on a stringified channel list, not the array.** Convex hands back a new array identity on every update, so keying on the array would tear down and rebuild every subscription on each one — closing and reopening REQs the relay was perfectly happy with.

**Mounted in `AppShell`, not on a page.** The working set belongs to the person; navigating from Desk into a topic must not tear it down.

Subscribing marks nothing read — read state moves in `useMarkRead`, driven by *opening* a topic. Projecting into a topic nobody is watching raises its unread count, which is the point.

549 tests, 9 new.

## What is left in this track

**PEE-1, PEE-2 and PEE-3.** Their role has changed: filed as the cheap mitigation while the socket was still ahead, they are now the *fallback*. PEE-8 returns `relayState` from `useTopicView` precisely so PEE-1's interval can idle against it rather than polling underneath a live socket.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Done.** Confirmed working on production after four rounds of feedback, every one of which found something real.

PRs: #66 (the feature), then #67, #68, #69, #70.

## The finding, and it is not in the ticket

Every piece of feedback was **the same mistake in a different place**: the indicator crying wolf during entirely normal operation.

| reported | cause |
| --- | --- |
| amber on the Desk on every load | no socket had been asked for yet — `polling` means the *fallback is carrying the load*, and nothing was being carried |
| blue flashing on every topic click | every topic open starts a backfill; on a healthy connection it finishes in well under a second |
| blue stuck for minutes offline, then nothing | see below — a real defect |
| amber for a moment during the first connect | the socket passes through `connecting` on its way to `live`, doing exactly what it should |

An indicator built from *"is everything perfect right now?"* fires at every transition, and a badge that lights during normal use is one people stop seeing — which defeats this ticket's whole purpose. **Each state now has to earn its way onto the screen by persisting**: 5s for catching up, 5s for a first connect, 20s for a dead credential, 30s before "catching up" expires into "stuck".

That principle is worth more to PEE-10 and PEE-11 than any of the individual numbers.

## One report was not cosmetic

*"Offline shows the blue dot for a minute, then no dot at all."*

`liveRelay` learns about disconnection **only from `onclose`** — and a WebSocket whose peer has become unreachable stays `OPEN` until TCP gives up, minutes later, while devtools' offline mode frequently never closes it. So the socket reported `live`, the derivation believed it, and nothing showed through a total outage.

**The wrong dot was the smaller half.** Reconnection is driven by `onclose`, so a socket that never closes never reconnects: live delivery would have stayed silently dead after any network blip, with the app insisting it was live. That is the exact failure shape this track has chased since PEE-5, and it would have shipped — it surfaced only because somebody sat in offline mode long enough to watch the dot disappear.

Fixed by making the browser's `online`/`offline` events the authority, plus `LiveRelay.reconnect()` so coming back online retries at once instead of waiting out a backoff grown to half a minute. `navigator.onLine` is trusted one way only — `false` is reliable, `true` merely means an interface is up — so the stalled-backfill bound still covers "online and unreachable".

## Against the ticket

Four states, visibly distinct, surfaced once in the nav rail, mapped onto `ShellReason` rather than a second vocabulary. `token_rejected` never reads as "signed out" — asserted as the *claim* rather than the word, because the shell's own copy contains "expired" inside "rather than an expired session".

`polling` is worded and coloured as a working state and carries the age of the last successful sync — and only a **real** sync moves that timestamp. `syncTopicFromRelay` returned `void`, so soft failures were recorded as successes and could have made "synced a few seconds ago" a lie at the moment it mattered most.

527 tests. `npm run build` caught type errors the suite passed on four consecutive tickets in this track.

## Assignment

Assigned to **Katerina**; picked up at Miky's direction rather than silently, after checking for work in flight (no open PRs, her branches five days old). Worth a word to her — the feature grew a fair way past what the ticket describes.

**Confirmed on production, with an event that could only have arrived through this routing.**

A `kind:9` signed by the agent and POSTed straight to the relay (`accepted: true`, `954c83b3…`) appeared in an open Peek topic within a second, no reload. Peek's Convex was not touched on the way in, so the path was necessarily socket → `liveProjection` → `importChannel` → reactivity. This ticket's done-when — *a message landing in Convex and appearing in an open topic with no HTTP relay read* — is met.

Worth adding for anyone who tests this again: an earlier attempt with two browser windows of the same account proved nothing, because both share one Convex deployment and a reply propagates by reactivity alone. It looked exactly like success. The event has to originate outside Peek's database — Ship, the agent, or a second identity.

```
signing as b38fd2687b17…
message event id: 954c83b303251679  kind 9
POST /events → HTTP 200
relay said: {"accepted":true,"event_id":"954c83b3…"}
```

It appeared in an open Peek topic **within a second, with no reload**. Nothing touched Peek's Convex on the way: socket → `liveProjection` → `importChannel` → Convex reactivity is the only route it had to the screen. PEE-5 through PEE-8 are proven end to end on production.

## The first test looked like success and was evidence for nothing

Two browser windows signed in as the same person, one posting and the other receiving. It worked. It proved nothing.

**Both windows share one Convex deployment.** A reply sent in one reaches the other by Convex reactivity alone — exactly as it did before any of M3 existed. None of the socket path is involved in that. The relay is only in the loop when an event originates *outside* Peek's own database.

The correction matters beyond this ticket, because it is a convincing mistake: the observable behaviour is identical, fast, and looks like the feature working. Anyone verifying this track has to publish from Ship, the agent, or a second identity. It is now written into the roadmap's §"Verified against live systems" rather than left as something to rediscover.

## Deployment verified against the bytes, not the image id

The container started 37 seconds after the publish job finished, which is close enough to be worth checking rather than inferring. The served bundle was fetched and grepped:

```
assets/index-C9eB-FYh.js
  "live topic subscription unavailable"  ✓
  "not a channel uuid"                   ✓
  "22242"                                ✓
```

An image id matching a local tag would not have said anything about what is being served.

## Found while testing, filed separately

**PEE-13** in `Peek: Feedback & Bugs` — a deleted message can stay visible in another tab until reload. Not this ticket's doing and not the relay path: Peek deletes the Convex rows *before* publishing the `kind:5`, and the reload clearing it proves the row was already gone, so it is stale rendered state in the merge layer. Very likely older than M3 and only visible because nobody normally watches two windows at once — flagged as unproven rather than assumed.

## Still not observed

The offline/online leg — that the app keeps working with the socket down and resumes without a reload. Unit-covered, and the reconnect path itself was exercised against production in PEE-5, but nobody has watched that cycle in the app. PEE-9 renders exactly that transition and should confirm it in passing.

root.body:
**Done.** PEE-8 shipped the wiring (`183d036`) and the chain was confirmed by hand in two browsers on peek.estiva.app: a message posted in one appears in the other within a second or two, live, with a clean console.

This ticket's done-when — *a message from Ship landing in Convex and appearing in an open topic with no HTTP relay read* — was never observable while nothing imported this module. It is now, and it works.

## The finding, restated because it is the one worth keeping

The ticket's routing table said `kind:9 → importChannel`. **Messages are kinds 9 and 1111.** Ship's comments moved to NIP-22 with REW-10, and a Ship comment is posted into the project's Folder — which *is* a Peek topic's channel. Routing only `kind:9` would have made every Ship comment vanish from live delivery: no error, no empty state, just a conversation that stops updating.

It was caught only because PEE-6's live two-channel check happened to show the first real events arriving as **kind:1111**, not `kind:9`. Reading the ticket alone would have shipped it broken, and the HTTP path — which already asks for both and explains why at length — would have kept working, so the two paths would have quietly disagreed about what a topic contains.

`KIND.COMMENT` now exists so both paths cite one constant rather than a literal.

## Still true and worth carrying into M4

**No profiles reach `importChannel` on the live path.** `kind:0` is not channel-scoped, so a `#h` subscription never delivers one and there is nothing to pass. A first-time author renders under a placeholder until `pubkeysMissingProfile`/`recordProfiles` fills it in.

The HTTP path fetched `kind:0` per author in the same run, so this is more visible now than it was: someone speaking in a topic for the first time can appear as `nostr:<8 chars>` until that pair runs. That is PEEK-72's gap, not a regression, but live delivery is what makes it noticeable.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Merged: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/65 → `183d036`. Live on peek.estiva.app and confirmed working in two browsers.**

M3's first desired outcome is met: a topic open in one window updates from another within a second or two, over the socket, with no interval involved.

## Verified against the bytes production is serving, not the image id

The container started 37 seconds after the publish job finished, which is close enough to be worth checking properly rather than inferring. The served bundle was fetched and grepped:

```
assets/index-C9eB-FYh.js
  "live topic subscription unavailable"  ✓   the effect's guard
  "not a channel uuid"                   ✓   PEE-6's channel-key guard
  "auth-required"                        ✓
  "22242"                                ✓
```

An image id matching a local tag would not have proved this; the strings do.

## What the ticket asked for that does not exist

**There is no M1 interval to idle.** PEE-1/2/3 are unstarted, so today's behaviour is one sync per topic open and there is no focus/visibility/interval refetch to keep active or idle. The fallback is therefore the unconditional mount backfill plus a **backfill on every reconnect**, which is strictly better than what was there.

That reconnect backfill is not in this ticket and is the half the socket cannot cover: while the connection is down, events are missed, and the restored subscription then delivers only what is new. Without it the gap would be invisible and permanent — a topic quietly missing whatever was said during an outage.

`relayState` is returned from `useTopicView` rather than rendered. **PEE-9 should consume that rather than deriving its own**, and PEE-1 should idle its interval against it. Either opening a second socket would double the AUTH round trips for nothing.

## Two design points worth keeping

**One connection per tab, as a module singleton.** A client created inside a component is one per mount, and StrictMode mounts everything twice in development. A module instance is built once and *watched* twice — which is exactly what PEE-6's refcounting handles, so the double mount needed no special case anywhere.

**The late-backfill trap is avoided structurally, not with a cancellation flag.** Every import is keyed by `topicKey` and nothing in this path touches component state, so a run landing after `topicId` changed writes the previous topic's history to the previous topic. Said in the code so nobody adds ceremony for it later.

## What was observed, and what was not

Confirmed by hand: live delivery between two browsers, and a clean console — no reconnect chatter, no listener errors.

**Not separately reported: the offline/online leg** — that the app keeps working with the socket down and resumes live delivery without a reload. It is unit-covered (reconnect restores every channel with a live refcount) and the reconnect path itself was exercised against production in PEE-5, but nobody has watched this specific cycle in the app. Worth a moment during PEE-9, which will be rendering exactly that transition.

## The gate that keeps earning its keep

`npm run test:run` is the only PR gate here; `tsc -b` runs solely on a push to main. It failed twice on this ticket while 478 tests passed — a missing `ViewSlots` field and an early-return path that did not carry it. Third ticket in a row. **Run `npm run build` before merging anything in this repo.**
