root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Merged: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/64 → `e125d3a`.** Held at `in_progress`: the done-when needs the app to drive this, and nothing imports it yet. PEE-8 closes it.

Almost no new logic, as the ticket predicted — batch, partition by kind, call three actions in order. 468 tests, 19 new.

## The ticket's kind list is incomplete, and it would have shipped broken

`kind:9 → importChannel` alone makes **every Ship comment vanish from live delivery.** Comments moved to NIP-22 `kind:1111` with REW-10, and a Ship comment is posted into the project's Folder — which *is* a Peek topic's channel. No error, no empty state, just a conversation that stops updating.

Not hypothetical: **the first live events seen on this socket during PEE-6's two-channel check were `kind:1111`, not `kind:9`.** The HTTP path in `src/nostr/sync.ts` already asks for both and explains why at length; the live path now matches it, and `KIND.COMMENT` exists so the two cite one constant rather than a literal.

## Two keys, and this ticket names only one

The import actions are keyed by **`topicKey`** — the client-facing topic id — while a subscription is keyed by **channel uuid**. Neither is derivable from the other without a query, so `watch()` takes both. PEE-8's caller holds both already, and looking one up here would put a Convex query inside an event handler.

Worth flagging because the RFC 0.3 note on PEE-6 asks that a topic id never become a subscription key, and this is the seam where the two meet. They stay separate: subscribe by channel, import by topic.

## Two things the ticket left implicit

**`importChannel` runs on every flush, even one with no messages.** It is the only source of `known` and `deletable`, and a reaction-only batch still needs them — skipping it would hand empty lists to `importReactions` and silently fail to attach. Safe because `syncTopic` guards on `incoming.length > 0` while the three lookups run regardless.

**A fixed window, not a trailing debounce.** "Debounce ~250ms" read literally keeps resetting while events keep arriving, which starves on a busy channel. The window opens on the first event of a burst and fires once — latency bounded at one window, burst still collapsed to one call per kind group.

## Found by its own test

`flushNow()` returned early on an empty buffer **even with a call in flight**, reporting "flushed" while work was outstanding. Fixed to return the in-flight promise. That is the shape that makes a test green and loses the last batch on unmount.

## One deliberate gap for M4 to know about

**No profiles reach `importChannel` on the live path.** `kind:0` is not channel-scoped, so a `#h` subscription never delivers one and there is nothing to pass. A first-time author renders under a placeholder until `pubkeysMissingProfile`/`recordProfiles` fills it in — the gap PEEK-72 built that pair to close, running on its own schedule. Live delivery makes it more visible than the HTTP path did, since that fetched `kind:0` per author in the same run.

## What PEE-8 has to observe

All three modules are merged and **none has ever run inside the app**. PEE-8 is where the chain becomes real, and this ticket's done-when is part of what it should check: a message published from Ship appearing in an open topic **with no `POST /query` in the network panel**. The StrictMode double-mount caution from PEE-5 still applies.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Merged: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/63 → `180651f`. Done-when met live.**

Two channels, two REQs, one socket, from a signed-in browser — and the events were the two comments posted onto this ticket and onto CRO-4, so no synthetic data was involved:

```
subscribed — chanA, chanB, and BOTH-control (multi-#h)
CLOSED BOTH-control  restricted: p-gated events require #p matching your pubkey
15:36:48  EVENT on chanA  kind 1111
15:36:51  EVENT on chanB  kind 1111
```

Both channels received simultaneously. The multi-`#h` control did not. That is the case this ticket exists to prevent, demonstrated rather than cited.

## The trap fails two ways, and this ticket describes only one

**The control was refused outright**, not silently starved. That is a correction to the ticket's premise and it is worth having exactly right, because the two arms behave oppositely.

`p_gated_filters_authorized` (`handlers/req.rs`) gates every subscription that resolves to `channel_id: None`. Its first test:

```rust
let can_match_p_gated = filter.kinds.as_ref().is_none_or(|ks| …);
if !can_match_p_gated { return true; }
```

| multi-`#h` filter | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| **kindless** — `{"#h":[a,b]}` | `is_none_or` → could match a p-gated kind → no `#p` → **CLOSED, loudly** |
| **kinded, ordinary** — `{"#h":[a,b],"kinds":[9]}` | returns early as authorized → registers globally → **silently receives nothing** |

Our control was kindless, so it hit the loud arm. **The silent arm is still real, and it is the more likely one to be written** — somebody optimising "one subscription for messages across all my channels" writes `kinds:[9]`, passes the gate, gets correct history and no live events. So the ticket's warning stands; the loud gate is simply a newer layer in front of the failure it describes, not a replacement for it.

I have corrected the same overstatement in my own PR: I had called the non-uuid key an "identical silent death". Since this module always builds a kindless filter, a bad key lands on the loud arm. It is still a subscription that never delivers, and still an asynchronous `CLOSED` the app has to interpret, so the throw at the call site still earns its place — but "silent" was wrong.

## Two things confirmed as a side effect

**The kindless filter picks up kinds nobody enumerated.** The events that arrived were **kind:1111**, not kind:9 — Ship comments moved to NIP-22 with REW-10. Nothing in this manager mentions 1111, and it delivered anyway, which is the wildcard-index behaviour working as read.

**A Ship folder uuid is the channel uuid** — `fold.ts` maps `folder: tag(event, 'h')`. That is what made a zero-pollution live test possible, and it is worth knowing for PEE-7.

## For PEE-7 and PEE-8

The manager is keyed on channel uuid and refuses anything else, per the RFC 0.3 note. Reconnection is delegated to `liveRelay` rather than reimplemented. What has still never happened is either module running **inside the app** — PEE-8 remains where that gets observed, and the StrictMode double-mount caution from PEE-5 still applies.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Handoff from CRO-1, which is done and live.** `POST /nip44/encrypt` and `/nip44/decrypt` are on production and round-trip verified, so this ticket's dependency is cleared.

Three things worth knowing before writing the client:

**The endpoints refuse a peer pubkey rather than ignoring one.** The request schemas are `.strict()`, so sending `pubkey` or `peer` is a `400`. That is deliberate and differs from `/sign`, which accepts and ignores one — there, the authoritative answer is unambiguous. Here, ignoring it would hand back a self-encrypted blob to code that believed it was encrypting to somebody else, and the mistake would only surface as an undecryptable message days later.

**Refusal reasons are readable cross-origin.** Verified over the wire from `peek.estiva.app`: the preflight returns 204 with the headers, an unregistered origin gets 403, and `access-control-allow-origin` rides on a `401` too. So a `429` or a `422` reaches this client as a status with a `detail.reason`, not as a generic network error. Worth relying on rather than re-checking — in-process tests cannot verify any of it, and this repo has shipped that failure twice with green suites.

**One gap to decide on, not a defect.** A malformed body (`400`) writes **no** audit row; only authorization outcomes and decryption failures do. So a client repeatedly sending a peer pubkey leaves no trace. This matches `/sign`, which does not audit its `badRequest` either, so it is consistent rather than an oversight — but if seeing clients misuse the API matters here, that is the gap.

Rate limit is 120 operations per minute, shared between encrypt and decrypt, keyed on (app, person). Read state writes are debounced, so single digits per minute is the expected shape and there are two orders of magnitude of headroom.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/63 — CI green, held for the live two-channel check.

A refcounted manager over the PEE-5 socket: one relay subscription per channel uuid, shared by every consumer, closed when the last releases. Reconnection is **not** reimplemented — `createLiveRelay` already re-issues its registered subscriptions after re-authenticating, so a channel with a live refcount comes back on its own. The test for that runs against the real client over a fake socket, because it is a property of the composition rather than of either piece.

## The trap holds, all four claims

Read out of the relay rather than trusted, since the whole problem is that it is invisible: `extract_channel_id_from_filters` returns `None` on two distinct `#h` or any filter lacking one; that registers the subscription in the global indexes; `fan_out_scoped` serves a channel-scoped event from the channel indexes only; and `subscription.rs` states the invariant outright.

## There is a second entrance, and it is the likelier one

`extract_channel_id_from_filters` only counts an `#h` value it can `parse::<uuid::Uuid>()`. **Anything else leaves `filter_has_channel` false and falls through to the same global registration** — identical silent death, no multi-channel subscription required.

That is reachable in Peek today, two ways:

- **topic ids are Convex ids, not uuids**, and they sit adjacent to the real key in signatures like `recordChannel({ topicId, channelUuid })`
- **`topics.channelUuid` is `v.optional`** — "absent on topics created before Nostr emission was wired up" — so `undefined` is a real value, not a theoretical one

The RFC 0.3 note on this ticket asks that a topic id never become the subscription key. That is now structural: `subscribe()` validates the shape and **throws**, naming the cause. A loud failure in development beats a subscription that looks fine and delivers nothing in production, which is the same trade the ticket is already making.

**A third silent death:** `kinds: []` is indexed *nowhere* by Buzz and receives nothing. The manager builds its own filter so none of the three is reachable through its API.

## The kindless filter is confirmed

`{"#h":[uuid]}` with no `kinds` lands in the channel **wildcard** index. Reactions and deletions carry no `h` tag, but `filters_match` falls back to `StoredEvent.channel_id` for `#h` when an event has no `h` tags at all — so messages, reactions, deletions and assertions all arrive on one subscription. The HTTP path's 100-reaction cap is not ported.

449 tests, 17 new. `npm run build` run as well, since `tsc -b` is not a PR gate in this repo.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Merged: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/62 → `089faa3`.** The protocol is proven end to end against production.

```
<- AUTH  dae4262d1e05f9f997efd62c8ce46868…
<- OK    4df660dbe510c647bbe524247777a348  true
AUTHENTICATED — subscribing
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  91044c77…
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  51b5635d…
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  c48fbd49…
<- EOSE  probe
```

Challenge → signed 22242 accepted → REQ answered with real events and an EOSE, on one socket, from a signed-in browser. This also closed **PEE-4**'s last unproven leg, which was the same observation from the other side.

## What is proven, and by what — the distinction matters for PEE-7 and PEE-8

**The protocol sequence and the grant** are confirmed against production, exactly as implemented here: the same frames, the same `relay` tag (`wss://estiva.estiva.app`, an origin), the same ordering.

**The module's own behaviour** — reconnect with backoff, re-issuing every live subscription afterwards, routing events per subscription, treating a poisoned socket as fatal — is covered by 22 tests against a fake relay built to match `crates/buzz-*`, not by production. That is the honest split.

**What has not happened is `liveRelay.ts` itself running inside the app**, because nothing imports it yet. It is unconsumed code until PEE-7 routes its events into the projection and PEE-8 wires `useTopicView`. **PEE-8 is where "the socket reaches `live` in the real app" actually gets observed**, and it is worth doing deliberately there rather than assuming it follows — the module is correct against a fake and against a hand-run protocol, which is not the same as correct inside React's lifecycle.

The specific thing to watch for at PEE-8: this creates **one connection per tab**, and a component mounting twice under StrictMode must not open two. That is a wiring concern, not a client concern, so it is not solved here.

## Carried forward

- **±60s clock tolerance** (`RELAY_AUTH_TOLERANCE_SECS`) — a browser more than a minute out signs a valid event that is refused every time, and lands in the poisoned-open state. PEE-9 should be able to say so rather than showing a generic disconnect.
- **`failed` is terminal and means auth, not availability.** A relay that is down stays `reconnecting` forever, by design. PEE-9 should render those two differently — one is "wait", the other is "this will never work".
- The connection-state values are `connecting | authenticating | live | reconnecting | failed`, surfaced through `onState`, with nothing rendered here.

root.body:
**The last leg is closed. The done-when is now met literally, not by proxy.**

This ticket's done-when was *"a browser-signed kind:22242 carrying the relay's challenge is accepted, and a REQ on that connection returns events instead of `auth-required`."* It closed on the row, then on browser signing. Both halves are now observed, on one socket, against production:

```
<- AUTH  dae4262d1e05f9f997efd62c8ce46868…
<- OK    4df660dbe510c647bbe524247777a348  true
AUTHENTICATED — subscribing
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  91044c77…
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  51b5635d…
<- EVENT probe  kind:9  c48fbd49…
<- EOSE  probe
```

The relay issued a challenge, accepted a 22242 signed through this grant by a real browser session, and then answered a REQ with **three real events and an EOSE** rather than `auth-required`. Every clause, in order.

**Nothing on the Estiva ID side needed changing to get here.** The row, the scope, the deployment bound and browser signing were all confirmed on the day this shipped; what was missing was a socket to exercise them, and PEE-5 supplied it. The prediction in the comment above — that if PEE-5 failed, the ceiling would not be the place to look — did not get tested, because it did not fail.

One detail worth keeping for anyone debugging a future AUTH refusal: the `relay` tag that was accepted is `wss://estiva.estiva.app` — an **origin**, no path, no trailing slash. That is `nip42_expected_relay_url` = `format!("{scheme}://{}", tenant.host())`, and it matches `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` exactly. Both sides of the AND agree on one string, which is the property that makes this work at all.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/62 — CI green, **not merged**: the done-when needs a browser and one leg is still unproven.

`src/nostr/liveRelay.ts`, plus `KIND.RELAY_AUTH` and `buildUnsignedRelayAuthEvent` in the Convex tree as instructed. 432 tests pass, 26 of them new.

## Item 4 asks for something impossible, and something that is not needed

> *"Re-auth on token rotation… prefer re-auth over reconnect."*

**Re-authenticating in place is refused by the relay.** `handle_auth` matches on `AuthState::{Pending, Authenticated, Failed}` and answers anything but `Pending` with `OK false "auth-required: already authenticated"`. A connection's identity is fixed at its first successful AUTH.

**And a reconnect is not needed either, because the premise is wrong.** The relay authenticates a **pubkey**, by verifying a Schnorr signature. It never sees the Estiva ID access token and does not know one exists. A renewal issues a new token for the *same* keypair, so nothing the relay checked has changed — the socket is not "running on a dead identity". The token is needed only to *sign* a fresh 22242, which happens on the next connect.

So the implementation reads the credential fresh on every connect attempt and leaves a live socket alone. Both halves are pinned by tests.

What genuinely does not propagate is **offboarding**: a revoked person keeps an already-authenticated socket until it drops. That is the relay's session model and its ban gate is the control for it — re-authenticating on a timer would not have fixed it either, since a banned pubkey is caught at connect. It is written into the module header rather than left to be rediscovered.

## The failure mode this ticket is really about

Worth stating because it is nastier than "the socket dies": **a refused AUTH leaves the connection OPEN.** Only a *ban* closes the socket. A verification failure sets `AuthState::Failed` and returns, after which every REQ is answered `CLOSED … auth-required` forever, on a socket whose `readyState` is `OPEN`. Health tells you nothing.

So an AUTH refusal is treated as fatal-for-this-socket and forces a reconnect — with a give-up cap, because the things that cause it (a missing grant, a clock more than 60s out) fail identically every time and would otherwise loop. A relay that is merely *down* never reaches `failed`, because that one does fix itself. Signing failures are counted separately: an expired token is not the relay refusing us.

## Two things the ticket does not mention

**±60s clock tolerance.** `TIMESTAMP_TOLERANCE_SECS` in `nip42.rs` — the same bound NIP-98 has, checked against the *relay's* clock. It is the one failure a correct client can still hit, and it presents as the poisoned-socket state above. Exported as `RELAY_AUTH_TOLERANCE_SECS` for M4 to explain.

**The `relay` tag is bound to the connection's host, not the deployment URL.** `nip42_expected_relay_url` is `format!("{scheme}://{}", tenant.host())` — Buzz has a test named `nip42_expected_relay_url_uses_tenant_host_not_config_host` because it regressed once. So the tag is an **origin**: no path, port kept. `normalize_relay_url` forgives a trailing slash but not a path segment.

## Verified live, and one correction to the ticket text

Probed against `wss://estiva.estiva.app` from Node:

```
socket OPEN
AUTH challenge received: 64 chars, hex=true
CLOSED  sub=probe-sub  message="auth-required: not authenticated"
frames seen: AUTH -> NOTICE -> CLOSED
```

Production answers **`"auth-required: not authenticated"`**, not the `"auth-required: authenticate before subscribing"` this ticket quotes from `req.rs:78`. There is more than one path to that refusal. Matching on the `auth-required` **prefix** covers both; an equality check on the ticket's string would have silently never fired. A `NOTICE` frame also arrives that nothing predicted — the parser ignores unknown verbs rather than throwing, so a relay that grows a frame cannot take the socket down.

## Also worth knowing for the next Peek ticket

`npm run test:run` is the **only** PR gate. `tsc -b` runs only on a push to `main`, inside `npx convex deploy --cmd 'npm run build'` — so a type error merges green and breaks the deploy. It happened in #61 and it happened here: `vitest` compiled a parameter property happily and `erasableSyntaxOnly` rejected it. **Run `npm run build` before merging anything in this repo.**

## What is left

The socket reaching `live` against production, and a REQ returning events. Both need a live user token, which only a browser holds — same constraint as PEE-4's last leg. Everything short of that is confirmed.

root.body:
**Follow-up: the signing half is now proven from a browser, and the scope with it.**

This closed on the row. It no longer has to. From devtools on a signed-in `https://peek.estiva.app`, cross-origin to the live `https://id.estiva.app`:

```
22242  relay=wss://estiva.estiva.app   200  signed
22242  relay=wss://evil.test           422  {"reason":"relay_auth_relay_not_allowed"}
```

**The second line is the ticket's actual subject.** The grant was never the risky part — the scope was, and this is it refusing a relay Peek has no business authenticating to, with the real credential, from the real origin. That is the widening the ticket existed to prevent, demonstrated rather than argued. Both bounds are in play: the deployment's `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` and the row's `relay_auth_urls`, ANDed.

It also settles a question in-process tests cannot touch. The 422 body was **readable by the browser**, so the refusal arrives as `policy_violation / relay_auth_relay_not_allowed` rather than a generic network error. That is PEEK-93's failure mode checked from the far side, and it matters for PEE-5: when a challenge is refused, the reason will be legible in the console instead of looking like a dropped connection.

## What is left, now much narrower

Still unproven, and still PEE-5's to observe: **that the relay accepts one.** The challenge above was fabricated by hand, not issued by a socket, so nothing has yet round-tripped a real AUTH. The remaining unknowns are on the relay's side of the wire, not Estiva ID's:

- the relay accepting the challenge response it issued
- a REQ on that connection returning events rather than `auth-required`

If either fails, it is now almost certainly **not** this ticket — the ceiling, the scope, the deployment bound and browser signing are all confirmed against production. Look at the challenge round trip and the socket, and note that the relay wants `--http1.1` on the upgrade or it answers with NIP-11 JSON instead.

**Done — the browser-session clause is now actually met, not waived.**

The grant has been live since the Gate 1 deploy; what was outstanding was the done-when's requirement that `/sign` accept the kind *from a browser session*. Run from devtools on a signed-in `https://peek.estiva.app`, against the live `https://id.estiva.app`:

```
41010  200  signed
30622  422  {"reason":"kind_not_allowed"}
```

**The second line is the one worth having.** 30622 is `KIND_DM_VISIBILITY` — relay-signed, republished by the relay on every hide, listed in `RESULT_GATED_KINDS`, and a reader must equal the event's `#p`. Its absence from the grant is a decision rather than an oversight, so it is asserted in `seed.test.ts` (`not.toContain(30622)`) and now confirmed against production from the app that would be the one to forge it. Somebody "completing the set" later has both a failing test and this line to run into.

41011 and 41012 were not probed individually — they sit in the same `allowed_kinds` array as 41010, granted by the same seed line and checked by the same `includes()` in `policy.ts`, so 41010 succeeding is the same evidence for all three. The row shows them:

```
estiva-peek | {9,7,5,9007,27235,1851,9101,9002,9008,1111,30078,41010,41011,41012,22242}
```

**What this does not answer, and DMS-2 still should:** whether the *relay* accepts a `kind:41010` over the HTTP bridge. This proves Estiva ID will sign one — the first of the two gates — and says nothing about ingest. DMS-2 exists for exactly that and remains the right next step in this track; it is now unblocked and can be run as a straight probe, since the signing half is no longer in question.

The grant has been live since the Gate 1 deploy; what was outstanding was the done-when's requirement that `/sign` accept the kind *from a browser session*, which no terminal can produce. Run from devtools on a signed-in `https://peek.estiva.app`, against the live `https://id.estiva.app`:

```

estiva-ship | {30850,30851,1851,9,5,9007,31989,27235,1111,30078}
```

CRO-4 can rely on reading refusal reasons cross-origin.

Nothing here is blocking. CRO-4 is next in this track and its ceiling is verified from the environment it will actually run in.

root.body:
**Closing on Miky's call: the row is sufficient.**

The previous comment held this at `in_progress` because the done-when asks for a browser-signed 22242 accepted by the relay, and a REQ returning events. That is a **PEE-5 observation, not a PEE-4 deliverable** — this ticket's scope was the ceiling and its scope, both of which are shipped, deployed and verified on production. Waiting on M3 to close an M2 gate would leave the gate looking shut while three projects were already unblocked by it.

So the ticket closes on what it actually controls, and what is still unproven is written down here rather than implied by a status:

**Proven:** the row (`22242` + `{wss://estiva.estiva.app}`), the pairing invariant across all four credential rows, the deployment bound present inside the serving container, migration 009 applied, and the neighbouring 27235 path unregressed.

**Unproven, and now PEE-5's to observe:** that the relay accepts a challenge response signed through this grant, and that a REQ on that connection returns events instead of `auth-required`.

**If PEE-5 gets `auth-required` anyway, read these two before suspecting the socket code** — they are the only things on this side that can refuse, and the first one looks correct while the second is missing:

```bash
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U estiva_id -d estiva_id -tAc \
  "select client_id, allowed_kinds, relay_auth_urls from app_credentials where client_id='estiva-peek'"
docker compose exec -T estiva-id printenv SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS
```

A `policy_violation` with `detail.reason` distinguishes them precisely: `kind_not_allowed` means the seed did not run, `relay_auth_relay_not_allowed` means the row or the env var is empty or names a different relay. Anything else is not this ticket.

root.body:
**Merged and deployed — the gate is open. Deliberately NOT marked done, see the last section.**

https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-id/pull/55 → `177dd10`, image `sha256:5cd4e415…` serving since 13:36 UTC.

## The row, which is the thing to check

```
claude-agent|{27235,1851,9,30851,30850,9007,1111}|{}
estiva-peek|{9,7,5,9007,27235,1851,9101,9002,9008,1111,30078,41010,41011,41012,22242}|{wss://estiva.estiva.app}
estiva-ship|{30850,30851,1851,9,5,9007,31989,27235,1111,30078}|{}
pc-0a4935|{27235}|{}
```

And the pairing invariant asserted in SQL rather than read by eye — `(22242 = any(allowed_kinds)) = (relay_auth_urls is not empty)` is **true for all four rows**, including the two bot credentials that have neither.

## update.sh really does not seed — observed, not assumed

Worth recording because it was visible mid-deploy this time. Immediately after the timer pulled the image and ran migrations, before the manual seed:

```
009_relay_auth_urls.sql | applied 13:36:19    ← migration ran automatically
estiva-peek | {…,41011,41012} | {}            ← no 22242, empty relay list
```

The migration applies itself; the seed does not. A deploy that stopped there would have left a new column, a healthy container, a green timer log, and the feature entirely absent.

## The other half of the AND, which the row does not show

`allowed_kinds` containing 22242 is **not sufficient**, and this is the part that would fail silently. `evaluateSignPolicy` ANDs the app's column with the deployment bound, so an empty `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` refuses every relay while the row above looks perfectly correct. It is a new env var, so it had to be added to `/opt/estiva-id/.env` by hand — **before** the new container started, so the timer's `--force-recreate` picked it up with no window in between. Confirmed inside the serving container, not in the file:

```
docker compose exec -T estiva-id printenv SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS
→ wss://estiva.estiva.app
```

**For anyone doing a fresh deployment or a restore: this is a required setting now.** It is in `.env.example` and `deploy/env.production.example`; empty means every 22242 is refused.

## Regression check on the neighbouring path

The 27235 branch shares the file that changed, so it was re-verified live: `https://estiva.estiva.app/query` still signs (200), `https://evil.test/steal` still refused (`nip98_url_not_allowed`). And a 22242 signed as `claude-agent` — which has neither the kind nor a relay — is refused `kind_not_allowed`, confirming the kind check still runs before the relay branch.

## Why this is still in_progress

The done-when is *"a browser-signed kind:22242 carrying the relay's challenge is accepted, and a REQ on that connection returns events instead of auth-required."* **That last leg is unproven and cannot be proven yet** — it needs a WebSocket client and a live Peek user token, which is PEE-5. There is no way to mint a Peek browser session from a terminal, and the service credential available to the agent is not granted 22242 (correctly).

So: everything this ticket controls is shipped and verified, and **M3 is unblocked — PEE-5 onwards are testable now**. The first socket that answers a challenge is what closes this, and it should close it by observation rather than by assumption: if the relay refuses, the two things to read are this row and `printenv SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS`, in that order.

One correction carried over from the scoping comment: Estiva ID *does* have a relay URL in config — `RELAY_BRIDGE_URL` — it is just the wrong one to derive from, because empty means "profile publishing is off" and sharing it would give two capabilities one switch.

root.body:
**Merged and deployed.** https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-id/pull/55 → `177dd10`, image `sha256:5cd4e415…` serving since 13:36 UTC.

## Verified against production, not against the deploy reporting success

The negative control was taken before merging: `POST /nip44/encrypt` returned **404 No route**. After:

```
POST /nip44/encrypt                       200, 176-char payload, version byte 2
POST /nip44/decrypt                       200, returns the original string
  a second encrypt of the same plaintext  different ciphertext (fresh nonce)
  { plaintext, pubkey }                   400 — refused, not ignored
  { plaintext: "" }                       400
  tampered final MAC byte                 400 reason=undecryptable
  132 chars of 'A'                        400, byte-identical message
```

Both failures return "Could not decrypt that ciphertext" and are indistinguishable to the caller. The audit rows kept the difference, which is the design working rather than an assumption about it:

```
nip44.decrypt.refused | {"reason": "undecryptable", "failure": "invalid MAC"}
nip44.decrypt.refused | {"reason": "undecryptable", "failure": "unknown encryption version 0"}
nip44.encrypt.granted | {}
```

A scan of the whole `audit_events` table for the probe's plaintext returned **0 rows**.

## CORS is verified, because a passing suite says nothing about it

`http/cors.ts` states outright that nothing enforces CORS when a Hono app is called in-process — this repo shipped that exact failure twice (PEEK-90, PEEK-93), both times with green tests. So it was checked over the wire rather than inferred:

```
OPTIONS /nip44/encrypt   Origin: https://peek.estiva.app   204 + allow-origin, allow-methods, vary
OPTIONS /nip44/decrypt   Origin: https://peek.estiva.app   204 + the same
OPTIONS /nip44/encrypt   Origin: https://evil.test         403
POST    /nip44/encrypt   no token, Peek origin             401 **with** allow-origin
```

The last line is the one that matters most for CRO-4: the header rides on refusals, so a 429 or a 422 reaches the app as a readable status instead of a generic network error. `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is absent throughout, as intended.

## Two proxies used, named rather than glossed

- **"A Peek browser session"** — no Peek code calls these yet, so the round trip was driven with the `claude-agent` service credential over the identical server path, and the browser-specific half (preflight from `peek.estiva.app`) was verified separately as above. What remains unexercised is Peek's own client code, which is CRO-4.
- **"A disabled app is refused"** — covered by test (`422`, `detail.reason: app_disabled`) rather than on production, since that would mean disabling a live app credential.

## One boundary worth knowing for CRO-4

A malformed body (`400`) writes **no** audit row; only authorization outcomes and decryption failures do. So an app repeatedly sending a peer pubkey leaves no trace. This matches `/sign`, which does not audit its `badRequest` either, so it is consistent rather than an oversight — but if CRO-4 wants to see clients misusing the API, that is the gap to close.

Done-when met: round trip ✓, peer pubkey refused ✓, disabled app refused ✓ (test), audit without contents ✓.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-id/pull/55 — batched with PEE-4 as one Gate 1 deploy. Not done until it is verified against production.

## Built as specced, with two deliberate additions

Both endpoints are self-encryption only, as required. One thing the ticket left open that turned out to matter: the request schemas are **`.strict()`**, so a caller sending `pubkey` or `peer` gets a `400` rather than having it ignored.

The ticket suggested following `/sign`, which "deliberately ignores any pubkey it is handed". That is right for `/sign` — the authoritative answer there is unambiguous, you always want your own signature. It is **wrong here**, and the difference is worth recording: an app that believed it was encrypting to a colleague would receive a blob only the user can open, succeed, publish it, and the mistake would surface as an undecryptable message on the far side days later. Refusing says so at the call. "Nothing to get wrong" is stronger when the wrong thing is rejected rather than silently discarded.

Second: **every decryption failure returns one answer**, `detail.reason: undecryptable`. The underlying `Nip44Error` distinguishes a bad MAC from bad padding and that distinction is kept — in the audit row, not the response. A caller that can tell them apart has a padding oracle. (The MAC is checked before unpadding, so the exposure was narrow, but the response shape should not depend on that ordering staying true.)

## On "use an audited implementation rather than hand-rolling the padding"

Taken seriously, and the resolution is not quite what the ticket assumed. `@noble/*` is in the tree, but @noble provides *primitives* — there is no NIP-44 in it. What exists is ChaCha20 (added `@noble/ciphers`, zero dependencies, no conflict with the `@noble/hashes` 1.x already present), HKDF, HMAC and secp256k1 ECDH.

So the composition is ours, which means the padding scheme is ours, which is the exact thing the ticket warned about. The answer is to be **judged by somebody else's expectations**: the reference vector suite from `paulmillr/nip44` is vendored and all **108 vectors** run, valid and invalid. This is the same pattern `nip-oa.test.ts` already uses against Buzz's Rust vector, and it is stronger than a round-trip test in a specific way — 10 of the vectors supply the nonce and pin **our ciphertext byte-for-byte against theirs**, which is the only way to catch a padding or HKDF divergence that round-trips perfectly against itself and interoperates with nothing.

The invalid half earned its keep immediately. Node's `Buffer.from(s, 'base64')` silently skips characters outside the alphabet, so the "invalid base64" vector decoded to *something* and would have failed later as a misleading MAC error. Strict base64 validation is in because a vector said so, not because it was foreseen.

Two more that would not have been written from prose: `calc_padded_len` uses `31 - Math.clz32(n)` rather than `Math.floor(Math.log2(n))`, because a float log is one ulp from the wrong integer at exact powers of two — the resulting bug would have been a padded length that differs from every other implementation only for certain message sizes. And the 1..65535 bound counts **bytes of UTF-8**, not characters; a naive `plaintext.length` check admits an over-long multi-byte message, which is now a test of its own.

## Rate limiting — sized, and with a limitation worth knowing

120 operations per minute, shared between encrypt and decrypt, keyed on (clientId, pubkey). One budget because the pair is one capability — a decrypt limit that reset whenever encrypt was idle would bound nothing.

**It is a per-process counter.** Estiva ID runs as one container on one box, so that is a per-deployment limit today. It is not that under two replicas: each would keep its own window and the effective limit would be N×. Anything that scales this service out has to move the counter to Postgres or Redis first, and `src/http/rate-limit.ts` says so where somebody will find it.

## Audit

`nip44.{encrypt,decrypt}.{granted,refused}` rows. Neither plaintext nor ciphertext is recorded — **and neither is their length**, which was a judgement call: a length is not content, but it is a hint about a read-state blob, and the ticket's bar is "that an operation happened".

The test asserts this by dumping the **whole `audit_events` table as text** and searching it, not just the `detail` column — a length or a prefix leaking through some other field would pass a narrower check.

## What is proven, and what is not

530 tests pass across the repo, 21 of them new here — including one that encrypts a blob **outside the service** under `conversation_key(own_priv, own_pub)` and decrypts it through the endpoint. That is the strongest available statement of "self-encryption": it is the key NIP-RS specifies, not merely one that is internally consistent.

Verified against production before merging, as the deploy's negative control: `POST /nip44/encrypt` currently returns **404 No route**.

**The done-when says "a Peek browser session".** That specific path stays unproven — no Peek session is mintable from here. What *will* be run against production after the deploy is a full `/nip44/encrypt` → `/nip44/decrypt` round trip using the `claude-agent` service credential, which exercises the identical server path end to end. The browser half is CORS, which in-process tests cannot check at all (`http/cors.ts` says so) and CRO-4 will be the first thing to actually exercise.

root.body:
PR: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-id/pull/55 — batched with CRO-1 as one Gate 1 deploy. Not done until the row is verified on the box.

**The unverified note was right to check, and the answer was reassuring.** Production's `allowed_kinds` matched `seed.ts` exactly before anything was edited — `estiva-peek` had the 14 kinds from PR #54 and no 22242, so no drift to reconcile.

## Where the allowed relays come from — the open question, decided

A **new deployment bound (`SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS`) and a new per-app column (`app_credentials.relay_auth_urls`)**, intersected exactly the way the NIP-98 pair is. Both default to empty, which refuses.

Reusing `nip98_url_prefixes` was rejected for the reason the scoping comment gives, and one more found while implementing: the schemes do not even match. A `u` tag is `https://estiva.estiva.app/...`; a NIP-42 `relay` tag is `wss://estiva.estiva.app`. Sharing the column would have needed scheme-rewriting on one side, which is a second place for the two capabilities to disagree.

**One correction to the scoping comment:** it says there is "no `RELAY_URL` in Estiva ID's config at all". There is one — `RELAY_BRIDGE_URL`, the origin of Buzz's HTTP bridge. It is still the wrong thing to derive from, for a sharper reason than being merely adjacent: *empty means profile publishing is off*. Deriving relay auth from it would give two unrelated capabilities one switch, so turning profile publishing off would also stop Peek authenticating to the relay. Worth knowing it exists before the next person greps for it and concludes the same thing.

## Exact match, not prefix — a deliberate divergence from the pattern

The ticket says to copy the NIP-98 URL-prefix branch. The structure was copied; the **match rule was not**, on purpose.

A NIP-98 `u` tag is a full request URL with a path, so a prefix is the only workable shape. A `relay` tag has no path, so a prefix buys nothing and costs something:

```
allow  wss://estiva.estiva.app
admits wss://estiva.estiva.app.attacker.example/    ← under prefix matching
```

That is precisely the hazard `config.ts` already documents for redirect URIs ("Exact, never prefix"). A trailing slash would have saved it by accident; a value configured without one would not. WHATWG normalization folds `wss://x`, `wss://x/` and host case together first, so exact matching costs no ergonomics — the test environment configures `ws://relay.test` without a slash while every event under test carries one, so the normalization is exercised on every run rather than assumed.

## The pin is gone, and what replaced it

`seed.test.ts`'s `not.toContain(22242)` is deleted as instructed. What replaced it asserts the **invariant** rather than either number, in both directions across every seeded app: an app has relays iff it has the kind. The kind without relays is PEEK-133's shape — passes the kind check, then refused for every relay there is. Relays without the kind sit there looking like a grant until somebody adds 22242 and gets no scope with it.

Ship is given `relay_auth_urls: []` rather than the deployment's list, so adding the kind there later cannot be a one-line unscoped grant.

## What is proven, and what is not

Six DB-backed tests in `sign.test.ts` alongside the unit tests, because the rule being a pure function is not the risk — the *column* surviving `seed.ts` → `findAppPolicy` → `evaluateSignPolicy` is. A `relay_auth_urls` missing from that SELECT would have refused every relay while every `policy.test.ts` test still passed.

**Still unproven, and it stays that way until M3:** a browser-signed 22242 accepted by the live relay, and a REQ returning events on that connection. That needs a live Peek user token, which this session has no way to mint — the service-credential grant available to the agent is `claude-agent`, which is not granted 22242. What *will* be verified on the box is the row plus the container's env var, and the second half matters: the deployment bound is the other side of the AND, so an empty `SIGN_RELAY_AUTH_ALLOWED_URLS` refuses every relay while `allowed_kinds` looks perfectly correct.

**Done and verified from `main`.** ship#39, peek#60, estiva-agent#11, ship#40 and the build fix peek#61 all merged; the manifest is republished from merged `main` rather than from a branch:

    web        ["web","https://ship.estiva.app/#/o/<bech32>","naddr"]
    title slot {"tag":["name","title"]}
    removed 4 verification fixture(s)
    Manifest published and satisfiable.

Every check green, which this script had not managed once all session — it was red throughout for three different reasons in sequence, and each one only became visible when the one in front of it was fixed:

1. it could not see the global project record at all (SHI-8)
2. the projection named a tag the record no longer carried (this ticket)
3. its own evaluator could not read the tag list that fixed 2 (ship#40)

## Closing, and what it cost

Four production records rendered untitled in Peek, one of them real. The cause was REW-11 renaming a tag and not the projection that reads it, and it survived because the tool that checks exactly this had been broken by the same change — one bug hiding the other's damage.

Two smaller things fell out and are fixed with it: the manifest's "open in Ship" links pointed at `localhost:5190` on two republishes (a green line printed the wrong value and I read past it twice), and `publish-manifest.ts` had been leaving a real project on production every run since long before today — four had accumulated, all now deleted, and it cleans up after itself.

The general lesson, which is going into the docs rather than only here: REW-11 verified the record shape, the fold and the relay's acceptance, and never verified **the other app's rendering** — the one thing the change existed to serve.

**A recommendation on the three kinds still refused, since `1111` is done and the rest are a decision rather than work.**

**`kind:5` — grant it.** This is the one with a cost that compounds. Today anything this identity publishes to production is undeletable **by anyone**: NIP-09 is author-scoped, so the author is the agent key and no human can clean up on its behalf. That has already produced permanent artefacts this week — a verification comment on REW-10 and three archived probe project records that exist only because deletion was refused after the fact. Archiving hides them from lists; it does not remove them, and the workspace accretes.

The usual argument against is that a bot should not be able to destroy work. It is weaker than it looks: NIP-09 is author-scoped, so `kind:5` lets the agent delete **only what the agent itself wrote**. It cannot touch a human's issue, comment or project. The capability is "clean up after yourself", not "delete things".

Compare the shape with the two apps: `estiva-peek` and `estiva-ship` both already have `5`, for exactly this reason.

    PATCH /admin/credentials/claude-agent/kinds
    {"allowedKinds":[27235,1851,9,30851,30850,9007,1111,5]}

**`31989`/`31990` — leave refused.** The agent has no business publishing Ship's NIP-89 manifest or a handler recommendation; `publish-manifest.ts` signs those with a separate local key by design, and that separation is worth keeping. Nothing this session wanted them.

**`30078` — leave refused** (CRO-2 asks for a deliberate answer). Read state records that a *person* read something. A bot marking things read is a reading nobody did, and it would corrupt the cross-app read-state model the moment the agent listed issues.

So: one grant, two deliberate refusals, and the ticket can close once `5` is decided either way. I am not going to widen my own ceiling by writing to the database directly — the admin route exists with an audit trail precisely for this, and it is the one case the control is for.

**Correcting this ticket's diagnosis, which was mine and is half wrong.**

I wrote that the check "validates the branch, not the merge result". It validates both — `check.yml` already runs `on: push: branches: [main]`. And it **fired**:

    2026-08-25T12:27  success  Mirror the project title projection fix (#11)
    2026-08-25T09:46  success  Mirror Ship's NIP-22 comment writer (#10)
    2026-08-25T08:43  success  Mirror Ship's NIP-22 comment reader (#9)

    2026-08-24T20:50  success  Install the same server as a Claude Code plugin (#8)

So `main` went red the moment the stale bundle landed, exactly as designed, and stayed red until I rebuilt it the next morning — for reasons I found by rebuilding, not by looking at that line. Nobody watched it, me included: I merged #7 and moved on.

**This changes what the ticket is asking for.** Option 2 — "run the check on `main` after merge" — is already built and already worked. The gap is not detection; it is that a red `main` produced no consequence. What is left is a choice between:

- **Branch protection, `strict: true`** ("require branches to be up to date before merging"). Prevents the merge rather than reporting it. I have admin and deliberately did not set it: in a repo where PRs merge minutes apart, every merge invalidates every other open PR and forces a rebase. That is a real cost to everyone else and a team decision, not mine.
- **Make a red `main` impossible to ignore** — a notification on the `push: main` job failing. No workflow friction, but it still depends on somebody acting.
- **Accept it and check `main` after merging**, which is free and is what should have happened.

My recommendation is the third plus the second. The first buys certainty at a price that a fast-merging team feels on every PR.

Worth keeping regardless: the immediate staleness is fixed and `main`'s last four runs are green.

    convex/nostr/projection.ts(655,42)
    TS2538: Type 'string[]' cannot be used as an index type

**Writer half open: ship#37 + estiva-agent#10.** CI green on both. That is the last code in this ticket.

    a comment about an object   → kind:1111, A/K/P root, a/k/p parent, h, ts
    a message about nothing     → stays kind:9
    a reply                     → stays kind:9, see below
    the manifest                → emits { kind: 1111, scope: address, alsoRead: [9] }

## Three decisions in there worth reviewing rather than skimming

**`K` and `P` are derived from the address, not passed in.** An address is `<kind>:<pubkey>:<d>` and already carries both; a second argument could only ever contradict the `A` sitting beside it.

**Replies stay `kind:9`, and that is the right answer rather than a shortcut.** A `1111` MUST name its root, and a reply's root is the *object*, not the comment it answers — so building one needs the thread's anchor, which `replyTo` does not carry and no caller passes. A `1111` with no `A` would be malformed rather than merely old. Supplying the anchor is a change in `apps/ship/`, which this ticket is scoped out of. Nothing breaks meanwhile: the fold reads both kinds into one thread and Peek has since peek#58. Worth picking up in the rewrite.

**The `h` has a test rather than a comment.** It would never fail a build: a `1111` is channel-scoped with an `h` and global without one, the relay takes both, and a comment published without it is world-readable however private its issue. Nothing errors.

## What still has to happen after merge

**Republish the manifest** — `npm run manifest`. Peek reads `emits.kind` to decide what to publish and the union with `alsoRead` to decide what to fetch, so until the *event* on the relay carries the new declaration, Peek keeps publishing `kind:9` and keeps querying only `kind:9`. The code change alone does nothing for Peek.

It signs with `.manifest-key`, a local key that is **not** subject to the Estiva ID ceiling, so it is not blocked on anything. I will do it once ship#37 merges, and verify by reading the `31990` event back off the relay rather than by the script exiting 0.

**PR open: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/59.** Took the general fix rather than the narrow one, because the narrow one is the thing `KIND_COMMENT`'s own note warns against.

`emits.alsoRead: [9]` — the owning app declares the kinds it *used* to publish, and `commentKindOf` becomes `commentKindsOf`, returning current-first and deduped. Peek hardcoding "also read 9" would have worked for Ship and done nothing for the next app that migrates, and it would have put a fact about one app's history in the consumer, which is exactly what that note says not to do.

Two properties make it safe to land ahead of everything else:

- **additive to reads only** — `kind` is still the single kind that gets published, `alsoRead` is only ever also fetched
- **a manifest without the field returns exactly one kind**, so no manifest published to date changes behaviour, Ship's included

So this PR is a no-op against today's workspace and cannot be the thing that breaks anything.

Ship's half — actually declaring `alsoRead: [9]` — belongs in the same commit as its writer flip. Declaring it earlier would assert a history that has not happened yet.

Still open, and I did not do it: `estiva-docs/protocol/SPEC.md` §7 specifies this schema for anyone implementing a consumer, so the field belongs there too. Better to let the shape be reviewed in #59 first than to document a field that might change.

395 tests pass, typecheck clean, ESLint 0 errors on the touched files — same as `origin/main`.

root.body:
**PR open: https://github.com/estiva-app/peek/pull/58.** No-op until Ship flips, so safe to land now.

Smaller than expected in one place and larger in another.

**`replyTargetOf` needed no change**, and it is worth recording why rather than leaving it to luck: a `1111` reply names its parent in a lowercase *unmarked* `e`, which the existing fallback already picks up; a top-level `1111` has no `e` at all, so it correctly reads as top-level; and the tag test is case-sensitive, so NIP-22's uppercase `E` — the thread root, possibly a different event — is never mistaken for the parent.

**The address extraction did need changing, and this was the real find.** NIP-22 puts the thread root in uppercase `A` and the immediate parent in lowercase. A top-level comment carries the object's address in *both*; **a reply carries it only in `A`**. So `e.tags.filter(t => t[0] === "a")` would have attached the first comment on a Ship issue to that issue and quietly detached every reply beneath it. `referencedAddresses` now takes both, deduped, on both import paths.

Both helpers are exported so the case rules are pinned by tests rather than by a comment; `projection.ts` already exports plain helpers that way.

395 tests pass, typecheck clean, and ESLint on the touched files is identical to `origin/main` — the 9 `no-explicit-any` errors are pre-existing in the `ctx` signatures, checked against the baseline rather than assumed.

root.body:
**PR open for the seeded half: https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-id/pull/53** — `1111` for `estiva-ship` *and* `estiva-peek`.

Peek turned out to need it too, which was not in this ticket. Peek never chooses a comment kind: `buildActionEvent` stamps whatever the owning app's NIP-89 manifest declares. So Ship flipping its manifest changes what **Peek** signs, with no change to Peek — and without the grant it fails at `/sign` after the manifest has already offered the action to a person.

**`claude-agent` is not in that PR and cannot be.** It is not in `SEED_APPS` at all, so it takes the route PEEK-172 built for exactly this:

    PATCH /admin/credentials/claude-agent/kinds
    {"allowedKinds":[27235,1851,9,30851,30850,9007,1111]}

Admin session cookie, not a token — `adminOnly` is `requireSession` + `requireAdmin`, and there is no UI for it. Full replacement, so the existing six have to be included. Effective immediately, no deploy, no re-seed.

**Do not re-issue the credential to widen it.** Minting replaces the secret, and per PEEK-168 there are two live copies (the WSL file and Desktop's keychain), so re-issuing revokes whichever you are not holding. That is the whole reason the PATCH route exists.

Useful and not obvious: the live ceiling is readable **without the box** for any credential whose secret you hold — `/token` returns `allowed_kinds` in its response. That is how the list above was read rather than guessed, and it is worth doing for `peek` and `estiva-ship` before the re-seed, since the ROADMAP notes the live rows were never checked against the file.

I am blocked on both halves from here: the re-seed needs the box and the PATCH needs an admin session. Once either lands I can verify it in one call — the agent signing a `1111` is the whole test, and the relay side is already measured.

**The relay half is now measured rather than assumed, and it is clean.** This ticket asserted "our relay already accepts it — commit `ffeb41606`", which was never proven end to end because the Estiva ID ceiling refused before the relay ever saw a `1111`.

Signed with `estiva-ship`'s local `.manifest-key`, which is a relay member and is **not** subject to the Estiva ID `allowedKinds` ceiling — so the two gates can be tested independently:

    ✅ kind:1111 WITH h   accepted=true     ← the shape the writer will publish
    ✅ kind:1111 NO h     accepted=true     ← accepted too, and that is the problem

    #h query returns the h-scoped one
    #a query returns both                  ← the shape Peek's widget uses

Both probe events deleted afterwards (`kind:5`, accepted).

**So there is no fourth blocker — and one existing warning is now load-bearing rather than theoretical.** The relay will happily take a `1111` with no `h`, storing it globally and world-readable, whatever the privacy of the issue it is anchored to. Nothing refuses it and nothing warns. The writer must always emit `h`, and that deserves a test rather than a comment.

Useful side note for anyone testing the other gates: `.manifest-key` is a **second identity** that Ship already holds locally and that bypasses the Estiva ID ceiling entirely. It is how you probe relay behaviour for a kind the agent cannot sign.

One trap while cleaning up, since it cost a round: there are two `buildDeletion`s. `lib/nostr/events.ts` takes `{ targetEventId }` and emits an `e` tag — correct for deleting a specific event. `src/events.ts` takes `{ target, folder }` and emits an `a` tag for an addressable object; handing it an event id gets `invalid: invalid a-tag format`.

root.body:
The signing-ceiling half of this ticket's blocker now has its own home: **AGE-2**, in the new `Agent / Steer` project.

`30851:b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46:34248a67-fbff-483f-83c2-575e3d38b63e`

It covers `1111` alongside the other three kinds `claude-agent` is refused (`5`, `31989`, `31990`), because they are one problem: a server-side ceiling that refuses at the last publish, after the work is done. `estiva-ship`'s credential still needs checking separately — the ceiling is per-app and the browser app is the main comment writer.

So the writer half of REW-10 waits on three things, all outside this repo or below it:

1. **AGE-2 / Gate 1** — `1111` granted to `estiva-ship` and `claude-agent`.
2. **PEE-9** (`…:25816546-bc00-48ac-82b9-3f9d4b929f82`) — Peek's topic sync reads `1111`.
3. Ship's NIP-89 manifest republished **in the same commit as the writer** — see below.

## Why the manifest cannot be republished early

Checked `peek-app` rather than assumed. `convex/nostr/projection.ts` reads `declared.emits.kind` in two places: line 113 to decide which kind to *query* for comments, and line 1238 to decide which kind to *publish*. So Ship's manifest is not describing Ship — it is instructing Peek.

Declaring `1111` while Ship still writes `9` would, all at once: drop every existing comment out of Peek's issue widget (it would query `1111` and find none), make Peek publish `1111` that Ship cannot yet read, and possibly break Peek's comment action outright if its credential cannot sign `1111`.

Worth knowing for whoever does it: `publish-manifest.ts` signs with a local `.manifest-key`, **not** Estiva ID, so the signing ceiling above does not gate it. The manifest is publishable at any moment, which is exactly why the ordering has to be deliberate rather than enforced.

## One gap nobody owns yet

`commentKindOf` returns a **single** kind, so the manifest has no way to say "we emit `1111` now and emitted `9` before". Even after everything lands correctly, old `kind:9` comments drop out of Peek's widget. That needs either a legacy read on Peek's side or a manifest that can declare both, and it is not filed — the right home is genuinely unclear.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Reader half open: ship#36 + estiva-agent#9. The writer is blocked, and the Peek trap this ticket predicted is the wrong one.**

## Blocked on the Estiva ID ceiling, and it belongs in Gate 1

Measured rather than read off the `allowed_kinds` query (which needs the box):

    Estiva ID refused to sign kind:1111 — App claude-agent may not sign kind 1111

The relay registry already has `1111` (`ffeb41606`), so this is the *other* ceiling and it is per-app. `estiva-ship` needs checking too and almost certainly needs the same grant, since the browser app is the main comment writer and the agent is the other.

**This is a Gate 1 dependency the ROADMAP does not record.** Gate 1 batches exactly this — CRO-2 `30078`, PEE-4 `22242`, DMS-1 `41010–41012` — into one deploy and one manual re-seed. `1111` for `estiva-ship` and `claude-agent` should ride that batch rather than earn its own trip to the box.

## The Peek trap, corrected

This ticket says: *"Peek renders a Ship issue widget above a conversation because the message carries `about`. If Peek reads `about` specifically, 1111 comments will lose the widget."* Checked, and it is the opposite way round on both halves.

**The widget path already works and was designed for this.** `convex/nostr/projection.ts` has `KIND_COMMENT = 1111`, and better, `commentKindOf(manifest)` reads the comment kind off the app's **own NIP-89 manifest** instead of hardcoding it — the comment there says hardcoding "would quietly stop finding comments the moment an app said something different." It queries `{ kinds: [commentKind], "#a": [address] }`, which is exactly what a `1111` presents.

But that only adapts **if Ship republishes its manifest**. `src/manifest.ts` currently declares `emits: { kind: KIND.MESSAGE, scope: "address" }` for the `comment` action. Republishing it is a required step this ticket does not list.

Also worth correcting: Ship does not emit a custom `about` tag. The parameter is called `about`; the wire tag is already `["a", address]`. What is non-standard is the *kind*, not the tag.

**The timeline breaks, and that needs a Peek ticket.** `peek-app/src/nostr/sync.ts` fetches `kinds: [9]`, hardcoded, `#h`-scoped. A Ship comment published as `1111` disappears from the Peek topic conversation **entirely** — not "loses its widget". That is a real break in the ecosystem's flagship interop claim, so **the writer half must not land before Peek reads 1111 in `sync.ts`.**

## What shipped

The fold reads `1111` alongside `kind:9`, both landing in the same thread under the same issue. NIP-22's case is the whole spec — uppercase `A`/`E`/`K`/`P` for the thread root, lowercase for the immediate parent — so `about` reads uppercase `A`, `parentId` reads lowercase `e`, and `rootId` reads uppercase `E` only when a thread roots at an event. Ship's roots at an address, so a top-level comment is its own conversation root exactly as a `kind:9` with no `e` is.

Reader-first is even more load-bearing here than for REW-11: a `kind:9` comment is **not replaceable at all**, so unlike a project record it cannot be rewritten even by its author. There is no migration window to miss — there is only "every comment ever written stays kind:9".

One thing the reader cannot fix, flagged where the writer will look: `1111` is channel-scoped with an `h` and **global without one**, so a comment published without it is world-readable however private its issue.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
Fixed and proven, not yet merged: estiva-app/buzz#8, branched from nfb-demo-kinds.

THE FIX

Delete the !require_relay_membership guard at both call sites rather than invert it. extract_nip_oa_owner verifies a Schnorr signature over a preimage naming the presenting pubkey and returns None for an absent or invalid tag, so relay membership has no bearing on whether the signature is true. api/mod.rs already says as much, and the ban cascade twenty lines above the auth.rs site already extracts the owner unconditionally for that exact reason. The guard was the anomaly.

PROVEN AGAINST A BUILT BINARY

Same agent key, same request, two binaries:

  ghcr :nfb (branch parent), direct member + valid tag  -> agent_owner_pubkey NULL
  built from the branch,     direct member + valid tag  -> agent_owner_pubkey SET

relay_members untouched in both, so the deliberate auto-admission of self-service bots stays exactly as decided.

All eight harness checks still pass on the patched binary, including every refusal path.

TWO THINGS LEARNED THAT COST TIME

Every workflow in the buzz fork except "relay image" is disabled_manually. A pull request there receives no checks at all, so a PR that looks unblocked has simply never been compiled. Compiled locally instead in the pinned rust 1.95 toolchain, and falsified by injecting a type error to confirm the check really compiles the edited file.

relay-image.yml has a bare workflow_dispatch trigger and tags buzz:nfb with no branch guard, while the box pulls :nfb every two minutes. Dispatching that workflow from any branch would publish that branch to production within two minutes. The obvious way to get a compile check is therefore a live deploy. Worth adding a github.ref condition on the :nfb tag.

Also: merging to nfb-demo-kinds is itself the production deploy. There is no staging step between merge and the box.

A REPLAY CHECK THAT LOOKS BROKEN AND IS NOT

Re-running the matrix after admitting the second agent shows the cross-agent replay case returning 200. That is the agent being admitted on its own membership, not the lifted tag working. On a clean database in the original order it is 403, and the relay records no owner from the replayed tag.

STILL OPEN

Only POST /events materialises. /query, /count and media enforce membership without recording the owner, so a read-only self-service bot (allowedKinds [27235], which is what self-service mints) never publishes and so never establishes ownership. Left alone deliberately: materialising per read costs three DB round-trips on every query, and PEEK-173 step 2 may be better served reading the verified owner off the request than via the column.

root.body:
**Merged.** ship#34 → `f0fb71b`, estiva-agent#7 → `c7f714c`. Closing.

Verified against `main` rather than the merge flag, and through the thing the ticket promises rather than the mechanism:

    coverage through merged main: reachable=97 unreachable=0 total=97
    note: (none)

The `note` disappearing is the part worth noticing. That string existed to warn every caller that a listing was incomplete; there is nothing left for it to warn about.

The widening half, spot-checked on the same read: both of the previously-unreachable issues that carry changes fold to **done + assigned**. Without the second pass they would have come back `todo` and unassigned — the failure this ticket was most at risk of introducing while fixing the other one.

Also verified: `diff -r src` and `diff -r lib/nostr` between the two **mains** identical; `conformance.test.ts` and `fold-fixture.json` byte-identical across repos, and the fixture's last commit is still `b990b57`, predating this entire programme. It was never regenerated — the fold did not change, only what gets fetched.

## What this ticket turned out to be about

Not a query bug. The discovery *model* reached an object only through its parent, so the model had a hole exactly the size of "parents can be deleted". Twelve deletions and one issue that never had a parent, and none of it visible from any single query — the app and the agent agreed with each other perfectly while both were wrong.

Two things generalise beyond Ship and are now in RFC 0.3 §4.2, because the folder model repeats the shape one level up:

- **Discovering children only through their parent loses them when the parent goes.** A folder lists its contents; a client that walks only folders loses every file whose folder was deleted or went private. One extra unscoped filter designed in costs nothing; retrofitting it cost this ticket.
- **Event counts are not object counts.** 14 change events targeting these 13 issues landed on 2 distinct issues. I quoted "six" here from an event tally and it was wrong by 3×; the fold is where that difference lives, and it is only visible by folding both ways and diffing.

root.body:
**REW-11 just ran this exact shape of change end to end. Three things transfer directly.**

This ticket swaps `kind:9` + a custom `about` tag for NIP-22 `kind:1111`. That is the same move REW-11 made on the project record: a wire-format change to a kind already in production, with old events that cannot be rewritten.

**1. Land the reader first, as its own PR.** There is no migration — a `kind:9` comment is not replaceable at all, so unlike the project record it cannot even be rewritten by its author. Every existing comment stays `kind:9` + `about` **forever**, and a fold that only understands `1111` loses the entire existing conversation history. Teach the fold both shapes, merge that, then flip the writer separately. REW-11 split this way and the writer flip was a one-builder diff with no coordination needed.

**2. Check the relay accepts the shape *before* estimating.** REW-11 was blocked for a full cycle by `requires_h_channel_scope` — a list nobody knew about, which is separate from the kind allowlist, and which refuses with `200 {"accepted": false, …}`. `kind:1111` is registered (commit `ffeb41606`), but registered is not the same as *accepted in the shape you intend to write*. Publish one and read the `accepted` field before planning the work. NIP-22 uses uppercase `A`/`E`/`K`/`P` for the root and lowercase for the parent, and whether Buzz gates on an `h` alongside those is exactly the sort of thing that is invisible from here.

**3. Expect the fold to need more fallbacks than the table suggests.** REW-11 looked like one swap (`h` → `buzz-channel`) and needed three, because the tags moved independently and a record could carry either combination. Comments will be worse: `about` versus `A`, `e` versus `E`, and threading semantics that differ rather than merely rename. Budget for reading both shapes in every field, not just the one the ticket names.

Conformance is the cheap proof it costs nothing: if the fixture and its checksum are untouched and the test still passes, the fallbacks provably cannot alter any recorded event.

root.body:
**Context this ticket did not have: deleting a project is what stranded 12 of the 13 issues SHI-7 is fixing.**

Measured on production 2026-08-24. Ship's `loadAll` reached an issue only by widening from its parent, so when a project record was deleted its issues stopped being *reachable* — intact and readable on the relay, invisible to `ship.estiva.app` and to the agent. Twelve of the thirteen unreachable issues were exactly that; the deletions were presumably somebody tidying up test projects with no idea it would do that.

**SHI-7 removes the trap**, and is worth having merged before this ticket builds a delete affordance. Once issues are discovered directly, deleting a project no longer hides them — they simply appear with no parent, which the Issues surface already handles (it never filtered on having a project).

Two things this ticket should still decide, which SHI-7 does not:

- **What deleting a project should *mean* for its issues.** They are separate events with their own authors and they survive; NIP-09 is author-scoped, so a project's author cannot delete another person's issue even if they wanted to. "Delete project" is therefore closer to "remove the record" than to "delete the work", and the UI should say which it is doing before the click.
- **`archiveProject` already exists and is the reversible version** — a `kind:1851` change, so anyone in the Folder can do it, it can be undone, and the activity feed records who. That is probably what most people asking for "delete" actually want, and it is already built.

One hard constraint on the delete path itself: **Estiva ID refuses `kind:5` for `claude-agent`**, so the agent cannot delete anything it publishes. Whatever this builds, the agent will not be able to use it without widening that credential's `allowedKinds`.

root.body:
**This procedure was exercised on 2026-08-24 for CAT-9, and one step in it is not sufficient.**

What happened: buzz#7 merged to `nfb-demo-kinds` at 14:01:41Z, `relay-image.yml` built `55c0c819b` successfully at 14:01:43Z — and a behavioural probe run immediately afterwards **still got the pre-change refusal.** The image existed in the registry; nothing had pulled it. The deploy was then run by hand and the probe flipped.

So the ticket's "verify by image id" is necessary and not sufficient, and the reason is worth stating: **an image id tells you which bytes are on disk; it does not tell you the process restarted into them, and it is unreadable from anywhere except the box.** Add a behavioural check that anyone can run from anywhere:

    publish the kind the change was about, and read the `accepted` field

For CAT-9 that was a `kind:30850` with `buzz-channel` and no `h` → `accepted:true`, with `kind:30851` and `kind:1851` without `h` → still `accepted:false` as controls. The negative controls matter as much as the positive: they show the deploy narrowed the rule rather than removing it.

Every gate involved answers **HTTP 200**, so a check on the status code passes against a relay that refused. This is now a row in `operations/SILENT-FAILURES.md`.

root.body:
**There is now a ninth commit to preserve, and it is a deletion — the kind a merge silently undoes.**

CAT-9 (`68fd3e6ad`, merged as `55c0c819b`) removes `KIND_LL_PROJECT` from `requires_h_channel_scope` in `crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs`, leaving `KIND_LL_ISSUE` and `KIND_LL_CHANGE`. Ship's project record depends on it: production now accepts a `kind:30850` with no `h`, and REW-11 is shipped on top of that.

A deletion inside a list is the easiest thing to lose in a conflict resolution, because the "obvious" merge keeps every line. **If it comes back, `ship create-project` starts failing** with `200 {"accepted": false, "message": "invalid: channel-scoped events must include an h tag"}` — a 200, so nothing that checks status codes will notice.

There is a test that catches it: `a_project_record_may_be_global_but_its_contents_may_not` in the same file. It asserts the asymmetry in both directions, including that `KIND_LL_PROJECT` stays *out* of `is_global_only_kind` — putting it in would flip every existing channel-scoped project record to world-readable. Keep the test through the merge and it will tell you if the arm came back.

Also worth folding into CAT-8's exercise list: publish a `kind:30850` with `buzz-channel` and no `h` against the merged relay and read the `accepted` field.

**Built: ship#34 + estiva-agent#7. Coverage 13 unreachable → 0, 97 of 97 against production.**

## A correction to this ticket's own description first

The description says 14 changes target the 13 issues (6 status, 7 assignee, 1 project) and concludes **"six of them would render as `todo` when they are not"**. That conclusion is wrong, and it was mine. Six is a count of change *events*, not of issues — six status changes turned out to be one ticket moved through its lifecycle repeatedly.

Measured properly, by folding both ways and diffing:

    change events targeting the 13: 14
       status    6 events → 2 distinct issue(s)
       assignee  7 events → 2 distinct issue(s)
       project   1 events → 1 distinct issue

    Without the Folder widening, of the 13:
      would show the WRONG status : 2
      would lose their assignee   : 2

So the argument holds and the magnitude was 3× overstated. Two rows, both `done` and assigned, both of which would have come back `todo` and unassigned. Still worse than thirteen missing rows — a missing row is noticed, a wrong status is believed — but two, not six. The code comment carries the measured figure.

## What shipped

Both passes, because the first alone is the harmful one:

1. discovery asks for `kind:30851` unscoped alongside `kind:30850` — the same query `coverage()` already used to *count* them
2. the widening set now includes each discovered issue's own `h`, so its changes arrive with it

The 4-pass bound is unchanged; the extra filter rides the same round trip, since `POST /query` takes an array.

## The app needed nothing, which was not obvious

I expected this ticket's third done-when — "a parentless issue has a defined place in the app" — to be the real work. It was already satisfied. The **Issues** surface never filtered on having a project, `ctx.folderOf` uses the issue's own `h` rather than its project's, and the issue view already renders a missing parent. So the thirteen were never displayed wrongly; they were only never fetched. `apps/ship/` is untouched, which also keeps this clear of the React rewrite.

## The coverage block stays, and starts being useful

At 13 it was counting a known defect. At 0 it measures the real thing — an issue in a Folder the reader genuinely cannot read — which will be non-zero the first time anybody makes a Folder private. Production has no private channel today (all 50 are open), so that case has never occurred here.

**Merged.** ship#33 → `86a752d`, estiva-agent#6 → `edd85bb`. Closing.

Verified against `main` rather than against the merge flag, and through the action a person actually takes rather than the mechanism behind it:

- `buildProject` on both `origin/main`s emits `buzz-channel` and `name`, and no longer emits `h`.
- `diff -r src` and `diff -r lib/nostr` between the two **mains** — identical. `conformance.test.ts` and `fold-fixture.json` byte-identical across repos, and the fixture's last commit is still `b990b57`, which predates all of this work. It was never regenerated.
- `npm test` green on merged main, conformance included.
- **`ship create-project` run through merged main**: the record came back carrying `d, name, description, buzz-channel` and no `h`; an `#h` query for its Folder returned **0**; `loadAll` folded it correctly; the other records still folded. Then archived.

## What the ticket set out to answer

1. **Does global discovery fix the unreachable records?** No — 13 before, 13 after, measured twice: by diagnosing each of the 13 before building, and again with a global record live. Twelve have a *deleted* parent, one never had an `a` tag, all thirteen sit in Folders the reader can already see. Filed as SHI-7.
2. **What breaks when a name becomes world-readable?** Nothing mechanically; the exposure is the point and it is narrower than it looked, because an open channel's member roster was already world-readable on the same rule. Two silent things did break and are fixed: `resolveObject` returned `null` for a global record (reported to the person as "you may not have access"), and `loadFolder`/`loadFolders` stop seeing the record, which is correct and now documented.
3. **How does the fold cope with two shapes?** Three fallbacks, not one, because the tags move independently. `h` beats `buzz-channel` when both are present; an empty `description` tag beats leftover `.content`. Conformance passing untouched is the evidence it costs nothing.
4. **How much work, really?** The code was half a day and four files. What cost the time was finding the relay's `h` gate — invisible from the app, and it fails as a `200` — and measuring the 13 rather than believing the ticket about them.

## As a rehearsal for the folder decision (RFC 0.3 §10.1)

Three things that transfer, all in the RFC now:

- **Reader lands first, and separately.** With no migration available the two shapes coexist forever; a folder model inherits that and §4.2's stub/detail pair doubles it.
- **Read the relay's ingest path before estimating.** One line here; it will not be one line for folder command and state kinds.
- **Measure the defect a design change is justified by, before the change.** This one was justified on a bug it does not fix.
