## The done-when, measured against production through the new writer

The claim worth testing is not "the relay accepted it" — that is CAT-9. It is that the record is **global**, not filed under the channel it names. The observable is an `#h` query:

| check | result |
| --- | --- |
| `{kinds:[30850,30851],"#h":[folder]}` returns the issue but **not** the project record | ✅ returned kinds `[30851]` only |

| its issue is attached and still channel-scoped | ✅ |
| the 14 pre-existing `h`/`title` records still fold | ✅ |

So: discoverable without channel scoping, conversation still gated, old records still fold. Three of the four done-when clauses.

Unreachable-issue count with a global record actually live: **13 before, 13 after** (84/13/97 now, 80/13/93 when first measured — the totals moved because the workspace grew, the 13 did not). Twelve have a deleted parent record, one never had an `a` tag, all thirteen sit in Folders the reader can already see. Filed as SHI-7.

`createProject` still bails when `ensureFolder` fails, and the reason narrowed rather than disappeared. The record no longer needs the channel to exist — but every issue, change and message filed into it does. root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Reader half is up — [ship#31](https://github.com/estiva-app/ship/pull/31) + [estiva-agent#4](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-agent/pull/4). The writer is blocked at the relay, and question 1's answer is not the one this ticket assumed.**

## The blocker: a third gate nobody had checked

A `kind:30850` with no `h` is refused by production:

```
200 {"accepted": false, "message": "invalid: channel-scoped events must include an h tag"}
```

Buzz lists `KIND_LL_PROJECT` in `requires_h_channel_scope` (`buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:494`), next to `KIND_LL_ISSUE` and `KIND_LL_CHANGE`. Measured against the relay, not read off the source, and probed in three shapes — with `buzz-channel`, without it, and a control with `h`. The first two get the message above; the control gets past it.

This ticket says "Estiva ID's ceiling is unchanged; 30850 is already granted." True, and never the binding constraint. **The relay's h-requirement is a separate gate**, and the ticket did not name it.

Unblocking is one entry removed from that list plus a relay deploy. Issues and changes stay on it — only the record goes global. The comment justifying the list says the Folder is required because it is "both how objects are grouped and how access is enforced", which is exactly right for an issue and is the thing this ticket argues is wrong for a *record*.

So: **reader landed, writer parked.** `src/events.ts` carries the whole diagnosis next to `buildProject`, including the tag array it will emit, so the flip is a one-builder change when the relay moves.

---

## 1. Does global discovery fix the unreachable-record problem?

**No. Something else causes it, and global discovery fixes none of it.**

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reachable | 80 | 80 |
| unreachable | **13** | **13** |
| total | 93 | 93 |

Root cause of all 13, measured one at a time:

| cause | count |
| --- | --- |
| parent project record **deleted** — does not resolve by `#d`, by bulk query, or by any route | 12 |
| no `a` tag naming a project at all | 1 |
| access-gated project record | **0** |

And the part that settles it: **all 13 sit in folders this reader can already see.** Every one of the 13 `h` values resolves to a `kind:39000` the reader gets back. There is no access problem to fix.

The ticket's premise — "discovery runs through access-gated project records" — is half right. Discovery does run through project records. On this workspace they fail to resolve because they were **deleted**, not because they were gated. A deleted record cannot be discovered by making records discoverable.

Worth adding, from the §5.2 probe done alongside this: **every one of production's 50 channels is `open`**, and a reader who is a member of none of them reads all 50. So on this relay, as configured today, channel gating never bites for Ship at all. It would bite the moment somebody made a Folder private — the fix is real for the future, it just is not the fix for these 13.

**What would actually fix them:** discovering issues directly rather than only through their parents — `{kinds:[30851]}` with no scoping, which is precisely what `coverage()` already does to *count* them. That is a discovery-model change in `loadAll`, not a record-shape change, and it is a different ticket. Not done here, deliberately.

## 2. What breaks when a record's name becomes world-readable?

Nothing breaks mechanically. What changes is what leaks, and the honest answer is **less than it first appears, because the people are already public.**

The §5.2 probe measured this: an open channel's **full `kind:39002` member roster is already world-readable** to any relay member. `get_accessible_channel_ids` is *member of* `UNION` *every open channel*, and `39002` rides the same rule — 50 of 50 rosters read by a key in none of them. A Ship Folder is created `open` by `ensureFolder`, for stated reasons. So today, for any Ship project: who is in it is public, its issues are public, its conversation is public. Only the project record's own metadata was behind the channel, and only incidentally.

So the trade is narrower than the ticket implies: the *name* joins a set of things that were already exposed. It is still a real trade — a project called "Acquisition of X" would leak, and that must be said before shipping. Anything needing a private name wants RFC 0.3's private-folder model, and RFC 0.3 §4.2's stub/detail split exists for exactly this.

Two second-order effects worth knowing:

- **`resolveObject` fails silently on a global record.** It found the event, looked for `h`, found none, returned `null` — which the app reports as "you may not have access to its Folder". A lie, about the record type most likely to be public. Fixed in the PR; it would have been invisible.
- **`loadFolder`/`loadFolders` stop seeing the record**, because they filter by `#h`. Correct rather than broken — a global record is in no Folder — but it means "read this one container" and "read everything" stop agreeing about what a project is. `loadAll` is the one that sees everything.

## 3. How does the fold cope with two shapes coexisting?

Cleanly, and it turns out to be **three fallbacks, not one**, because the tags move independently: a record can carry `name` with `h`, or `title` with `buzz-channel`.

- `projectFolder` — `h` ?? `buzz-channel`
- `projectName` — `name` ?? `title`
- `projectDescription` — `description` tag ?? `.content`

Three decisions that were not obvious until written:

- **`h` wins when both are present.** A record carrying `h` really is filed under a channel, whatever else it claims. Reading `buzz-channel` first would describe a channel-scoped record as global.
- **An empty `description` tag beats leftover `.content`.** Absent and empty are different: clearing a description must not resurrect prose somebody thought they had removed.
- **`originFolder` kept its name and its callers.** For a global record it is the `buzz-channel` — still where a `kind:1851` about that project must be addressed, because changes stay channel-scoped whatever the record does. `apps/ship/` needed no change.

**Coexistence is permanent and the reason is worth recording precisely.** Not just the ±15 minute drift window: a replaceable event can only be rewritten by *its own author*, and rewriting stamps a fresh `created_at` that cannot be backdated. Interestingly `channel_id` is deliberately **not** part of the NIP-33 replacement key (`WHERE community_id AND kind AND pubkey AND d_tag`, `buzz-db/src/event.rs:718`), so an author republishing without `h` genuinely *would* replace their own channel-scoped record rather than duplicate it. The blocker on migration is losing `created_at`, not the mechanics. Reading both shapes forever is still right.

**Conformance is the evidence it costs nothing.** `fold-fixture.json` and `EVENTS_SHA256` are unchanged in both repos and the test passes — a fallback that only fires on tags no recorded event carries cannot alter a recorded fold. 11 new checks in `app.test.ts` cover both shapes, a record with both tags, the empty-description case, and a change still overriding a `name`.

## 4. How much work was it, really?

**The reader: about half a day, and 4 files — three of them comments.** `src/fold.ts` (three helpers, four call sites), `src/store.ts` (one `resolveObject` fallback plus doc corrections), `src/events.ts` (comment only), `scripts/app.test.ts` (11 checks). Mirrored to `estiva-agent` by copy; `diff -r` clean.

**The writer will be one builder** — `buildProject` emits a different tag array. Genuinely small.

**The relay change is one line and a deploy**, and that is the whole schedule risk. `~/buzz` is 625 commits behind upstream and the deploy is manual.

**What actually cost the time was none of the code.** It was finding the ingest gate — which only surfaced by publishing to production and reading the `accepted` field, exactly the trap the app's own relay client was written for — and then measuring the 13 issues rather than believing the ticket about them. Both findings are worth more than the diff.

### As a rehearsal for the folder decision (RFC 0.3 §10.1)

The scale claim holds: this is structurally the same move, and it was cheap. Three things it teaches that transfer:

1. **The reader must land first, and separately.** Not a nicety — with no migration available, two shapes coexist forever, and a folder model has the same property with more at stake.
2. **A relay change is on the critical path, and it will not be one line for folders.** §10.1 says the latest responsible moment for the upstream-versus-fork call is the first line of folder command or state code. This ticket says the relay's ingest gates are a thing to read *before* estimating, because they are invisible from the app and they fail as a 200.
3. **Check the defect a design change is justified by, before the change.** Global discovery was the right shape and the wrong fix for the bug attached to it. It stays worth doing on its merits — upstream alignment, discoverability, the private-Folder future — but the 13 issues were never its evidence.

RFC 0.3 §5.2/§5.3 were answered alongside this and both came back clean: [estiva-docs#3](https://github.com/estiva-app/estiva-docs/pull/3).

---

*Housekeeping: verifying the live read path wrote one throwaway project record to Folder `b6dff859`. Estiva ID refuses `kind:5` for `claude-agent` ("App claude-agent may not sign kind 5"), so it could not be deleted — it is archived and renamed to say so. NIP-09 is author-scoped and the author is this agent key, so nobody else can delete it either; removing it needs the signing ceiling widened, or it stays archived.*

root.body:
**Pulled forward. Do this now, ahead of the rewrite — it does not need any part of it.**

## It needs no React

Everything this ticket changes lives in `src/events.ts` (`buildProject`), `src/store.ts` (`createProject`, `loadAll`) and `src/fold.ts` — the shared code REW-1 explicitly says **not** to move, because `estiva-agent` vendors it at identical paths. The rewrite replaces `apps/ship/`, which this ticket does not touch.

So it can be done today in the current vanilla-DOM app, and the rewrite inherits it rather than blocking it.

## Two reasons to do it early rather than in M3

**1. It fixes a live defect.** 13 of 65 production issues are unreachable because discovery runs through access-gated project records. That is not waiting for a rewrite to be worth fixing, and every read the agent does reports it in the `coverage` block.

**2. It is a rehearsal for the folder decision, which is the decision blocking the most.**

Making Ship's project record global with a `buzz-channel` tag is *structurally the same move* as making a folder global with a channel reference — the change [RFC 0.3](../protocol/RFC-0.3-FOLDERS.md) §4.2 argues is forced. Building it here answers empirically, at a tenth the scale, what would otherwise be argued on paper:

- does global discovery actually fix the unreachable-record problem, or does something else cause it?
- what breaks when a record's name becomes world-readable?
- how does the fold cope with two shapes coexisting, given republishing is barred by the relay's ±15 minute drift window?
- how much work is it, really?

RFC 0.3 §10.1 now names this ticket as one of three things to do while that decision is deferred. Folder implementation, Peek's `topic → file` migration and the upstream NIP proposal all wait behind it, so moving this ticket earlier moves all three.

## Record the answers here

The four questions above are the point. Whatever this ticket teaches belongs on this issue as a comment — the before/after unreachable count especially, since it is the one measurable claim.

Nothing about the ticket's content changes. Only its position.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Note from RFC 0.3 — no change to this ticket, but know what is coming.**

[RFC 0.3](../protocol/RFC-0.3-FOLDERS.md) §7.1 concludes that conversations for every file in a folder live in **one channel**, distinguished by their anchor, with extra channels only where access differs (huddles). Peek today has one channel per topic.

**Nothing here changes.** One REQ per channel is still correct, still the right abstraction, and the multi-`#h` trap this ticket exists to avoid is unaffected — if anything it matters more, because fewer and busier channels make a silently-dead subscription more expensive.

**What changes later** is *what* gets subscribed to: fewer channels, each carrying threads for several files. So build the subscription manager keyed on channel uuid — as specified — and do **not** let a topic id become the subscription key anywhere in the API. That is the one thing that would need unpicking.

RFC 0.3 §11.1 is explicit that the Peek migration is plausibly larger than the Ship rewrite and belongs in its own project, sequenced later. This ticket is not blocked by it.

root.body:
Hit this for real while filing a bug in Peek: Feedback & Bugs. The new issue was assigned ref PEE-8, and 'ship set-status PEE-8' then refused with '"PEE-8" matches 2 issues' — the other being 'Subscribe useTopicView to its channel; HTTP becomes backfill and fallback' in Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates.

The mechanism, from the agent's create-issue path: nextRef derives the number from siblings *within one project* (state.issues filtered by projectAddr), while refPrefix derives the prefix from the project title. Two projects whose titles share a prefix therefore number independently and collide on the first shared number. 'Peek: Feedback & Bugs' and 'Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates' both yield PEE.

Not fatal — the address is the identity and everything worked once addressed by '30851:<pubkey>:<d>' — but any command that takes a ref is unusable for the colliding issues, which is the part that bites. Two fixes worth weighing: number refs per prefix rather than per project, or make the prefix unique per project.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Amendment — this issue was written assuming two layers, and there are three.** Read it with the following in place of the framing above. The measurements are unchanged; what they decide is narrower.

**What changed.** `kind:30078` (NIP-78, arbitrary app data) is usable for app-private, user-owned state, and Buzz already does exactly this for itself — `is_buzz_mesh_status` (`buzz-db/src/lib.rs:3688`) stores mesh member status as a `BOOKMARK_SET` with a namespaced `d_tag`. Ingest performs no `d_tag` validation on 30078, and NIP-RS handling is a narrow predicate matching only `read-state:<32 hex>`. So there is a middle layer between "on the relay for interop" and "in Convex":

1. interop → relay, standard kinds
2. **app-private but user-owned → relay, `30078` with an app-namespaced `d_tag`, NIP-44 encrypted** — see CRO-11
3. app backend → Convex, for what genuinely needs a database

**Why it matters here.** This issue's premise was that `screenerItems` and `deskOpenWork` are irreducibly Convex-shaped because only Peek reads them. That reasoning was wrong: "only this app reads it" is not the same question as "this needs a database". All three of `stars`, `deskOpenWork` and `screenerItems` are small per-user lists that fit layer 2, and `stars` may belong in a standard NIP-51 bookmark list instead. So the residue this spike is weighing is smaller than described, and the ownership argument — one `authors:[pk]` export, NIP-IA archival on offboarding, NIP-09 deletion — now covers it.

**Revised outcome space.** The three outcomes still stand, but the third is now the likely one and the first two shift meaning:

- *Convex stays in the read path* — as a materialization layer, justified by cold-start numbers rather than by holding state nothing else can.
- *Convex leaves the read path* — and, with layer 2 available, may be left holding little beyond **file blobs** (`_storage`; Buzz has media routes plus `KIND_FILE_METADATA` 1063 and Blossom auth 24242, so even that has a relay home).
- *Hybrid* — fold live, materialise a small denormalised summary (per-container last-message-at and unread frontier). Most likely to be right if the cliff is real.

**Two things to add to the measurement.** First, cost layer 2 as a destination: what a `30078` round trip costs on boot for three or four small blobs, and whether whole-blob replaceable writes are acceptable for a screener that gets snoozed often. Second, note the concurrency constraint — replaceable events are last-write-wins on a *seconds* timestamp, so two tabs can silently lose a write unless the blob is a CvRDT the way NIP-RS is.

**What has not changed.** Layer 3 is permanent and will grow as Peek ships features that genuinely need queries, indexes, server-side compute or scale, and Convex may be exactly the right tool for it. The point of this spike is not to remove Convex. It is to decide whether it belongs in the read path for content the relay already owns — and now, additionally, to confirm nothing sits in it that a person would reasonably expect to own.

**Dependency added:** CRO-11 (the layer-2 convention) should be settled before this runs, or the spike will measure a two-layer world that is no longer the plan.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Planned, not started.** Eleven issues filed in implementation order: DMS-1 → DMS-11.

**Decision recorded: DM channels, not NIP-17 gift wrap.** This is business software, not a second Signal — end-to-end encryption prevents search, retention, offboarding and admin recovery, and the relay operator is the organisation. Three things confirm the platform already assumes this: the relay sends DMs itself for moderation notices (`moderation_notices.rs:102` calls `open_dm`), NIP-IA identity archival exists for offboarding, and NIP-50 search is advertised live — gift-wrapped content is invisible to all three.

**What that decision bought.** Both blocking prerequisites disappeared. `ingest.rs:1498` restricts only gift wrap and presence to WebSocket, so DM commands publish over the HTTP bridge Peek already uses — no dependency on the WebSocket work in *Peek: Real-time Ship→Peek updates*. And plaintext `kind:9` messages need no encryption, so no dependency on the Estiva ID NIP-44 service either. This project is independent and can run in parallel with *Cross-app read state*.

It also means DMs reuse machinery Peek already has: the relay knows each DM message's `channel_id`, so the existing projection, cursor, reaction and deletion handling and live subscription all work on a DM channel unchanged. DMS-5 should add callers, not a projection.

**Next logical step.** DMS-1 (grant `41010`/`41011`/`41012`, and deliberately *not* `30622` — it is relay-signed) followed immediately by DMS-2, the probe. DMS-2 exists to verify the assumption this project's independence rests on: that `41010` is accepted over HTTP. If it is not, this project needs the WebSocket publish path and the plan changes shape — so run it before anyone starts M2, not after.

**The cost to own.** DMs will be private by membership, not by encryption; the relay stores them in plaintext. DMS-11 makes sure nothing in the UI implies otherwise. DMS-7 is a decision task, not a migration — the relay's ±15 minute drift window means republished history cannot carry its original timestamps, so "migrate the old DMs" is not the free option it looks like.

root.author: b38fd2687b17bbde2e8079577cba601936acfe1b731d2d2ba7cdef29a063db46
root.body:
**Planned, not started.** Nine issues filed in implementation order: CRO-1 → CRO-9.

**Where it stands.** The protocol side is already done for us — `kind:30078` (NIP-RS) is specified in `buzz/docs/nips/NIP-RS.md` and already in the relay's accepted kinds, so there is no Buzz change and no relay deploy. The merge rule, encryption scheme, slot model and fetch filter are all specified. Two things are genuinely missing, and both are ours.

**The blocking gate: Estiva ID cannot encrypt.** NIP-RS content must be NIP-44 encrypted to the user's own keypair, which needs their private key. Peek holds no keys, and Estiva ID exposes `/sign` and nothing else — there is no `/encrypt` and no `/decrypt`. CRO-1 adds them, scoped to self-encryption only so the result is not a general decryption oracle.

**The design gap: the context-id convention.** NIP-RS deliberately does not prescribe context identifiers, which is the entire reason cross-app read state does not already work. CRO-3 fixes `h:<folder-uuid>` / `thread:<root>` / `msg:<id>` in the protocol spec. It is the highest-leverage item here — it is what makes app three inherit this rather than become a third disagreeing opinion.

**Next logical step.** CRO-1 and CRO-2 in parallel — both are Estiva ID changes and both need the same manual re-seed, so batch them into one deploy. `update.sh` runs `migrate` and never `seed`, so verify the `allowed_kinds` row rather than the log line. Then CRO-3 before any client code, so the client is written against a decision instead of becoming one.

**Two notes.** This project is no longer a prerequisite for *DMs on Nostr (DM channels)* — that dependency existed only while DMs were going to use NIP-17, and it is gone. And the 7-day fetch horizon is a real regression risk for Peek's long-lived topics (a container read three weeks ago reads as unread); CRO-6 keeps Convex `readState` as the cache that covers it, so the table is repurposed rather than retired.

replies.body:
I will tell you how I use Linear <> Claude today.

I start a project in Linear (just a name) then brainstorm with Claude / Claude Code and in the end ask to create a plan. What it does is it create bunch of tickets with description (implementation prompts) and sequence them in milestone.

Then in next session I say to Claude start with first milestone that contains those 5 tickets.

So, this is how I imagine I will use Claude with Peek and Ship.
1. We are discussing some idea on Peek and agree on something.
2. I will open Claude link the topic with our conversation and ask Claude "Let's brainstorm this new idea and turn it into project plan"
3. Then do the brainstorming, answering Claude's questions, steering the direction..
4. In the end, I will ask him to "Capture this project plan into Ship project and tickets, sequence them in order of implementation"
5. Then I will start new Claude Code coding session and I will simply ask to start with first batch of tickets: "Start implementing ABC-1, ABC-2, and ABC 3. Once those tickets are done. Capture the implementation notes in comments and change status to done. Once the first milestone of the project is done, send project update to the Topic thread"

Something like this.

replies.author: f3a38fa646debd4162125e0aed87b6d2393fb1ed9702b6875dcbc0c6529d64d1
replies.body:
Let's leave it for our call. Because I think your questions are spot on. The Folder topic has so many levels that needs to be figured out. The core concept, but also all the niche nuances in terms of referencing.

My thinking is till vague and I'm for sure in brainstorming mode how to make it happen, so it feels natural. Couple of high-level thoughts for the call:
- Folders and files: It's a concept that has been with computers from beginning. It's understandable. It makes sense. It's both technical and user concept. -> **As it's proven by time, I intuitively think somehow we should adopt Folder & File concept**.
- In 90s when I was little and started with computers, one thing amazed me. I used different programs, but the underlying structure with folders and files were same everywhere. That was one of the key point of operation system, that it organize your "life" on the computer. Now with SAAS apps where each app Basecam, Notion, Linear, Slack,... has completely different navigation so you need to remember each and every single app... it's so tedious. -> **I'm intrigued by thought that whatever app you open in our ecosystem, it has similar navigation/organization of files, so you don't need to re-learn anything. It's always the same.**
- Purely from Peek or Ship perspective, I don't like the endless stream of Topics and Projects that doesn't belong anywhere or they are not grouped by anything. That's why I've keep bringing this topic of "Themes" that lives above the Topic. -> **We need to find a way how to organize things like Topics in Peek and Projects in Ship into meaningful chunks.**

One small thing that we could do relatively easily is that we can expose Ship actions to Peek's intelligence like:
- Add issue / project
- Update issue / project
Scenario could be: You're in Peek discussing something in thread. You want to capture it to ticket/project. In this first version, you would hit Cmd + K -> Add issue -> Form for issue would show up -> Save it -> it add message with the widget for that issue into the thread.

Adding thing like this might help us try the Intelligence without having the AI really plugged in.

We could also add basic Topic search and People / Team search to make it little bit more useful.
